item.title: Wasted or Worth It? Alumni Views on Baylor’s Liberal Arts
item.description:
“I think there is something that permeates throughout the Baylor Honors College environment as a whole. It is a culture of faith and seeking reason and knowledge,” said alumna Josiah Padley when I interviewed her about the liberal arts at Baylor. Baylor Honors College has been classified as a “hidden gem” by the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, and with most students in Baylor’s College of Arts and Sciences—which comprises the majority of majors on campus—having to take at least two Great Texts or English courses, the liberal arts take a prominent role at Baylor and impact the lives of many students.

Many liberal arts majors have been asked a seemingly obvious question: What are you going to do with that? Great texts? Philosophy? Who is going to hire you? At face value these seem like logical questions, though often implicit within them are assumptions that there is not anything one can do with that sort of major. How does a degree that entails little to no technical training prepare people for career success? Given the impact of the liberal arts on Baylor’s student body, I interviewed four alumni on their experiences with Baylor’s liberal arts.

How does a degree that entails little to no technical training prepare people for career success?

First, I talked to Grayson Meyers, a class of ‘25 University Scholar with concentrations in political science, history, and philosophy. On the general importance of liberal arts, he said, “I think having a good handle of these sorts of foundational topics… prepares you to be able to engage civically and ask policy questions, like what are particular policies for?…I think a lot of people don’t really think too deeply about the values they have, or question them, or engage with them correctly. They just kind of accept them as obvious.”

Indeed, the liberal arts are meant to provoke thought on life’s deep questions. Not only questions on a grand scale, such as politics, but even those in our daily life. The faculties that the liberal arts cultivate have a profound impact on how we behave socially as well as professionally.

Class of ‘24 political science and communications major Daniel Escobedo’s thoughts were that “part of the liberal arts education is the professor being like…stand up, tell the class your beliefs and defend them, and I think that’s a very vital skill. Not just in the political world, obviously, because that’s kind of what it all is, but also in the corporate world.” He elaborated further on how the liberal arts, rather than merely showing students how to do a job, teaches them to answer the questions of why they take certain actions. Ideally, education illuminates both the means and ends, not simply one or the other, though without a clear vision of the ends, the means remain aimless.

But who cares? Are Grayson and Daniel right? To address the critics of the liberal arts, I asked two alumni to respond to those who insist that a business or STEM degree guarantees a six-figure starting salary or a job at all: Mike Ortiz, a class of ‘25 University Scholar with concentrations in political science, great texts, and philosophy, and Josiah Padley, a class of ‘23 University Scholar with concentration in classics, political science, history, and great texts.

“Some degrees may place limitations. …if you’re wanting to go into med school, …it is difficult to not just study something in the natural sciences…but in other fields it is not so crystal clear,” said Mike. “I have a buddy of mine who is currently working in DC, and he was hired by some bank, I don’t remember which, having studied not just economics but philosophy and he was hired primarily because in an interview, as he was talking about his philosophy course work, his boss was so interested in it that he genuinely just wanted someone he could talk to…that seems like an idiosyncratic story that doesn’t apply to everyone… but is just an example of [how] the kind of thing you end up doing in college may or may not land you that job that you think the degree is or is not designed to get you.”

“He was hired primarily because in an interview, as he was talking about his philosophy course work, his boss was so interested in it that he genuinely just wanted someone he could talk to…” —Mike Ortiz, class of ’25

Josiah echoed that sentiment, explaining that, “If one is studying ancient Greek and ancient Greek alone, it is quite unlikely that they will end up working as an economist somewhere because they simply do not have the background or the training for that…When you’re thinking about how to successfully get a humanities degree and how to successfully leverage it in your career afterwards, what you need to be thinking about is doing things as excellently as you can and doing as many things as well as you can.”

In addition to excellence, anyone majoring in the liberal arts ought to have measured expectations. Each alumni stressed the importance of intentionality when pursuing these degrees. Josiah continued, “where I think people get in trouble is when they get a very basic humanities degree and they don’t do these amazing extracurriculars like writing, or researching, or getting involved with your community.”

Liberal Artists, according to ChatGPT

With all this being said, what does your degree say about you? Probably not much, if we are being honest. A college degree is a certificate which demonstrates that you have learned the fundamentals and some specialized knowledge in a particular field. Of course, the actual value of that degree does depend on the quality of the institution and by extension the quality of the teaching faculty. However, the greater part of the degree’s value is what you do in the time in between starting and finishing the formal curriculum.

The most important take away from my conversations with these alumni is the importance of excellence and how Baylor’s liberal arts curricula help foster that environment. The liberal arts will not help you get a job in the sense that majoring in accounting will. No. It will not train you to do specific iterative tasks; there is no such position at any company titled “liberal artist.” And in spite of this each of them have found employment, Josiah is working in education policy, Mike is a Ph.D. student at Duke, Daniel is working as a paralegal while starting law school, and Grayson is doing likewise. Each of the alumni agreed that Baylor’s liberal arts helped them work better with people, something unavoidable in any career. Degrees do not inherently destine someone to destitution or riches beyond their wildest dreams. For those skeptical of the liberal arts, try taking some; you just might grow greatly as a person. And for those in the liberal arts thinking that giving minimal effort in college will naturally result in a well-paid corporate job, you are sorely mistaken.

item.title: Baylor Alumnus Gives Firsthand Account of Artemis II Capsule Recovery – The Standard
item.description:
At 5:07 p.m. PDT on April 10, 2026, the Orion capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego. The crew of four was completing a nine-day journey that had taken them farther from Earth than any human ever before. Stationed on the frontlines of this final stage of the mission—capsule recovery—was a Baylor alumnus.

Ensign Henry Banaghan graduated Baylor in 2024 with a B.S. in Engineering. Banaghan is stationed at US Naval Base San Diego where he serves as Fire Control Officer aboard the USS John P. Murtha (LPD 26). As an amphibious transport dock, the ship is commissioned to transport Marines to foreign shores for military operations or deliver humanitarian supplies and personnel. Rarely, the vessel assists in spacecraft recovery operations.

According to Banaghan, the USS John P. Murtha is uniquely suited for NASA recovery operations. Its well deck, a lower deck of the ship often flooded to receive or launch vessels, served an instrumental role in the recovery mission. “[As] a landing platform dock, we do well deck operations all the time. We flood the back of the ship, [and] we bring different craft into the back of the ship. So, bringing something like the capsule back in the back of the ship, [is] different, but pretty similar,” Banaghan said. Another capability of the USS John P. Murtha is helicopter-based personnel recoveries—an essential element of the Orion capsule recovery operation. The physical condition of the astronauts upon returning to earth is such that they cannot weather a boat ride.

Photo from the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service

The USS John P. Murtha launched six small boats and four helicopters hours before splashdown. The boats waited a distance from the splashdown target zone to avoid falling debris. After hearing the capsule reenter Earth’s atmosphere with a sonic boom and watching its parachutes deploy, slowing the capsule’s descent, the sailors waited for the clear to approach.

Once given the greenlight, “all the small boats race over and start doing hazard assessments,” Banaghan recounted. “They’re checking the capsule to make sure it’s safe for them to approach it because some of the chemicals they use to cool the capsule and protect it are hazardous. They have to wait for those to dissipate, so they can approach it.”

After determining it is safe, the boats approached. Upon reaching the capsule, a flight doctor immediately entered and performed a full physical assessment of the astronauts. Once the astronauts were determined to be healthy, they were lifted into the recovery helicopters and transported back to the ship.

By 7 p.m., with the astronauts safely aboard, the crew then focused on capsule recovery, rigging the capsule to be towed. On the ship, the well deck was flooded, and towing lines for the capsule were readied.

At midnight, with Banaghan at the helm and the astronauts receiving medical attention aboard, the USS John P. Murtha began approaching the capsule. Banaghan needed to maneuver his 684-foot-long ship within 150-200 feet of the capsule without touching it whatsoever.

This critical step of the operation did not go as planned.

Photo from the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service

“But right as [the capsule] was getting close, late at night, the lights of our ship and then the lights of the small boats around it kind of lit it up … And being that close to it, all of a sudden, it being, 200 or 300 feet away, and just floating right there as our small boats are hooking up the tow lines. That was a really cool experience but was also kind of scary as we were having problems,” Banaghan said.

The crew was having trouble detecting the ship’s distance to the capsule. The pitch-black night prevented the laser rangefinder from functioning effectively. The other systems typically used to get ranges were also struggling.

Banaghan had to think on his feet. “On the fly, I came up with a new way to use the equipment that we had to get a range … And then I was able to call out ranges to the capsule and help us maneuver to get close enough to it for the tow line to be hooked up,” Banaghan said.

After fastening towing lines to the capsule, small boats guided the capsule to the flood deck, at the rear of the ship. A motorized winch hauled the capsule into the ship as more lines were attached to steady the capsule. Once the capsule was positioned above its cradle, the USS John P. Murtha was brought back up and the water receded. Finally, the boats returned to the ship—a full 11 hours after splashdown.

Banaghan believes his time at Baylor equipped him with foundational skills that he uses every day as a naval officer. “Having my engineering background, like the problem-solving skills…and the project management skills I learned at Baylor, when I was doing senior design, and different engineering classes … those are some of the most effective skills that I use on a day-to-day basis. That alone has made a huge impact on my career so far.”

A sixth-grade visit to NASA Space Camp in Huntsville, Alabama, first introduced Banaghan to the Artemis program. “Finding out that I would be on the team recovering the Artemis capsule, all these years later, and having that full circle moment of, wow, going from being that little kid, seeing the scale model and being awestruck by [it], being at space camp, being like, ‘Oh man, I want to be an astronaut, I want to be on this mission,’ to actually being on the mission in a different role … God brought me full circle and that was a really amazing experience.”

item.title: The Science of Memes: How One Professor Studies Digital Culture
item.description:
After seeing Donald Trump’s AI-generated meme of Trump portraying himself as Jesus, I knew I had to ask Dr. Leslie Hahner, a professor of Communication Studies, to ask her opinion on it. I met Hahner last semester in her class entitled, “Theories and Methods of Visual Communication.” I took her class because I needed another rhetoric class for my major; little did I know I would come away with so much more knowledge about how people communicate with digital media positively and negatively.

I met with Hahner during her office hours last semester to have her assign my honors contract. As I told her about my potential research topic, she encouraged me to pursue it even though there was little research on it. I could tell from the start she wanted students to push themselves to be the best they could be.

As it turns out, Hahner is a well-known visual rhetorician who studies misinformation, disinformation, and propaganda. She specifically studies memes to understand how memes influence people to believe one way or another.

After a semester and a half and one research project later, I sat in Hahner’s office in Morrison. Her office is a quiet, relaxing, and welcoming space with a window that overlooks students walking to class. Hahner sat across from me, enthusiastic to talk about her field of study – memes.

President Donald Trump’s AI-generated image, originally posted on Truth Social.

Her interest in memes first began in 2011, after she had completed her PhD in visual rhetoric. Shortly after, Hahner saw LeBron James memes following his announcement of leaving the Cleveland Cavaliers. Additionally, there were riots that year in Canada over the Stanley Cup, and a meme emerged of a couple kissing amid the riots. So, she began to write about memes and the public arguments they make, and how memes work off people’s emotions.

After her daughter’s birth, Hahner became even more intrigued by memes. “My daughter was born in the end of 2012, and I was home a bunch for her early days. I started to look more into how memes were working, and that’s when I started to notice that there were entire collectives, testing memes in a political sense. And that really drew me in quickly,” Hahner said.

When thinking about memes, many people imagine the typical funny picture with the bold text making a joke about something. However, Hahner uses a two-pronged definition of a meme:

“One, a meme is any replicable unit in society–that is brought to us by behavioral biologists who study human behavior, which will argue that memes are any repetitive behavior. So, if you wore a snap bracelet in elementary school, and then all of your friends wore a snap bracelet, that would be a meme. But an internet meme is a replicable unit typically done in a visual unit … that seems iterative, right? It’s taking something that already exists and playing with it. And that tries to simplify messages to a great degree. So, I usually say a meme is a visual commonplace that is a replicable unit.”

“A meme is a visual commonplace that is a replicable unit.”

With this definition, it seems memes arise when something happens. According to Hahner, for a meme to go viral, it must be timely, in line with a cultural or social trend, and have a humorous or some sort of emotional resonance in a way that aligns with our day-to-day experiences as humans.

“An internet meme is a replicable unit, but it is typically done in a visual style. It is taking something that already exists and playing with it,” said Hahner.

For example, a famous meme that is often replicated features a little girl giving the stink eye in her car seat. People often reuse this image to make fun of a situation or get a point across.

The “Side-eyeing Chloe” meme.

In the years to come, memes will evolve, especially with the rise of AI-generated content. They may look a little different, and humans may have a harder time sensing what is AI and what is not AI.

“Most of the meme culture that is developing right now is going to rely heavily on AI-generated content. We’ll be used to seeing children’s toys mashed up with politics, we’ll be used to seeing our contemporary culture sent back to us through this uncanny image of AI. And that can be more effective or less effective depending on how people manage that. Some people think that AI-generated mimetic propaganda will become overwhelming, such that humans won’t be able to resist it. There’s also a school of thought that suggests that AI-generated propaganda is merely ‘slopaganda,’ and it will be ineffective, and people will hate it over time,” Hahner said.

Hahner feels that AI-generated propaganda will “present a new obstacle,” and this new tactic could be more or less successful, but it will also make propagandists’ jobs much easier in the long run as well.

This new tactic could be more or less successful, but it will also make propagandists’ jobs much easier in the long run as well.

“Right now, we’re really poised to learn a lot about what humans are attracted to, and what types of persuasive messages will actually work. Mimetic propaganda has operated in a long time through the vein of authenticity. This is an actual human expression,” Hahner said.

When using the word authenticity, it refers to how “real” or “memorable” a meme appears. Right now, people are constantly confusing AI-generated memes with factual evidence. This presents a new obstacle insofar as older people may not be able to decipher real news from fake news if AI-generated memes continue to be circulated. This raises the concern as to what is ethical to post as a meme and what is not. The answer to this remains somewhat unclear, though it may be argued that any AI-generated meme is unethical to post. A basic piece of advice Hahner recommends in all of her classes is to post things that promote human flourishing instead of posting something that could be problematic.

For those of you still wondering if the AI-generated image of Trump as Jesus that I referred to at the beginning of this article is a meme, according to Hahner, yes, it is a meme.

item.title: “All Are Neighbors” Event Platforms LGBTQ+ Advocates who say Inclusion is Faith-Motivated
item.description:
Over 350 students, faculty, staff, and alumni attended the “All Are Neighbors” event on Wednesday, April 22. The student-organized event featured several speakers who advocated for LGBTQ+ affirmation, opposed the Trump administration’s immigration policies, and lauded religious diversity.

More than a third of attendees were Baylor faculty and staff, and Baylor alumni also made a strong showing at the event. Speakers ranged from high-profile LGBTQ+ advocates to Baylor faculty to undergraduate students.

Rev. Paul Brandeis Raushenbush, president and CEO of Interfaith Alliance, viewed his identities as a Baptist and as a gay man as compatible and divinely bestowed. “My faith teaches that each one of our lives—in all of our complexity and diversity—are divinely and beautifully created,” Raushenbush said.

In contrast, the weaponization of faith and politics against people in vulnerable communities is the “blasphemy” and “sin” we must stop, Raushenbush said.

Rev. Susan Hayward, Minister for Justice Organizing and Adult Faith Formation at Creekside United Church of Christ in Minneapolis, Minnesota, emphasized human diversity as a reflection of God. “In learning and celebrating our differences, we can understand better a God who is bigger than any one race or culture or nation or religious tradition, a God who does not belong to any one of us, but to whom we all belong,” Hayward said.

Additionally, Hayward challenged the audience to stand in solidarity with immigrants. She recalled how she and her community in Minneapolis stood against Operation Metro Surge with nothing but their whistles and phone cameras, and how the community had helped feed and hide illegal immigrants.

Dr. Greg Garrett, the Carole Ann McDaniel Hanks Chair of Literature and Culture at Baylor’s English department, recalled being named to TPUSA’s Professor Watchlist 2 years ago. “They don’t comprehend my deep faith,” Garrett said.

Referencing Matthew 25, Garrett emphasized that what matters at the end is whether we have served “the least of these.” To then redirect attention away from those on the margins is an affront to the faith, Garrett said.

“I am a straight white Christian male, and I am not one of the least of these. Even though some white American Christians claim to be persecuted, or that Christianity is under siege, this is not reality,” Garrett said.

Kelley Robinson, president of the Human Rights Campaign, said her faith is foundational to her work. As a queer person who grew up Catholic, Robinson said church taught her how to build community and to advocate for others. She challenged the audience to have a “civic faith” that “together we can bring forward a world that we all deserve.”

“One day, my kids will feel just as safe surrounded by the American flag as they do when they’re surrounded by pride flags,” Robinson said.

Robinson praised the All Are Neighbors organizers for offering an alternative to the TPUSA event. “This moment … exists because … the community decided that if harmful ideas were going to have a platform, then by God, the truth would have one, too,” Robinson said.

All Are Neighbors served as Robinson’s chance to remind listeners that “the power of the people is always greater than the people in power.”

Director for Pastoral Care and Associate Chaplain Dr. Sara Barton delivered the event’s benediction. She reminded students that the chaplains around Baylor’s campus offer care and support—whether that means sharing snacks or discussing the big questions. “I’m here on behalf of our office to say especially to the students who are here: we are here for you,” Barton said.

Finally, Barton concluded the formal portion of the event with a poem decrying global conflicts in Ukraine, Syria, and Iran. “And into this world of violent retribution … God explodes, not as a czar or hero of war, but as an infant weak and a servant poor,” Barton said.

She highlighted texts from various religions that echoed the idea of loving one’s neighbor. Baylor Spiritual Life has not responded to a request for comment.

After the formal portion of the event concluded, attendees moved to the Quadrangle to exchange stories about what neighborliness meant to them. People who were not able to attend the formal portion of All Are Neighbors joined attendees in swapping stories. Some held posterboards supporting All Are Neighbors.

Lauren W., a staff member in the Film and Digital Media department who wished to withhold her last name, held up a double-sided sign which read, “Baylor [hearts] Druski,” and, “Spew your LIES elsewhere, eriKa KirK.”

Lauren explained that Druski, an online comedian and influencer, had recently posted a skit poking fun at conservative women such as Erika Kirk. “She has not been very excited about that and wants him to not have free speech to continue in those activities. So, I wanted to support free speech,” Lauren said.

Lauren was heartened that Baylor had allowed both TPUSA and All Are Neighbors to have a platform, even if she personally aligned more closely with the views expressed at the latter.

“We’re allowed to say what we want and what we think in this country, and as long as we’re not hurting somebody else or inciting somebody else to hurt other people, then we deserve to be heard,” Lauren said.

Hanna Al-Hayek, a social work major from Houston and a Palestinian American, was one of the student speakers and student organizers of All Are Neighbors. While she supported free speech, Al-Hayek was troubled by speech that led to hatred or advocated for genocide.

Al-Hayek initially worried that Baylor’s acceptance of the TPUSA event on campus indicated Baylor’s support for its message. However, when it came to getting permission for All Are Neighbors, Al-Hayek said, “They approved it almost immediately. … And, we had a lot of faculty and staff on our side who showed up and helped make this happen.”

Both the All Are Neighbors event and the TPUSA event displayed official expressive activity signage from Baylor. Both events hung flyers around campus. The week prior to the events, some of the flyers from TPUSA at Baylor had been ripped up or graffitied.

item.title: The Honors Thesis that Became a Muse-ical
item.description:
On Saturday, April 11, crowds filled up the North Village Community Center to see Te Kalliste, a musical production featuring songs from each of the nine Greek muses representing their philosophies of beauty. Written by senior University Scholars major Annalise Shero for her honors thesis project, the musical blends music, philosophy, and friendship in a stunning reflection of Shero’s education as a whole person: a scholar, an artist, and a friend.

In the beginning of the musical, Eris, the goddess of discord, arrives at the wedding of Thetis and Peleus and presents the apple labeled Te Kalliste: for the most beautiful. Each of the nine muses reflects in turn on what beauty is and how one should respond to it. Shero began her work in her sophomore year at Baylor by filling up journals with ideas, studying Greek myths, the muses, and philosophies of beauty, and developing a creative vision for each muse. Then she began composing, carefully making musical choices that reflect her philosophical message for each muse.

Live musicians played the score of Shero’s musical

Garrett Woodbury, senior composition major and Shero’s music director, remarked on Shero’s “very diverse” set of compositions which nevertheless “sounds like it’s all supposed to fit together.” In fact, the diversity of Shero’s compositions is no coincidence, but reflects some of her philosophical ideas. She said “By the end of the musical I’ve kind of made the case for dissonance as a form of beauty. It is within clashing voices that we can have conversation.” As Shero’s friend and roommate, I can attest to her personal philosophy that we hold truth in two hands; there is truth in apparent dissonance, and the musical diversity and dissonance in her compositions reflects this belief.

Woodbury pointed to the lyrics in Calliope as another testament to the integration of Shero’s ideas and her music. The lyrics read, “Restless souls, how will we find our way, wandering lost, far from home. Odysseus captain braving, wide ocean, waves all around, crashing down.” He notes that “the meter is this 6/8 lilty feel, which makes it feel like you’re on a ship.”

As Shero continued to compose, making musical choices with care, her friendships played a significant role in her process. Senior Peyton Louise Robuck recalled that “[Annalise] would be playing us… the Muse Score [composition software] in sometimes skeletal parts… and you kind of saw the skin coming on the bones.” Woodbury began working with Shero in Dr. Taylor’s orchestration class in the fall of 2025, where they “became closer on a musical level” as he watched her develop her compositions and gave her feedback.

The full cast celebrates after the performance

When rehearsals started, it felt like the culmination of years of friendship. Each week, we set aside our schoolwork, worries about the future, and, for some of us, our own theses, and met together to make music. Like our friendships, our rehearsals started out a little awkward and unsure. But we were patient and listened to each other, and over time, we learned what we sound like, what to listen for, and how we fit into the whole group. Robuck observed that she saw references to moments from the past years of friendship reflected in the lyrics, saying that it was “really neat to see a lot of the seeds of friendship and discussion from [past years] [come] to fruition senior year.” In that sense, the musical was a gift to all of us.

item.title: Of Hobbits and Heroism: Joseph Loconte on the Inklings and the World Wars
item.description:
As late afternoon sunlight streamed through the stained-glass windows of Armstrong Browning Library, a standing-room-only crowd of more than 200 students and faculty gathered to hear Dr. Joseph Loconte recount how C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien used imaginative literature to resist the moral disillusionment of their age.

Loconte, bestselling author of The War for Middle-Earth, delivered the Annual Ethics & Culture Lecture on Wednesday, across the street from the controversial Turning Point USA rally.

Freshman Lucy Pritchett, a Great Texts major from Waco, Texas, found in the lecture lessons for our current cultural tensions. She noted that widespread division has made it harder for students to envision a common good: “We aren’t trying to imagine…what can redeem us from this brokenness. And we aren’t talking about it together.”

In his address titled “War, Friendship, and Imagination: J.R.R. Tolkien, C.S. Lewis, and the Fight for Civilization,” Loconte situated both writers in the aftermath of World War I, when faith in ideals like beauty, virtue, and heroism had eroded. As another global conflict loomed, they united in a deliberate rebellion against this prevailing cynicism: “The long shadows cast by the second world war invaded their minds…it is the tragedy of war that brings these two amazing authors together in friendship, and it is their friendship that makes possible the creation of their epic works.”

More than a dozen students sat on the floor after seating was filled

This resistance appears vividly in The Lord of the Rings, where rising political threats find a literary expression: “The Ring of Power is the mode of force behind Sauron’s intent to enslave or destroy anything that stands in its way. . . it sounds like a political ideology: totalitarianism.”

However, the war also provided models for the forces of good. The London air raids brought four girls to Lewis’ home in Oxford for refuge, and those children served as inspiration for the Pevensies in The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe. Through unassuming figures like hobbits and children, both authors portray heroism as rooted in everyday sacrifice and moral choice rather than strength alone.

Beyond their fiction, Lewis and Tolkien embodied this vision through their literary circle, the Inklings. Loconte called them a bulwark against cultural fragmentation: “At a moment in history when the moral foundations of Western civilization seemed to be disintegrating, here are two trying to reverse the rot.”

“At a moment in history when the moral foundations of Western civilization seemed to be disintegrating, here are two trying to reverse the rot.” Dr. Joseph Loconte

In an interview with The Standard, Loconte argued that their work remains especially relevant today. In a climate marked by political polarization and institutional distrust that mirrors the era of the Inklings, he suggested that their stories continue to resonate because they speak to enduring human longings for beauty and purpose. “If people are exposed to great literature or art,” he said, “there’s going to be an instinctive response, no matter how cynical you are.”

For sophomore Jack Malone, a Science Research Fellow from St. Louis, Missouri, the lecture prompted a personal response. “It inspired me to read more Tolkien…[and] it made me think about my vocation. What can you do in your vocation to forward the love of God?”

For students interested in exploring these ideas further, Baylor English professor Dr. Richard Russell will offer an “Oxford Christians” course this fall, guiding students through the works of C.S. Lewis, J.R.R. Tolkien, and Dorothy Sayers. In the course, Russell invites students “to enter into various and strange worlds of whimsy and fancy that ultimately lead to an appreciation of the eucatastrophe that is the crucifixion and resurrection of Christ.”

That vision of courage, rooted not in power but in what is worth defending, continues to resonate with students facing their own moment of cultural and political uncertainty. As Faramir says in The Return of the King, “I do not love the bright sword for its sharpness, nor the arrow for its swiftness, nor the warrior for his glory. I love only that which they defend.”

item.title: Baylor Shouldn’t Have Allowed the TPUSA Event. Here’s Why.
item.description:
Baylor has reached a missional crisis—a “turning point,” if you will. Baylor students and administration need to decide what the purpose of a university is, and the place politics has in pursuing that purpose. If we don’t choose our answers to those questions, Baylor will drift, unintentionally but inevitably, into an answer none of us would have chosen.

I believe that the purpose of a Christian university is to seek the truth rigorously, through research and socratic discussion, and to foster Christian virtue in its students. By and large, the TPUSA event (and the “alternative” event it inspired) didn’t help advance that purpose, and because of that, I believe that Baylor shouldn’t have allowed it on campus.

I didn’t go into the event expecting to come to that conclusion, but after reflecting on my experience, I truly believe it. It’s not because I’m a “psychotic, castrated lib,” as right-wing political commentator Benny Johnson called members of the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC). It’s not just because I think it’s wrong for Johnson to respond to a student who farmed cows and pigs by commenting that he’d be “very familiar with how to deal with liberal women.” It’s that the people being insulted and argued against didn’t have a chance to defend themselves to the 438 people who attended. That is contrary to the spirit of the university.

A university should encourage students to engage with topics, even political ones, in the spirit of an academic, not a politician. This seems obvious to me. Because of the nature of elections, political figures have a vested interest in engaging with ideas and policy in a way that makes their side seem better than it is, and the other side to seem worse than it is. As citizens of a classically liberal democratic republic, it’s something we have to deal with. However, bringing that spirit to a university isn’t wise, and Baylor, on paper, recognizes this.

A university should encourage students to engage with topics, even political ones, in the spirit of an academic, not a politician.

According to the Baylor Student Organization speaker event policies, “particular concern should be taken that the University not be politicized.” Both the TPUSA event and the counter event were political, but they also fostered politicization. There’s a distinction. Voting is political, listening to primary debates is political, running for a Student Government position is political.

Politicization, on the other hand, creates “omnicauses,” wherein people are bound to hold the party’s views on disparate issues, and where to disagree with one issue is to deny the entire omnicause. Both the left and the right are guilty of creating omnicauses. Each omnicause entails a specific opinion on hot-button, controversial topics, and there are social consequences if an individual in the cause decides to change their mind. Meaning, this grouping of causes can lead people, especially students, to engage issues as “America-First Republicans,” or as “LGBTQ+ advocates,” rather than as truth-seekers.

Johnson was not afraid to lump people into political categories. He spent time during the event on several conservative “wins,” including congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s fraud charges, Virginia’s redistricting being blocked by a judge, and the federal indictment of the SPLC for funding extremist groups. I would guess that most liberals aren’t even familiar with the SPLC. But Johnson’s (potentially satirical) advice was to say to a liberal who may approach a future TPUSA tabling event, “what’s it like funding the KKK, biatch?”

To his credit, the president of Baylor’s TPUSA chapter, Peter Fernandez, gave a speech at the event in which he decried “[surrounding] ourselves with people who think exactly like us” and “[thinking] the other side is evil.” At the same time, he called the people at the counter event “opps” and said there’s probably only “tens or twenties of people there.”

Two notes before a final point on Baylor’s purpose as a university.

One, these are certainly not “unprecedented times,” but they are important ones. Back in 2019, the Baylor Young Americans for Freedom hosted Matt Walsh. A Change.org petition to cancel Walsh created by Baylor grad Patrick Hill II received 2373 signatures, but it failed, and Walsh was still able to speak. A counter event was also held, where Baylor’s left-leaning community used a party for recovering addicts, called the “Love Feast,” as a place for LGBTQ students to gather at the same time as Walsh’s event.

This time, the response to the event centered on countering the TPUSA event, rather than cancelling it. The new petition demanded “equal expression rights,” and contained a thorough written justification, unlike the 2019 petition:

To be clear, we don’t want to silence others; we want the same access they have. We recognize that no institution is neutral. However, by granting exclusive ‘unrestricted’ space to one political arm (TPUSA), Baylor has abandoned its role as a place of rigorous inquiry and has become a site of ideological indoctrination of a specific perspective of Christianity. We demand the same ‘unrestricted’ space for counter-narratives.

Here, the petitioners recognize that the solution to disagreement is not cancellation, something that I believe the attendees and speakers at the TPUSA event realize as well. This is an important step in the right direction in terms of national politics, but the issue of needing to bring in a counter-event could have been avoided, had the TPUSA event not been held on campus.

Two, about attendance—using the Lariat’s numbers, the All Are Neighbors event had 352 attendees, and TPUSA had 438, so a combined 790 people attended. Most of the attendees were students, although there were faculty, staff, and community members at both. Meaning, out of Baylor’s 19,858 students, a generous estimate would be that 4% attended. That is an incredibly low number. The reason these events matter is not because they will shape student viewpoints significantly right now, but because of what they represent for the direction of the school, politically and academically.

So, is it possible for Baylor to avoid politicization, while at the same time protecting free speech and academic freedom? Yes, if the university doesn’t make Wednesday’s events the new norm on campus.

President Livingstone’s email on the Thursday following the events mainly lauded that both events had been conducted safely, but she also wrote: “I want to thank each of you for engaging respectfully as a demonstration of Baylor’s Christian mission, our commitment to academic freedom and to civil discourse.” I didn’t see a clear representation of any of those three things at the TPUSA event. If Dr. Livingstone truly did, then she and I have very different conceptions of Christian mission, academic freedom, and civil discourse.

I believe that the closest the event came to any of these three ideals was during Johnson’s interview with Border Czar Tom Homan. I went into the event with low hopes for Homan. But, for the most part, he defended his actions and beliefs cogently and methodically. He referenced stats related to border security, his personal experience with children being taken across the border, and his habit of praying nightly for both border patrol agents and “aliens” crossing the border.

Homan is not an angel; he did call the Biden Administration “treasonous” for what he saw as purposeful mismanagement of the border. That’s a claim that really deserves a foil by someone who disagrees. Maybe a student would have asked a question on it, but there was not enough time to answer every question, or to discuss the questions that were asked in depth.

Of course, university regulation of politicization could be a slippery slope. If the university is the arbiter of what counts as politicization or not, doesn’t that severely restrict the academic freedom that I’m advocating for? No. It is not actually very hard to tell in most cases whether an event is intended to politicize. When it is difficult, the university should err on the side of allowing the event. It’s clear that the nationwide TPUSA tour is being held in order to rally young people around the MAGA cause, allowing for only minimal discussion (in the Q&A). It’s also clear that allowing political candidates like Ken Paxton to campaign on campus, as Baylor leadership has promised to allow, is intended to politicize students.

While I think this particular event should not have been allowed on campus, I am not condemning the existence of the Baylor TPUSA chapter itself. The chapter’s mission, according to its constitution, is admirable:

Turning Point USA at Baylor’s mission is to educate Baylor University students about the importance of fiscal responsibility, free markets, and capitalism through innovative campus activism and non-partisan, thought-provoking discussion.

It’s theoretically possible for Baylor’s TPUSA to stay true to this mission, even if it tends to attract right-wing students. Joining a TPUSA chapter doesn’t necessitate joining the right-wing omnicause. This same logic applies to all political student associations, even the College Democrats and Republicans. Their existence doesn’t necessitate undue politicization, but the holding of a rally, where students are explicitly asked to hold up posters of Charlie Kirk and begin chanting “USA,” does.

The mission of the university is primarily to be a place for students, even if free speech calls for apologists and ideologues to have a chance to air their opinions. By all means, students should hold and advocate for their individual beliefs. But we ought to do it not just respectfully, but respectably. We should allow opposition to be heard—not in another building across campus, but in the room in which they are being criticised. This may require some Liberals to grow a thicker skin in political conversation and some Conservatives to give views they see as “psychotic” a chance to be defended.

When Alexander Hamilton called on George Washington to break his treaty with France during the American revolution, he did so not on grounds that the French cause was altogether wrong, but that the way in which it was being sought was misguided. I would echo his words to TPUSA:

A struggle for liberty is in itself respectable and glorious. When conducted with magnanimity, justice, and humanity, it ought to command the admiration of every friend to human nature. But if sullied by crimes and extravagances, it loses its respectability.

Liberals and Conservatives, be respectable, and by all means don’t stop talking. To fulfill its mission, Baylor needs students like you and I to be true students of politics and each other, something the TPUSA event didn’t foster.

item.title: The Event to Attend Instead of TPUSA or its Left-leaning Alternative
item.description:
The echoes of applause from competing political rallies on Baylor’s campus Wednesday evening will likely reach into Armstrong Browning Library, where a renowned Lewis and Tolkien scholar will speak about how the trenches of WWI and Hitler’s civilizational threat shaped the imagination and wisdom of generations. That is where I will be on Wednesday, and you should join me.

Dr. Douglas Henry, the Dean of the Baylor Honors College and one of the key planners of the Lewis and Tolkien event, argued that it “expresses what universities at their best ought to be about: questions, critical reflection, intellectual and moral formation… entertaining the prospect that one might be wrong… none of those things are typically on offer at partisan rallies.”

On the evening of Wednesday the 22nd, two contentious political events will be hosted on Baylor’s campus: Baylor’s chapter of Turning Point USA will host right-wing speakers Donald Trump Jr., Benny Johnson, and Tom Homan. In response to the Turning Point event, several Baylor student organizations, including College Democrats and the NAACP, will host a competing event titled “All Are Neighbors.” The event will feature two high-profile Christian LGBTQ advocates.

At 7 pm, across the street from the Turning Point event, Dr. Joseph Loconte will deliver the Annual Ethics & Culture Lecture, titled “War, Friendship, and Imagination: J.R.R. Tolkien, C.S. Lewis, and the Fight for Civilization.” It will be based on Loconte’s recent NYT bestselling book, “The War for Middle Earth.”

Dr. Richard Jordan, a Baylor political science professor, taught a class last semester on War, Politics, and Literature in which he recommended Loconte’s book. He called Loconte a “dazzling” speaker. “Like CS Lewis, he possesses a talent for making deep ideas accessible and compelling to just about anyone. Like Tolkien, his imagination is rich with centuries of tradition.”

Dr. David Corey, a Baylor professor who teaches classes on political philosophy, also recommended the Loconte event over the political events. “Politics is good and liberal learning is good. But we have too much of the one and hardly any of the other, so it’s not a hard decision.”

I agree with Dr. Corey that politics is worth pursuing. In a few months, I will be moving to Washington, DC to advocate for a political cause I believe in. I am not attending the Loconte lecture because I believe political problems are unimportant. Rather, I am attending it because I believe it will help form me into the kind of person who can solve political problems well.

According to Dean Henry, the increase of political conflict makes learning about lasting truths even more important. “We’re going to make mistakes with the conflicts that confront us unless we are shaped by the wisdom of the ages.”

The writings of Tolkien and Lewis contain vast resources of wisdom for those facing political contention. Their stories speak to a generation that faced the very real possibility of Hitler taking over the world.

As Dr. Jordan put it, “There’s a reason these two authors still fortify our souls and defend us against the cynicism creeping into our politics and culture. They were tried by fires none of us have ever experienced.”

In October of 1939, one month after the start of WWII, C.S. Lewis spoke to students at Oxford about why learning matters in wartime. His arguments included an appeal to the importance of learning about the past to understand the present. We need the past to remind us that “the basic assumptions have been quite different in different periods and that much which seems certain to the uneducated is merely temporary fashion. A man who has lived in many places is not likely to be deceived by the local errors of his native village: the scholar has lived in many times and is therefore in some degree immune from the great cataract of nonsense that pours from the press and the microphone of his own age.”

I am looking forward to hearing about the political events on Wednesday, especially from our Standard writers who will be covering both. But I would rather sit in the quiet foyer of the most beautiful building on campus, being fortified by the hard-won and time-tested wisdom of two of the people I trust most. I hope you join me.

item.title: Who’s the Better Worker: You or AI? The Intelligence Advantage in the Judgement Economy
item.description:
A few weeks ago, I attended a Baylor Alexander Hamilton Society lecture by American Enterprise Institute scholar Brent Orrell in which he called AI development the next industrial revolution and claimed that this transformation would occur far faster than the industrial and managerial revolutions. Regardless of whether you’re apprehensive or accepting of this technology, Orrell is right. Like all technologies before it, AI is here to stay. And unlike those earlier technologies, it directly challenges our most uniquely human attribute: our own intelligence.

The digital revolution of the 2000s and 2010s accelerated a similar trend, a move away from the manufacturing-based economics of the industrial revolution to a knowledge-based economy. With each innovation, the cognitive threshold needed to maintain a comfortable lifestyle appears to shift heavily in favor of those with greater intelligence. Human intelligence will become increasingly vital to be a shareholder in this new revolution rather than its victim as AI’s entrance reduces people’s ability and drive to think critically, let alone at all.

Human intelligence will become increasingly vital to be a shareholder in this new revolution rather than its victim as AI’s entrance reduces people’s ability and drive to think critically, let alone at all.

The selection pressure from this AI revolution compared to the industrial, managerial, and digital revolutions could be much more severe. As more basic administrative tasks and lower-level white-collar jobs are replaced by AI, the credentials and level of intelligence needed to secure stable employment that provides for a comfortable lifestyle increases. At the same time, AI allows more and more people to feign higher levels of competence, even as their actual ability to retain and acquire information decreases. The consulting firm Tyton Partners found that as of the spring 2024, 59% of students use AI at least twice per month. Data published by AI detection software company Turnitin claims that just over 1 out of every 10 papers submitted (11%) through the software contained AI generated content. And while not all of these uses are detrimental to the students themselves or society at large, many of them are.

Junior supply chain management and Russian major Stewart Gaydosik had this to say regarding the impact of cognitive decline attributed to AI: “I think it’s definitely accelerated it in some way with younger students. People that should be above average, or significantly above average [are] using AI to their detriment … people that are already below average intelligence [are using AI to] appear smarter than they actually are.”

Using AI effectively without outsourcing one’s thinking requires not only higher cognitive ability, but also restraint.

The implications for the world outside the academy also appear dismal. As white-collar jobs that require lower cognitive ability and little “critical thinking” to perform are replaced with AI, large segments of the population face obsolescence. Junior political science major Alex Kelley commented on the potential impact on employment. “I think when students use the AI to answer questions…and it’s everything that their future job can be…if they use AI to answer questions now, their boss can use the AI to answer those questions in the workplace…you are allowing the AI to be your cognitive limit.” Those who let AI think for them defer to the answers it deems “the best.” This means that the machine then becomes the standard, something which none of us should subordinate our own ideas to. Using AI effectively without outsourcing one’s thinking requires not only higher cognitive ability, but also restraint.

In his lecture, Mr. Orrell introduced us to what he called “the judgment economy.” Those who are well suited to this economy will be those who can think creatively, critically, and exercise good judgement. Our ability to think creatively is one of the primary differences between us and AI. Even more so than animals that live instinctually, AI operates mechanically, without creativity or true innovation. However, not every person is endowed with equal cognitive ability.

Psychologists traditionally suggested that an IQ of 120 is the threshold at which people gained creative or higher level cognition. More recent scholarship places the peak of the IQ-creativity association between approximately 110 and 120 after which this association remains relatively constant. Because the overall average IQ is 100 with a standard deviation of 15, only about 25% (~86 million people) of the American population possess the cognitive faculties to surpass or, at the very least, compete with AI. And while IQ doesn’t determine all outcomes across all jobs, it is a useful proxy to attempt to quantify the issue. Although there is no data for or good way to test this, the number of Americans who are both smarter than AI and willing to resist outsourcing their thinking is likely much lower than any of us would like.

Already, unemployment for recent graduates between the ages of 23-27 is just under 5%, up from 3.25% in 2019. Roughly 55,000 layoffs have already been at least partially attributed to AI. The present lack of quality employment for college graduates, which may degrade further, leaves the skilled trades as reliable, well-paying alternatives. Or so we are told. A simple supply and demand issue arises: America does not need millions more tradesmen. And if it had them, those wages would suddenly decline and become far less attractive, as happened to the salaries of computer scientists and coders. So what jobs will be left for people? This is a question that will loom over the horizon for as long as AI continues to improve.

AI has long-term potential to free humanity from much needless toil.

With this in mind, the future seems quite bleak. And it could be, though there should be some emphasis on could. The likelihood that AI causes mass labor displacement in the near future is dubious. For as long as it continues to make things up, cobble quotes together from multiple books and pass them off as verbatim, and struggle with basic math at times, we are far from a dystopia in any real sense. That being said, AI is not going away, and it will only continue to improve, meaning that this potential displacement is possible on a long enough timeline. AI has long-term potential to free humanity from much needless toil. Although, as in Mr. Orrell’s “judgment economy,” discernment will be needed to ensure that AI benefits the society generally, not merely the 25% who are lucky enough to escape its encroachment.

item.title: Trade in the Shadow of China: Dr. William Chou on Chinese-American Trade
item.description:
“China is a disruptor, but not a builder.” If that observation is true, the opportunity to strike a hammer blow against Chinese trade is fleeting. With the dragon rearing its head toward disrupting American influence throughout the global economic theatre, a reasonable administration ought to take immediate action to uphold our national interests. The most sensible, and arguably the strongest, being our ability to use trade as a tool against China.

William Chou, senior fellow and deputy director of the Hudson Institute’s Japan Chair, delivered a lecture at Baylor on Thursday, March 5th about economic competition between China and the United States. Hosted by Baylor’s chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society, the lecture centered on a simple question: Is Trade a Tool Against China?

China’s economic trading strategy sharply differs from the foundations that guide Western trade policy.

China’s economic trading strategy sharply differs from the foundations that guide Western trade policy. Rather than viewing commerce as a mutually beneficial exchange, Beijing often treats it as an instrument of leverage. “In terms of application in how the Chinese use economic power, they align themselves with coercion,” Chou said. This dynamic can be seen in strategies such as the Belt and Road Initiative, a massive infrastructure program that some argue saddles developing countries with unsustainable debt in exchange for Chinese investment and influence.

Western concern over China’s predatory economic initiatives demands immediate action. Chou argued that the United States still possesses a powerful lever in the global financial system: “American capital markets are our greatest weapon. If there’s one way to really hit the Chinese hard, it is to cut them off from foreign financing.” Foreign investment accounts for a substantial share of Chinese trade – cash flows reach into the trillions of dollars. Combined with measures such as tariffs and sanctions, which have been a common note of the current administration, such limits on Chinese access to foreign capital could significantly constrain Beijing’s ability to expand its geopolitical influence.

Economic competition between the United States and China will consequently hinge primarily on financial power rather than simply manufacturing alone. Global markets operate on access to capital and investment, areas where the United States still holds the upper hand. As Chou bluntly summarized during the lecture, “Unless you control the money, you cannot really change anything.” If Beijing’s ambitions are fueled by access to global capital and expanding markets, then restricting that access may prove one of the most effective tools available to Washington in aligning the future with American interests.

f the United States hopes to preserve its geopolitical position, it cannot disregard its own economic agency in the present battle.

If the United States hopes to preserve its geopolitical position, it cannot disregard its own economic agency in the present battle. The administration must instead recognize what trade has become: an instrument of strategic competition. The Chinese Communist Party has demonstrated a particular willingness to use economic coercion and capture to advance their geopolitical aims, and the United States should not hesitate to respond definitively. Maintaining American influence in the global economy will require more than simply passive participation in the global market. If Beijing continues to treat economic relationships as instruments of geopolitical leverage, the United States must respond forcibly and decisively using tariffs, investment restrictions, and financial pressure to ensure that American economic power serves American strategic interests. If the United States fails to act while the dragon rises, it will find that the moment to strike has already passed.

item.title: Waco Authors Burst the Baylor Bubble at Fabled’s Author Fair
item.description:
The evening of Feb. 19, Fabled Bookshop and Cafe opened their floor to eighteen local authors to display their books to the Waco community during their annual Local Author Book Faire. This event drew a large crowd — nearly 300 people — and the store became crowded with attendees walking around the bookshelves, perusing the different displays and exhibited books.

Events such as this one emphasize the benefits of engaging with the larger Waco community, an important

reminder for Baylor students who struggle to step outside of the “Baylor Bubble.”

‘Baylor Bubble’ is a term which has been around for at least a decade and refers to the insular, privileged environment that Baylor’s campus creates. This bubble creates a buffer between Baylor students and the Waco community, which can create a narrow-minded perspective and an echo chamber which inhibits personal growth. Benefits such as fresh perspectives, empathy from hearing other people’s stories, and a wider understanding of how the real world works are lost when students confine themselves to the ‘Baylor Bubble’.

Kai Jackson, the communications manager for Fabled who was overseeing the Author Book Faire, says the event grew out of a desire to create space for local writers.

In a KWBU interview, he said this event is more than just selling books, it’s about community. “Most authors tend to be introverts,” Jackson said. “So to have a space not just to celebrate their work, but also to connect with the other authors … just to know that they’re not alone in the work.” The Author Book Faire builds the Waco community as well as creating a space for local authors to feel represented and seen. Mary Beth Talley, author of non-fiction memoir Not Bad, Just Different was a first-time participant in Fabled’s event. “They’ve been very gracious hosts,” she said. “It’s been wonderful, it’s a really great opportunity. I’m meeting all kinds of different people and other authors..”

Talley’s book was published in October and navigates grief and post traumatic stress in the aftermath of the Wedgewood Baptist Church shooting, which Talley experienced when she was 17. One reviewer describes how the book brings light into a dark situation. “It’s a good reminder of God’s power to redeem even the worst situations,” the reviewer said, “We are never without hope.”

“It’s a little surreal,” Talley said, “I have a book that has the story of my life, and it’s out there for people to read.” Reyna Shanks, another author featured at the book fair, echoed the astounding reality of having a book published: “This started out as me just writing in my room,” she said.

Shanks stands apart from the other authors highlighted at the event as one of three child authors showcased. Chapter 10 is a poetry collection published last April, the assembly of poems from when Shanks— now twelve— was just 10 years old. Chapter 10 invites readers into the mind of a child, seeing the simple things of life—trees, pets, moments of quiet—as magical.

“I’m not used to this attention,” Shanks laughed. “It’s a little intimidating, but it’s exciting to see where I could be someday.”

Fabled Bookshop & Cafe places important emphasis on the visibility of local authors, whether it is through events such as the Book Faire or their bookshelf for local authors only. Reading local authors such as the ones Fabled highlights teaches valuable lessons. Stories like Mary Beth Talley’s Not Bad, Just Different show readers how to have hope and empathy in hard times, and stories like Reyna Shanks’ Chapter 10 encourage readers to step out of their perspective and see the beauty in the mundane— particularly for older, college students engaging with her poems. While Baylor students are only in Waco for four years, these years should be expanded beyond campus. Listening to the stories of local writers reminds students that the community around them is filled with voices worth hearing if they take the time to step outside of their own perspective and pick up a book.

item.title: The HRC’s Monday Chapel: Reorienting a Mandatory Credit
item.description:
Rather than reminiscing on the various tasks of the day, at 9pm on Monday nights the Honors Residential College (HRC) gathers to worship on the third floor of Memorial in our chapel. The bustle of what many claim is the most dreadful day of the week is finally over. We come together to affirm, through smiles and laughter, exhaustion and frustration, a fundamental truth: we are nothing without Christ.



The HRC is composed of college students, and our chapels are the same. HRC students create and enact all the night chapel services that occur Monday through Thursday of every week. I knew coming to Baylor that all students are required to take at least two semesters of chapel to graduate, and I did not expect the HRC chapel to change the way I viewed my college experience. I assumed it was just another box that I needed to check off my list. I am grateful that I was wrong. Monday chapel has had a profound impact on how I view the HRC and the broader Baylor community. Rather than being another activity I simply go through the motions of, it has become a thoughtful time of peace and recentering with the people I live alongside.

Monday chapel has had a profound impact on how I view the HRC and the broader Baylor community.

We begin our time together with an excerpt from the hymn “Veni Sancte Spiritus” (Come Holy Spirit). Yes, the HRC’s Monday night chapel begins with an excerpt from a hymn in a dead language—quite fitting for Honors students. Following the hymn designed to quiet our minds and bring us to a place prepared for communion with the Lord and each other, we mourn the brokenness of this world together. Like St. Francis prayed, we too pray to be peacemakers and to love others as Christ first loved us. Senior Rebecca Tietze said “these prayers affect our view of the world, and when we repeatedly say the same words, they become ingrained in us. They serve as a reminder that one day when inevitably ‘there is hatred or discord, we have the choice to sow love and union.’”



The evening continues with a responsive hymn acknowledging that although this world is broken, it has been overcome. Then, we join in an ancient Judeo-Christian tradition. We recite a Psalm which proclaims the goodness of God and reminds us of the nature of the God we serve. Following a communal confession where we acknowledge our collective faults in the presence of a merciful God, we bless Him with humble hearts for the love which caused His Son to die for us, that we might be forgiven. These practices are powerful because they draw us into the church. It is through liturgies and confession that we are invited to participate in the historical representation of Christ’s body.

These practices are powerful because they draw us into the church. It is through liturgies and confession that we are invited to participate in the historical representation of Christ’s body.



Then comes the part which changed the way I view my college experience. We pray for the HRC and for the “5th Floor.” Senior Andrew Parks said there is “no 5th floor in the HRC, it is a reference to the general community of Baylor and Waco, the people we interact with daily and those we work with abroad.” We pray that we may love others well, that the Gospel may be shared, that healing might come where there is injury and brokenness, that the outcast may be given a home, and that we, the members of the HRC, would be strong enough to pursue above all else “the love of God, love of neighbor, and love of learning,” and that Christ may use us as his hands and feet in a world which needs hope and truth. Fittingly, following a prayer full of our supplications, we pray as Jesus taught in Matthew. It was incredible to me that a group of college students so very different from one another, living different lives, would pray so intentionally for the needs of others. It has helped rightly reorient my heart and my loves. It is good, true, and beautiful.

To end our time together, we sing to proclaim the truth about the God we serve. We serve a loving God. A God we are called to love with all our heart, soul, mind and strength (Matthew 22:37), a God we love because He is Love (1 John 4:7-8), and a Love that bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:4-8). In a world that desperately needs Truth, we are blessed to have the opportunity to share it, in part, through song. The altos go first proclaiming the truth that we love because God is love, followed by basses who proclaim love bears and believes all things, followed by the tenors who sing that God is love, followed by the sopranos who share the Greatest Commandment. Once every part has had its turn, we arise and face each other, each person, each part, proclaiming truths over each other in one beautiful song. Every voice has something different to bring, but we are all singing the same thing. We serve a good God and we need Him. At the close of this song is the benediction where we beseech God to “grant us a quiet night and perfect end.” And thus, the day is complete.

item.title: Standing in the Rain: If it Worked for Jane Bennet and Guy Montag—Why Not Give it a Try?
item.description:
You would think the rain on this planet is acid the way we all bolt for shelter as soon as the first drops fall. But leather shoes and pristine jackets aside, I suggest that we consider going boldly forth every once in a while into the rain to recover a little sanity and imagination.

Being inundated by a shower is a useful thing, especially if you catch a violent cold that allows you to stay at your rich neighbor’s house for a few days. But aside from getting to know single men in possession of large fortunes (who are thereby in search of a wife), there are other benefits.

When you get out into the rain, for a brief moment, nothing else matters. You can’t take pictures, not if it’s really raining. In fact, you can’t so much as have your phone out. So you’re perfectly cut off from distraction and forced to live in the present. There is nothing that can claim your attention except what’s happening around you—the rain, the leaves bouncing as each drop falls, the rivulets that start to form. You get to experience a little of the joy older generations may have felt, who perhaps knew better how much we need rain for our livelihoods.

It’s a time to stop and breathe. We are always doing something, going somewhere, meeting with someone. While these may be valuable things, we aren’t machines, and we can’t keep going all the time. Let us pause and enjoy what’s happening around us. Like rain. Especially rain in the spring. Rain is beautiful, but it’s even more marvelous when it chivvies winter away, soaking the ground so that the wildflowers come and the world bursts into green.

It’s a sad day when we all hurry through the rain with heads down and umbrellas up. It’s a sign that we are one step further in our dehumanization if we never stop to consider the miracles of nature happening around us. But if, like Guy Montag in Fahrenheit 451, we dare to taste the rain now and then, perhaps we will rediscover something precious:

“I’m still crazy. The rain feels good. I love to walk in it.”

“I don’t think I’d like that,” he said.

“You might if you tried.”

“I never have.”

She licked her lips. “Rain even tastes good.”

“What do you do, go around trying everything once?” he asked.

“Sometimes twice.”

item.title: A Young American Religion: The Catholic Baylor Professor Seeking to Understand Mormonism
item.description:
Mormons and Christians often have a limited understanding of each other’s beliefs. For Christians to engage in better apologetics, they must be more charitable to Mormons. A deeper understanding of each faith’s history and theology is necessary for better dialogue.

This week I had the opportunity to interview Dr. Francis Beckwith, Baylor Professor in Philosophy and Political Science, Resident Fellow of the Institute for Studies in Religion, and author of A Catholic Engagement with Latter-day Saints. Like me, Dr. Beckwith is curious about the interaction between Mormon and orthodox Christian theology.

When defending any faith against another, both perspectives ought to be understood well. Without this clarity, people make arguments against a version of the faith that they have created, rather than the faith as it is currently and historically understood.

Because Mormonism is so young, its doctrine has shifted a lot over time, causing large amounts of variation in beliefs, especially between younger and older members. However, there are still places for debate between Christians and Mormons where terms are more clearly defined. One of these places is the debate surrounding the nature of the Trinity. Beckwith finds, “for Latter-day Saint theology, especially the later works by Joseph Smith, he talks about God as being an advanced version of the species that we belong to. That’s where I think the real difference is. There’s nothing like the classical doctrine of the Trinity. Mormon theology has an understanding that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are only triune insofar as they’re one in purpose, but not because they are the same substance. [In] the Nicene Creed, it says that the Son is one in substance with the Father. That’s something that the LDS would reject.”

In its own theology, Mormonism needs to solidify its doctrine on ongoing revelation. Mormonism is one of the most well known restorationist movements that began during the Second Great Awakening. Joseph Smith claimed to have received revelation from God that all other Christian denominations were false, and that the true Gospel would be restored through modern-day prophets, which have the authority to receive true knowledge from God. Like Roman Catholics, they place a strong emphasis on church authority for establishing doctrine. However, Beckwith pointed out that their approach to revelation is very different. “they don’t have [the same understanding as] the Catholic Church and the papacy…The Pope is only infallible if he speaks ex cathedra, which only happened twice in the history of the Catholic Church. Most of the doctrines that are considered infallible are those that were issued by councils like the Council of Nicaea. And so in a weird way, the pope is actually more constrained in what he can do [than Mormon prophets].”

The lack of constraint on the Mormon prophets allows contradictions between past and present revelation. These contradictions suggest the existence of a bipolar, chaotic God who changes His mind at random.

Beckwith explained that Mormonism has not yet had a movement like the Protestant Reformation that has aided in clearly solidifying the doctrine of the church. Because of this, he argues, “where Latter-day Saints sort of fit in the wider Christian world is difficult to say.”

“Most of the book is a dialogue. We want to better understand Latter-day Saint theology and also want [them] to be able to read the book without feeling that we’re attacking them.”

Though clear disagreement exists, there is still a lot of debate between Mormons and Christians that ought to be more clearly defined, especially for the parts of Mormon doctrine that have yet to develop. In these places, charity, humility, and intellectual open-mindedness are required for both Christians and Mormons to have greater understanding of each other. Dr. Beckwith explains how he has done this in his book, A Catholic Engagement with Latter-day Saints. He reports, “what we did in the book is we recruited about a dozen Catholic scholars to write chapters on aspects of Mormon theology. Most of the book is a dialogue. We want to better understand Latter-day Saint theology and also want [them] to be able to read the book without feeling that we’re attacking them.”

It is this kind of understanding of Mormonism and orthodox Christianity that I hope occurs through a deeper understanding of each religion. This can only occur through curiosity, humility, and charity for our neighbors and perspectives.

item.title: Weil, Heidegger, and the Kind of Thinking AI Can’t Help Us With
item.description:
“Y’all are self-deceived rational utility maximizers.” This is how Alan Jacobs addresses his students at the beginning of each semester. It’s his lighthearted way of explaining why, despite our best intentions at the beginning of the semester to do the reading for the sake of joy and wisdom, we will eventually start reading for the sake of our grade.

Dr. Jacobs’ diagnosis of his students really indicates a much more pervasive cultural disease, one with bigger consequences than a few tedious reading quizzes. While utility maximization is helpful in some areas of life, letting it become our only way of thinking could compromise our very humanity. But guidance from Martin Heidegger and Simone Weil has given me hope of a cure: a greater, second type of thinking which trains us for prayer.

Our entire culture is built on utility maximizing, from our economy to our government and even to our own weekly lives. And this is not necessarily a bad thing. With market prices being automatically dictated according to computer calculations of consumer demand, ordinary people can take meaningful financial action in real time, with confidence that consumer sentiment is efficiently and accurately represented. Without such computer calculation, the market would be much more exclusive, uncertain, and ultimately less productive.

While our government is definitely not known as the most speedy institution, it too is built around utility maximization. Rather than prioritizing quantitative measures like our economy does, the government revolves around maximizing certain qualitative values. Checks and balances make legislation take longer to pass, but they keep our system stable and representative of the people. While certain utilities like speed are sacrificed, other utilities are nevertheless being maximized at all times.

And in both of these cases, we should be extremely glad for utility maximization! Otherwise, most of us would benefit far less from market success, and all of us would have to worry more about government stability. The real question is whether the utility maximizing in our own lives is just as beneficial.

Most of us order our weeks according to the things we value most, be those assignments, parties, church, video games, etc. However, our weekly calculation of what we intend to allot our time and energy to is often unreflective and even appetitive. We deceive ourselves in thinking that our calculations help us make the most of our time, but in reality we have not even begun to reflect on what our criteria are in our calculations.

Many of us hide under a vague notion of ‘rationality’ as our guiding principle. We tell ourselves that we are ordering our lives ‘rationally,’ but I do not think we know what that word really means or why it is valuable. Is rationality just thinking and acting according to reason? But then what is reason? Is reason ultimately just logic? But then what is logic? Does logic exist as the systematic structure of reality, or is it just something we have just made up in order to make sense of reality? These are the types of reflective questions we must ask ourselves in order to go beyond our blind utility calculations.

In his Discourse on Thinking, Heidegger puts forth a dichotomy of thought. On the one hand, he argues that modern culture is overrun with calculative thinking, the thinking which “plans,” “computes,” and “never stops, never collects itself.” On the other hand, he argues that our culture is deprived of meditative thinking, the “thinking which contemplates the meaning which reigns in everything that is.” This is problematic because Heidegger believes that man is fundamentally a “meditative being.” And if we let this dichotomy develop further, someday calculative thinking may be “the only way of thinking,” and “man would have denied and thrown away his own special nature.”

Martin Heidegger

Unfortunately, it has been 70 years since Heidegger made this observation, and for 70 years we have only become more calculative and less meditative. To make matters worse, the rise of artificial intelligence threatens an exponential decline in meditative thought. AIs are calculative machines, with efficiency unlike anything we have ever seen. As we use them and come to rely on them more, not only will we continue to forsake meditative thinking, we will begin to outsource even our calculative thinking, causing us to stray further from our nature as meditative beings.

However, it is still not too late to heed Heidegger’s warning and grow out of our reliance on blind utility calculation.
