But to do so, we must understand what meditative thinking is and why we should practice it. Thankfully, Simone Weil articulates one way of practicing meditative thinking which offers a clear and final end. In her essay “Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God,” she argues that the end of all activities, especially challenging activities like mathematical calculations, is “increasing the power of attention that will be available at the time of prayer.” For Weil, every activity is an opportunity to train our faculty of attention, so that when we enter into prayer, we can more fully meditate on and attend to God.

Simone Weil

We can think meditatively by focusing our attention as much as possible on each activity that we undertake. Rather than only focusing on outcomes, like we would with calculative thinking, Weil encourages us to meditate by immersing our attention in the activity itself. Ultimately, this will bring us into deeper meditative thought in our prayer to the True God, the “living Truth, the very Truth that once in a human voice declared: ‘I am the Truth.’”

item.title: Growing together: A Defense of Human Conversation From Baylor’s AI & Faith Symposium
item.description:
“What’s the difference between having a conversation with Socrates vs ChatGPT?” If treated like an interlocutor rather than merely an answer machine, might it be possible for modern students to engage with AI in much the same way that Athenian youth might engage with Socrates? Which is more likely to “corrupt the youth”?

This line of questioning was raised by Dr. Christina George during a Q&A session at Baylor’s recent AI and Faith Symposium. Baylor’s Institute for Faith and Learning invited scholars from across the nation to deliver over 200 presentations on AI over three days. Topics ranged from whether AI should be used in elderly care to explanations of mathematical processes behind artificial “intelligence.” Throughout all the presentations I attended, Dr. George’s question followed me. In their own way, each presenter helped me to understand the unique value of human conversation.

In her presentation, Dr. George offered the beginning of an answer: “Socrates allows for his own mind to change throughout the course of many of his dialectics!” AI, however, does not have any mind to change.

Sam Byassee, a Baylor senior who chaired the Crane Scholars panel at the symposium, described AI as “a conversation partner who collates information for you to sift through.” You can use AI to enable your own thinking, but if “you want someone with whom to contemplate the realities about which you are speaking, then there is going to be a stark difference between the kinds of conversations you can have.” Since AI does not think for itself, it can never be the kind of partner, like Socrates, who grows alongside you.

However, this is not the kind of difference we can calculate and measure. Sam Byassee observed “there is something demonstrably different” between human and AI conversations, but this might not be something that “shows up directly on any of our observation charts.” Byassee’s comment expresses a common theme that I observed during the conference sessions I attended: it is clear that humans and AI are different kinds of things, even sharing certain capacities, but there is great difficulty in locating exactly where we are different.

The Crane’s Scholars panel at the Baylor IFL AI and Faith Symposium

Dr. Ian Gravagne, associate chair of Baylor’s school of engineering and computer science, gave a presentation that helped me to better understand exactly what we mean by “intelligence” when we apply that word (rightly or not) to AI. AI processes human language by turning human words into numbers (a lot of them!) through a process called “tokenization.” Then these number representations of words are assigned specific locations within a “vector space.” Through this process, AI can make mathematical associations between words. For example, the input “teacher + PhD” can output “professor” because the inputted words are related to one another insofar as they are situated near one another in the vector space. When “added together,” they direct the AI to the vicinity of “professor.”

Granting that both humans and AI possess a capacity for respective kinds of intelligence—the latter being a purely calculative kind—then the question of Socrates vs ChatGPT reveals itself as far more complex than attributing greater reasoning capabilities to one or the other.

“The fact that AI cannot be interested is perhaps one of its greatest benefits to humanity as well as one of its greatest dangers.”

In his presentation, Dr. Phillip Donnelly of Baylor’s Great Texts Department compared AI to the oracles of the ancients: Just as the ancients went to an oracle for answers and had to decide whether to trust the oracle’s advice and how to interpret it, so also moderns go to AI for a kind of “prophecy”—though this prophecy is generated by crunching numbers rather than communion with gods.

Dr. George noted that we are quick to accept what AI tells us as if it is plain fact: “It is not always approached with the same skepticism that we bring to a Google search,” or in Dr. Donnelly’s analogy, the same skepticism one might want to bring to an oracle.

One feature of Socratic dialogue is that Socrates is interested in the welfare of his interlocutors. In fact, Socrates, as history records, was perhaps too interested. By contrast, AI is, in Dr. George’s words, “not interested, whatsoever, in the implications that result from its ‘teaching.’”

The fact that AI cannot be interested is perhaps one of its greatest benefits to humanity as well as one of its greatest dangers. Insofar as AI is disinterested in people and in itself, it can be used to perform those tasks that humans might not want to do themselves—cleaning, caretaking, etc.—or would perform more effectively without error. What societal operations would we prefer be performed by humans with interests vs disinterested AIs? Do we prefer that Socrates “corrupt the youth” or ChatGPT?

item.title: The Church Should Teach, Not Control the State, Karl Barth Panel Explains
item.description:
Would you be brave enough to mail a declaration of the separation of church and state straight to Adolf Hitler’s mailbox?

Karl Barth, a 20th-century Swiss Protestant theologian, did just that. Barth’s work on the relationship between church and state was the topic of a panel discussion hosted by Baylor University’s Institute for Faith and Learning on February 25.

For Barth, the divide between church and state goes beyond mere institutions; it reflects a fundamental gap in knowledge and a clear separation of roles. One of the three panelists, Gerald McKenny, a professor of theology at the University of Notre Dame, explained, “The state has no knowledge of the fact that it’s a kind of proleptic anticipation of the kingdom of God. … The state is ignorant, and the state does all that it does in entire ignorance of the message of the gospel.”

In other words, the church possesses knowledge of the Gospel and Scripture which the state does not understand on its own. This gives the church the distinct role of proclaiming the truths of God to the state, a role analogous to teaching. But the church can only educate the state properly if the church itself is living in line with God’s word. Matthew Lee Anderson, an assistant professor in the Baylor Honors College, said, “The state really can learn something from the church so long as the church … has integrity. The church has to learn to live beneath the word of God because if it doesn’t do that, then, as it speaks to the state, it’s going to be vain and fruitless and actually bring defamation on the church.”

The church can only educate the state properly if the church itself is living in line with God’s word.

The distinct roles of church and state must prevent one from collapsing into the other. In the lead-up to World War II, Barth opposed the Third Reich’s totalitarian overreach into the church. The Barmen Declaration, which Barth largely authored and personally mailed to Hitler, decried totalitarian states and their attempts to usurp the church’s role. Likewise, the Declaration rejected church bids to overtake the state’s functions. Either way, to Barth, the church’s prerogative to the declare the Gospel and the state’s duty to secure peace and justice preserve the separateness of each.

While institutionally distanced, Barth stressed that both church and state are underneath Christ’s reign. Kimlyn Bender, a professor of theology at the George W. Truett Theological Seminary, explained that Barth focused on the relationships between the state, the church, and Christ. Indeed, Christ sits in judgment over the state, but He also created the world for His own glory. This means that God has a positive relationship with the state, not just one of judgment. Yet, state and church alike can be made into idols by sinful human hearts. “[Barth] doesn’t want to divinize the state, [and] he doesn’t want to demonize the state,” Bender said.

Karl Barth. Photo from Wikimedia Commons.

Thus, when it comes to Christian involvement in government, Barth proceeded with care. Bender said that a relational understanding of Christ, church, and state “means that Christians can never be entirely reconciled to everything in the state, but it also cannot be entirely oppositional between them and the state.”

Barth further warned against conflating theology with a particular political ideology. Barth was dismayed to see his teachers and peers rally behind national identity rather than the Gospel during World War II. And, when controversy later arose between countries on either side of the Iron Curtain, Barth urged unity around the supremacy of the Gospel.

As Bender elaborated, Barth opposed the baptism of any specific political order. No program should be deemed uncontestably “Christian” or placed above criticism. “There has to be a transcendence to the gospel such that it stands over any politics of any side and gives the ability to judge it,” Bender said.

“There has to be a transcendence to the gospel such that it stands over any politics of any side and gives the ability to judge it.”

Paul Taussig, a freshman from Mokena, Illinois, appreciated that the panel discussion brought together different viewpoints on Barth’s work. “We’re all dealing with Barth, but you can read Barth in different ways, apply him in different ways. … They all approach him a little differently, but the message can still be applied,” Taussig said.

Taussig said the panel highlighted the important and distinct roles of church and state. Barth’s work centered the church’s duty to engage with the state wisely, which means picking its battles rather than devolving into white noise, Taussig reflected. The Institute for Faith and Learning hosts events like the “Barth, Church, and State” panel regularly, which are usually open to undergraduates. More information can be found on the Institute for Faith and Learning’s website.

item.title: Why Is There Evil? Ratio Christi’s Waco Apologetics Conference Defeats the Problem of Evil
item.description:
Why does an all-good and all-powerful God allow evil to exist? On Saturday, February 21st, the Waco Apologetics Conference addressed one of the most pressing objections against Christianity: the problem of evil. Ratio Christi at Baylor, a Christian apologetics student organization, partnered with Columbus Avenue Baptist Church to host the conference, which was titled, “Defeating the Problem of Evil.” The conference’s keynote speaker, Scott Christensen, an associate pastor at Kerrville Bible Church, presented on free will and the greater-glory theodicy.

In his presentation, Christensen argued that one of the most popular responses to the problem of evil falls short. For context, the problem of evil argues that the existence of evil disproves or renders unlikely the existence of an all-good and all-powerful God. After all, if God really is all-powerful and all-good, why does He allow evil and suffering to persist? One popular response to that question is known as the free will defense. This counterargument posits that God has good reasons for allowing humans to have free will, but also that free will brings with it the possibility of evil. The free will defense usually requires a definition of free will known as libertarian free will. According to Christensen, libertarian free will operates under the assumptions that our choices must be autonomous to be free and that we have to be able to make an alternative choice under the same set of circumstances. Christensen denied this understanding of freedom, saying it undermines what the Bible says about God’s sovereignty, total depravity, God’s character, and divine foreknowledge.

As an alternative, Christensen turned to compatibilist free will. Christensen defined compatibilism as the idea that there is a dual explanation for every human choice. He said that, ultimately, God determines our choices. He is the primary or formal cause, and He is the remote cause of our actions. However, Christensen also said that our moral responsibility is tied to the intentions of our hearts, and that we are the immediate causes of our actions. Simultaneous with God’s ordering of our actions, we cause our choices. Christensen clarified that God never coerces anyone to act against their will, but that there are simply two explanations for our actions. To defend this idea, Christensen used the biblical story of Joseph, the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart, Acts 2 and 4, and Romans 1.

Christensen concluded the conference with a discussion of the greater-glory theodicy, which showed how God’s goodness can coexist with evil and suffering. An example he gave for how this works is our redemption in Christ. He used this analogy: the redemption of the world is shaped like a “J,” not a “U.” The story of the world and humanity does not start at one point, stoop down into fallenness, and become redeemed simply to end up back where it started. Rather, we are redeemed to an even greater state than humanity was in the first place. Christensen further explained that Jesus’ redemptive work on the cross is truly what magnifies God’s glory the most—that by defeating death and sin, redeeming us and saving us, God is most glorified. For that to be necessary and even possible, however, the world must be fallen, sinful, and in need of a redeemer.

“The redemption of the world is shaped like a “J,” not a “U.” … We are redeemed to an even greater state than humanity was in the first place.”

Christensen’s God-centered explanation for evil and suffering emphasizes our need to know that we are not the center of the universe. God created everything and works everything out for his greater glory. However, this does not leave us on the sidelines—rather, what most magnifies God is also what gives believers the most satisfaction, joy, and redemption. What most glorifies God is also what brings us the most good, for it glorifies God to bring his followers good and to show His love to them.

Samantha Hockaday, a Baylor seminary student from Sacramento, California, commented on the event, saying, “I enjoy getting to talk about the problem of evil… It brings a lot of hope.” She thought that Christensen’s presentation especially made clear “free will and individual agency and how we are to interpret sin after the fall.” Throughout the conference, Hockaday was reminded of how “God’s justice and God’s provision will always prevail, and that we can always have faith that he will make all things right in the end.” This is a great summary of what “Defeating the Problem of Evil” was all about. Apologetics serves as a great way to remind ourselves of God’s work and promises in our lives, and it helps both believers and nonbelievers alike to make sense of the broken world around them.

The conference also included a student symposium, in which current students with Ratio Christi presented on topics of their own. Zach Aston, a Baylor freshman from Boerne, Texas, presented his very own theodicy, integrating an explanation for why evil exists in the world with how Christ defeated evil’s power on the cross. Joshua Schultz, a Baylor senior from Fort Worth, discussed the difference between theodicies and defenses and examined Van Inwagen’s free will defense as a solution to the problem of evil.

Scott Christensen delivered the conference’s keynote presentation. Photo by Caitlyn Beebe.

Ganesh Venkataramanan, a 52-year-old resident of Katy, Texas, drove up to Waco just for the conference. Venkataramanan noted that his favorite aspect of the conference was the student symposium. Each student’s “depth of knowledge on deep questions” encouraged and amazed him. He commented that “I think there’s a lot of people who have a deep desire for something authentic, especially students,” and he thought that Ratio Christi’s conference succeeded in fulfilling some of that desire for depth.

The conference also explored adjacent topics through breakout sessions covering topics like divine authorship and the problem of evil, the necessity of the Trinity for the problem of evil, original sin as the roots of evil, and difficult passages in the Bible pertaining to evil. Breakout speakers included Houston Christian University apologetics chair Austin Freeman, Ratio Christi International Director Bill Scott, Baylor graduate accounting student Saul Winebrenner, Reasoning Through the Bible podcast host Glenn Smith, and more.

Ratio Christi is an apologetics organization on campus which helps students to answer the question, “Why do you believe?” Every week, Ratio Christi at Baylor hosts on-campus lectures, small-group discussions, and tabling events. Students may also enroll in Ratio Christi’s chapel section to receive chapel credit for participating.

item.title: Is D.C. Intern Culture Really as Cutthroat as You Think?
item.description:
Impersonal, cutthroat, and full of egos. That’s the reputation most people associate with the workplace culture in Washington, D.C. When it comes to internships, this reputation increases tenfold because every young intern is trying to find a way to break into the tough, network dependent world of Washington. However, this reputation is not necessarily reflected in reality. While it depends on the office, generally the internship culture is much friendlier and more encouraging than one might expect.

Internship opportunities abound in Washington, and they aren’t just limited to government. While many students in the Baylor in Washington program work on Capitol Hill—ten out of the 18 students participating this semester are—plenty of students work elsewhere, in places such as think tanks and nonprofits. Interning on Capitol Hill often has the worst reputation when it comes to intern culture, as all the interns are vying for a permanent job offer on the Hill. However, as interviews with Baylor students currently working on the Hill demonstrate, the intern culture really depends on the office.

One student, Liv Tantalo, a junior from Little Elm, Texas, who works for a Senator, stated, “There are a couple [interns] that are very driven in their work, and… they are only focusing on work during this time.” She explained that some interns avoid talking about their personal life, which can make it difficult to have close relationships and can contribute to the more intense culture that most think of when they think about D.C. She said that this stays true the higher up you get within the office. “Once you start kind of getting up to the Chief of Staff and those areas, it’s definitely very ‘we are here to work and not [to have a] personal relationship,’” Tantalo said.

Overall, she described her office culture as “a very driven and passionate environment” and added, “They can be very intense when it comes to getting the work done the way they would like it done.”

However, this does not reflect all of the Hill office experiences. Jacob Jones, a junior from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is another student in the Baylor in Washington cohort who works in the House of Representatives. Jones described his office as laidback. He said when it comes to the relationship between staff and interns, “In the personal office, it’s like [there’s] no barrier—everybody’s like really good friends.” When it comes to the dynamic between interns, Jones said that they also were all “really good friends.”

A hallway inside a U.S. congressional office building. Photo by Stella Tognocchi

Arianna Latterel, a sophomore from Plymouth, Minnesota, and a Baylor in Washington student working for a nonprofit, has also had a positive experience with her internship. “On an average day I do my own research, depending on what research project I’ve been put on. I handle a lot of spreadsheets, a lot of point of contact lists, as well as preparing for school tours and events,” Latterel said. She described her office as “dynamic because everyone is always helping each other out.”

In contrast with Tantalo and Jones, who work with at least five other interns, Latterel works with only one other intern. When asked about that dynamic, she said, “It’s really good, we help each other out a lot, we give each other feedback, and we cheer each other on. We have different departments we work underneath so we get to support each other without having competition within.” She also added that, “Everyone is there to help you learn and they want to give you as many opportunities as you can.”

In the end, despite its reputation, interning in D.C. is not as cutthroat as people may think. Generally, the environment is not as competitive, and interns are made to feel like part of the team rather than like people just there to perform grunt work. Every office is different, and some offices can be more impersonal than others, but most interns feel they are given the opportunity to grow and learn without having to undermine their fellow interns.

item.title: A Trap in Tehran: Why the War in Iran Might Be a Bad Idea
item.description:
It’s easy to get caught up in the excitement about the war in Iran. The Iranian government is a brutal theocratic regime hellbent on fighting American interests and allies in the region. It’s hard to find anything bad happening in the Middle East which isn’t covered in Iranian fingerprints. They finance terrorists across the region. They bolster the Russian war machine and provide energy to our enemies in Beijing. The possibility of eliminating this regime and writing a new fate for the Iranian people should ignite passions in all freedom-loving people. Optimism becomes even easier when admiring the capabilities and effectiveness of the US military, which time and time again proves itself to be in a league of its own.

Despite these feelings, I become increasingly pessimistic the more I think about the war and its potential outcomes. Prior to Operation Epic Fury, the Trump Administration’s uses of force in Iran and Venezuela were successful because they were limited missions with clearly defined objectives and strategy. This war, however, is different. I believe that while it may be justified, it is not wise or prudent. It is built on a plethora of bad assumptions, and I have doubts about the operation’s chance at success and how it fits into the larger strategy of US foreign policy.

The Folly of Air Superiority

Air power alone is not enough to win this war. Since the end of the Second World War, the US has often overrelied on air power to prompt the collapse of adversarial regimes, and time and time again this approach fails. War is not simply about winning every battle, or causing more death and destruction than the other guy. War is about accomplishing your objectives, and if the objective of this war is a decisive victory and collapse of the Iranian regime, history proves this approach to be unwise.

War is not simply about winning every battle, or causing more death and destruction than the other guy. War is about accomplishing your objectives, and if the objective of this war is a decisive victory and collapse of the Iranian regime, history proves this approach to be unwise.

The US believed technological superiority and control of the skies would guarantee victory in Vietnam. It did not. In 1999, the US believed that overwhelming air power against the Serbs would collapse the rule of Milosevic and keep him out of Kosovo. It did not (further threats of a NATO ground invasion and lack of Russian support did). Without the use of boots on the ground, achieving enough control to collapse a regime like the one we are fighting in Iran is highly unlikely.

The AHS panel on the war in Iran.

“Air power is best used at an operational level,” said Clay Parham, a PhD student in political science here at Baylor. “The assumption behind [strategic] air power, which is that you can use destruction to gain domestic support without other elements of control, I think is where faith in air power as the only tool falls apart.” If the US continues on its current trajectory of only relying on the skies to collapse this regime, without showing the Iranian people an alternative, there will be no chance at sparking a revolution or diminishing the control of the current government.

The Munitions Problem

One common concern about the war is the possibility of depleting our military’s stockpiles of munitions. These concerns are valid. To this point, advanced air defense systems and cruise missiles, namely tomahawks and interceptor missiles, have been the backbone of the war effort. Because of this massive uptick in usage, many in Washington worry about what this means for US deterrence moving forward. Russia might seize this opportunity to ramp up operations in Ukraine knowing the US could be stingier about providing missiles. These stockpiles are also pivotal for defending Taiwan against a Chinese attack, and those in Beijing may see this as their own opportunity to strike.

This administration seems to dismiss this problem. In a post on Truth Social, President Trump stated that US stockpiles are “virtually unlimited.” Whether or not this is truly a representation of the administration’s belief or simply a common display of bravado from the President, this statement should be a cause for concern.

While we will not lose the war in Iran due to lack of munitions, depleting our resources leaves our deterrence weak and our warriors underpowered in future conflict.

Overspending the Will of the American People

My biggest concern about this war is what I believe it will do to the psyche of the American public if it fails. The public’s confidence in regime change through the use of military force has already been shattered by the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. I believe in an active America abroad. The use of force is a tool which we should be willing to use to strengthen our nation’s interests. Therefore, when we enter unwise conflicts, and we fail, this hurts the prospect of its use in the future. If this war fails, will we be willing to defend Taiwan? Probably not.

Operation Epic Fury is surely the boldest foreign policy move the United States has made since the invasion of Iraq. It is bold and well intentioned, but I don’t think we will succeed in creating a freer Iran aligned with the west. For the country’s sake, I hope I’m wrong. For the fate of the Iranian people, I hope I’m wrong. As much as I would love for this war to succeed, I simply doubt that any robust and meaningful change will happen because of it.

The Importance of Civic Discourse

It can be hard in the modern world to feel politically active without relying on social media to voice your concerns and listen to the opinions of your fellow countrymen. The loudest on social media are often the most obnoxious, and it’s difficult to engage in honest and meaningful discourse when this is the only medium you have to interact. To combat this problem, the Alexander Hamilton Society’s chapter at Baylor hosted a discussion event on March 4th to provide an opportunity for students to learn, listen, and discuss this war and its ramifications with their peers.

Students attend the AHS panel on the Iran war.

Events like these are a breath of fresh air for those wanting to talk politics without the noise of social media. “The Iran panel was a great opportunity for me to dive deeper into a significant world event I had previously only encountered on the news and social media,” said Graham Icasiano, an Edmonds, Washington, sophomore who attended the event. “It was especially helpful to hear different perspectives on the conflict and its global impact. The event equipped me to really think deeply.”

item.title: Echoes of Rome in Armstrong Browning: Why We Perform Plautus in a Dead Language – The Standard
item.description:
On January 29th and 30th, the walls of Armstrong Browning Library resounded with the original Latin text of a second-century BC Roman comedy. The Baylor Classics Department, in collaboration with Baylor’s chapter of Eta Sigma Phi, performed Plautus’ Casina as a part of their yearly tradition of performing Greek and Roman plays in their original languages.

Casina tells the story of Lysidamus, an old man desperately in love with a young slave girl, to the consternation of his wife, Cleostrata. Their opposing plots to marry Casina to their favored slaves involve hilarious hijinks that culminate in a ridiculous wedding. Cleostrata dresses up her male slave as Casina and sends him to the wedding as the bride; let us say that Lysidamus and his slave Olympio exit the play without much dignity left.

The staging of such a show presents inherent difficulties. The Classics Department chose to perform in a language that almost no one speaks, leaving the audience only with visual clues. The plots and themes of Roman comedy are also somewhat uncomfortably situated on a Christian campus. Unlike last year’s Antigone, which portrays the triumph of devotion against corruption, Casina puts to the stage lecherous old men, wedding nights gone wrong, and characters whose passions always trump their morals. In other words, the project might initially seem a complete fool’s errand.

I have been involved with these shows every year, from timidly working the teleprompter for Cyclops to starring as Antigone and helping to direct Casina. These shows, and the people who make them happen, have been one of the brightest highlights of my undergraduate life.

Samantha Wren, who played Cleostrata in Casina, told me, “This is what I look forward to most out of spring semester.” In fact, she started her Classics minor because she was enthralled by Cyclops. “Performing a really old play in a dead language just feels really special,” she said. It’s not just from the students’ side, either. Dr. Jacqueline Jones, a co-director of the play, said, “[Directing] brought me so much more joy than I was expecting. It’s been absolutely delightful to work with all of the students.” An experience so unique and singular must bind people together.

One motivation of our forays into theatre is undergraduate interest. Dr. David J. White, another co-director of Casina, said, “I’m always astonished and gratified by the enthusiasm of the students for doing this.” We always throw the show together in one and a half weeks, which is an incomprehensible miracle to me. Within one week, we go from tripping over unfamiliar words to delivering dramatic monologues. And somehow, in the middle of all that hard work, we have time to laugh until we cry, design and create a set, and stay on top of our courseloads. “The secret,” Dr. White said, “is getting the students invested, so that it’s their play and not my play that they’re doing.” We receive no course credit for our endeavors; we do it only out of passion for the subject, and that passion is palpable. Not such a fool’s errand, then, after all.

For students who have been reading and translating these plays, performance is a chance to interact with the material in the way it was meant to be experienced.

The benefits go beyond the blessing of community; Dr. White described the play as a “pedagogical exercise.” For students who have been reading and translating these plays, performance is a chance to interact with the material in the way it was meant to be experienced. Isaac Bostic, who played Lysidamus, explained, “This is the closest I feel to living in that time. You’re talking like real people would have talked.” We students get to live in ancient Greece and Rome for a moment and feel a bit of what they might have felt. And on a more practical note, memorizing texts has been shown to be beneficial in language learning .

To translate a work is to change it fundamentally. And so, this one time a year, we don’t.

There’s also philological backing for keeping the original text. Translating comedy is notoriously difficult, and Plautus’ work is no exception. So much of comedy relies on wordplay, something nearly impossible in translation and usually inelegant when achieved. The original work and each translation of it are, simply put, different works of art. The phrasing, the word choice, and even the music of the words themselves are all intentional choices on the part of the artist. To translate a work is to change it fundamentally. And so, this one time a year, we don’t.

But why should anyone care to see a play they cannot understand? If we actors do our job, the audience should understand more than they expect. Wren described to me how her mother is still able to pick up the general ideas and emotions at play, and my own family has a similar experience. Dr. Jones noted, “Many of my students…were still able to follow a lot of the action just because it was so well acted.” Like an opera, it is a lesson in the tradition of storytelling. Dr. Jones explained it as a multicultural experience, saying that we all “need to be able to experience things in cultures very different from our own.” That is what these plays offer us: the ability to compare our culture to another, to recognize commonalities and differences. And most of the time, what we discover are not differences, but rather what Bostic called “the similarities in the human experience, the understanding of love and misery.” These plays offer a supreme example of stepping into another culture, since we must bridge 2,000 years of separation. It is a difficult but endlessly rewarding exercise.

Human nature is deeply troubled, twisted, and ugly sometimes. The comedic aspects of it help us understand that better.

If we care about the continuity of the human experience, we also should give a nod to the continuity of comedy. Both Wren and Dr. White mentioned that Roman comedies show us the same kind of plot we would see in a modern sitcom. The same stock characters appear, the same misunderstandings and misdirection. “A lot of the humor that we get in Plautus has directly given us a lot of our conventions of modern comedy,” Dr. Jones said. And modern comedy bases much its humor in the ridiculous aspects of humans themselves. “It’s not terribly deep,” said Dr. White, “but it says a lot about human nature.” And human nature is deeply troubled, twisted, and ugly sometimes. The comedic aspects of it help us understand that better.

This is our justification for performing somewhat raunchy and problematic comedy on a Christian campus. The Roman world was a violent world. Slavery was normal, sexual violence was common, and the hierarchy of society was unjust. Casina does not shy away from these facts. “We shouldn’t pretend like these things never happened,” Wren stated. Bostic echoed her words: “Comedy points out to us problems and points out to us why we shouldn’t cause them.” We watch comedy, not just to laugh, but also to evaluate the actions of the characters. And in Casina, we see a subversion of the problematic elements of Roman culture, for the lecherous old man does not carry the day.

For Christians, there is an added level of importance to entering the world of Rome: Jesus was born under Roman rule.

Finally, for Christians, there is an added level of importance to entering the world of Rome: Jesus was born under Roman rule. Dr. White spoke about how this world of slavery and violence was the world the early Christians were dealing with. “What was it like for the early Christian church?” he asked. “What were the cultural assumptions that they had to interact with?” The plays that we put on answer those questions. They give us a window into the ideas that the early church had to dismantle in order to preach the Gospel. And they give us a window into how vastly the Gospel has changed the world in the intervening millennia.

As she was praying before our final performance of Casina, my dear friend and co-actor Rachel Jageman laughingly said, “Lord, may even this honor you.” I, for one, believe that prayer was answered in spades.

item.title: Become Not a Bot: Advice From Baylor Professors and a Drunk Russian on Maintaining Your Humanity
item.description:
AI is amazing at sounding right. It can give you a polished, logical answer to nearly anything you might ask, something I doubt any of your classmates (or students) can do. So why not use it to bring more coherence into the classroom? Is there really any reason to stumble through a question that should be obvious to a class?

To be good classmates, we ought to both be able to love our classmates for their nonsense and to be confident enough to share potential nonsense. Baylor Great Texts professor Dr. Kirsten Welch, an upcoming presenter at Baylor’s Symposium on AI, faith, and the human person, defended the classroom condition without AI: “When we insulate ourselves from that pain of making mistakes and giving the wrong answer, we are depriving ourselves of a tremendous opportunity to form ourselves into better human beings.”

As I explored this issue of human value and AI with Baylor professors and students, I found a unique theme running through our conversations—the value of idiosyncrasy. Each professor I interviewed affirmed what Zach Miyazaki, a junior who will be presenting at the AI and Faith Symposium elucidates: “Christianity has the resources to say that human work is valuable insofar as it’s an expression of that God-given gift of creativity and of imagination.” This idiosyncratic creativity, this eminently human nonsense, is exactly what AI is not capable of and what we ought to be fostering in the classroom, over and above recitation of information.

The point here is not to elevate senseless babble. That is to say that, when someone has reasoned their way to an answer that turns out to be nonsense, we ought to tolerate it—insofar as it’s a contribution to the class discussion from a real, singular, human. Just as Plato’s Republic would be less impactful without the indifference of Cephalus or wrath of Thrasymachus, so too would classmates lose an opportunity for growth without that one kid.

When AI is brought into a classroom, not only could it hurt critical thinking (as this study and this study suggest), but it could create a profoundly boring classroom environment.

A few weeks ago, one of my quietest classmates gave a well-informed answer to my instructor’s question, which pleasantly surprised me. Later, I noticed ChatGPT on his screen. While my classmate’s use of AI may have added helpful information to our class discussion, he also flattened it and cut it short.

Baylor’s Associate Director for the Academy for Teaching and Learning, Dr. Christopher Richmann, takes the implications of these incidents seriously. Many people’s idea of an “AI apocalypse” looks something like The Matrix or The Terminator. But for Dr. Richmann, “the most likely dystopian or apocalyptic future as a result of AI” might be that “more and more people become thoroughly uninteresting… because they’re not engaging in the same kind of thinking and friction and pushback that you get from real human interaction.”

For advice on how to avert this apocalypse of boredom, there is nowhere better to turn than the musings of a drunk Russian college dropout. In Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment, Razumhikin, a well-meaning friend of the main character, delivers a poignant speech on the value of “nonsense” in the midst of his intoxication:

“Not one single truth has ever been arrived at without people first having talked a dozen reams of nonsense, even ten dozen reams of it, and that’s an honourable thing in its own way; … Talk nonsense to me, by all means, but do it with your own brain, and I shall love you for it. To talk nonsense in one’s own way is almost better than to talk a truth that’s someone else’s; in the first instance you behave like a human being, while in the second you are merely being a parrot!”

A classroom full of humans may not be as informed and intelligent as one full of chatbots. We will talk more nonsense, and that’s perfectly alright. If we are to believe Razumhikin, it’s good and even worthy of love.

Incentivising AI use over potential nonsense would create an artificially frictionless environment, hostile to the development of truth and to our nature. AI will affirm you, even when you’re clearly in the wrong. If we’re not careful, we may come to expect this extreme lack of friction in the people around us.

Miyazaki’s upcoming talk at the AI and Faith Symposium centers on this idea of supplanting our conception of the real with the artificial. For example, a serendipitous moment is “just like a movie” and a sunset is “as beautiful as a painting.” Early twentieth-century French author Georges Bernanos develops this concept as applied to emerging tech:

“The danger is not in the multiplication of machines, but in the ever-increasing number of men accustomed from their childhood to desire only what machines can give.”

If generative AI supplants our idea of what a classmate or friend ought to be, nonsense and friction may become intolerable.

How should higher-ed then live? Should we become Luddites advocating for the abolition of AI (and smartphones while we’re at it)?

No, at least not in every sphere of life and education. The relative value of AI compared to human nonsense is very different in Business and Biology compared to Great Texts and Philosophy. Likely in recognition of this, Baylor has not adopted any blanket policies on AI. In fact, Baylor leaves AI policy completely up to the instructor, although they do provide guidelines and example syllabi clauses.

In November of last year, the Academy of Teaching and Learning brought on Dr. Megan Alstot as a post-doc in AI and emerging technologies to help guide Baylor’s approach to AI. She recommends that responsible AI users keep in mind the “three Cs”: cognition, creativity, and connection. Be aware of how new technology may be affecting the way in which you think, your capacity to create, and how you relate to other people.

While Dr. Alstot advises caution when it comes to the “three C’s,” she is a regular user of AI and is “equal parts enthusiast and skeptic.” She emphasizes that “we need to be learning how to work with it and thinking about ethically what is appropriate.” We shouldn’t run for the hills, but we also shouldn’t assume that generative AI is perfectly compatible with Baylor’s educational values.

Over the next three years, whenever I’m struggling to navigate my education in the midst of chatbots, I will go back to Razhumikhin. I will engage with my idiosyncratic classmates, strive to love them for their reams of nonsense, and be brave enough to spew some of my own. I ask my professors to leave space for this honorable pursuit, and for them to ask more of me than a machine could give. In everything I do in and outside the classroom, I will strive to become not a bot.

item.title: Lent: Reframing the Easter Feast
item.description:
The season of Easter is fast approaching and with it the palpable excitement of the Christian community. Oh wait—I forgot. We don’t anticipate Easter months ahead of time like we do Christmas. No one is counting the days until it is permissible to sing “Christ Arose!”—and certainly not like how we furtively hum Nat King Cole in October. For those who have grown up in a Christian home, the Church calendar’s story of Easter is old news. It seems everything has already been said: Christ was crucified, died, and then rose again on the third day. Each year rolls out nothing new but the same overabundance of chocolate and a headache the next day. Most of us probably have a vague sense that this apathy is dangerous, knowing that Easter is the basis for the hope of Christians. But we don’t know quite what to do. As a tonic to this passivity, I suggest the season of Lent.

Lent is about recognizing what our sin has done to us

Lent, a long-standing tradition of the Church, is mentioned at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and even earlier, as pointed out by Dr. Paul Gutacker, Executive Director of Brazos Fellows. “One way to think about where it came from,” he said, “and really the meaning it has carried down through the centuries is that it is a time for us to seek to turn back to the Lord.” He went on to expand on the purpose of the season: “Lent is about recognizing what our sin has done to us…as we get close to Christ’s Passion and Crucifixion and Resurrection, his triumph over death and satan, his great work in undoing our sin, it’s an appropriate time to pay more attention to that, to really look hard at the way in which we are enslaved to sin, subject to death.” As Dr. Gutacker put it, Lent is a time to realize the extent of sin’s damage in our lives, and the control it has that leads to both spiritual and physical death. Lent is a forty-day period of fasting that prepares us for the magnificent fifty-day feast of Easter. We examine ourselves and repent so that we can properly celebrate the death and resurrection of the Savior who has delivered us from sin.

Giotto di Bondone, Lamentation (The Mourning of Christ), c. 1304–1306, fresco

The failure to recognize Lent doesn’t diminish Easter as much as it transforms Easter. Easter becomes a different kind of holiday when it just happens and you haven’t been preparing for it

Dr. Scott Moore, Associate Professor of Philosophy and Great Texts, comes from the Baptist tradition. He also stressed the importance of Lent, lamenting the loss which he believes his tradition experiences from neglecting the season. In remarking on how the practice of Lent affects Easter, he said, “The failure to recognize Lent doesn’t diminish Easter as much as it transforms Easter. Easter becomes a different kind of holiday when it just happens and you haven’t been preparing for it, you haven’t been thinking about it, you haven’t been looking forward to it. I think that’s where the danger of ignoring Lent is… If I take forty days to get ready for it, I’m going to think about it differently.”

But what does this look like? A vague thought of, “Oh, I suppose I’ll think about my sin every so often for the next forty days,” will not take us very far. Along with our firm resolutions to be released from the tyranny of our phones and stop staying up late enough to be singing “Good Morning, Good Morning” with Gene Kelly, this one too will be passionate and short-lived. We make excuses for this, saying “there’s too much going on to add another task.” But the beauty of Lent is that it does just the opposite.

Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, The Entombment of Christ, c. 1603–1604, oil on canvas

Dr. Gutacker explained that the Anglican practice of Lent is encapsulated in three things: Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving (Charity).

Yes, I know that that looks like adding three things. But hear me out. The second element, fasting, is the key. Fasting is not limited to giving up food (which some may not be able to do for health reasons) but includes giving up something in order to spend that time in prayer and almsgiving. This could mean food, but it could also mean social media.

As Dr. Moore said, “The point of giving up something of course is to focus your mind on the preparation for the great feast that is Easter. We only give up something, not because it’s intrinsically valuable to give something up, but as a way of focusing our attention. When I’m inclined to want to look at Instagram or eat the piece of chocolate or whatever it might be, that becomes a very easy way for me to refocus my mind.” In other words, the fasting of Lent is not mere privation. It is giving up one thing for the sake of something better.

We don’t only fast for our own well-being, though. Dr. Gutacker notes the connection between fasting and almsgiving when he said, “Part of the point of fasting is going without what you need for your own good, for your own healing, for your own growth, but also for the sake of others.”

For most of us, however, our minds are not always very pleasant places. “Look, I already know how broken I am,” many of us might say, “My mistakes are always before my eyes, I know I’m not enough and never can be. And you want me to devote forty days to pondering the depths of my sin and depravity?” Or perhaps, “It’s really better not to go there—I haven’t really thought about it deeply and once I start, it will only end in despair.” As someone who has struggled with these questions, I’d like to offer a possible solution: community.

Dr. Gutacker said, “You don’t do it alone. There is a time and place for prayerful self-examination, but I think you always want to avail yourself of what God gives us to help us do that well.” In other words, the practice of Lent is not a solitary endeavor. Dr. Gutacker explained that we desperately need our priests, spiritual mentors, and fellow believers to help us through Lent:

Rembrandt van Rijn, The Return of the Prodigal Son, c. 1668–1669, oil on canvas

We have to get out of our own heads and that’s why God gives us ministers

“We probably let ourselves off the hook about things that are much more insidious. And so I think we have to get out of our own heads and that’s why God gives us ministers. So I would encourage people during Lent that it is a very good time to prepare for and make a confession to a priest. And this is not about earning forgiveness that you can’t get otherwise, it’s about healing.”

If Lent is new to you, there are practices you can begin to incorporate into your life. Fasting can include not only food but social media or any habit which might be an undue source of distraction. For those looking for a devotional, Christopher Richmann’s Stretched: A Study for Lent and the Entire Christian Life is a great place to start. For any who love art, I have included some of my personal favorite works to contemplate during Lent: Rembrandt’s The Return of the Prodigal Son, Caravaggio’s The Entombment of Christ, Giotto’s Lamentation, and the Crucifixion from the Isenheim Altarpiece.

item.title: More Than a March: Waco’s MLK Peace March Answers Dr. King’s Call to Action
item.description:
On Monday, Jan. 19, 2026, more than two hundred Waco residents gathered to honor the legacy of Martin Luther King Jr. The MLK Peace March fostered unity through reflection from prominent community leaders, worship, and a shared responsibility to act.

Over the past 27 years, the march has become a longstanding tradition sponsored by the City of Waco, TFNB, Caritas, NeighborWorks, and more.

The event begins with participants marching across the Waco Suspension Bridge while singing African American spirituals, then becomes a town hall where each organization is recognized and delivers a call to action. The event concludes with a gospel extravaganza, which was a celebratory program pulling from the Black Church tradition of gospel music and praise dance to celebrate the King’s work. The organizations present at this year’s March included the Masonic Lodge, the Eastern Stars, the Community Race Relations Coalition (CRRC), the Nation Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), and all Greek organizations of the Divine Nine National Pan-Hellenic Council.

The first speaker, Waco NAACP president Peaches Henry, set the tone with a fiery speech. “If we allow our history to be whitewashed or erased, America will never confront its mistakes and will always be reaching back for a past filled with inequality, unfairness, and violence. … So, we must stand and fight for the weakest among us. We must fight,” Henry said.

Photo by Jesenya Rose Hernandez Wrightsil

The rest of the speakers shared similar sentiments, calling for voter participation, immigrants’ rights, increased diversity, and, most importantly, a call to action rather than stagnation. But the most repeated message was one of unity and love.

Many of the speakers recognized that our country faces bittersweet times marked by both sorrow and unity. Amid divisive policies, growing uncertainty within the Department of Education, and intensified ICE enforcement, Americans find themselves drawn together not by celebration, but by shared concern and grief. The once-hopeful America our grandparents knew seems to have become increasingly distant. Yet in these moments, we are reminded that there is unity in our struggle, and hope for the future. Olga Rogers, one of the first Black female graduates from Baylor and president of the Alpha Rho Sigma Chapter of Sigma Gamma Rho Sorority, Inc., said, “In a world filled with turmoil, some things still transcend our differences, and one of those is the dream.” So, we must work to keep the dream alive.

In these moments, we are reminded that there is unity in our struggle, and hope for the future.

Truett Seminary student and member of Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc., Kendall Petteway reminded us that a hopeful future does not arrive on its own—it requires us. “The present is today. The past has happened; and the future needs us, so it starts with you,” Petteway said.

“If you ask a room full of people, ‘Who here thinks the world needs to be changed?’ every hand will go up. But if I asked who needs to do the changing, half the hands would go down. … Yet you need to ask yourself, ‘What changes do I need to make? Who do I need to love better? And how can I be a better advocate for my community?’” Petteway said.

The MLK Peace March’s keynote speaker and Pleasant Olive Missionary Baptist Church pastor E. Shaun Williams put it perfectly:

“Dr. King called communities to rise above bitterness and become bearers of light in dark places. Honoring Dr. King’s legacy means more than just remembering his words—it means living them out, choosing love over hate, service over selfishness, and hope over despair.”

The MLK Peace March concluded with a gospel extravaganza, which was a joyous way for people of all ages to truly celebrate Martin Luther King Jr.

Photo by Jesenya Rose Hernandez Wrightsil

Several students from Baylor University attended the MLK Peace March. Sethlyn Pappoe, a Prosper junior and member of the Nu Iota chapter of Zeta Phi Beta Sorority, Inc., said “the event is a great way to unify the community.”

Petteway said, “The ability to march with Blacks, Whites, and Hispanics in 2026 is an important thing that should happen more often.”

All in all, what started as an idea between a few women dedicated to the principles of Zeta Phi Beta Sorority, Inc.’s motto of being a “community conscious action-oriented organization,” grew into an over two-decade-long tradition, where people of all cultures and beliefs can unite and keep Dr. King’s dream alive and to change our world for the better. How will you contribute to the change? Will you become bearers of light? Or be so disenchanted that you let the dream die?

Keep the dream alive, I say. Work to keep the dream alive.

item.title: “Why Are We Here?” Jennifer Frey on the University’s Search for Purpose
item.description:
Will this be on the exam? How will I use this in real life? Why am I even here?

These are the perennial questions of the college student, especially those sitting in the pesky core curriculum classes like Christian Heritage or U.S. Constitution, two required courses in Baylor’s College of Arts & Sciences.

Dr. Jennifer Frey, a professor of philosophy at the University of Tulsa, addressed these exact questions when she delivered the annual Drumwright Family Lecture on Wednesday Nov 11, aptly titled: “Why Are We Here? A Liberal Arts Education and the Pursuit of Wisdom.”

Frey began with the assertion that we are at college, first and foremost, to pursue wisdom. To buttress her bold claim, she juxtaposed two competing visions of the university: Max Weber’s research ideal and John Henry Newman’s liberal arts college.

Jennifer Frey

Beginning with Weber, the twentieth century German sociologist, Frey connected his idea of the “knowledge worker” to the mission of the modern university: “Weber gave an account of scholarship as mere expertise, undertaken with no ultimate horizon of meaning, purpose, or goal.” For Weber, the work of scholarship is specialization in a narrow and exclusive mode, the foundation for the knowledge-production ethos of research institutions. Today, similar views are held by prominent thinkers like Stanley Fish, who argues that the professor’s role is merely to impart the technical skills of an intellectual trade.

This is precisely why questions of meaning and value in the modern university go entirely unasked. Higher education becomes a soulless machine. For an alternative to this clinal approach to education, Frey directed our attention to US history.

Frey explained that higher education in the United States began with small, liberal arts colleges run by clergy and grounded in classical curriculum. (Harvard was one such institution.) The university was not a factory churning out the product of “knowledge-workers,” but a garden for the nurturing of good human beings and citizens: “The moral formation of these pupils was paramount to the entire enterprise.”

This all changed when the model of the German research university hopped the Atlantic: “The telos of the university was transformed, it was now to create new knowledge, rather than to pass on received wisdom or the cultivation of personal morals.”

The renowned theologian and Catholic Saint John Henry Newman shared the educational principles underlying America’s first colleges, Frey argued. “Newman is most concerned that the university be a place for the whole of liberal knowledge to be presented and handed on. This knowledge must form a whole or be comprehended as a unity.”

John Henry Newman

Truth is not simply grasping the facts, but understanding those facts as part of a universal, comprehensive system—a sharp contrast to Weber’s silos of specialization. “All the partners within this ideal university should understand themselves as making a necessary but radically incomplete contribution to the whole of knowledge.”

This “whole of knowledge,” according to Newman and Frey, may also be defined as wisdom: “Newman’s ideal knower is not an expert or a technocrat, but someone who possesses an intellectual virtue of wisdom in his mode of study.” Pursuit of wisdom is a good in itself because it aligns with our nature as beings possessing an intellect. Thus, Frey insisted, “as we acquire this habit of mind in our university study, we are advancing in our own flourishing or perfection as a human person.”

“Newman’s ideal knower is not an expert or a technocrat, but someone who possesses an intellectual virtue of wisdom in his mode of study.” Jennifer Frey

In Newman’s model, university education is training for a life, not just a job. But today, many would like to reduce it to just that. Frey concluded with a call to upraise and support this vision of liberal education, a difficult task that she herself faced as the founder and leader of a Great Books Honors College.

In a guest essay for The New York Times, Frey revealed how her position as inaugural dean at the University of Tulsa’s Honors College was abolished by the administration—not because of decline in student interest or lack of funding for its Great Books enterprise, but because of administrative disfavor.

In an interview with The Standard, Frey criticized the University of Tulsa administration. “It’s clear that [liberal learning] is not valued; I would like them to just admit it—the people making decisions about how to allocate resources.” For Frey, hostile administrators pose the present threat to liberal education. These administrators are withholding the formative education that students need in an age of doomscrolling, A.I., and a “loneliness epidemic.”

Baylor’s current strategic plan, Baylor In Deeds, brings Baylor one step closer to becoming one of the outcome-oriented academies that Frey critiques. In prioritizing research initiatives, is our beloved Baptist R-1 university susceptible to losing its liberal arts origins? Will Baylor’s story be the same as Tulsa’s?

In the past, Baylor has claimed to occupy both realms, insisting that the tension between Weber and Newman is not as rigid as it seems. While emphasizing impactful research, Baylor has nonetheless retained its focus on personal formation through the core virtues in the College of Arts & Sciences, and various Honors College programs that engage the Great Texts of the past under the motto “love truth, kindle faith, and cultivate virtue.”

As soon as the university forgets her past and purpose, then our research will be just as directionless as our lives.

If virtue remains at the core of Baylor’s mission, then students, faculty, and administrators will be able to answer the question “why are we here?” But as soon as the university forgets her past and purpose, then our research will be just as directionless as our lives.

This loss will not be abstract. It will be felt by the student entering a required core class already convinced it is useless and leaving with no reason to think otherwise. For her, the question “Why am I even here?” is no longer ironic or rhetorical. It is the most serious question a university can either help her face, or quietly teach her to ignore.

item.title: An Unlikely Flannery Fan: How Did I Get Here?
item.description:
Flannery O’Connor wrote stories about murder, self-blinding, death on the horns of a bull, and worse. The darkness of sin and violence in her works understandably repulses many readers. But her hauntingly powerful portrayal of grace in that context is a beautiful testament to—and encouragement toward—devout faith.

As O’Connor put it, “To the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost blind you draw large and startling figures.”

I was indeed startled when I first read O’Connor at the beginning of high school. I don’t know about you, but confusing violence is not usually my cup of tea. But over the years I went from being an apprehensive bystander to an avid student to now planning a screening of a film about her life (February 12th, 6:30 pm, Draper 152, CAE Film Credit, be there!).

It all began in eighth grade with a prayer that makes me chuckle now:

“Please,” I begged God, “anything but O’Connor.”

My online school was starting a house system, and all the other houses were named after Christian authors I already loved. I could be thrilled with St. Augustine, Jane Austen, and C. S. Lewis. But Flannery O’Connor? I knew basically nothing about this (apparently?) author except that one of our pastors was not sure what to do with her, per the recent sermon anecdote. (“A Good Man Is Hard To Find”: if you know, you know.)

Of course, I was placed in O’Connor House, and I think God knew he was answering my prayer in a better way than I could have imagined.

Three years later, I was a fervent house leader, coordinating spaces for “fellowship and fun” and championing Flannery while at the same time frantically warning my little peacocks (as we called the members of this marvelous O’Connor House) to consult their parents before reading her astonishing work. “O’Connor portrays the radical brokenness of the world,” I would echo my own first house leader, “in order to portray the even more radical grace of God.” Yes, it will shock you. It’s supposed to—not gratuitously, but insofar as “Christ crucified” surprises and befuddles like a “stumbling block,” as Paul would say.

Part of a mosaic from an early Christian church in Syria, Getty Museum

O’Connor perceived the twentieth century’s need to be shocked out of sentimental stupor to remember again and again that Jesus was born into our brokenness for us: the unshiny grime of a stable, of poverty, of oppression, of prostitutes and tax-collectors, of hypocrites and demons, of false witnesses and torture. Her stories are vivid, perplexing, hilarious, terrifying, convicting. She is a jarring, saving reminder to us of the Lord’s steadfast love that pursues his lost sheep even when we turn aside to our own remarkably grotesque ways. I know I have needed that reminder—that revelation of my own sin and need for a grace that all “human nature vigorously resists . . . because grace changes us and the change is painful.” As uncomfortable as it is, it can be healing and good to sit with that.

I’ll leave you with one of my favorite passages from her Prayer Journal that I continue to return to praying myself. I hope you enjoy this taste of Flannery and traipse on over to Draper 152 on February 12th for more.

“Dear God, I cannot love Thee the way I want to. You are the slim crescent of a moon that I see and my self is the earth’s shadow that keeps me from seeing all the moon. The crescent is very beautiful and perhaps that is all one like I am should or could see; but what I am afraid of, dear God, is that my self shadow will grow so large that I block the whole moon, and that I will judge myself by the shadow that is nothing. I do not know you God because I am in the way. Please help me to push myself aside.”

Event Details

Wildcat Film Screening

February 12th, 2026

6:30 pm in Draper 152

CAE Film Credit

item.title: Reason or Dignity? A Refutation of Locke Provides Firmer Footing for Human Equality in the American Founding
item.description:
John Locke and other Enlightenment philosophers often present rationality and autonomy as the basis for human equality. The American Founders used these arguments to justify their revolution. However, American philosopher and law professor Martha Nussbaum argues that this basis is insufficient. Recognizing human dignity as an additional basis for equality would fortify our founding values against tyrannical manipulation.

I read Locke and Nussbaum side by side this month after I attended the American Enterprise Institute Winter Honors Program. The three-day seminar celebrated the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution and recalled the modern influence of the ideas that inspired the Declaration of Independence. The program included a seminar on Locke and his influence, especially that of The Second Treatise of Government.

Locke bases human equality on all being endowed with reason by a Creator. From this premise, he derives natural rights, the consent of the governed, and the social contract. He writes, “Men being…by nature all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent.” According to Locke, equality and rationality allow people to recognize tyrannical governments with “a long train of abuses” against its people and the justification to rebel when legitimate abuse occurs.

I agree with Locke that the possession of reason is a proof for universal human equality. However, basing human equality on an internal characteristic opens the door to reason being redefined such that not all humans are equal. The philosopher Martha Nussbaum finds, “The classical theorists all assumed that their contracting agents were men who were roughly equal in capacity…They thus omitted from the bargaining situation women…children, and elderly people—although the parties might represent their interests.” Something external to humanity must give a source for its equal political value in terms of the social contract in order to account for all humans who are able to consent. As Locke acknowledges a creator, equality can be found in the conferred value humans have because all are made in the image of God.

John Locke

Conferred dignity brings additional grounds for political equality in moral equality, an observation shared by Nussbaum. She finds that Locke’s understanding of the social contract is underdeveloped. If Locke had continued in his line of thinking, he would have arrived at a dignity-based entitlement theory for equality and consent. Additionally, Locke equates moral equality and equal political power. Nussbaum writes, “Whether we should grant that equal powers entail moral equality is profoundly unclear. The right way to ground moral equality almost certainly does not involve reliance on a putative power-equality.”

Rather than rights to equal political power being the basis for moral equality, equal dignity forms the basis for moral equality and the right to political equality. Humans are valuable because they are created by God, which means their moral equality comes from an external source. Because all have equal dignity and value, humans have the claim to political equality and can form a social contract in which they can remove their consent if their dignity-based rights are violated. Dignity thus creates a social contract based on the real moral equality of persons and not just manufactured political equality.

Dignity thus creates a social contract based on the real moral equality of persons and not just manufactured political equality.

Nussbaum provides an additional concern about the disabled and political equality based on reason. She writes, “No social contract doctrine, however, includes people with severe and atypical physical and mental impairments… such people were simply not included in society. They were excluded and stigmatized; there was no political movement to include them.” This is notable not only because the disabled have a role in political society because they are citizens of nations, but also because of the potential manipulation of reason being the basis of equality.

If a person is deemed to be without reason, either because of disability or if one’s views are deemed “unreasonable,” their rights can be unjustly violated.

Suppose a tenant of reason was the belief that what is reasonable is fully determined by the government. If one disagreed with the government, such a citizen could be deemed unreasonable, removed from the social contract, imprisoned, or worse. Because this citizen was removed from the social contract, they would have no ability to resist or escape their situation. After all, such an unreasonable person has no ability to consent in the first place. Without reason, one cannot consent to the social contract and cannot receive the benefits of protection of the government. That protection is even more important to the disabled who can easily be and often are marginalized in political society.

When God made humans in His image, he gave them dignity that provided an external basis for their political equality. This external basis creates a clear and stable foundation because it comes from a Creator rather than a human concept which can be manipulated for tyrannical gain.

item.title: The Bronze Age Collapsed. Does Our World Have To? The McGee Lecture at Baylor
item.description:
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes.

In his lecture titled “1177 BC and After: The Collapse and Survival of Civilizations,” Dr. Eric C. Cline borrowed Mark Twain’s famous phrase, “if history does indeed rhyme, then we are swiftly approaching the end of a rhyming couplet.” And he pointed to the similarities between our modern, globalized world and the world of the Bronze Age—a flourishing network of trade, diplomacy, and culture that essentially collapsed overnight.

“If history does indeed rhyme, then we are swiftly approaching the end of a rhyming couplet.”

Dr. Cline, a world-renowned archaeologist and Professor of Classics and Anthropology at George Washington University, visited Baylor University on Thursday, October 30th to deliver the Department of Religion’s annual McGee Endowed Lecture. Established to honor the legacy of Dr. Daniel McGee, the lecture invites leading scholars from around the country to speak on issues relating to ethics.

The collapse of civilizations at the end of the Late Bronze Age—Dr. Cline’s topic—may at first appear remote from the pressing ethical issues of our time. But the problems that led to the downfall of those ancient nations are strikingly similar to problems we face today: climate change, famine, political unrest.

Dr. Cline began his remarks by painting a picture of the cosmopolitan world-system at the end of the Late Bronze Age (roughly 1500-1200 BC): “[It was] what I would call the globalized Mediterranean…In today’s terms, that’s roughly from Italy on one side, to Iran, Afghanistan on the other, and from Turkey down to Egypt.” This international network was made up of Egyptians, Babylonians, and others. Through this web of trade, King Hammurabi of Babylon could even source a pair of leather sandals from the island of Minos (and return them, as the story goes.)

Map of the late Bronze Age world

But why consider civilizations that seem so distant from us? Cline argued that such global interconnection is rare in human history, and thus the Bronze Age may be closer to us than its 3,200-year distance would suggest.

In a matter of years, it all fell apart. “In about 1200 BC, and in the decades after throughout the 12th century, everything that they had enjoyed just went south. They collapsed. [The system] would have been happily working for 500 years, and suddenly it went away.”

Photo of Cline giving the lecture (with his own books on the screen)

The cause? Drawing on research from his award-winning book 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed, Cline argued that the collapse was a result of a kind of “polycrisis.” While some historians attribute its cause to invasions, famine, or disease, Cline proposes a compound of disastrous factors: “My answer is yes, it’s all of the above…What if you have more than one at once, or you have them in rapid succession? What if you’re suffering from a drought which has weakened the populace? That leads people to invade you, and then you get hit by an earthquake.”

“My question is, are we going to be anti-fragile Phoenicians? Or are we going to be unprepared Mycenaeans?”



But not every civilization crumbled. While some failed to adapt, others appear to have regrouped and transformed. Dr. Cline pointed to the civilizations that adapted as models for us today—if our current crises are similar to those of Bronze Age civilizations, then perhaps the solutions are too: “My question is, are we going to be anti-fragile Phoenicians? Or are we going to be unprepared Mycenaeans?”

Indeed, avoiding the mistakes of the past is one reason to study history in the first place. When I interviewed Dr. Cline, he spoke about the vital importance of understanding history. Cline argued that “if you don’t know your own past and other people’s past, you’re in no position to figure out where we should go.” The past is a treasure trove of resources, and ignoring our ancestors because we assume they were unenlightened is like refusing a priceless gift because we think it is beneath us.

“if you don’t know your own past and other people’s past, you’re in no position to figure out where we should go.”

It can seem pessimistic to imagine that we’re heading toward collapse. But instead of hopelessness, Dr. Cline offered seven practical goals, based on the societies that adapted, to guide us away from disaster. They included crafting multiple contingency plans, preparing for extreme weather, and securing dependable water resources—nothing that hasn’t been thought of before, as Cline pointed out, but concrete objectives for our generation nonetheless.

Photo of the seven societal lessons

But if you have enough people working on enough issues, then you can make a big difference…. It’s the sum of the effort

Abigail Miranda, a freshman Electrical Engineering major from Lufkin, Texas, left Cline’s lecture with a hopeful outlook. When I interviewed her, she shared how she sees her future career as a way to meet these goals, doing her part to work toward a flourishing global society: “In the field of study that I’m in, I’m looking for ways that I can apply my skills. Solar energy is a big interest of mine. I [like to ask] how do famine and the energy crisis relate? How do they play together? Because it is all interconnected, right? It’s a web—not that solving one issue will solve all the issues. But if you have enough people working on enough issues, then you can make a big difference…. It’s the sum of the effort.”

That’s what it’s really about: grasping the interconnectedness of things. How the past is tied to the present, how the Mediterranean Sea is related to Lake Waco, how an aspiring engineer can work to provide sustainable energy for an entire continent. As Wendell Berry once wrote, “History overflows time…. Every shakable thing has got to be shaken. In a sense, nothing that was ever lost has been replaced. In another sense, nothing is ever lost, and we are compacted together forever, even by our failures, our regrets, and our longings.”

If the Bronze Age collapse teaches us anything, it’s that the future depends on ordinary people making thoughtful choices in an interconnected world. As student Abigail Miranda put it, “it’s the sum of the effort.” Her words, along with Berry’s reminder that “we are compacted together forever,” might be the real lesson of 1177 B.C. History may rhyme, but the rhyme is ours to write.

item.title: R.U.R.: What a Baylor Play About Robots Tells Us About Humanity
item.description:
The word “robot” was used publicly for the first time ever on January 25th, 1921 when Czech author Karel Čapek premiered his play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots). Čapek took the word from an old Czech word (rabu) meaning “slave.” On December 7th, 2025 in Baylor’s Mabee theater, Rossum’s Universal Robots took the stage once again.

Although the play was known for its technological imaginativeness, it is more about humans than it is about robots, says Eva Hruska, a Baylor Russian professor who provided the translation of R.U.R. used in Baylor’s production. Hruska described the plot succinctly: “human-made beings, now for the first time ever called ‘robots,’ wipe humanity off the face of the earth, only to be succeeded by Robots-turned-human—the new Adam and Eve… it is not the progress and the humanoid robots themselves that Čapek warns about. It is the surrender of humans to greed, power, and money in the name of progress.”

“it is not the progress and the humanoid robots themselves that Čapek warns about. It is the surrender of humans to greed, power, and money in the name of progress” Eva Hruska

The mere thought experiment of robots allowed Čapek to gain profound insights about human nature. Čapek contrasted humans with robots, and asked what was unique to humans. In this age of AI, we should all be doing what Čapek did, and we are better equipped. We don’t need to have his brilliant imagination to explore the concept of the robot, we only need to read the news. Anyone interested in what it means to be human should research what human tasks AI can and cannot complete. Like Čapek, we should ask what makes us different.
