In this age of AI, we should all be doing what Čapek did, and we are better equipped.

Kiley Towne, a Baylor student pursuing a Master’s of Fine Arts in directing, chose R.U.R. as her final project because she loved “how timely it is for our contemporary society.” Towne noted that the play was also relevant to the time it was written—in the midst of the rapid technological acceleration of the Industrial Revolution. The recurring question the script prompted among the actors and creative team was “what’s the difference between these humanoid, bioengineered robots and a human?” Towne said.

Robots Primus and Helena wonder what they are (photo by Jared Tseng)

Parker Wallace, a Baylor sophomore who played Primus, one of the lead robots, had to wrestle with this question very practically. Throughout the play, Parker said, “we play with the evolution of robots becoming human.” Parker’s own character begins as merely a robot, but develops human traits like fluid movements and emotion over the course of the play.

Ashton White, a junior, played Builder Alquist, a human who expresses reservations about running society on robot work. White reflected that “every character, robot or human, has something to say about the human experience.” White said that Alquist “believes in the human ability to work and create, and that he thinks that’s what separates us from the robots, but he also thinks that’s what defines humanity.” When Alquist’s friends want to transfer human labor to robots, Alquist believes they are “giving up one of the greatest aspects of being human.”

When asked what Alquist might think of our current society, White laughed. “I think Alquist would absolutely despise AI right about now. Alquist would ask: ‘what do humans do besides consume?’ He has a bit of an aside where he starts to talk about the fact that humans do nothing but eat, but the robots are feeding people.”

Alquist and Harry Domin, the robot factory owner

Kiana Pantellaleaver, a junior, played two characters: Helena, the beautiful wife of the robot factory director, and the beautiful robot Helena, created in the human Helena’s image. Both Helenas are repeatedly described as useless. “In the robot world,” Pantellaleaver said, “her beauty means nothing to them.” Robot Helena was created to be beautiful, but “a robot’s only use is to work, to build things, and to create.” However, in the end of the play, Helena is one of only two robots that is able to become human.

The robots in R.U.R. are not engineered only to be like humans, they are made to be better. Harry Domin, the director of the robot factory, tells Helena that the best worker is “the one that is the cheapest.” In order to build this worker, the engineer had to “take out everything that did not directly serve the purpose of work. This way he actually took out the human and created a Robot.” Helena seems to doubt these high aspirations, observing that “they say that a human is the work of God.” Domin responds with the flippant arrogance of a utopian: “God did not have a clue about modern technology.”

Harry Domin displays his robot to Helena (photo by Jared Tseng)

The robots were created in the image of man, and, in the end, they fail because they are both too similar and not similar enough. Over the course of the play, the engineers discover that the qualities they were so quick to discard—happiness, love, pain, and beauty, may have been more important to humanity than they thought.

But in some ways, robots are more like man than their engineers anticipated. When the robots have killed every human but one, the remaining human asks why they destroyed them. A robot responds, “you have to kill and rule, if you want to be like people. Read your history!” Humans fell because they aspired to be like God. Čapek’s robots fell because they aspired to be like the corrupted likeness of God in man.

Alquist, the last human left alive, questions the robots (photo by Jared Tseng)

Philosophers throughout history, most famously Aristotle and Cicero, studied humans by comparing them to animals. Čapek is doing the same thing with his hypothetical robots. Which qualities can humans and robots share? Which are unique to humans?

Čapek seems to propose that, if a robot is better than humans at factory work, then maybe factory work is a less human occupation. If AI can get a passing grade on an essay, then maybe the way we do education isn’t as human as we thought it was. If ChatGPT is better at bedside manner than human doctors, then maybe the way we show love to strangers needs to be more human. Observing AI’s capabilities can teach us what is and isn’t uniquely human, and where we are deficient.

If ChatGPT is better at bedside manner than human doctors, then maybe the way we show love to strangers needs to be more human.

As a writer, I have found this personally convicting. When I write lazily, I choose my words like an LLM does: based on common word associations I have heard rather than an intentional examination of the word’s meaning. My favorite writing, especially my favorite poetry, places words next to each other that are usually not associated but advance the writer’s unique meaning. For nature writer Robert MacFarlane, crow calls “hex” off of cliffs rather than echoing. For humorist P.G. Wodehouse, a man with a hangover sees his butler “shimmer” into the room rather than stride.

AI ethicist Mark Coeckelbergh wrote that “robots are used as purification tools: instruments that keep open the divide, that guard the borders between human and nonhuman.” However AI ends up harming or helping our society, our understanding of AI has the potential to inspire real advances in the philosophy of what it means to be human.

item.title: What does Baylor’s Student Government Actually Do?
item.description:
The busyness of college life makes it difficult to keep up with all the activity happening around Baylor’s campus. Unfortunately, this means many students are unaware of how their Student Government impacts their experience at Baylor. Some students wonder: is Student Government just political science majors cosplaying as politicians, or are students’ representatives actually doing meaningful work?

Baylor’s Student Government is modeled after the United States government with three branches: legislative, executive, and judicial. However, Student Government’s legislative branch is only a senate. These senators are elected by the class they represent. The Senate is where most of the tangible work originates. Here, the most common way Student Government helps the student body is by providing funding for events. This money comes from the Student Government Allocation Fund (SGAF), which began with around $380,000 in funds this year. The SGAF can be used to subsidize student events like Howdy, for example. Another feature of the Student Senate is its various committees. These committees, such as Campus Improvements and Affairs (CIA) or Public Relations (PR), help organize projects.

Last year, some of the most notable projects included CIA leading a project to improve lighting on campus, PR creating suggestion boxes, and Academic Affairs (AA) renovating the lobby of Sid Richardson. Current Senator and chair of the AA committee Jaclyn Ebeling said one of the Senate’s biggest allocations this year was for creating a cycle studio in the Student Life Center (SLC) by converting one of the racquetball courts.

Photo by Stella Tognocchi

However, Student Government’s impact does not just come from the Senate. The executive branch which includes the External Vice President, Student Body President, and their respective cabinets, has its own projects. Landon Self, the current Student Body President, ran on the promise to bring back an airport shuttle for students. This shuttle launched before Thanksgiving break and will offer rides to and from the DFW airport for Winter Break with tickets only costing $35. Self said that this is the project he is most proud of so far this year. “We were able to provide a needed service to the students and I’m very proud of our team for working hard on this,” Self said.

In addition to funding and projects, Student Government advocates for students in administrative settings. Senator Ebeling stated, “We can be a voice and a bridge between students and faculty and staff. … We’re thankfully at a university that the staff and faculty respects students, and they really respect Student Government..”

Self emphasized, “Student Government can do a lot for the student body. … We can advocate for our peers in areas that other people can’t. … We get into spaces and get to not only lead, but we get to represent and advocate for the voices and opinions of our peers.”

Photo by Stella Tognocchi

When asked what they wished students knew about Student Government, Self said, “I wish people knew about the heart behind Student Government, that we are motivated, that we are passionate, that we have ideas, we are thinking of ideas on a regular basis, and we are constantly striving… to deliver results for our peers.”

Students looking to become more aware of Student Government activities can follow their Instagram account, @bustugov, which regularly posts about upcoming events, projects, and initiatives.

Photo by Ada Mathias

Students of all majors are always welcome to get involved in Student Government. There are a variety of positions available, including some that do not require an election or campaigning. Student Government is a great way for students to become involved in Baylor and make their voices heard.

item.title: How Can We Celebrate America in the Shadow of Slavery? A Revolution-Era Poet Finds a Way
item.description:
“On the cusp of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, the same question that Frederick Douglass posed in 1847 is still being asked today, ‘What country have I?’” This question was posed by Dr. Matthew Reising, a visiting UT professor, in his talk at Baylor about slavery, the American Revolution, and the poetry of Phillis Wheatley.

Dr. Reising was quoting a speech Douglass gave less than a decade after his escape from slavery. Douglass goes on to lament: “I have no country, for the institutions of this country do not know me nor recognize me as a man. Therefore, in a country such as this, I cannot have patriotism.”

As an Afro-Hispanic woman in this country, I have sometimes felt as Douglass did. I know people both Black and White that have felt it as well — the scornfulness toward the country built on scarred backs that carried the burdens of America and made its birth possible.

Amid such political divisiveness, should we direct scorn towards our nation? Should we turn our backs on America? Dr. Matthew Reising, a speaker for Baylor’s “America 250” initiative, explained why the enslaved, Revolution-era poet Phillis Wheatley Peters said “no.”

On October 27th, ten days before the unveiling of The Memorial to the Enslaved Persons, Dr. Reising visited Baylor to speak on Phillis Wheatley at an event jointly hosted by the Alexander Hamilton Society, The Standard, and Baylor’s “America 250” initiative. Before his current teaching position at the University of Texas, Dr. Reising earned his PhD at Baylor, where he won the award for Best Graduate Student Instructor and The Best Dissertation in Humanities Award.

Dr. Reising began his talk by acknowledging the tension Frederick Douglass saw in the American founding. He highlighted two beloved notions of the Founding: first, human equality as presented in the Declaration of Independence, and second, Madison’s contention in Federalist 39 that the American experiment is a hopeful one. However, he also recognized the darkness in the Founding by reading a shocking quote from Thomas Jefferson, where he calls the Black imagination “dull, tasteless, and anomalous.” Jefferson says that “religion indeed has produced a Phyllis Whatley [sic], but it could never produce a poet.”

Phillis Wheatley, despite all the odds stacked against her, proved Jefferson wrong.

Wheatley was born in West Africa and was captured into slavery at the age of seven. In 1761, she was sold to John and Susanna Wheatley, who were New England evangelicals and thought it was necessary to teach Wheatley how to read and write to engage with the Bible.

By 14, she had her first poem published in a colonial newspaper, and as tensions rose between England and the American colonists, she published her first book of poetry in 1773, where she argued fervently against British rule. She was freed from slavery the very next year.

Over the next ten years, Wheatley published internationally renowned poems about the Revolutionary War, education, slavery, and more. She became a celebrity in her time and corresponded with Ben Franklin and George Washington, but today she is a mere ghost in both academia and the literary world.

Her Letter to Mary Wooster, the wife of Revolutionary General David Wooster, reads:

“Forever grateful let them live to thee And keep them ever Virtuous, brave, and free — But how, presumptuous shall we hope to find Divine acceptance with the Almighty mind — While yet (O deed ungenerous!) they disgrace And hold in bondage Africa’s blameless race; Let virtue reign — And those accord our prayers Be victory ours, and generous freedom theirs.”

Such beautiful work from such an inspiring woman, and yet why is she so neglected?

Dr. Reising argues that it is due to “Bad academia, and the allergy academics have to the notion that someone would want to be Christian more than anything else — even more than their freedom.” He pointed specifically to her poem On Being Brought from Africa to America, where she thanks slavery as the means through which she encountered Christianity — a sentiment many scholars find uncomfortable and often misinterpret.

According to Dr. Reising, most academics interpret Wheatley as either:

1. Brainwashed to love America

2. A rebel who used her religion and patriotism as a ruse to further the abolitionist movement

Dr. Reising holds a different view: that Phillis Wheatley was a genuine patriot, as well as a genuine Christian. When we dismiss authors like Wheatley as unserious, Dr. Reising said, we miss the opportunity to learn from them. In an interview with The Standard, Dr. Reising reflected on an African American Political Thought class he taught at Baylor a few years ago. In that class, he said he was “very intentional about including literature as a means for understanding politics because I’m a firm believer that the serious books and essays from the African American tradition give the best accounts of what it means to be an American. I think they just cut to the heart of what America stands for and is trying to live up to.”

“I’m a firm believer that the serious books and essays from the African American tradition give the best accounts of what it means to be an American. I think they just cut to the heart of what America stands for and is trying to live up to.”

To support his interpretation of Wheatley, Dr. Reising read from her letter to the Reverend Samson Occam, where Wheatley shares her view of freedom, and states that slavery is diametrically opposed to the character of the United States.

“In every human breast, God has implanted a principle, which we call love of freedom. It is impatient of oppression, and pants for deliverance, and by the leave of our modern Egyptians, I will assert that the same principle lives in us. I assert this not for their hurt, but to convince them of the strained absurdity of their conduct, whose words and actions are so diametrically opposite.”

She echoes the sentiment implied in her letter to Mary Wooster: America’s future depends entirely upon our citizens’ continued and genuine commitment to freedom for all. Now, whether all Americans are truly committed to freedom as such, is something only time can tell.

I asked Dr. Reising why he thought Wheatley chose to stay in America when she could have left. “Phillis Wheatley saw America’s founding principles, and thought this nation could be everything human beings had been striving for. But, it needed someone who could point out its problems and hypocrisies, which was her. She loved the country for what she believed it could be, and saw the kernel of a great nation. And that’s why she was an American by choice: because she was hopeful about what America could become.” [emphasis added]

“That’s why she was an American by choice: because she was hopeful about what America could become.”

Wheatley saw the Revolution not as a distant movement, irrelevant to her, but as the vehicle through which justice, equality, and freedom could be achieved; all while noting the fact that many Americans were failing to live up to its principles.

Wheatley’s most controversial poem, On being brought from Africa to America, proves her sincere Christian faith.

Wheatley chose Christ-like commitment and patriotism over liberty, over her own desires, because she had the eyes to see what almost none of us in today’s age can see — what the true America could be. Not eyes of blind complacency, nor those of scorn, or of unrealistic optimism, but the Spirit of what this country should be.

Phillis Wheatley was a genuine Christian and American patriot. To answer the question Douglass posed, “What country have I?” She would boldly proclaim: America. A land which we should not abandon, nor turn our backs on. She had several opportunities to emancipate herself in London or return to Africa, but she chose her country. She chose America — a country that had failed her constantly, yet one that she looked at with hope and adoration. Like her, we should search for and work diligently to reclaim the spirit of liberty that America calls for. Not necessarily “my” or “our” America as individuals or interest groups, but a genuine one: united in spirit, rooted in liberty and celebrating our differences, a place where a Phillis Wheatley could become a renowned poet, regardless of her sex or race, and make the conscious choice to truly be an American.

Phillis Wheatley made that choice as a slave, in the most adverse conditions, with all odds stacked against her. If she could do it, so can you.

item.title: Baylor C.S. Lewis Biographer Has a New Subject: Dorothy L. Sayers
item.description:
For three magical hours every week, tucked away in a tiny conference room with four other students, I attend a class entirely dedicated to a writer many have never even heard of: Dorothy L. Sayers. Sayers, the witty and versatile British novelist, essayist, and playwright, has been overshadowed by contemporaries like C.S. Lewis for whom, in many respects, she paved the way. Throughout her life, Sayers pursued her many interests with courage, producing a canon of varied and insightful work. We forget her at our peril.

Dr. Alan Jacobs, the Baylor Great Texts professor who made the unusual choice of teaching an entire undergraduate course on a little-known female author, is himself a prolific and versatile writer. In 2005, he wrote one of the most famous biographies of C. S. Lewis and has chosen Dorothy Sayers as his next biographical subject. In addition to being the Distinguished Professor of Humanities in the Baylor Honors Program, Dr. Jacobs is also a Senior Fellow of the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture at the University of Virginia.

Each work we examine in Dr. Jacob’s class is carefully placed in the context of Sayers’ life. Sayers was born in 1893 in the town of Oxford. After growing up in the country, she returned to Oxford and graduated from one of the few women’s colleges. Following university, she worked in a variety of jobs including teaching, advertising, and publishing.

I had not been reading Sayers long before I was wondering how on earth she was not more celebrated. I asked Dr. Jacobs why she did not spark interest in more students. One reason, Jacobs said, may be her reputation as a detective novelist. “A lot of people in academic circles don’t think detective stories are serious enough to be worth studying.” But Sayers was much more than a detective story writer. According to Jacobs, “when she turned to writing as—well many people say a Christian apologist, but I say a Christian catechist—at the time in England she was really popular, really widely read. But eventually, C.S. Lewis, her contemporary and friend, kind of took over that role, so everybody started paying so much attention to Lewis that there wasn’t a whole lot of time left over for her… people just didn’t realize how gifted she was…So her reputation kind of remained confined to England and didn’t really spread in a serious way in the USA.”

What Sayers was able to accomplish with the genre of detective stories was by no means unacademic. “She’s the person who is responsible more than anyone else for turning the detective story into serious literary fiction,” Dr. Jacobs said. He explained how Sayers paved the way for more recent writers such as P. D. James, who is lauded as a great English novelist despite writing “only” detective stories. Sayers’ detective stories went beyond the conventional bounds for the genre, writing not just mysteries, but social commentaries. In particular, Gaudy Night and The Nine Tailors introduce worlds in which the whodunit is but a small aspect, and the relationships and social questions of the day are the real focus. The questions Sayers explores in these novels are strikingly relevant to the present day, including struggles of personal integrity and tensions between a woman’s vocation and family.

“She’s the person who is responsible more than anyone else for turning the detective story into serious literary fiction”

Sayers was not only a pioneer in detective stories but also in radio. “There had been radio dramas before her but nothing that had the kind of impact that her twelve plays on the life of Jesus had,” Dr. Jacobs remarked. He explained that Sayers paved the way in radio drama and religious broadcasting before Lewis ever gave the lectures that turned into Mere Christianity. “The idea that that radio presentations of the Christian faith could be intellectually substantive and artistically substantive we get from her…she was someone who was trying out new genres, new forms of artistic work, she was very much exploratory and innovative and pioneering, and I just don’t think that is recognized as much today.” He attributed this neglect to the bad reputation inevitably earned by her Christianity, and the misconception that her work in mysteries and radio was not academically valuable. She was not taken as seriously as writers like Virginia Woolf, since the genres in which she wrote, detective fiction and radio, were not then considered high quality literature. “But it is serious,” Jacobs said, “it’s brilliant stuff and I think it’s not well enough known now.”

Sayers certainly had an exploratory spirit, writing in multiple genres, including detective stories, plays, essays, and radio. Readers who have never heard of Sayers before may very well wonder where exactly to start. Dr. Jacobs recommended her novel The Nine Tailors for those who are not particularly interested in detective fiction per se, because while there is a mystery, it is not the heart of the novel. There are also her polemical writings, including the pithy essay Are Women Human? which my classmates and I found extremely thought-provoking and relevant for the questions women continue to struggle with today. Other essays include The Greatest Drama Ever Staged, and The Lost Tools of Learning, the latter being foundational to the classical Christian homeschooling movement. My personal favorite is Gaudy Night, from her delightful Lord Peter Wimsey series. I recommend the BBC TV adaptation starring Edward Petherbridge and Harriet Walter.

“The thing that has really stood out to me more than anything else is just how courageous she was on so many levels, how situations that would have defeated a lot of people didn’t defeat her.”

On a personal level, one of the most impactful parts of the class has been hearing about the character of Sayers herself. It is clear from how he talks in class that Jacobs has been deeply affected by Sayers’ character as well. Through the process of writing Sayers’ biography, Jacobs said, “The thing that has really stood out to me more than anything else is just how courageous she was on so many levels, how situations that would have defeated a lot of people didn’t defeat her.” He described how she abandoned writing detective stories to try her hand at writing a religious play. Writing those detective books was safe. It paid the bills, and Sayers was the main provider for her family. But she took the risk and pursued something new. Then, years later, she happened to read Dante during a WWII air raid and decided to translate The Divine Comedy: “she was passionate about it. she was fascinated by it, she just couldn’t stop thinking about Dante… she had no reason to think that that was ever going to be lucrative for her and it never really was…She was just fearless about stuff like that and it didn’t make sense on the practical level but it made sense to her internally and that’s just really, really admirable I just don’t think that there are very many people who are that courageous.”

As a college student, Sayers’s fearless character is particularly inspiring to me. The task of finding my vocation is intimidating. Dorothy Sayers never hesitated to follow the paths she felt called to, even when it meant leaving what was safe to explore new horizons. One of the first women educated at Oxford, she developed her writing in the midst of bearing a child out of wedlock and struggling through a difficult marriage. The exhaustion of living in today’s world, where we are told to calculate the probability of a successful marriage, how many children one can afford, and how to save enough to retire comfortably, can be debilitating. The adventurous life of Dorothy Sayers is bracing. She invested her talents boldly, pursued her passions, and kept forging ahead, regardless of circumstances. She is an exemplar to the modern man and woman alike to take one day at a time because we cannot anticipate the golden opportunities we may miss if we chart our path too carefully.

item.title: Finding Your Tahini: The Baylor Marriage Pact and Psychometric Theory
item.description:
Can you predict compatibility with an algorithm? Can you quantify love?

Baylor has a reputation as a “Ring by Spring” school. But what about those without a BU beau? On November 5 at 5:08pm, 1,622 Baylor students received an email with the name of one other Baylor student, informally entering an agreement to marry that person if they remain Ring-less by Spring.

These emails were sent out by the Marriage Pact, a matchmaking organization that uses a unique questionnaire and algorithm to identify your most compatible match (the history of the Marriage Pact is discussed in a previous article).

Ryan Marsh, a sophomore at Baylor, met up with his match last week.

He decided to fill out the Marriage Pact questionnaire “just for fun” but “didn’t expect anything to come of it.” He met up with his match at George’s and said he had a fun time. Ryan said that the results of the algorithm this year were “almost perfect, which is scary. We have the same cat.”

“You have the same cat?” I asked.

Ryan continued, “I emailed her and she didn’t email me back for a whole day because she was adopting a cat. I’m a very big cat person, so I asked for pictures of the cat and she sent them to me and we have the same cat.”

Including cats, Ryan and his match had a lot of similar interests, but Ryan didn’t think the questionnaire was completely perfect. “They didn’t really ask a lot about your personality, just your beliefs and what you were studying in school. It was more observable traits rather than internal traits,” such as interests or personality.

Ryan suggested adding questions like “Why did you choose your major?” “What’s your favorite childhood memory and why?” or “What’s your favorite TV show and what makes it your favorite?” which he says would be more difficult to put through an algorithm.

Overall, Ryan said, “I can see us being good friends, but I can’t see us being anything more than friends,” but he is open to taking the questionnaire again next year for fun.

Ryan’s suggestions raise some interesting questions about the Marriage Pact’s methods of data classification. Can you really predict compatibility with an algorithm? How do you find one set of questions that works for everyone? For these questions, I went to an expert: Baylor professor and psychometrician Dr. Grant Morgan.

Morgan describes classification as “a very natural process that we as humans engage in because we are surrounded by so much data all the time that there’s no way we could attend to it all. Classification is really a data simplification process.” (Though this, also, he notes, is a simplification of the subject.)

Morgan teaches graduate level Quantitative Methods and researches psychometrics and classification. He also goes to HEB for his groceries, where he puts classification into action to locate an unusual ingredient.

“I went to the HEB on Hewitt Drive in Woodway, and I needed tahini. I’d never bought tahini before and so I thought as I walked into the store, ‘Where is tahini?’ If grocery stores weren’t structured the way they are, you would just start at the place closest to the door and just walk up and down aisles until you saw tahini.”

First, Morgan asked, “What is it? What things is it similar to? It’s not something we eat a lot in the American diet, so I’ll go to the aisle labeled ‘International.’”

He went there, but didn’t see it. Then he pondered further, “What is tahini? What is it exactly? It’s roasted sesame seeds. It had been ground up with probably a little oil, let’s see, roasting things and grinding them up—sounds like peanut butter.” (On the nut butter aisle, he did in fact discover the sought after tahini).

These qualities (in the case of tahini, roasted and grinded nut butters) are examples of “salient features of some observation that help us to classify” tahini, or another subject of interest. For the Marriage Pact, the subjects of interest are the people profiled through the questionnaire.

“I think that [The Baylor Marriage Pact] has got a kind of metaphorical grocery store. They’ve got the items all set up or the shelves all set up. They’re administering this instrument to figure out which shelves to put people on.”

Morgan says, “I think that [The Baylor Marriage Pact] has got a kind of metaphorical grocery store. They’ve got the items all set up or the shelves all set up. They’re administering this instrument to figure out which shelves to put people on.” He added, “I really don’t like that metaphor, but I think it actually kind of fits.”

“And everyone’s trying to find their tahini,” I added.

“That’s the title of this article—Finding Your Tahini,” Grant said.

In the case of the Marriage Pact, “There’s this set of items that are intended to be manifestations of all these different aspects of a person’s personality, values, interests, those kinds of things” which is a sort of “profiling.” Morgan added, “That verb (profiling) has gotten a negative connotation over time, but mathematically that’s what is happening—you’re creating these profiles based on what we know from the empirical literature.”

Classification is a process used in psychometrics, another research focus of Morgan. And what is psychometrics? “Psychometrics as a discipline is focused on how we can make decisions about latent variables, [which are] variables that we believe exist but can’t directly measure. And the way we do that is we develop these instruments that are hopefully reflective of the latent variable.”

The Marriage Pact is one of those instruments, and in this case, the latent variable is theoretical compatibility. How then does the Marriage Pact identify the salient features by which to profile, classify, and arrange those who take the survey? Here’s what the Marriage Pact’s Data Principles and Practices have to say:

“Based on your values, the Marriage Pact algorithmically ‘interviews’ all other participants at your school on your behalf to find the best person with whom you could make a marriage pact…Your long-term compatibility with a person depends not on your surface-level traits, but on your core values—what you care about deep down.”

Your long-term compatibility with a person depends not on your surface-level traits, but on your core values—what you care about deep down. Marriage Pact

To acquire this “values data,” the Marriage Pact asks 50 questions, each of which can be answered on a scale from one to seven. Questions from this year’s survey include:

I find politically incorrect humor funny (1- strongly disagree; 7 – strongly agree)

It’s okay that my partner drinks

It is more important to protect someone’s feelings than to tell the truth

I’m comfortable with my child being gay

Exercising is an important part of my identity

My partner can be “just friends” with an ex

Are you smarter than most people at the university?

It’s important my child(ren) be raised outside of the U.S. for some period of time

I always vote (1 – never; 7 – even in local elections)

The world needs (1 – more realism; 7 – more imagination)

How are these responses scored? The Marriage Pact is built on a variation of the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm (a foundation shared by the dating app Hinge), which “seeks to orchestrate a stable match between two equal-sized groups of participants, typically men and women. The objective is to secure a stable matching, where no two participants would desert their current partners for one another.” (However, this does not exclude the possibility of a stronger unrequited desire among matches.)

In addition to empirical weighting (which psychometricians call “loadings”), Morgan says, “There can also be a weighting imposed on scoring so that if ‘You believe in God’ is one item and ‘You like macaroni and cheese’ is another item, they probably shouldn’t be weighted equally if the purpose of the answers is to find a life partner, hopefully.” We don’t know if the Marriage Pact has imposed importance onto various questions. Is one’s stance on politically incorrect humor as important as one’s ideal parenting approach?

Even with a seemingly objective questionnaire and algorithm, Morgan says, “The results of this are an expression of some value system.” The Marriage Pact acknowledges the importance of values, claiming to determine matches “based on your values,” but really it determines matches based on your values within their values. The framework of their value system is formed by the questions they find important. “So I hope people are aware that they’re accepting a value system by accepting the results. I’m not saying that’s bad, I’m just saying be aware of it.”

Even with a seemingly objective questionnaire and algorithm, Morgan says, “The results of this are an expression of some value system.”

Whether determining which questions hold the most importance, or what results to accept, we are faced with what Morgan calls a balancing act: “Do you let the data make every decision or do you say ‘This is what we believe’?”

This is easier said than done. According to Morgan, “Even doctoral students are hesitant to impose their values on decisions. They want to be the translator for the data.”

Most of us aren’t PhD students, but many of us still face the temptation to offload the responsibility for our most important decisions.

Morgan encourages his students to resist that temptation. “Just this week in class, I reminded students who are hesitant to make decisions: ‘You’re pursuing a terminal degree, you’re going to have to make decisions. And is it scary? Sometimes it is. Is it hard? Sometimes it is. But you wanted this. That’s what comes along with being an expert.’”

The Marriage Pact is an easy opportunity to give up our agency, but I believe it is better to have courage and make our own decisions. Even the wrong ones can be instructive.

After an illuminating breakup, I formulated a questionnaire of my own to reflect my revised understanding of my values and preferences. I identified the qualities I was looking for and transformed each data point into a question, resulting in my The Questionnaire (which I do use on dates). I believe that one of the many merits of dating is how it teaches you about your own preferences, character, and values. In searching for someone to complement ourselves, we are also searching for ourselves.

As someone who took the Marriage Pact questionnaire “for the bit,” I honestly don’t really like the way this instrument turns people and matchmaking into economics (though I am a big fan of my own DIY psychometrics). Even though it has some success and the end decision does belong to the users, I disagree with this system on principle. One of the selling points of the Marriage Pact (and online dating platforms) is the opportunity to allow data to make decisions for you. Whether people are truly handing over the keys of their dating life to economics or not, I take issue with the attitude of submission. I do not want to give up the search just to find myself in the machine. Instead, let us own our agency, make decisions, and become the expert interpreters of our lives’ date-a.

item.title: Diplomacy in the Shadow of AI: Former USAID Administrator Speaks at Baylor
item.description:
Artificial intelligence alters the balance of power abroad and tests the moral and institutional stability of the United States at home, former USAID Deputy Administrator Bonnie Glick argued.

On October 16, the Baylor Chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society hosted a lecture titled “AI and Diplomacy” in Kayser Auditorium. Before she took the stage, Glick outlined her argument in an interview with The Standard: AI is not a peripheral innovation but a powerful instrument that will reorder geopolitics and expose America’s moral perimeter.

Glick’s central claim is that U.S. adversaries already exploit AI’s capabilities. “Do not be so naive to think that our adversaries do not use AI for nefarious ends,” Glick said. The point was not speculative. For years, authoritarian states have been deploying technology first and rationalizing it later.

“Do not be so naive to think that our adversaries do not use AI for nefarious ends.”

The most explicit case she highlighted was China. In her view, Beijing races not only for a commercial or technological advantage but also for a potent instrument of social control. Surveillance against persecuted minorities is not a distant dystopian future but is rather being actualized in the current day, especially against groups like Uyghur Muslims. Glick argued that China’s AI strategy collapses the distance between software and state power, a relationship once seen as mutually beneficial.

Students question Glick after her lecture. Photo by Stella Tognocchi

Her warning extended beyond foreign adversaries to the American policy dilemma itself. “We are at a moment in history where people are taking a deep breath to analyze what is available to us,” she said. The U.S. must decide whether it will “stay ahead of China or take a responsible road with technology to put regulation on it.” Delay favors regimes that do not restrain themselves.

Glick expects the current administration to press for rapid deployment out of Silicon Valley without any sense of restraint on technological innovation. If a figure like JD Vance were to become president in 2028, she suggested, the direction of AI policy would continue in that vein.

The choice between acceleration and discipline is not partisan in the conventional sense but rather civilizational in scope. The costs of acceleration are not abstract, Glick argued. “There are rules in our society that will become undervalued, and that takes away from the special thing that is America.”

If AI displaces or dispossesses workers across the spectrum from “blue-collar to academics,” the social fabric that underpins our societal order weakens. Economic dislocation erodes shared purpose, strains public trust, and leaves citizens more vulnerable to populist or anti-institutional movements. Any serious adoption of AI requires a commitment to upskilling “to enhance the workforce for the 21st century.”

Glick addresses AHS event attendees. Photo by Stella Tognocchi

Glick sees the prevailing public mood as careless rather than malicious. “I think people are willfully blind in regard to AI,” she said. The desire to “move fast, to make money, to advance” is not new, but the domain is new. Diplomacy, in her view, is not immune to the costs of speed. Glick drew a hard boundary: “Diplomacy is the room for diplomats. And AI should be used as a tool for things such as translations… The human skills of brokering peace, the human skills of public diplomacy, of sharing American culture — that cannot be done through ChatGPT.”

“The human skills of brokering peace, the human skills of public diplomacy, of sharing American culture — that cannot be done through ChatGPT.”

AI may assist, but it cannot substitute for the human work that stabilizes political order. The lecture that followed in Kayser Auditorium reflected the same logic that AI is not a neutral technical instrument. It is a venue in which rival models of governance are already in contest. Authoritarian states such as China deploy AI without hesitation, while the United States is caught in indecision. If that hesitation persists, the terms of diplomacy will not be set by diplomats at all. They will instead be set by the systems that outpace them.

item.title: Marriage Pact: The Matchmaking Program Sweeping Baylor’s Campus
item.description:
Like many at Baylor, I thought the emails from an alleged “secret admirer” filling my inbox last fall were a scam. However, the source, the Marriage Pact, has been an established campus phenomenon for 8 years and is built on a Nobel-Prize-winning algorithm. Last year, almost 2000 Baylor students participated, and many have found dates and potentially even partners from the process.

The (love) story begins in 2017 in a Stanford University economics course. Originally a final project for ECON136: Market Design, the Marriage Pact was created by Liam McGregor ‘20 and Sophia Sterling-Angus ‘19, utilizing the Nobel-Prize-winning Deferred Acceptance Algorithm. Within days, they had over 4,000 responses. To this day, almost 70% of Stanford students fill out the survey every year. Soon, the Pact spread to campuses all across the United States. The program is currently run by volunteer students selected from each operating campus. The Marriage Pact is independent and largely unfunded.

But what is a marriage pact? The program proposes the following definition: “An informal agreement between two people—if both parties remain unmarried and without prospects after a certain period of time—to simply marry each other.” There’s no pressure to commit to your algorithmically allocated match, but the Marriage Pact seeks to provide a safety net for those without a ring by spring.

“Look around. College is the best place to meet *the one*. But we’re not going to be here forever…If someone better comes along in your 20s, more power to you. We hope you don’t need us. But… better safe than sorry.” (Baylor Marriage Pact)

In November 2024, the Marriage Pact reached Baylor. Approximately 578 men and 1,160 women filled out the questionnaire for a total of 1,738 people. In December, students received an email announcing their “match,” the name of one Baylor student with whom they had the most compatibility. The Marriage Pact’s flirtation with Baylor didn’t end there. In April, they released their “Campus Report,” highlighting the demographic preferences of students, drawn from the anonymous results of the questionnaire.

One Baylor senior (who asked to stay anonymous) took the questionnaire last year, and despite some skepticism has decided to try out the Marriage Pact again this year. Reflecting on the questionnaire experience, she says, “It was strongly value-focused rather than interest-focused. Maybe I would’ve preferred a better balance.” She went on just one date with her match, which was “fairly unremarkable,” but also “appreciated the opportunity to meet someone new and gather more data about what a first date should feel like.”

Overall, she added, “I would definitely do it again and I’ve already filled it out for this year.” There are only a few days left to sign up for this year’s Marriage Pact. The questionnaire closes this Tuesday at 10 am.

(In a forthcoming article, I will examine how the MP works, from latent variables to value systems with insights from Grant Morgan, PhD, a psychometrician here at Baylor).

item.title: Motherhood in the Shadow of Academic Achievement: The Desire Left Out of Campus Conversation
item.description:
Why do young women no longer feel proud of, or even comfortable with, expressing their desire for motherhood? And why is this exceedingly prevalent at a Christian university?

To answer the first question, Nadya Williams—a homeschool mom, writer, and editor—explains that it all started with the abortion movement, though not in the politically divisive sense. Williams says that the “choice to prioritize conversations about whether abortion is a form of healthcare, instead of directing further resources to support expecting mothers and their babies, is a dramatic statement about our society’s undervaluing of babies and mothers, regardless of where one stands on the political spectrum.” In other words, the healthcare system’s language surrounding pregnancies not only dehumanizes the child, but also ignores the woman, making her feel as though she is unhealthy and unfit for motherhood. The emphasis on choice in the context of motherhood immediately encourages the mother to feel diminished because of her “condition.”

Now it is easier to understand why women—particularly young women—feel that a call to motherhood is something to be embarrassed about. Society tells them that they are essentially hoping for a “condition” that will strain them mentally, physically, and emotionally.

It was through the birth of Isaac that she was given the joy and fulfillment she had longed for.

Of course, this completely ignores all the good that comes from creating life. Not to mention, the great fulfillment that women gain through becoming mothers. It is not a burden, it is something to celebrate. More than that, it is something to be proud about desiring. This is displayed in the Bible repeatedly. Genesis 21 tells the story of Sarah and Abraham. When Sarah finally gave birth to a son after decades of barrenness she exclaims, “‘God has brought me laughter, and everyone who hears about this will laugh with me.’ And she added, ‘Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.” (Genesis 21:6-7). Their son is named Isaac—which means laughter—because of the prophecy of Sarah’s pregnancy. Isaac’s birth brought Sarah so much joy, it reduced her to laughter. As she says in the verse, God brought her laughter in more than just that one moment. It was through the birth of Isaac that she was given the joy and fulfillment she had longed for. There are many other similar stories to this in the Bible, like that of Tamar, Hannah, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary.

The female students at Baylor University, many of whom have studied these stories in the Bible and understand the goodness of motherhood, have fallen prey to the message of the world that the desire for motherhood is detestable. I believe this is partially a result of Baylor’s recent push towards academics and research, which seems to have left the cultivation of faith behind.

“First Steps” by Arthur John Elsley

In the last few years, Baylor has made major moves towards becoming and maintaining its status as an R1, or ‘Research 1’ university, which is “the highest ranking awarded by the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education. The rankings are based on particular benchmarks in research activity, such as the number of research doctorates awarded and the amount of money allotted to research at an institution.” To put it simply, Baylor basically wants to become the Baptist version of the University of Notre Dame—both competitive schools that will not let go of their religious affiliations despite very evidently putting more time, money, and effort into academics. Surely, the role of the university is to focus on academics. But it is concerning, particularly for a school that has a clear mission to integrate academics and Christianity, that the focus seems to have shifted heavily towards presenting only its academic achievements to the world.

This brings us to the motherhood issue: female Baylor students feel as though their call to motherhood is less important than their career, a result that aligns with the unfortunate mainstream narrative and the pressure from academic glorification. It is one of several examples which show how students feel they must give all their attention to academic achievements as they relate to their own professional reputation and Baylor’s.

Baylor Students Walking on Campus

I was first clued in on the issue on Baylor’s campus through conversations that I had with other female students. At the start of the conversation, they automatically list all of their achievements, along with the many academic and career goals they have for themselves. On the one hand, their goals have shown me how amazingly driven and passionate women at Baylor are. However, these aspirations usually involve remaining in school for the better portion of the next decade of their lives or immediately getting swept into the corporate world after graduation.

Eventually they ask me what I would like to do once I graduate. If I’m feeling prepared to have a controversial discussion, I explain that the only job I really desire to have is to be a wife and a mother. Nine times out of ten, the girl will light up and immediately agree with my goals, saying that at the end of the day that’s all she really wants as well. It’s amazing to watch her get both more excited and more relaxed at the same time, as she feels comfortable discussing her innermost wishes. She can discuss those dreams without feeling the need to prove herself academically or professionally first.

Students who want to pursue callings that will not necessarily bring acclaim to themselves or the University, but rather solely bring glory to God, should be just as communally praised as those who do great things for the academic world.

These conversations have taught me that the gap between striving for academic excellence and pursuing one’s passions and vocation through faith must be reconciled at Baylor University. Students who want to pursue callings that will not necessarily bring acclaim to themselves or the University, but rather solely bring glory to God, should be just as communally praised as those who do great things for the academic world. Women who want an education as a step towards fulfilling their calling to motherhood should not be looked down upon as wasting time and money. Rather, they should be seen as boldly taking hold of the opportunities that the modern Christian university offers them.

item.title: How Reading Homer Helps the Homeless: A Case for the Liberal Arts
item.description:
My close friend and I often discuss our classes, though our courses of study couldn’t be more different. She is majoring in Urban Studies, enrolled in a Civic Leadership Program, and taking a class this semester titled Poverty, Justice, & Transformation. Her educational path is preparing her for community-based non-profit work, a tangible and direct way to help others. Meanwhile, I spend my school days reading Wordsworth, translating Cicero, and studying the paintings of Botticelli. Compared to her selflessly practical focus, my academic pursuits feel indulgent and gratuitous. My studies are worthwhile, perhaps, but they appear distant from the needs of the world.

I’ve always felt this tension between my thirst for truth and my desire to serve others. At times, it seems like I must sacrifice serving others to study what I love—literature, philosophy, languages, art. Having the freedom to shape my own academic path as a college student only sharpens this tension. If I want to think with Plato about the definition of justice, how can I ignore the injustice unfolding right outside my door?

Liberal learning has long been falling out of favor. Critics of the liberal arts make reasonable arguments—why care about literature or philosophy when people can’t get food on the table? Why study something “useless” when other fields offer tangible ways to improve the lives of others? Ultimately, the criticisms come down to one central question: can the liberal arts serve others, or are they merely a selfish luxury?

This question is one that every serious scholar must consider. Luckily, the wisdom of thinkers from ages past can guide us toward an answer. It begins with correcting society’s beliefs about what the liberal arts are and what they offer us. To help reform society’s understanding, I turn to the 20th-century Catholic philosopher Josef Pieper.

Image of Josef Pieper

In his book Leisure: the Basis of Culture, Pieper writes a compelling defense of the liberal arts as meaningful and necessary. He defines the liberal arts as “ways of human action which have their justification in themselves…The ‘liberality’ or ‘freedom’ of the liberal arts consists in their not being disposable for purposes, that they do not need to be legitimized by a social function, by being ‘work’” (41). In other words, the liberal arts are those things that are done for their own sake, not in the service of separate ends. Their value is intrinsic, not instrumental. For Pieper, the foundation of liberal learning is leisure, which he defines not as idleness or escapism, but as “the disposition of receptive understanding, of contemplative beholding, and immersion—in the real” (50). While leisure may take place in the classroom, it is certainly not confined to one. Pieper argues that this contemplative and receptive posture requires a particular inner attitude, a “celebrating spirit” (52). In this way, all leisurely activity, including the liberal arts, depends upon a joyful affirmation of reality. One must acknowledge that the world is a wonderful place—rich with truth, goodness, and beauty, even amidst suffering—before one can genuinely pursue liberal learning.

One must acknowledge that the world is a wonderful place—rich with truth, goodness, and beauty, even amidst suffering—before one can genuinely pursue liberal learning.

A proper conception of the liberal arts defeats the argument that they are selfish to pursue. In fact, liberal learning nurtures an outward-facing disposition in a number of different ways. First, the leisurely activity at the heart of liberal education is itself a process of “un-selfing.” Pieper writes that leisure is the attitude of someone “who opens himself; not of someone who seizes but of one who lets go, who lets himself go” (51). In studying the liberal arts—whether it be philosophy or geology or art history—one becomes completely absorbed in some fascinating feature of existence. For a time, the self recedes, suspended in attentive appreciation.

Second, contemplation perfects not just the individual, but society. Dominican priest and philosopher A.G. Sertillanges agrees with this social dimension of liberal education: “The time of a thinker, when he really uses it, is in reality charity to all; only thus do we appreciate it properly. The man of truth belongs to the human race with truth itself; there is no risk of selfishness when one has isolated oneself jealously to serve this sublime and universal benefactor of mankind.” Liberal education shapes good citizens, preparing people for productive political contribution. It equips students with skills of reasoning and self-expression that are essential for democracy and shared life.

Dr. Elizabeth Corey, Professor of Political Science and Director of the Honors Program at Baylor University, has much to say about the value of a liberal education, especially for the person living in a democratic society. When I interviewed her, she shared that she had recently been called to serve jury duty for a man that was on trial for committing a felony: “I realized in that trial that I had things to bring to the jury that were really helpful because of what I have learned through liberal education—how to have a conversation, how to set the parameters for people who are very different to come together and dispute some really weighted issues.” For Dr. Corey, liberal education is not something set apart from the needs of our society; rather, it equips us to respond to them with empathy and equity.

Lastly, liberal education is not selfish because it elicits a burning desire to invite others into the contemplative life. Witnessing a startling sunrise or listening to a Tchaikovsky concerto is definitely self-fulfilling, but it also turns one outward towards other people. Like the enlightened man in Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, the liberally educated person yearns to guide others toward the light to share in their contemplative experience of truth and wonder.

But as essential as contemplation is, it does not encompass the whole of a well-lived life. The liberal arts do not ask us to retreat from the world indefinitely, nor are they properly practiced in isolation. A true liberal education equips us to return to the world, ready to see it more vividly and love it more passionately. When conducted properly, liberal learning nurtures friendship between the student and the world. The world offers itself up to the student by revealing its beauty, truth, and goodness in moments of leisure. In return, the student responds not with grasping but with gratitude, as he seeks to love and serve the world and its inhabitants.

A true liberal education equips us to return to the world, ready to see it more vividly and love it more passionately.

Work in the world is a necessary part of life. Unlike leisure, it is purely instrumental, but similar to leisure, it is crucial to fulfilling our purpose as human beings. Sertillanges supports this idea: “A country priest who devotes himself to his parishioners, a doctor who turns away from study to give help in urgent cases, a young man of good family who adopts a calling to help his people and in doing so has to turn his back on liberal studies, are not profaning the gift that is in them, they are paying homage to the True which is one and the same being with the Good.” When one works to love others in true charity, it can never be contrary to the vision of goodness and truth which the liberal arts point to.

The conviction that true liberal learning turns us outward points to a potential resolution to the tension between study and service.While fields like social work and public health are urgent and valuable, studying the liberal arts shapes how we see the world and ignites a desire to act in it. Literature stretches our human sympathy, philosophy reminds us that everyone wrestles with meaning, and science intensifies our reverence for all creation.

Dr. Rebecca Flavin, Senior Lecturer of Political Science and Director of Engaged Learning Curriculum at Baylor University, has a foot in both worlds. As a lecturer in the College of Arts and Sciences, she studies and teaches political philosophy, but in her role in the Office of Engaged Learning, she seeks to integrate scholarship with service. She points out another crucial reason why liberal study must predicate service in the world: “In order to understand why people are sleeping on the streets, you need a liberal education . . . you’re not going to remedy the problem of people sleeping on the streets if you don’t understand the complex causes that contribute to . . . homelessness, as an example.” An education in the liberal arts gives one the prerequisite understanding to serve others in a productive manner.

I do not seek to diminish the important work of non-profit organizations or global relief efforts. Relieving the suffering of the diseased, the poor, the hungry, and the unhoused is a noble and necessary cause. But to what end? When the people you are helping are freed from poverty, what will they do with their lives? We know what they are freed from, but what are they freed for? As various research reports on the mental health of middle-class Americans will show, economic security and a comfortable lifestyle do not guarantee happiness. Relief efforts must be conducted with a fuller understanding of the human person, acknowledging that mankind does not live to survive, he survives to live.

It must have been this view of the human person, as understood by the liberally educated man or woman, that sparked the desire to serve others in the first place. Tragically, mankind will often do what is most advantageous or pleasurable for himself instead of what is right. But liberal study alerts one to the transcendent reality that lies beneath the surface of our existence. The liberal arts instill a sense of wonder toward others and implant a desire to serve and contribute to civilization. In her essay How Should One Read a Book?, Virginia Woolf eloquently captures this idea: “But that pleasure [we get from reading]—mysterious, unknown, useless as it is—is enough. That pleasure is so curious, so complex, so immensely fertilizing to the mind of anyone who enjoys it, and so wide in its effects, that it would not be in the least surprising to discover, on the day of judgement when secrets are revealed and the obscure is made plain, that the reason why we have grown from pigs to men and women, and come out from our caves, and dropped our bows and arrows, and sat round the fire and talked and drunk and made merry and given to the poor and helped the sick and made pavements and house and erected some sort of shelter and society on the waste of the world, is nothing but this: we have loved reading.” Study of the liberal arts results in a mysterious outpouring of love, rooted in gratitude for the miracle of the world we live in.

But liberal study alerts one to the transcendent reality that lies beneath the surface of our existence.

Lady Philosophy Presenting the Seven Liberal Arts to Boethius

This is how the liberal arts can inform and elevate the work of service. Focused on establishing material security, service runs the risk of being solely directed towards the incomplete purpose of survival. We become susceptible to approaching the population we serve as a problem to be solved or a statistic in a sociological study. Meanwhile, the liberally educated man or woman will conduct service with a full vision of human flourishing. The liberal arts cultivate a receptiveness to the world’s goodness, thereby enabling us to see the beauty in suffering people. This combats the tendency towards surface-level service. Instead, it motivates and enriches service by expanding our capacity to see the inherent mystery and complexity of other people.

The liberally educated man or woman will conduct service with a full vision of human flourishing.

Liberal study and service work should not and cannot exist apart from one another. Instead, they belong together when they are rightly ordered. Openness to wonder allows true service to transform the servant in the same way that liberal learning transforms the learner. When we pursue the liberal arts hand-in-hand with service in the world, we love our fellow inhabitants of this world with our utmost. People are miracles—not problems to be fixed, but mysteries to behold.

item.title: Baylor alumni working in D.C. face government shutdown with peace
item.description:
Millions of government workers over the past few weeks have found themselves in a position of empty inboxes, phones not ringing, and fingers drumming on the desk waiting for the next steps to take. The government shutdown has halted much of Washington, D.C.’s activity, and no one seems to have a clear answer. Since October 1, two million employees have been working with suspended pay and no clear end in sight. Baylor University has historically prided itself on postgrad employment rates, placement rates usually hovering around the 90% range. That includes a full-time job, graduate school, and the military. Of these many students who enter the workforce, a handful of them go on to work in Washington, D.C., either immediately postgrad or years down the line.

Baylor prepares students in many ways for success in the real world through cultural experiences, faith practices, relationships with peers and professors — the list goes on and on. What Baylor doesn’t (and can’t) prepare you for is a government shutdown, let alone one that threatens your job. When the idea came to me to interview government workers in D.C., I wanted to explore how Baylor prepared them for their individual careers. I was riding the elevator in Draper while texting a friend and former Standard writer about my idea, and he asked if I was going to address the government shutdown in my interviews. I quickly switched tabs, opened Safari, and simply Googled “government shutdown.” Article after article, having been posted mere minutes and hours prior, placed panic in me that it seemed the rest of the country was also feeling. When asked about the shutdown, however, my interviewees seemed not to break a sweat.

“I think … everyone is holding things very peacefully, recognizing that we can give guidance, and it may change within a few hours or by the end of the day, so just be flexible, be adaptable, be patient as much as you can,” said Zane Zovak, a 2019 Baylor alumnus. He now works in the Department of Commerce and has spent much of his time in D.C. focused on national security and Chinese foreign policy.

Photo generated using ChatGPT and Photoroom

Two recent grads, as of May 2025, didn’t envision their first few months on the job involving a nationwide government shutdown. Caroline Williams, staff assistant for Texas Senator Ted Cruz, and Reagan Havel, staff assistant for the U.S. House of Representatives, both shared their thoughts.

“The entire office is still coming in because we’re still continuously working around the clock to help Texans because that is the senator’s priority. He cares first and foremost for Texans. … I really think everyone’s still happy to come in and do the work and realize that it’s a privilege to work for who we work for and just continue keeping on to save the country,” Williams said.

“I really think everyone’s still happy to come in and do the work and realize that it’s a privilege to work for who we work for and just continue keeping on to save the country.”

Havel drew the same conclusion about the attitude in her workplace. “Everyone on the outside is freaking out. But I think in this case, it just seemed kind of inevitable from the get-go. And I think it’s probably because the House passed their budget that things just seem less stressful over here, because we’re like, ‘we did our job.’”

Former U.S. Representative Jack Fields has worked in and around the government since he graduated from Baylor as an undergrad in 1974, and from the law school in 1977. His attitude was unwavering and one of someone who has seen the ebb and flow of government over the years. “Changing government is not bad. I believe God’s given us the greatest government that’s ever existed. And forefathers I think were enlightened by God because otherwise how could they have created a system of such good checks and balances?… So, when people look at our current situation and, you know, think, ‘Is this the way America is going to be?’ It’s not. It’s going to go back and forth. And that’s what our forefathers envisioned. And I think that’s the genius of our system. It all reflects back to people utilizing their right to participate and vote. People make the change.”

“So, when people look at our current situation and, you know, think, ‘Is this the way America is going to be?’ It’s not. It’s going to go back and forth. And that’s what our forefathers envisioned.”

Photo generated by ChatGPT

These low-stress responses had me scratching my head on why there was no external panic or anxiety from them. Apart from the obvious lack of control over the turnout, the answer pointed back to their responses on what Baylor taught them and how the school shaped their lives.

Fields had nothing but kind words to say about the school. “I believe that everything that has a truth in God. God has a has a plan for everything. Baylor is a very important part of who I am and what I’ve accomplished. Without Baylor, none of that could have been possible. Baylor is a laboratory of success. Baylor breeds success. I’m very proud to say I’ve gone to Baylor. I never felt like I was ever outclassed by somebody from Harvard or Yale or Stanford or any of those schools.”

“Baylor is a laboratory of success. Baylor breeds success.”

Zovak’s response was not far from that, either. He bragged on the professors and the relationships that were formed over the years of his time at Baylor. “Something I take away from Baylor, it’s Thursday professionalism, but also emphasis on interpersonal nature and that only proves to be more and more true as I’ve left Baylor.”

A bit later, he mentioned the impact that Baylor’s faith culture has had on him. “Something that also was a key factor of my time with Baylor was having a church small group and community that could support you in all the different ways, but also just kind of keep you grounded. People that, even when other things that were out your control took a dip, reminds you that, hey, eternally, you know, things are still as they always were,” Zovak said.

Several of them also spoke highly of the bipartisan friendships and relationships that occur in the city. There’s the idea that Capitol Hill is constant arguments and backstabbing, but they were quick to shut that down.

“There’s a lot more bipartisanship than people ever realize, which is so cool … I mean you’re always going to find that, but it’s a lot less than what I thought. It also just depends on who and what you want to surround yourself with,” Williams said. It’s clear that Baylor fosters a sense of perseverance and groundedness that is often tough to find in a largely secular world, and especially in what can be a tense and fast-paced environment such as Capitol Hill. In the midst of circling questions like back payment, job security, and the future of the government, these Baylor alumni are in no rush to panic. Taking the lessons they have learned from their time in Waco to the workforce has left an ease in the air that is, without a doubt, impacting their work attitude for themselves and those around them.

item.title: The Campus Crucible: Gen Z and America’s Realignment
item.description:
If you want to see where U.S. politics is going, walk across a college quad. The tidy split that defined the Bush/Clinton years (neoliberal technocrats vs. neoconservative hawks) has fractured. In its place, two coalitions are emerging in parallel: a reorganized left (labor-forward, intersectional, antiwar) and a reorganized right (populist, post-liberal, openly religious). Even at a Baptist university like Baylor, the new alignments are unmistakable.

The old consensus is out of favor

Polls show the ground moving. Americans’ positive view of capitalism has slid to 54%, a series low in Gallup’s tracking, with Democrats especially skeptical (only 42% favorable). At the same time, Democrats are more open to “socialism” (about 66% favorable), reflecting a broader re-think of economic orthodoxy among younger voters. (AP explainer on the poll.)

Trust in institutions is also scraping bottom among the young. In the Spring 2025 Harvard Youth Poll, only 19% of 18- to 29-year-olds said they trust the federal government to do the right thing all or most of the time; the U.S. military (40%) and Supreme Court (29%) aren’t much better, and only 39% of enrolled four-year students feel comfortable sharing their political views on campus without fear of repercussions.

On foreign policy, the generational split is starkest around Israel/Gaza and Ukraine. Younger adults sympathize less with Israel than older Americans and are more likely to say U.S. leaders are too favorable to Israel, trends that have intensified since 2024. And while the public overall still backs aid to Ukraine, Millennials and Gen Z show the lowest enthusiasm for sending economic assistance compared to older cohorts.

The younger generation is shifting their beliefs on issues their parents took for granted. The political coalitions they belong to have shifted to meet them.

The new left: labor, liberation, and antiwar energy

On campus, the reorganized left is not a monolith: it’s a coalition. First, there’s a labor-forward revival: young people are now the most pro-union Americans, with around three-quarters of 18–34-year-olds approving of unions in 2024 Gallup data, per a summary from the Center for American Progress. Overall union approval remains near historic highs.

Second, there’s an intersectional protest wing that links racial justice, LGBTQ rights, climate action, and anti-imperialism. That energy has increasingly flowed into Palestine solidarity work since Oct. 7. At Baylor, two seniors organized a cease-fire demonstration at Waco City Hall days after the attacks, hoping to “educate on the Free Palestine movement.” Baylor’s administration, for its part, joined other university leaders in a statement “standing with Israel” and calling the fight against Hamas “a fight against evil.”

Context matters at Baylor. As a professor of political science at Baylor, David Bridge notes that “there’s relatively fewer left… Democrat students at Baylor,” and those who are left-leaning are often closer to old Southern Democrats: “still a little socially conservative, economically liberal.” “You don’t really get as much of that progressive Ocasio-Cortez wing of the party,” he said. Bridge also sees frustration on Baylor’s left: “[They’re] frustrated by their complete inability to win elections… Why should I try? Why should I vote?”: a mood he described as “a resignation that the party leadership is poor.”

Dr. David Bridge

The new right: populist, post-liberal, and unafraid of state power

The right has diversified. The MAGA-populist strand prioritizes immigration and crime and leans into anti-elite sentiment common to modern populism; it also frames campus free speech as a counter-power and eagerly hosts provocative speakers (e.g., YAF’s Ben Shapiro lecture tours). A smaller but noisy post-liberal/NatCon wing embraces religious traditionalism, argues for conservative-leaning industrial policy, and favors foreign-policy restraint over liberal-imperial nation-building.

At Baylor, these factions are visible. Bridge notes that today’s right-leaning students are more likely to question free-market dogma and accept a larger state role than in the pre-2016 GOP, even as abortion and gender remain red-line issues. In practice, he says, MAGA has shifted the agenda to immigration, and many religious conservatives have made peace with that emphasis while keeping their own priorities. He observes that Christian conservatives still have a “good faith view” on things like immigration and tax policy, issues which don’t present saliently to them.

The department chair of Political Science at Baylor, Patrick Flavin, adds that outsiders often imagine Baylor as a monolith, but the student body now runs “from super liberal to super conservative,” and club activity reflects that pluralism. He notes that “there’s probably more enthusiasm for different conservative student groups… there are… several different conservative groups.” In the classroom, he sees intra-right clashes that didn’t surface a decade ago: “a more traditional Republican free-market view sort of clash[es] up against… a Republican push for more government intervention in a way that… ten years ago, I would not have expected from more right-leaning students.”

“A more traditional Republican free-market view sort of clash[es] up against… a Republican push for more government intervention in a way that… ten years ago, I would not have expected from more right-leaning students.” Dr. Patrick Flavin

Where the lines blur

Free speech

Students across the spectrum feel chilled: just in different ways. Only about 39% of four-year students say they feel comfortable sharing political views on campus without fear, per the 2025 Harvard Youth Poll. Longer-running work by the Knight Foundation tracking post-2016 student perspectives on free speech finds similar apprehension about speaking freely online and in class. Interestingly, the same report noted the “politically diverse” perspectives on speech restrictions: “no single party emerges as a dominant supporter of restrictions on either issue.”

Foreign policy

An anti-war skepticism now stretches from democratic socialists to libertarian conservatives and some post-liberals. Younger Americans are consistently more critical of U.S. policy toward Israel/Gaza than their elders, and recent polling shows younger cohorts least supportive of arming Ukraine.

Baylor as microcosm and exception

Baylor University, with its conservative Baptist heritage, might seem an unlikely venue for avant-garde political change. But in many ways, Baylor encapsulates the currents of this realignment, albeit filtered through its unique context. Students and faculty say outsiders often misread Baylor’s climate. “They think Baylor is monolithic, like all our students are Bible-thumping Republicans,” says Dr. Patrick Flavin, “but that’s certainly not the case”. In classrooms, he sees the full spectrum “from super liberal to super conservative,” and notes that ideological diversity has grown as Baylor expanded and attracted students from around the country. Yet, Flavin also notes polarization: “For both left and right, at least the most vocal and visible … those on the left [are] moving further to the left, and those on the right … moving further to the right … there does seem to be sort of a greater distance between the two sides.”

Dr. Patrick Flavin

Indeed, both Flavin and Bridge indicate that political discourse on campus has intensified post-2016, with more stark clashes but also more energy. Flavin senses “more enthusiasm” for conservative clubs after Trump’s rise, and Bridge remarks that Baylor’s left-leaning students have become somewhat demoralized by constant losses in red-state Texas (leading to apathy), whereas MAGA-type students tasted victory and remain highly mobilized.

Where Baylor differs from, say, Berkeley or even UT-Austin is in its institutional constraints. The administration and board are vigilant to keep the university’s Christian values intact, as noted in the University’s mission statement. That means certain activist causes face obstacles here that they wouldn’t elsewhere. The LGBTQ+ research grant episode is one example; another is the long struggle by Baylor’s LGBTQ student group to receive official recognition (Baylor only recently allowed an unofficial group, and it still must navigate strict rules).
