On the other hand, Baylor’s mission also creates openings for cross-ideological alliance on issues like peace, ethics, and even skepticism of power.

Baylor’s cross-cutting religious identity thus sometimes reshuffles the coalitions: a progressive Baptist student and a traditionalist Catholic student might find themselves agreeing on the importance of peacemaking abroad, even as they diverge fiercely on abortion or LGBTQ issues. And Baylor’s emphasis on respectful discourse, repeatedly noted by interviewed faculty, provides a forum for these debates to occur more civilly than at many secular campuses. “Baylor students really want to hear each other out… it’s admirable, the level of civil discourse,” Dr. Bridge said.

The same Gen Z impulses (disillusionment with elites, search for authentic community, left-wing yearning for solidarity, right-wing desire for order) are all present, but channeled through Baylor’s Christian collegiate culture.

In sum, Baylor shows how the national realignment filters through a local lens. The same Gen Z impulses (disillusionment with elites, search for authentic community, left-wing yearning for solidarity, right-wing desire for order) are all present, but channeled through Baylor’s Christian collegiate culture.

What comes next

Two scenarios feel plausible. One is a pro-worker, anti-war left facing a pro-family, America-First right, leaving centrist establishments stranded. Another is a cross-ideological civil-liberties coalition: students who disagree on nearly everything but agree that open inquiry and pluralism are worth fighting for. Either way, this generation is reshaping the terms of debate.

The question for universities is whether they’ll make room for the realignment to unfold without turning every disagreement into a speech code fight or a donor-driven veto. And the question for students is whether they’ll translate campus coalitions into durable politics off campus.

If the quad is the preview, the next decade won’t look like the last one.

item.title: “Don’t Wait to be Taught.” A Workforce Expert on Why All Baylor Students Should Learn How to Use AI
item.description:
Workforce expert Brent Orrell has a message for all college students, regardless of their major: “You’re not going to have the option of not learning how to use AI.”

Orrell, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, has worked on workforce development policy for more than 20 years, including as Assistant Secretary at the Department of Labor. In the past few years, his research has focused on how AI will change the job market, and how we can respond.

In an interview with The Standard, Orrell shared his advice on how college students can make themselves more employable in an AI economy and how to make AI “work for you without substituting for you.”

Brent Orrell

Orrell highlighted the unique challenges facing college students who will graduate in the next few years. “We’re clearly seeing a slowdown in hiring for entry-level, white-collar positions. Those are the kinds of jobs that recent college grads have specialized in filling.”

While Orrell noted that AI is only one of several factors that have likely contributed to this slowdown, AI competency will be a “big factor going forward” in how employers evaluate recent graduates.

“We’re moving away from the knowledge economy and toward the judgment economy,” Orrell explains. AI will produce a “real tidal wave of information analysis.” Employers will need “people who have the ability to assess that information.” Employers will need people who can think a level deeper than ChatGPT and ask “Is it true? Is it wise? Is it moral?” rather than “plugging numbers into a spreadsheet.”

“We’re moving away from the knowledge economy and toward the judgment economy,” Orrell explains. AI will produce a “real tidal wave of information analysis.”

So what can we do to prepare? First, undergrads should “do whatever they can to familiarize themselves with some of the major tools: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity.”

Orrell recognized that most Baylor students are not allowed to use AI for school assignments, and instead recommended they weave AI into their everyday tasks like chore lists and trip planning. He also recommended using online courses to teach yourself AI skills. “Don’t wait for somebody else to teach you. There’s so much of this you can learn on your own.”

Orrell’s advice is backed up by the numbers. The major consulting firm PwC reported in June that AI-skilled workers benefited from an average 56% wage premium in 2024, double the 25% wage premium the year before.

Baylor provides several AI resources for students, including a Canvas-based AI literacy course and a student guide to generative AI.

Additionally, Orrell encouraged undergrads to use their remaining time in college to develop a broader set of skills than they may have initially planned. “Most undergrads don’t end up using their degrees in a specific sense. It’s the underlying skills that you want to emphasize if you’re a history major, research and writing. If you’re a psychology major, human insights and relationships.” Orrell emphasized “soft,” personal skills over “hard,” technical skills. “If you’re a finance major,” Orrell added, “I would make darn sure that you understand what’s going on in the finance sector relative to AI.”

Orrell encouraged students of all majors to research the current state of the job market in their intended fields and locations. If they need help, he suggested they “ask AI.” Give a chatbot a little information about your future plans, and ask what skills you should be developing to prepare.

“The number one thing that employers are concerned about is, do you work well with others and can you communicate?”

Orrell shared some specific tips on adapting your resume for an AI job market. He identified two things students should emphasize: first, “your agility with and ethical use of AI” and second “that you have a broad set of skills that make you a good learner on the job when confronted with new technology or new questions that you have to answer.” To demonstrate a broad skillset, Orrell recommends that students should incorporate their broader interests and hobbies toward the top of their resume. Hobbies that demonstrate social skills, like organizing a pickup basketball league, are especially important. “The number one thing that employers are concerned about is, do you work well with others and can you communicate?”

Every Baylor student will need to learn how to compete in a job market saturated with AI. Instead of waiting for their classes to give them those skills, they should take the opportunity to learn on their own and get a headstart on the AI future.

Orrell plans to visit Baylor for an Alexander Hamilton Society speaking event in February.

item.title: Bourbon Bluegrass and the Bible: The Hillbilly Thomists Visit Baylor
item.description:
Imagine the look of surprise on the faces of Baylor’s founders at the sight of five Dominican priests calling themselves The Hillbilly Thomists playing bluegrass music in long white robes at Jones Concert Hall. On September 24th, the bluegrass-chart-topping band hosted a concert at Baylor as part of the Baylor Nicea Symposium, hosted through the Institute for Faith and Learning. These friars from the Catholic Order of Preachers, founded in 1216, used guitars, a fiddle, a banjo, even a metal washboard to make a joyful chorus. Three hundred people broke the Baylor rule against dancing that ended only 50 years ago, all on their feet, dancing and clapping. With the songs “Bourbon, Bluegrass, and the Bible” and “Holy Ghost Power,” they got our dry campus rocking like an old-time revival. Very old-time, as in 13th century.

Fr. Justin, the vocalist and guitar player for the band, explained that bluegrass is “a fitting vehicle for the Gospel because of its joy.” This joy was apparent. Children, professors, and college students clapped and danced to the lyrics of “Heaven or Tennessee” and “Weight of Eternal Glory.” They had come to preach the gospel through joy and bluegrass. Their voices shouting in falsetto highs and to a low bass, were as far away from auto-tune as possible. For Fr. Justin, this “earthiness” found in bluegrass makes the proclamation of grace only more clear.

According to Fr. Justin this “earthiness” can be found in their namesake, Flannery O’Connor, the original Hillbilly Thomist. She was a Catholic Appalachian oddity living on a farm in the mountains of Georgia. She wrote bizarre stories of God in the lives of hillbillies in the 1940s and 1950s. As Fr. Justin explained, O’ Conner sought “to explore the way grace breaks into the world and often disrupts it, she wanted to do that through earthy examples in down-home, kind of southern experience; she loved painting those pictures of how grace moves in that.”

Many Christians are tempted to withdraw from the world in pursuit of God. Yet Fr. Justin believes that Christ has expanded our choices. “We inherited original sin, but grace is the very form that restores the integrity of our nature, body, and soul. Grace makes us more human.”

This revival of grace, Fr. Justin explained, is how we can balance following Christ while still living in the world. The band harmonizes this in their music. He explained that “there’s a temptation going towards one side of our human nature, angelism, I need to be perfect, or on the other side, the animal, the hedonist.” Many Christians are tempted to withdraw from the world in pursuit of God. Yet Fr. Justin believes that Christ has expanded our choices. “We inherited original sin, but grace is the very form that restores the integrity of our nature, body, and soul. Grace makes us more human. That is our nature. We are human.” These Dominicans believe Christ’s grace completes us and fulfills us. Christ wishes for us to be what we already are: human beings.

One of The Hillbilly Thomist’s most popular songs, “Bourbon, Bluegrass, and the Bible,” celebrates grace in everyday life. They are“talking about grace and talking about sin,” finding revival in the middle of the world. In the song, God speaks to the Southern protagonist who discovers through his banjo and Bible a revival of grace, and a desire to live for the other side. Flannery O’Connor believed that the human thing is beautiful because grace transforms everything. O’Connor believed that if we look past the human to find God, we are missing Him, and if in the sinner we only see sin, we miss again.

O’Connor believed that if we look past the human to find God, we are missing Him, and if in the sinner we only see sin, we miss again.

O’Connor illustrates this in her famous story “Parker’s Back.” The protagonist, E.B. Parker, burst into Sarah Ruth’s life in an explosion of curses and tattoos. The pair couldn’t be more different. Sarah Ruth’s plain face and judgmental eyes, “forever sniffing up sin,” make her incapable of ever finding grace in this world. Because of his worldliness and her fixation on sin, both think of God as absent. To her, his tattoos are “a heap of vanities” because they are colorful, while to Parker they awaken the uniqueness of a human person. He covers himself in tattoos, everywhere besides his back, for “he does not readily see it himself.” He has reserved a space for the view of others. Despite their differences, the couple marries. Parker suffers months of her judgmental and sharp ways. After falling into a trance-like state and crashing a tractor, he feels he must fill the empty space on his back with “God.” On returning to Sarah Ruth, Parker uses his full name, “Obadiah Elihue,” “God’s servant.” He hopes Sarah Ruth will love the image of God on his back. But instead she repeats, “It ain’t anybody I know.” She screams in anger at him, “Idolatry! Inflaming yourself with idols,” and beats him senseless. O’Connor shows that the sinner Parker finds Christ moving in the world, yet his wife is unwilling to see Christ in anything. She can’t see grace in odd places because she has limited grace to her narrow view.

Flannery O’Connor

The Hillbilly Thomists want us to see Christ in everything and in ourselves. In our strangeness, quirks, fears, and ugliness, we are living for the other side. Like Parker, we are a canvas for the image of Christ. The same can be said for these priests who seem so bizarre on stage: they are truly letting Christ transform their talents into instruments of grace. Fr. Justin believes that this idea of transformational grace should fill us with joy. When I asked Fr. Justin how Christians should go about enjoying life, he responded excitedly. “Go out on Saturday night and be joyful. But how do we do it virtuously? Grace lets us.” This sentiment is echoed in the lyrics of their song “Saturday Night,” where they sang “Like old Hank Williams, I saw the light / because I found salvation on a Saturday night.” The band believes that to live “for the other side” requires celebrating well: dancing and singing with God’s creation.

The Hillbilly Thomists want us to see Christ in everything and in ourselves. In our strangeness, quirks, fears, and ugliness, we are living for the other side. Like Parker, we are a canvas for the image of Christ.

Yet joy is not the whole story of our lives. Sorrow is evident in both our lives and the gospels. Does the cheerful tone of bluegrass miss the sorrow of life? Fr. Justin said no: “the lyrics [of bluegrass] are sad and are about even death, but in a jubilant register. I think that’s weird, but also Christian, that there is suffering and even great suffering and suffering of death, that final suffering.” Fr. Justin shows that life and joy and sorrow are mixed in the gospels. He continues: “we are confident in the Lord’s victory over death and that our souls will go on. So to live in grace is to live in the Lord. He has us on the next side and the next part of the journey. The virtue of hope really comes in here.”

The Hillbilly Thomist’s song “Veronica” tells the story of Saint Veronica, the woman who wiped the face of suffering Christ on his walk to Calvary, and saw his suffering face appear on her cloth. They pray that, like her, someday they “will see him face to face.” Suffering always graces our lives, and as the band said in the concert, “Christ’s suffering allows us to see and be taken to heaven so that we may be like him and fulfill who we really are.” Christ’s sacrifice brings a harmony to our sorrow and joy. This hope “strengthens the soul to cling to God and to go towards what is good, even when things are difficult.” The Hillbilly Thomists are calling all who live under the weight of eternal glory, regardless of your strengths or interests, to live for the other side.

The Hillbilly Thomists, an unlikely troupe of friars, bring together theology and music to preach a grace that redeems man in all his strangeness. They sing that we must “live for the other side” by being truly ourselves. The strange and beautiful will be redeemed.

“When it’s a question of love and survival

Bourbon, bluegrass, and the Bible.”

item.title: Religion in Government: Lessons From a Supreme Court Attorney and Charlie Kirk
item.description:
Every successful nation must be founded on religious principles, otherwise, the only authority lies within a government run by imperfect people. The United States must honor this tradition or risk falling into the vicious cycles of immorality that have destroyed empires.

Our first guarantee as Americans is freedom of religion. Why did the Founders include this before anything else? In his book, The Right to Be Wrong, Seamus Hasson argues that our religious beliefs and practices are a part of our conscience. It’s something that we don’t get to choose, it is rather a deeply ingrained part of who we are. Our religious beliefs are our motivation, they are what inspire us to keep moving, growing, thinking, and feeling. The Founders of our nation understood the power these beliefs have over the human conscience, and they showed their reverence for it, Thomas Jefferson once writing, “For I have sworn upon the altar of god eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man.”

William Haun is an attorney at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the firm that Seamus Hasson founded in 1994, and most recently, he successfully argued Mahoud v Taylor in front of the Supreme Court of the United States. His appellate work in defense of our first amendment freedoms is extensive, and his knowledge of our country’s history and religious liberties runs deep.

Will Huan, Attorney at Becket

When asked about the inception of religious liberty, its foundation within our nation, and the effect it has on our modern institutions, he first points to George Washington’s Farewell Address where Washington warns the American people about what he foresees for this nation. Haun acknowledges these warnings and notes that “we’re essentially aware of no example of a political community that has ever existed, let alone sustained itself, without a recognition of higher authority – a transcendent, God-given authority.”

The Soviet Union is a prime example of this. It actively removed religion from society and government, establishing a completely secular state. Many consider what happened in this country by one of its foremost leaders, Joseph Stalin, to have been a genocide. “If you don’t accept that there’s a certain power that transcends the state, you’ve embraced totalitarianism,” Haun explains.

“If you don’t accept that there’s a certain power that transcends the state, you’ve embraced totalitarianism”

When those who run a government don’t recognize a higher power, they begin to see themselves as their own god. Haun argues that communism is inherently atheist because it requires complete state control, and God cannot be controlled, so these leaders do their best to take religion out of public life. Believing in a higher authority requires putting complete trust into something that is not the state, understanding that some things must be left to Him rather than controlled by a government. Haun says, “Because religious duties transcend state power, there’s an inherent limit on what the state can do in that area.” It begs the question if a government rooted in atheism would be able to establish and protect religious freedom like the United States does.

Haun later referenced Justice Alito’s dissent in Yeshiva University v. YU Pride Alliance when asked how this idea of atheism in command affects our institutions. As Justice Alito explains in his dissent, Yeshiva is the premiere undergraduate university for Jewish students in the United States, honoring its religious traditions and living in accordance with them. However, they are now required to allow an official pride alliance group on campus despite their religious commitment.

Many universities fall to public pressure before they even reach the point of a legal battle. As our local, state, and federal governments turn more toward these atheistic tendencies, religious institutions often give in and willingly allow organizations like YU Pride Alliance to come onto their campuses before they risk losing federal funding. Baylor is one of them. In 2022, PRISM, an LGBTQ+ student organization, was granted a charter despite Baylor’s official policies on the “biblical understanding of sexuality” described in their Statement on Human Sexuality.

Justice Alito said in his dissent, “The First Amendment guarantees the right to the free exercise of religion, and if that provision means anything, it prohibits a State from enforcing its own preferred interpretation of Holy Scripture.” When a government, like the state of New York where this case originates, does not respect religious freedom, it undermines the foundation of who we are as a nation.

“The First Amendment guarantees the right to the free exercise of religion, and if that provision means anything, it prohibits a State from enforcing its own preferred interpretation of Holy Scripture”

Despite our forgetfulness of the necessary influences religion has on our governing system, Haun says there’s hope. “What we’re seeing is a much more religiously informed engagement with public life.”

Most recently, the assassination of Charlie Kirk has sparked conversations about bringing religious values into politics. Kirk claimed that there was a revival in the church, and in the weeks following his death, faith leaders reported an increase in church attendance. Matt Zerrusen, the co-founder of a Catholic nonprofit organization called Newman Ministry, claims that in many of the 200 campuses his organization operates in, they have seen 15% more students attending Mass.

An X post from Charlie Kirk in September

Kirk’s memorial service in Washington D.C. attracted dozens of congressmen and thousands of others, including myself, a student directly impacted by him. There were remarks by Speaker Mike Johnson, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr., and more. The consistent theme in each speech was how important religion is to our society. They applauded Kirk for his political outreach that brought thousands of young Americans to the faith. It was refreshing to hear politicians unafraid to announce their faith as they often conceal it to appear neutral.

As an intern at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty this semester, I have seen our justice system misinterpret religious freedom. It was given to us as a right, not to the government. The government doesn’t need protection from religion, but the Founding Fathers knew that our religious institutions and traditions needed protection from the government. Many of them were keenly aware that religion had to be the foundation of any great nation, but they also knew that our country would go through cycles of turning from religion, and those would be the times that our constitutional rights would protect us.

Even during times when religion declines in America, we still have these constitutional protections. Atheists have these protections too, but only because of the value that religious men put into their freedoms when drafting our governing documents. The United States and any nation who wishes to obtain the success that has made us a world power needs the same religious protections that can only be provided by people with a religious conscience.

item.title: The Alexander Hamilton Society hosts U.S.-Russian relations expert, invites student participation
item.description:
Since the end of World War II, U.S. relations with Russia have been a bumpy ride, ranging from competition for preeminence in a newly bipolar world to the U.S. identifying the Soviet Union as an “evil empire.” While both nations consider maintaining a relationship important, especially with nuclear weapons in the mix, Russia resents the hegemonic power of the U.S. and claims that alliances such as NATO create a security threat. According to Jeffery Edmonds, a former director for Russia in the U.S. National Security Council, “The Russian leadership’s ultimate goal is the creation of a new polycentric world order in which great powers have spheres of influence and privilege over smaller countries.” This drive to reassert Russia’s lost power and become a world power once again, combined with its autocratic regime, serves as a contrast to the U.S.’s interests.

With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, a sovereign democratic nation, the U.S. is now forced to take a blatant adversarial stance against the nation. According to The Center for Preventative Action’s Global Conflict Tracker, “Ukraine has received about $407 billion in aid, including over $118 billion from the United States.”

With U.S.-Russian relations being such an important part of foreign affairs, Baylor’s chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society (AHS) brought in Daniel Twining, president of the International Republican Institute and former foreign policy advisor to Senator John McCain, to speak on U.S.-Russian relations. Baylor political science professor Richard Jordan moderated Twining’s talk, asking questions ranging from the Ukraine war to what books would provide good insight into the mind of a Russian.

Danielle Miller, a Baylor senior and president of Baylor’s AHS chapter, described the enthusiasm of event attendees. Miller said, “We had about a dozen students stay after the event to ask Dr. Twining questions about his work, about his opinions on the war in Ukraine. They were just all gathered around him in a little circle, and he was really excited to talk to them. That just shows me how curious and sincere and invested our AHS members are.”

Photo by Stella Tognocchi

The Alexander Hamilton Society is a non-partisan, national organization that encourages dialogue and intellectual growth within higher education by analyzing U.S. foreign, economic, and national security policies. The national organization helps campus chapters bring in experts in a variety of fields and foster meaningful engagement with today’s pressing issues. Miller summarized the goals of the chapter: “To supplement the political science department at Baylor with experts who are working, working on this stuff, on governing political science, foreign policy on the ground, and who can provide our students with a concrete, rigorous glimpse into what’s going on right now in D.C. on a topic that they’re interested in and then to build a network of students who can learn from each other and provide each other with opportunities.”

This organization provides a great resource to students interested in foreign policy, as it is bi-partisan and does not require a certain number of attendance points to be a part of. Additionally, AHS has built an extensive network of alumni in Washington D.C.

Photo by Stella Tognocchi

Following the death of political activist Charlie Kirk, AHS held a panel on political violence, featuring professors from Baylor’s political science department. Miller moderated the event, and the professors shared insights on the history of political violence in the U.S. and globally, providing important context for how and why these things happen. Following every speaker event or moderated panel, students have time to ask questions.

When reflecting on the success of the event Miller said, “It convinced me once again that Baylor students are ready to engage with even the most controversial, emotional, hot-button topics in a reasoned, academic, open-minded, simple way, and that’s what I love about our club.”

“Baylor students are ready to engage with even the most controversial, emotional, hot-button topics in a reasoned, academic, open-minded, simple way.”

Baylor’s AHS chapter is a great way for students interested in U.S. politics, foreign policy, economics, and diplomacy to learn more about these topics and hear from experts in these fields. The club also holds movie nights which can provide Creative Arts Experience (CAE) credits, which are a graduation requirement, and hosts student discussions about relevant issues. The next AHS speaker event is set for October 16. There, students will learn about AI and diplomacy from Bonnie Glick, a non-resident senior advisor with the Project on Prosperity and Development at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

item.title: A Conversation with a Supreme Court Justice: Brett Kavanaugh Visits Local Community College
item.description:
On September 11th, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh visited McLennan Community College (MCC) as part of the Ken Starr Lecture Series. His visit drew a packed auditorium of students, professors, and local residents—as well as a line of protestors voicing their opposition to Justice Kavanaugh’s recent Supreme Court Rulings.

Justice Kavanaugh’s appearance consisted of a private conversation and a public event. He engaged with a limited number of students from MCC, five Tarleton State Honors students, and five students from the Baylor Honors College. Later that evening, Justice Kavanaugh addressed the public at MCC through a conversation moderated by MCC Professor Ashley Cruseturner. There were 2,500 seats reserved for the public event.

Alice Starr, the wife of former Federal Judge and Solicitor General Kenneth Starr, provided opening remarks at the event. Mrs. Starr noted her long-standing relationship with Justice Kavanaugh, sharing that “It was on 9/11/2001, 24 years ago today, that my husband, Ken, and I were to have lunch at the White House mess with Brett Kavanaugh.” Justice Kavanaugh worked under Kenneth Starr during his time as Associate Counsel in the Office of Independent Counsel. “Judge Kavanaugh is a man of complete integrity. Although his credentials are elite, he could not be more humble or more friendly and kind to others,” acclaimed Alice Starr.

Justice Kavanaugh with MCC’s Ashley Cruseturner

The Justice spoke on topics ranging from the role of the judiciary and the brilliance of the U.S. Constitution to his friendship with President G.W. Bush. “I think the genius of the Constitution is its separation of powers,” said Kavanaugh, “[the separation of powers] protects individual liberty by dividing powers, preventing concentration of power, and thereby ensuring that each person can live in liberty.” Justice Kavanaugh likened his role in the Supreme Court to that of a referee, noting that it is the role of the Judiciary to act as an umpire for the “teams,” or rather, the political parties. He said, “One of the things that makes a good umpire or a referee among others is consistency—calling it the same way for both teams.”

“One of the things that makes a good umpire or a referee among others is consistency—calling it the same way for both teams.”

Professor Cruseturner asked if there is a “sense among the justices that some cases are more important than others, that some are going to be more controversial than others, and some are going to be more contested than others? And what’s that like?” Justice Kavanaugh responded by outlining the important balance between remaining steadfast in decisions and being open to learning from the public. “You’ve got to not be afraid,” noted Kavanaugh, “You can’t worry about criticism. But at the same time, you can’t tune out responsible critiques. I always want to do better tomorrow than I did today, every day. I want the court to always do better.”

The Justice recalled how he learned some of his most valuable lessons in leadership. He pointed to one of his favorite books, To Kill a Mockingbird, and an insight from his elementary school teacher. “He said the lesson [in] To Kill a Mockingbird was standing in someone else’s shoes. And that’s a reminder to me. I think to be a good judge, to be a good person, to be a good citizen, we all have to stand in each other’s shoes to understand different perspectives.”

Justice Kavanaugh is well-known for his dedication to the Catholic faith. When asked a question regarding how he balances his faith with his duty as a judge, he explained, “my faith is central to me, my personal [life], but I take an oath to apply the Constitution and laws of the United States without regarding what my faith might dictate, what my moral views might be, what my policy might be.” His faith is “very helpful in reminding [him] of the bigger picture of life” and reinforcing how he operates and treats other people. However, Justice Kavanaugh emphasized the importance of an independent, impartial judiciary whose responsibility it is to say what the law is, not what it ought to be.

Justice Kavanaugh emphasized the importance of an independent, impartial judiciary whose responsibility it is to say what the law is, not what it ought to be.

The audience reacted very positively to Justice Kavanaugh throughout his conversation, even giving him a standing ovation at one point. Outside of the auditorium, however, was a line of protestors gathered with signs that read “We will not be quiet” and “Women’s rights = human rights” among others.

Protestors Stand Outside of MCC Auditorium

Jay Gordan Mitchell, a local resident who is running for the Texas Senate, was among the protestors. He voiced his frustration with the recent Supreme Court rulings, saying that “You do not get to legislate and dictate and direct policy or have policy directed by the executive branch to you, that’s not your job. Your job is to be the checks and balances.”

Jay Gordan Mitchell Protesting

The protest was promoted by several community and university organizations, including Waco Friends of the Climate and The College Democrats of Baylor. Baylor senior and President of The College Democrats of Baylor, J.W. Lastrape, commented on his involvement with the protest. He conveyed his dissatisfaction with the ICE deportations and the Supreme Court’s rulings on executive authority. He said “It seems like your goal isn’t to follow the law, your goal is to be vindictive and punish people, which for Christians I would expect better, but you know, it is what it is.”

Supreme Court Justices seldom make public appearances, let alone host private conversations and public speaking events at community colleges. Most notable in recent history, McLennan Community College hosted Justice Clarence Thomas in 2017.

item.title: The Red Mirage: Why Gen Z’s Communist Crush Blinds Them to Bloodshed
item.description:
“Wouldn’t it be fun to go to a protest this week?”

As I heard that while interning in Washington, D.C., I was immediately alarmed at the will of my young colleague. To engage in protest for the pure fulfillment it might bring to social status or weekend plans, unfortunately, wasn’t a new idea.

Advocacy is a pillar to the role of virtuous civic engagement. The butter to the bread of democratic success. Though, it has become more apparent that the motivation behind spreading that butter has long shifted beyond both the necessity and national nourishment it once served. As if the Founding Fathers’ ideal for a sacred right, born from conscious experience and revelation, and protected in the Bill of Rights, was morphed into a trendy pastime that served nothing beyond performative leisure.

The Founding Fathers’ ideal for a sacred right, born from conscious experience and revelation, and protected in the Bill of Rights, was morphed into a trendy pastime that served nothing beyond performative leisure.

By bending personal will in a way that satisfies merely cultural obligations, protest for the sake it once served has become old news among many young Americans.

Hearing my peers’ casual suggestion, I was not only struck by the trivial form protest has taken, but how deeply the language of activism, and in many cases revolution, has become ingrained into recreational ideology.

On TikTok, it seems that Karl Marx is having a moment. A history of oppression has now been adapted as a solution to the nation’s problems in just about every policy issue from environmentalism to gender gaps. A trendy solution to the downfalls of free markets, communist ideology has slowly crept its way back into classrooms and college campuses across the nation in the form of misaligned nostalgia that performatively seeks to correct injustice by blindly ignoring a history of, you guessed it, injustice.

In April, I stood in Tallinn, Estonia, among the Scot pines, many of which stood tall during the horrific days of Soviet occupation across Eastern Europe. I was visiting the Maarjamäe Kommunismiohvrite Memoriaal, or Maarjamäe Victims of Communism Memorial. I read thousands of names over a span of hours, all of whom succumbed to the brutal repression and political persecution of the Estonian Soviet Socialist Republic (ESSR) regime.

The memorial marked the end of Soviet occupation and persecution of more than 90,000 Estonians between 1941 and 1991, the year Estonia gained its formal independence. Yet it did more than signify an ending, but rather a new beginning free from the totalitarian control of the USSR.

A brief story of the Estonia Singing Revolution was engraved on a small plaque at the entrance to the memorial. I thought about what it would be like to be able to hear the sounds of over 300,000 brothers and sisters locked in arms resounding with symphonies of desired freedom. The type of freedom that doesn’t beg for attention or demand applause, but only asks to be preserved.

The type of freedom that doesn’t beg for attention or demand applause, but only asks to be preserved.

I thought about the fathers; those brave enough to speak out not for themselves, but their children, only to be rewarded with death in the noble pursuit against despotism. I thought about the mothers tucking their children in each night, only to be met with the reality that their child might not come back from school the next. Selfishly, I also thought about myself—the opportunities that have led me to be in a position to only vaguely imagine what enduring real, and visceral persecution is like.

Meanwhile, 4,000 miles away and 30 years later, the same type of advocacy and protest that ultimately freed millions from the shackles of tyranny was being touted around as a half-hearted attempt at gaining social clout before unlimited mimosas at brunch.

Behind the anonymity and comfort of screens in modern America, young people are concerningly aligning themselves with the same social systems that once choked any breath of free speech, extinguished political opposition, and brutally bulldozed the very freedoms students scroll past without missing a step.

Recently, students in particular are increasingly unaware of the very issues for which they are advocating. A professor of political science in the University of California system’s recent survey of students at Berkeley highlights this phenomenon.

Out of 250 students surveyed on whether or not they support the statement “From the River to the Sea” in response to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, most said they supported the chant. His survey suggests that some supported enthusiastically at 32.8%, and others to a lesser extent, totaling 53.2%. Yet, only 47% of the students who supported the slogan were able to name the river and the sea that correlated to the conflict.

Besides the sheer ignorance of student advocacy in issues related to war or social policies, many are alarmingly unaware of historical legacies of the very systems that often perpetuate such oppression.

The Cato Institute’s poll on the favorability of Americans’ views of various economic systems, including free market capitalism, socialism, and even communism, correlates to this growing concern. Among 2,000 Americans aged 18–29 surveyed, 62 percent view socialism favorably, while 14 percent feel the same about communism.

However, the broader question is not why many young Americans are favorable to socialism, but rather why they are tastefully distrustful of capitalism considering the social impacts it has had on lifting citizens out of poverty unlike any other system. The real question is why students in particular are disillusioned with American national resolve in an age of triumph and inherent natural progress. It is, however, most concerning to see students justify modern collectivism in pursuit of equality at the sake of individual liberties core to the American identity. As a graduate student, I often hear the defense of communism from my progressive counterparts as “a perfect system on paper,” though this is still fallible. Frederick Hayek’s stance on free market capitalism inherently highlights the danger that grows in collective economic systems that prioritize redistribution over reciprocity. He shares that no one group of citizens, no matter how intelligent or capable, will ever be competent enough to oversee planning of a centralized system that equitably distributes opportunity for human flourishing. This defense is precisely rooted in the issue of collectivism, but does not fully endorse the very real downfalls that exist in capitalism. Yet, highlighting the need for consumers to express feasibility through choice is a powerful reminder that, like any institution—whether economic, political, or social—must be structured to balance individual liberties with collective responsibility that makes certain human flourishing is achievable by both free will and the frameworks in place to support it.

No one group of citizens, no matter how intelligent or capable, will ever be competent enough to oversee planning of a centralized system that equitably distributes opportunity for human flourishing

Captivating the autonomy of its citizens, a collectivist society prioritizes nothing more than oppressing dissent in pursuit of state-driven equity, a pursuit far more harmful in the long run.

In an age of media and cultural wars dominating American identity, perhaps nothing is as important in shifting the narrative than civic education. An antidote to tyranny, civic education distinctly counters ideological blind spots by inviting students to the table of truth. Encouraging critical thinking over fast and often mistargeted advocacy is a noble way forward, and when paired with in-depth historical analysis and civil discourse, is perhaps the only way forward past a future legacy of polarization and insolence.

True progress respects both the historical and traditional institutions at the basis of culture, and does not sustain itself from disregarding uncomfortable truths. Communism has claimed more lives than any economic system in history. Millions of innocent people, from Mao’s brutal campaigns to Stalin’s tyrannical purge, have paid the ultimate price for centralized systems that disregarded individual rights and inherent human dignity for the sake of the illusion of pure equality.

True progress respects both the historical and traditional institutions at the basis of culture, and does not sustain itself from disregarding uncomfortable truths.

Beyond the social media hashtags and catchy protest signs is the shadow of mass graves where Communism promised equality but delivered ensnared ideological bureaucracy and buried the corpse of freedom.

Steering clear from dangerous idealism and into pathways that do not blindly accept the evident weaknesses of a free market system, but correct them by empowering prosperity through civic education and active, informed citizenship, is a good place to start.

item.title: Baylor Community Weighs Kirk’s Legacy, America’s Future
item.description:
Over 100 people gathered in prayer Wednesday night on Fountain Mall for Charlie Kirk, the Turning Point USA founder who was fatally shot while doing what he was known for: professing conservative values informed by his Christian faith.

Minneapolis sophomore Kate Kremer attended the prayer gathering after seeing plans for it on social media. She admired how Kirk’s faith informed his political positions, even as he defended them from a non-religious perspective.

“He was willing to talk about [his faith] and answer questions if anybody asked about it, but he was absolutely not forcing it down people’s throats,” Kremer said.

Kremer said Kirk was a model of how to engage in civil discourse with kindness and respect in the face of difficult controversies. Going forward, she hopes that students learn from Kirk’s advocacy of free and civil dialogue.

“When people stop talking and when people stop communicating about these issues and how to go about them, then that’s when wars start and that’s when violent things happen,” Kremer said.

Plano senior Nicky Rudd addressed the crowd at Fountain Mall, urging students to remember Kirk’s role in spreading Christian values on college campuses.

“He did not die just because of politics. He died because he preached the name of Jesus Christ. Charlie Kirk died a martyr,” Rudd said.

“He did not die just because of politics. He died because he preached the name of Jesus Christ. Charlie Kirk died a martyr.”

Although Kirk openly professed his Christian faith, the motives of his shooter remain unknown.

Rudd identified college campuses as places uniquely targeted by Satan, and he noted Kirk’s nationwide fight against the devil’s attacks.

“A champion of Jesus Christ and a champion for Christian values—his life, his love, his light was snuffed out. Let us remember that he did not die in vain. … He died so that we would carry on that torch,” Rudd said.

Two attendees fold an American flag, photo by Bella Vennare

Peter Campbell, associate professor of political science at Baylor, studies terrorists and insurgent organizations. He observed that, historically, these groups have used violence as a tool to provoke retaliation. While Campbell cautioned against jumping to early conclusions about motives behind killing Kirk, a similar principle applies. “Using violence in response to this violent act is probably exactly what the perpetrator would want you to do,” Campbell said.

Students like Kremer opened their phones after class, only to find their social media feeds and group chats flooded with news of Kirk’s death. On X, some videos showed graphic close-up angles of the moment Kirk was shot in the neck.

It’s natural to be rattled by the violence, Campbell said, but Christians shouldn’t be surprised when they face harm for their beliefs.

“Christ says, ‘If the world hates you, it hated me first.’ So, the fact that someone being open about their Christian faith gets them killed—and about their political opinions—isn’t actually that surprising from the Christian perspective. Only one of the disciples wasn’t martyred,” Campbell said.

Campbell said he gained peace with Kirk’s death after watching videos where Kirk discussed his relationship to Christ.

“You can’t live in fear. I think it’s one of the things that Charlie Kirk showed was that … he had numerous threats against his life, but it was more important to him to do what he saw was the work that God had put in front of him than to be safe,” Campbell said.

“It was more important to him to do what he saw was the work that God had put in front of him than to be safe.”

Kirk showed a new generation how to integrate faith and politics, Campbell said. Whereas previous generations used the idea of church-state separation to prevent religious principles from entering politics, Kirk demonstrated how to take both faith and politics seriously.

On this point, Kirk previously faced criticism for reinforcing Christian nationalism and supporting President Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

“He energized young people in a way that I don’t know if there’s anybody who could replace him, honestly. But there has to be, right? And it has to be from the people that he influenced. [Someone has] to not be afraid and step forward and continue. That’s how his legacy is going to survive,” Campbell said.

Kirk spoke near Baylor University, photo from Turning Point USA’s livestream, 2021

Turning Point USA at Baylor University posted a statement on their Instagram page following Kirk’s death.

“This is the turning point. Charlie Kirk’s assassination was a direct attack on our first amendment for freedom of speech and debate to what he was so passionate about. We know that many, including us, are absolutely heartbroken by the devastating news of Charlie’s death. Right now we ask for prayers over his family. We acknowledge that God’s hand is at work. May the Lord bless and comfort his wife, Erika, and his two young kids during this difficult time,” the post read.

Baylor University president Linda Livingstone issued a statement on Kirk’s death on Thursday, calling Kirk’s death “a senseless loss of life motivated by hate” and decrying political violence, especially on college campuses.

“A senseless loss of life motivated by hate.”

Kirk’s event at Utah Valley University was the first stop on “The American Comeback Tour.” The tour’s closest stop to Baylor would have been at Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, on October 27.

The last time Kirk visited Waco was part of his “Exposing Critical Racism Tour” in 2021.

item.title: Some Christians are Rethinking Women’s Suffrage. Here’s Why the Bible Says Otherwise.
item.description:
Conservative Christianity entertains a dangerous romance with far-right, patriarchal nationalism. At least, that’s the impression left behind by CNN’s interview with pastor and online personality Doug Wilson a few weeks ago.

The situation escalated when U.S. secretary of defense Pete Hegseth retweeted Wilson’s interview with the caption, “All of Christ for All of Life.” CNN also showed a clip of Hegseth attending Wilson’s newly opened church in Washington, D.C.

While Wilson’s interview with CNN focused on his advocacy for Christian nationalism, Wilson mentioned his positions on women in military roles, women’s function in society, and women’s voting rights. Wilson supported repealing the 19th Amendment, replacing women’s suffrage with a “household voting” system, under which only the head of the household can vote. Since Christianity teaches that husbands are the “heads” of their wives, Wilson’s system would exclude many women from voting.

In a separate reaction video, Wilson explained his position is not fundamentally about reversing women’s suffrage. “Our concern in all of this is not the enfranchisement of men over against women. Our concern has to do with the disenfranchisement of the covenant household,” Wilson stated.

Wilson believes that households are the fundamental units of political society—a view he believes contradicts universal suffrage. “If you recognize the family as a political reality, then the family will need to have a representative spokesman. … That household will be represented by its head,” Wilson explained.

To establish households as the fundamental political unit, Wilson appeals to the Bible. Wilson pastors Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, which currently employs a household membership system. The church’s “Book of Worship, Faith, and Practice” highlights biblical passages where households are greeted, evangelized, or judged collectively rather than individually.

The book further argues that household membership is necessary to combat excessive individualism in current culture. “We tend to think that the only legitimate units of membership in a church are individuals. Thus, what in Scripture is presented as an organic but diverse whole has become, in many of our churches, nothing more than a list, or roster of the names of individuals,” the book states.

The above argument resonates with conservative Christians who are disenchanted with liberal democracy and are eager to find straightforward answers. “A lot of the reason we’re getting the attention we’re getting is that people are hungry for answers that don’t just whitewash it, that don’t sugarcoat it. And, as I’m fond of saying, it’s Christ or chaos,” Wilson said on CNN.

According to Wilson, Christ Church’s location in Moscow, Idaho, has doubled in attendance since 2019.

Despite its allure for conservative Christians, the argument for household voting falls short on two main grounds.

First, the argument for household voting oversteps the support which Scripture appears to lend it.

The biblical passages that Christ Church’s page references support honoring households as important entities, but do not go so far as to structure church membership or political voting processes around them. Nowhere does Scripture explicitly prescribe household voting for either the church or for society. Just because the Bible acknowledges households as distinct entities does not immediately imply that household voting is necessary.

On purely logical grounds, this argument for household voting is far from watertight. Even if households are political entities, the argument does not explain why this entitles households to a vote. For example, corporations are arguably political entities, yet few suggest that corporations should be able to vote.

Furthermore, the argument gives no reason to believe that household voting and individual voting are mutually exclusive. For instance, one can imagine a system where individuals retain suffrage while the heads of household can cast an additional voting representing the household, a set-up reminiscent of Demeny voting.

These logical gaps force proponents of household voting to reckon with reality: household voting simply isn’t found in Scripture.

The second reason that the argument for household voting falls short is that it forgets the rationales behind individual voting.

Proponents of household voting rally against excessive individualism and feminism, neglecting the moderate, healthy forms of individualism and feminism. They throw out the baby with the bathwater.

The Bible is unequivocal: individuals are a fundamental political reality. Individuals are morally responsible beings who are accountable directly to God. At the end of time, God judges each person on their own; the Lamb’s book of life lists individual names, not household ones.

According to Romans 13, the administration of justice is the primary function of political community. If God administers final justice individually, human governments must at least acknowledge individuals as a core political reality.

Moreover, individuals are the kind of political beings that warrant suffrage. Classical liberalism points to individuals’ rationality as the spring from which voting rights flow—in addition to the idea that legitimate governance is based on the consent of the governed.

In terms more congruent to the Bible, individuals have both a sense of justice and a stake in how justice is administered. Humans’ innate sense of justice is rooted not in any collective group but is written on the heart of each individual. Households, strictly speaking, have no access to natural law, and there is no reason to privilege the head of household’s sense of justice over anyone else’s.

Furthermore, individuals have a stake in the administration of justice. In Scripture, God honored the case brought to Moses by the daughters of Zelophehad. These women brought their case as a group, but without representation by a head of household. Additionally, Deborah participated in Israel’s government as a judge without needing to be represented by her husband.

Both these qualities of individuals—their sense of justice and their stake in its administration—suggest that individual suffrage is a prudent and biblically justifiable system at the least.

Even if suffrage is not an inherent human right, a just government cannot capriciously privilege one class of people over another, especially when injustice and abuse are likely. In the case of household voting, the words of Abigail Adams ring true: “Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.”

In the end, Wilson’s remarks on CNN’s nationwide platform gratified illiberal audiences while misrepresenting biblical support for individual suffrage. Classically conservative Christians must combat the reactionist and illiberal impulse, lest the next generation be seduced by unbiblical extremism.

item.title: Liberal Education as Political Vision: Reimagining the Good Life in a Time of Migration
item.description:
The current migration crisis challenges us to decide what kind of society we want to be. Will we define ourselves by productivity, exclusion, and fear? Or will we embrace a vision of the good life rooted in dignity, leisure, and love? Liberal education equips us to choose the latter—not by giving us technical solutions, but by forming us to see differently.

This summer, I spent a week in Washington, DC studying liberal education alongside students from across the country through the American Enterprise Institute’s Summer Honors Program (SHP). My course was taught by Dr. David Corey and Dr. Elizabeth Corey, two Baylor professors who have taught classes on political science, philosophy, music, and art. Reading authors such as Josef Pieper, Michael Oakeshott, and A.G. Sertillanges, we asked: what does it mean to live well? How do we see the world not merely as a set of problems, but as a place of beauty, wonder, and meaning?

Liberal education, I realized, is not just about acquiring knowledge but about shaping how we see and who we become. It forms us either toward work—what Pieper calls “ratio,” reasoning aimed at production—or toward contemplation—what he calls “intellectus,” the receptive awareness that allows the world to enter our souls. Put differently, education doesn’t just determine what we know; it influences what kind of people we are.

Jazmine Fajardo in her SHP class on liberal education this summer

This philosophical debate sharpened when we considered whether education should prepare students primarily for work or for life. We framed this tension through two archetypes: “Herbert,” a graduate of critical pedagogy, and “Mary,” a graduate of liberal education. Herbert, shaped by Paulo Freire and Henry Giroux, sees education as a moral and political project—training students to resist oppression and act for justice. Mary, by contrast, embodies the liberal education tradition, living in leisure, contemplation, and joy. She attends to the world not as a set of problems to solve, but as a reality to encounter, delight in, and love.

We decided that neither mode of education is complete without the other. Herbert reminds us of the urgency of justice. Mary reminds us that life is more than work or politics; it is also friendship, beauty, and wonder. The conversation between them mirrors the debate our society faces today: is education about productivity and measurable outcomes, or about forming character and vision?

Is education about productivity and measurable outcomes, or about forming character and vision?

This question became concrete for me when I turned my attention to the U.S. debate over contemporary migration. Growing up as a first-generation student, straddling my Central American roots and American upbringing, I saw firsthand the divisions between immigrant and American communities. Trips to Honduras made these contrasts vivid. In Tegucigalpa, my family spoke not of dreams but of survival: food insecurity, violence, and political collapse left little room for flourishing. In the U.S., by contrast, people often spoke of the American Dream, though increasingly in terms of individual achievement, material success, and national identity.

This is not just my family’s story; it is the reality of many in the Northern Triangle. In 2022, nearly 250,000 Hondurans were apprehended at the U.S. border, many fleeing gang violence, corruption, and climate-driven food insecurity. Yet U.S. policy continues to reduce migrants to economic contributors or legal categories: workers, refugees, “illegals.” Missing is the recognition of their full humanity—their dignity, their longing for community, and their capacity to flourish.

Liberal education taught me that how we “see” shapes how we respond. Do we see migrants through Herbert’s eyes as problems to be solved, figures in need of justice-oriented reform? Or do we see them through Mary’s eyes as people whose inherent dignity eclipses even the consideration of economic utility? Both perspectives matter. Together, they remind us that migration policy is not only a technical or economic issue but also a moral and spiritual one.

Jazmine’s liberal education class on the front steps of the American Enterprise Institute in DC

Liberal education offered me a new lens to interpret the American Dream itself. For many, the Dream symbolizes self-realization through hard work. But through Augustine and Aquinas, I came to see its distortions. Augustine reminds us that “our hearts are restless until they rest in God,” pointing beyond material success toward eternal truth. Aquinas directs us toward the common good, calling us to prioritize justice, dignity, and community.

From this view, the American Dream, when reduced to individual achievement, risks becoming a form of what Pieper calls the “glorification of work.” It leaves little room for leisure, contemplation, or communion. It pressures people to justify their presence in terms of productivity. But true flourishing cannot be reduced to economic metrics. As Josef Pieper insists, leisure is the basis of culture because it allows us to encounter reality as a gift, not as a problem.

Our vision of education will inevitably parallel our vision of politics. If education is only about production, then politics will be reduced to management: controlling borders, calculating labor flows, maximizing economic gain. But if education is about shaping how we see, then politics, too, must be about shaping how we live together, how we pursue dignity and justice.

Thinkers like Augustine and Aquinas remind us that unjust systems are not merely flawed but disordered. To treat migrants as disposable labor or as threats to national identity is not just bad policy; it is a distortion of human dignity. An aim, then, must be transformation—of self and of society—toward love, communion, and justice. Aided by liberal education, we should expand our imagination to recognize migrants as fellow human beings called to flourish with us in community.

Aided by liberal education, we should expand our imagination to recognize migrants as fellow human beings called to flourish with us in community.

Understanding politics through the lens of liberal education reframes advocacy itself. Advocacy is not merely about solving problems (Herbert’s mode) but also about embodying the good (Mary’s mode). It is about forming communities where people can delight in life together—sharing meals, telling stories, worshiping, and creating culture. In this sense, migration justice is not only about securing rights or distributing resources but about reimagining political life as a form of communion.

My week at SHP ended with Oakeshott’s reminder that conversation itself is an “unrehearsed intellectual adventure.” That is what liberal education has been for me—an ongoing process of discovery, lived out in community and oriented toward the good life. In the context of immigration, this means engaging difficult questions not as battles to win or problems to solve, but as opportunities to enter into a shared adventure marked with humility and love of our shared human experiences.

For me, this has become a vocation. I no longer ask, “What do I want to be?” Instead, I ask: “How can I live in right relationship with others?” Liberal education has taught me that the most important things in life are found not in achievement but in communion. Applied to migration, this means creating structures that do not marginalize but invite all people—especially immigrants—into a community shaped by justice, belonging, and love.

item.title: Biblical Israel and Modern America: A Rabbi’s Take
item.description:
Like Biblical Israel, America is a covenantal nation. Abraham Lincoln saw this parallel, and how it compels us to press onward when we fail to live up to our creed.

This summer, I spent a week in Washington DC at the American Enterprise Institute Summer Honors Program (SHP). My SHP class, taught by Rabbi Dr. Meir Y. Soloveichik was titled “The Almost Chosen People: Lincoln, the Hebrew Bible, and the Meaning of America.”

Rabbi Soloveichik introduced us to a new paradigm for viewing the nature of America: contractual and covenantal. Most of us have some familiarity with the idea that America was founded on social contract theory: the people endow government with power for the protection of the people’s natural rights. However, many of us fail to realize that America is also covenantal—founded not only upon a “ceasefire” but upon a commitment to uphold certain ideals. As Rabbi Jonathan Sacks puts it, “Social contract is about laws and their enforcement. Social covenant is about the values we share.” Using this paradigm, we understand the Declaration as America’s covenant—the creed of freedom and equality that unites us—and the Constitution as the social contract. Or, as Lincoln puts it, the golden apple and the silver frame. A mutual agreement to sacrifice for a nation’s creed must underpin any covenantal society. America’s founding at a specific moment, expressly in the name of certain universal principles, sets it in a class with Biblical Israel alone.

America is also covenantal—founded not only upon a “ceasefire” but upon a commitment to uphold certain ideals.

In his 1861 address to the New Jersey State Senate, Lincoln refers to America as God’s “almost chosen people.” Lincoln clearly sees parallels between America and Biblical Israel, but why call Americans almost chosen? Rabbi Soloveichik believes that Lincoln uses this qualifier to denote a contingency. As Americans, our founding fathers chose to enshrine universal principles of equality and liberty in our covenantal creed, the Declaration. Our commitment to these principles makes America exceptional. If, as Americans, we fail to uphold these principles, we will no longer serve as a light to the nations. In contrast, Israel was sovereignly elected by God to be His among all nations. The Old Testament is filled with stories of Israel violating their covenant. Yet, Israel’s chosen status remains since it ultimately depends on God. As Lincoln saw it, we have more influence over our preeminence than did the people of Israel. Our distinctiveness fully stems from our covenant faithfulness.

As Americans, our founding fathers chose to enshrine universal principles of equality and liberty in our covenantal creed, the Declaration. Our commitment to these principles makes America exceptional.

Undeniably, we as Americans have failed to uphold our founding creed at times. Lincoln knew this. He saw the Civil War as an existential threat to America as a covenantal nation. In his Gettysburg Address, Lincoln soberly observes, “Now we are engaged in a great civil war, testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.” Yet, the nation has endured. The rebel cause that so vehemently rejected the American creed of liberty and equality in favor of slavery was defeated. It took another century for America to more fully guarantee our creedal promises to Black Americans by passing the Civil Rights Acts of the 1960s. Yet, the greatest visionary leaders of the civil rights movement—Frederick Douglass and Martin Luther King— recognized the inherent value of American ideals and called out America’s failures to uphold them.

We must not turn a blind eye toward America’s faults but instead call Americans to greater faithfulness to our founding creed.

Now, the mantle is passed to us. Rabbi Soloveichik explained that Judaism requires covenantal renewal with each generation, chiefly through Passover. So too, as God’s almost chosen people, we must affirm our willingness in this generation to uphold our covenant. Unfortunately, some Americans fail to see the goodness of our covenantal creed, arguing America was conceived in sin. In our generation especially, we passionately decry injustice and acutely perceive the manifold ills of our society. Yet, we must respond with Lincoln that our nation was “conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.” We must say this first because it is true—liberty and equality are the very DNA of America, despite our faults—and second because to do otherwise would be self-defeating. We must not turn a blind eye toward America’s faults but instead call Americans to greater faithfulness to our founding creed. That is the greatest form of patriotism. As we sacrifice and strive to better uphold our covenant, we show ourselves to be God’s almost chosen people.

item.title: Who Do You Choose as Your Neighbor?
item.description:
In Luke 10, the Law is summed up in two commands: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’; and, “Love your neighbor as yourself.’” An expert of the law, wishing to “justify himself,” then asks the Lord, “And who is my neighbor?”

Jesus responds with the parable of the Good Samaritan, calling the followers of God to show mercy to any vulnerable persons we encounter. We must make ourselves neighbors to those in need by seeing and loving them.

We must make ourselves neighbors to those in need by seeing and loving them.

Matthew 25 raises the stakes of this call to love our neighbor. Jesus describes the final judgement as a division between those who were neighbors to the vulnerable and those who passed them by, declaring that “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.”

Are Christians in America answering this eternally consequential call to love our neighbors, and in doing so, loving Christ himself?

Chasing the American Dream means striving for houses with porches, white picket fences, manicured lawns, and family cars. Each piece of “the good life” relies on one key factor: good neighbors. The ideal American neighbor gives a friendly wave from the porch next door, enters through the picket fence to deliver baked goods or borrow the occasional egg, and picks up after their dog. If the neighbors need too many favors or are too loud, however, you are rudely awakened from your dream.

Even when you exit the neighborhood, the American Dream expects a peaceful commute where any potential neighbors are separated by two panes of glass and only occasionally communicate through gesture or horn. When you arrive at your stable job, you might make small talk on the elevator or on your way to your office, but when you sit down at your desk, you hope that no coworkers will intrude to converse outside of the appropriate times. Nowadays, perhaps the ideal job may only require online interactions where potential neighbors appear merely as users on your screen.

I say all that to illustrate a core American ideal that millions of Christians have widely accepted: we value neighbors that are easy to love so we can live independently. When we look for housing or employment, we choose to surround ourselves with people who will not require much from us. And when we choose to put ourselves in taxing situations, we do so on our own terms: donating to charities of our choice, volunteering once a month, or going on mission trips.

Living the American Dream allows us to justify ourselves as the teacher of the law wished to in Luke 10 with the question “And who is my neighbor?” If we only surround ourselves with people who require little from us, then we easily answer the call to love those we encounter who are in need. If we happen to venture out of our way to what is labeled as the “bad part of town,” we may buy a meal for the woman begging with her children. Or if we go to a concert where they ask us to sponsor a child, we will oblige—at least the first time—to fulfill the requirement.

This is the question for Christians today: who do you choose as your neighbor?

This is the question for Christians today: who do you choose as your neighbor? Are you choosing to surround yourself with people who require minimal love from you, taking a safer road from Jerusalem to Jericho in order to avoid men in need? Are you only willing to encounter the least of these, and therefore encounter Jesus, on your own terms, but not at your inconvenience?

These are questions I never considered until my summer in Washington, DC. I was blessed to be a part of Baylor in Washington’s Summer Fellowship for Religion & Social Life, where I spent half of my week in seminars with guest speakers from around the nation and the rest of my time at an internship of my choice.

Baylor in Washington Religion and Social Life Cohort 2025

The House DC in Anacostia, Washington D.C.

In the first few weeks of seminars, the idea of integrated living was introduced by guest speakers Dr. Jeremy Everett and Ms. La Wonda Bornstein. Dr. Everett lived in impoverished areas where he came to know his neighbors on a personal level to understand and meet their needs. He told us stories of the coffee shop he started at the request of his neighborhood that provided free laptops, community events, and a safe space from gang violence. Ms. Bornstein is the president and CEO of The House DC, a haven located a few blocks away from Anacostia High School where students can receive services for personal and spiritual growth, meals and groceries for their families, academic mentorship, and job training. Like Dr. Everett’s coffee shop, The House is protected by gangs in the area, even though it is located on the street of houses known as “Murder Row.” These ministries were able to make deep and lasting impacts because they were integrated into their communities. They chose to be literal neighbors with the people God had called them to serve, even at the risk of their safety and comfort.

While I was learning the inspirational stories of our speakers, I had the privilege of experiencing integrated living firsthand at my internship. L’Arche is an international network of living communities that invites people with and without intellectual disabilities to live life alongside each other in Christ. There are approximately 150 communities in 37 countries, and each have core members (people with disabilities) living in the same house as assistants (people without disabilities) and going through daily routines together.

Ontario House is a four-story townhouse in Adams Morgan, a culturally diverse neighborhood in the Northwest quadrant of DC. It is currently home to three L’Arche core members, four assistants, and the husband of an assistant. While working as an assistant for two months at Ontario House, I got to experience the joy of choosing an unconventional dream. At L’Arche, people are fully interdependent with no white fences separating their lives. When sharing time with the core members, assistants support them with anything they need. For core members with greater needs, this means getting them dressed in the morning, helping them use the restroom, and brushing their teeth. Assistants cook meals, do laundry, and drive to activities or appointments. They bear through core members yelling, refusing to cooperate, or insisting on watching The Secret Life of Pets for the twentieth time…this month alone.

Why do assistants choose to live life at L’Arche? The answer is obvious after having just one dinner at Ontario House. While the core members depend on the assistants for basic physical needs, the assistants at L’Arche depend on core members for basic emotional and spiritual needs.

Eileen volunteering for a nonprofit

Of the current core members at Ontario, Ms. Eileen is the youngest and most active. She is a professional artist that sells her drawings and co-curates art shows, a community servant that volunteers for nonprofits, an advocate on Capitol Hill fighting for the rights of the vulnerable, and a L’Arche GWDC employee with the title “Friendship Builder.” The title is fitting because Ms. Eileen is truly a friend to everyone she encounters. Each morning, Ms. Eileen would greet me with a wide grin, an enthusiastic “Hi!” and a hug or squeeze of the hand.

Debora in one of her favorite dresses at L’Arche Southeast Regional Gathering

Ms. Debora is Ontario’s resident singer and fashion queen. She knows the lyrics to practically every 60s song (the Beatles are her favorite) and owns a total of 64 dresses (one of my summer projects was to count them). When we took a trip as a house to L’Arche USA Southeast Regional Gathering in North Carolina, I had the privilege of rooming with Debora. Although we were up at 5:30am every morning to use the restroom, our acapella duets to “Yellow Submarine” and “Have You Ever Seen the Rain?” while going through the rest of her morning routine gave me more than enough energy for the day.

Johnny is a Cuban immigrant in his eighties who speaks almost exclusively in Spanish. When describing English, he knocks twice on the wood table, indicating that it is “very hard.” When I first arrived at Ontario, I could not understand a word Johnny was saying. But, over time and with the help of the Lord, we learned to communicate with my limited Spanish and his limited English to the point of sitting and talking with each other for up to twenty minutes at a time. My favorite part of the summer was walking into the dining room in the morning when Johnny was at the table. He would beckon me over, I would kneel beside his wheelchair, he would put his arm around me, motion me closer, and give me a big kiss on the cheek. I would respond, “Gracias Johnny, te amo” and converse with him briefly before sneaking into the kitchen to wipe the egg or oatmeal off my face.

Johnny and Me

Michael Schaff, the founding core member of L’Arche Greater Washington, DC

A month before I came to the house, they lost their founding core member, Mr. Michael Schaff, at eighty years of age. Michael moved in with L’Arche Greater Washington DC in 1983. Though I never had the blessing of knowing Michael, he was known in Adams Morgan as a present and loving neighbor. His obituary tells that “Anyone who had the pleasure of accompanying Mike on his daily trip to McDonald’s got to witness how known he was in the neighborhood, and his incredible memory of each person’s family tree, how many grandkids, who was divorced, and who was engaged.”

If you decide to integrate yourself with people who require something of you, you might just see the face of God in their face and feel his love in ways you have yet to experience.

L’Arche taught me that choosing to be neighbors to “the least of these”—though it comes at the sacrifice of time, energy, and personal comforts—brings a multitude of blessings. Eileen, Debora, and Johnny showed me Christ unlike anyone had before through their unique personalities and gifts. As 1 Corinthians 12:22 tells us, “the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable.” As they relied on me to meet their physical needs, I relied on the sense of belonging and connectedness they abundantly provided.

So, who will you choose as your neighbor? If you decide to integrate yourself with people who require something of you, you might just see the face of God in their face and feel his love in ways you have yet to experience. Let us, as Christians in America, choose the unconventional dream of interdependence with Christ and his body.

item.title: The Resources Exist: Jeremy Everett on Faith, Justice, and Ending Hunger in Waco and Beyond
item.description:
We have the resources to end hunger in America.

Jeremy Everett delivers the line plainly—no flourish, no sermonizing—just the hard-earned conviction of a man who has stood in too many kitchens with empty shelves and too many living rooms where hunger is a daily guest.

Everett had my attention from the moment he opened our three-day seminar with that line. As part of the Baylor Fellowship for Religion and Social Life, I spent several days learning from Everett—an expert in food insecurity and the founding executive director of the Baylor Collaborative on Hunger and Poverty.

In the abstract, ending hunger sounds like the kind of pipe dream we assign to utopian idealism, a lofty ideal you might toss out when playing a game of “Three Wishes.” I don’t know many people who treat it like a tangible goal. Jeremy Everett does.

Everett’s own path began as an undergraduate with the dawning awareness of the injustices of the world and his own participation in them.
