As a third-generation preacher’s kid, he found himself sitting in pews growing more and more confused by the gaps in the church’s storytelling. “We talked a lot about Jesus’ birth and Jesus’s death and resurrection,” he told me, “but we really didn’t spend a whole lot of time talking about what happened in between.” That “in between” were the many years that Jesus moved toward the poor, the outcast, the dispossessed, and the forgotten, speaking to them as bearers of God’s image. “He saw who they were and called that out in them.” For Everett, this was not an optional addendum to the gospel; it was the center: “[Jesus] was trying to make crooked paths straight.”

When I asked Everett about the Church’s role in solving hunger, his response was quick: prophetic witness. The task, as he describes it, is first for the Church to tell the truth—to point at hunger and name it as an injustice and a moral failing. “In a world that produces enough food for everybody to have access to it… we should make sure that everybody has access to it,” he said. “Hunger is a litmus test for the soul and spirit of who we are as people of faith. If hunger is present, then sin is present — and it’s not the sin of the people who are hungry. It’s the sin of us, those of us who are not ensuring that they have enough food.”

“If hunger is present, then sin is present — and it’s not the sin of the people who are hungry. It’s the sin of us, those of us who are not ensuring that they have enough food.” Jeremy Everett

For Everett, fighting hunger is not an optional act of charity. It’s a theological mandate.

When I asked where this conviction comes from, Everett immediately went to Scripture. He recalled the prophets calling out nations that ignored the poor, and Jesus himself feeding the hungry, healing the sick, and sharing tables with those pushed to the margins. “Jesus talked about the kingdom of God as good news for the poor,” Everett said. “When he tells us in Matthew 25 that when we feed the hungry, we’re feeding him—that’s not metaphor. That’s the standard he’s holding us to.” For Everett, these passages aren’t background color to the gospel story; they are a core theme. Hunger is not merely a social issue, but a spiritual one—and the Church’s failure to confront it is, in his words, “a failure to be the Church.”

“We’re called to people who are experiencing injustice” Everett said, “that’s what it means to be Christian.” Everett pushed back against the idea that prioritizing justice turns faith into a “works-based gospel,” emphasizing that we are saved by grace alone—and that this very grace demands that we act in service and compassion.

For Everett, addressing injustice is the Christian’s “nonnegotiable.”



Having grown up in more conservative circles in the South, I am well acquainted with the arguments against government involvement in addressing hunger. So, I was curious to hear Everett’s perspective—both on these arguments and on the recently passed cuts to SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program), the federal government’s primary program aimed at reducing food insecurity.

Everett doesn’t hesitate when it comes to addressing the common objections to programs like SNAP.

“It’s one of the most efficient programs we have as a nation—less than a three percent error rate,” he explained. Fraud is rare and usually happens at the state agency level, not with individual recipients. And as for the idea that the church, not the government, should be the one to address hunger? For Everett, the point is not church or government, but church and government, alongside nonprofits, industry, and local communities. Ending hunger, he says, “is too big and too complex for one sector to address by itself.”

When I asked him why, if the resources exist, we have not acted, he paused. “We don’t see others as fully human,” he said quietly. If we saw the homeless man on the street as our own brother, the child in Gaza as our own daughter, “we’d probably be more motivated to do something about it.” So why do we often neglect this reality? Because if it’s true that what we do unto the least of these we do unto Christ then “we are obligated to actually do something.” It is an issue of the will.

As an undergraduate living in Waco myself, the pervasive reality of people experiencing homelessness, poverty, and food insecurity is all too real. Most of my friends feel the same way that I do—heartbroken, with a desire to help, but unsure about how to respond in a meaningful way.

I asked Everett whether giving food or water directly could do more harm than good. He was firm: “I think providing somebody a sandwich or water…that’s never going to be a bad thing. Immediate relief matters. But it’s not enough.” He explained that while handing out meals or groceries can meet urgent needs, it does little to address the systemic conditions that create hunger in the first place. This highlighted an underlying issue: students and others in the community want to help and have a lasting impact on others’ livelihoods, but without guidance, coordination, and a deeper understanding of the issues, even the best intentions, though good, often fall short of true solidarity.

This strategic guidance is what Everett and his team have developed through the Baylor Collaborative. Though they have piloted many groundbreaking programs across Texas and the nation, the most recent is the Hunger Free Community Accelerator which will officially launch September 3rd. The program trains leaders to address hunger in a systemic, sustainable way—from leveraging federal nutrition programs to uniting local organizations.

“It’s for people who say, ‘I want to end hunger in my community,’” Everett said. “We’ve been testing it for 15 years in Texas and now it’s being piloted nationally and even globally with the World Food Programme.” As this training program rolls out, the hope is that even a Baylor student could take the training, gather a group of leaders, and scale the solution to their town or community.

By this point in our interview, my throat felt tight and my eyes blurred—grief. I recognized the feeling: mourning the weight and sheer scope of suffering around me, in my own community, and feeling the sting of how little I had dared to shoulder that pain in the past.

Yet I had only spent three days listening to stories of the struggle against hunger and one hour in conversation with Everett. I asked him how he carries the weight, and he admitted that despair often creeps in. His antidote? Contemplative prayer, a loving faith community, and a redefinition of success.

“We’re not called to be successful,” he said. “We’re called to be faithful.”

For him, that means showing up each day, working alongside others, praying for those on the front lines, and making space to rest and recenter. “There will be times of despair,” he acknowledged, “and sometimes you have to give space to grief. But you get up the next day and you do it again.”

Everett frames hunger not as a problem of scarcity but of solidarity. The resources exist; the question is whether we will be the kind of people willing to use them.

Everett frames hunger not as a problem of scarcity but of solidarity. The resources exist; the question is whether we will be the kind of people willing to use them.

I left our interview deeply moved and convicted, but also encouraged. Through Everett and the many others working alongside him to serve those in need, I realized that part of the fight is just daring to hope in the middle of despair for the ongoing renewal of all things.

As I walked back to my car that day an old gospel song rang in my ears:

“Oh happy day,

When Jesus washed,

Washed my sins away,

He taught me how to watch, fight and pray!

Fight and pray!”

item.title: Can AUKUS Help the U.S. Pose a Real Threat to China?
item.description:
Over the past few decades, China has focused on building up its military. As their manufacturing and military capabilities progress, the threat they pose in the Indo-Pacific continues to grow. This creates concerns over the stability of the region and the United States’ ability to deter its rivals.

AUKUS is a trilateral partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, signed by President Biden and currently under review by the Trump administration. The agreement was designed around two main pillars and is projected to cost between $268 and $368 billion. While the agreement comes with a steep price tag, it provides too many benefits to not be implemented.

The first pillar focuses on building and strengthening deterrence capabilities in the Indo-Pacific, an epicenter of the global economy and the site of a possible conflict with China. Specifically, Pillar 1 aids Australia with obtaining nuclear powered submarines (SSNs) which would increase their undersea capabilities by adding range, endurance, and stealth. Australia will purchase U.S. Virginia-class submarines for their Royal Navy. While the agreement is not a promise by any nation to respond to a conflict, Australia’s acquisition of SSNs would greatly reduce response time to a crisis in the Indo-Pacific—increasing deterrence. However, the production of these submarines will take time. To bridge the gap between now and the completion of Pillar 1, the U.K. and the U.S. will provide rotational presence of submarines beginning in 2027.

Pillar 2 focuses on the interoperability of advanced and shared capabilities with focus on eight main sectors: cyber, artificial intelligence, quantum, undersea technologies, hypersonic, and electronic warfare. This pillar also provides the possibility to introduce additional partners, such as France or Japan, into the agreement. However, this possibility appears unlikely to occur.

President Joe Biden, British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the AUKUS meeting in San Diego, California, March 13, 2023

With the U.S. playing a large role in this agreement by providing Australia with SSNs, it’s important to note the condition of the Defense Industrial Base (DIB)—which is actually quite worrisome. While recent investments in our military and the DIB are aimed at aiding this crisis, those investments will take time to pay off. According to Seth Jones’ report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, China is acquiring equipment and high-end weapons systems at a rate five to six times faster than the U.S. In a near-future conflict with China, the U.S. would run out of certain munitions in less than a week. This causes those in opposition to the agreement to emphasize the toll it would place on the DIB, arguing it would deplete the U.S. military. However, AUKUS could actually help revive the DIB from its death spiral.

One of the biggest problems is a lack of sufficient funding since the “procurement holiday” post-Cold War. Not only are we still relying on the military investments made in the Reagan years, but Congress has exacerbated the problem by failing to provide appropriations bills on time.

The DIB faces many challenges when it comes to being adequately prepared for a conflict. One of the biggest problems is a lack of sufficient funding since the “procurement holiday” post-Cold War. Not only are we still relying on the military investments made in the Reagan years, but Congress has exacerbated the problem by failing to provide appropriations bills on time. This forces the military to rely on continuing resolutions which only allow for spending on existing projects—meaning no innovation or modernization. This is a big problem as our equipment continues to age and gets increasingly more expensive to repair. With the uncertainty and inadequate funding that accompany new projects, there is no incentive for companies to spend time and money on research and development. This means our facilities and equipment continue to age while the next generation of our workforce sees no security in pursuing education or a career in manufacturing for the DIB.

This creates cracks in the U.S.’s most relied-upon defense policy: deterrence. While testifying in front of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, William Greenwalt, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, emphasized, “If China knows we can’t produce and sustain our military forces in a great power conflict, the chance of warfare will be that much greater.” To fix this problem, companies and the Department of Defense need an indication that investments in production won’t go to waste—this is where AUKUS comes in.

To fix this problem, companies and the Department of Defense need an indication that investments in production won’t go to waste—this is where AUKUS comes in.

The AUKUS agreement provides many benefits to the United States, and aligns with Trump’s “America First” foreign policy strategy. As outlined above, one of the biggest roadblocks for the DIB is a lack of reliability when it comes to investment in production. AUKUS provides funding and long-term demand for expertise in submarine construction. Not only is Australia purchasing the submarines, but they have also pledged to invest in the DIB to increase production capacity. In order to fulfill the promises made in the deal, U.S. shipyards are being forced to modernize, which will benefit our DIB in the long-term. Pillar 2 of the deal also increases collaboration on research and development by lowering barriers between partners and increasing cooperation. The benefits from both pillars align with Trump’s “America First” agenda by rebuilding our military-industrial complex, creating American jobs, increasing allied burden-sharing, and strengthening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.

The benefits from both pillars align with Trump’s “America First” agenda by rebuilding our military-industrial complex, creating American jobs, increasing allied burden-sharing, and strengthening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.

AUKUS provides the U.S. with an opportunity to not only strengthen our alliances and deter our adversaries, but to also strengthen its own weak points within the military and its industrial base.

item.title: Baylor Reverses Course on LGBTQ+ Grant
item.description:
A previous version of this article was published by the Institute on Religion and Democracy

Baylor University rejected a $643,401 grant to study “the disenfranchisement and exclusion of LGBTQIA+ individuals and women” in the church. Baylor President Linda Livingstone announced the decision this afternoon, reaffirming that the viewpoints promoted by the research conflicted with traditional Baptist teaching on sexuality.

“As we reviewed the details and process surrounding this grant, our concerns did not center on the research itself, but rather on the activities that followed as part of the grant. Specifically, the work extended into advocacy for perspectives on human sexuality that are inconsistent with Baylor’s institutional policies, including our Statement on Human Sexuality,” Livingstone wrote.

The grant to Baylor’s Center for Church and Community Impact (C3I) originally aimed to develop training resources for churches and take “concrete steps toward genuine inclusion” of LGBTQ+ people.

Garland School of Social Work dean Jon Singletary and C3I director Gaynor Yancey have agreed to rescind their acceptance of the grant. The grant funds will be returned to the Eula Mae and John Baugh Foundation, a nonprofit that supports progressive causes and has previously donated to Baylor’s C3I.

Livingstone informed the Baylor community that the university remains committed to being “a loving and caring community for all—including our LGBTQIA+ students.” Livingstone also emphasized that the university continues to value academic freedom.

The announcement acknowledged the confusion and pushback surrounding Baylor’s acceptance of the grant.

“Please be assured that Baylor’s institutional beliefs and policies remain unchanged. … We affirm the biblical understanding of human sexuality as a gift from God, expressed through purity in singleness and fidelity in marriage between a man and a woman,” the Baylor president wrote.

item.title: Baylor University Receives Grant to Study LGBTQ+ Inclusion in the Church
item.description:
A previous version of this article was published by the Institute on Religion and Democracy

Update: since the publishing of this article, Baylor reversed course and rejected the grant

A progressive foundation has granted $643,401 to Baylor University to study “the disenfranchisement and exclusion of LGBTQIA+ individuals and women” in the church. The grantees hope their work will “nurture institutional courage and foster change,” according to the June 30 press release.

The funding comes from the Eula Mae and John Baugh Foundation, a private progressive faith-based nonprofit headquartered in Texas. The foundation explicitly prioritizes funding for progressive Baptist organizations, social justice advocacy and inclusivity initiatives.

The Center for Church & Community Impact (C3I) within Baylor’s school of social work will receive the funds and conduct the research. Using this grant, C3I researchers will interview a group of 50 university students and use the results to inform training resources for congregations. The study aims to have congregations take “concrete steps toward genuine inclusion” of LGBTQ+ people.

Baylor University’s C3I has previously received similar grants and has already produced LGBTQ+ resources for churches and social workers—including a “LGBTQ+ Discernment Guide.” In 2024, another C3I project funded by the Baugh Foundation sought to educate congregations in trauma care and LGBTQ+ discernment.

C3I director and Baylor professor Dr. Gaynor Yancey has a history of nudging students and churches towards LGBTQ+ affirmation. In a 2017 academic article geared towards advising Christian social workers, Yancey and Baylor professor emeritus Dr. Helen Harris noted that “It is possible to provide affirmative practice, even if the social worker has religious views that do not support homosexuality.”

In the same article, Yancey and Harris asserted that social workers should follow the principle that, “As a fallible being myself, I have no right to pass moral judgments on others,” quoting the influential Christian social worker and professor, Alan Keith-Lucas. Yancey and Harris later suggested that Christian social workers should be “culturally humble” when counseling LGBTQ clients.

Yancey and Harris’s 2020 article funded by the Baugh Foundation chronicled methods for churches to have conversations about LGBTQ+ discernment—with the lion’s share of the anecdotes coming from formerly “traditionalist” writers who embraced an LGBTQ+-affirming position.

As a prominent Baptist institution, Baylor University’s openness to LGBTQ+ affirmation sparks mixed reactions.

In Baylor’s press release, Dr. Jon Singletary, dean of the Garland School of Social Work, welcomed the grant. He hoped the grant would inspire churches to become “more just and welcoming communities.”

Meanwhile, the polemical Christian news site Protestia accused the recent grant of compromising Baylor’s Christian values. “The game is nearly up,” the Protestia article warned. The article pointed out the Baptist university’s previous friendliness towards LGBTQ+ causes, including allowing the first pro-LGBTQ+ student organization on campus.

Baylor University is associated with but not controlled by the Baptist General Convention of Texas. Texas Baptists affirm the historic Christian view that homosexuality and transgenderism are sins. The university is not affiliated with the Southern Baptist Convention.

item.title: Stuck in the Past? Reconsidering Faithful Political Engagement
item.description:
The 2024 presidential election ignited a strong wave of political engagement among college students and first-time voters, prompting many to align themselves with a specific party or candidate.

This political awakening, however, lacked thorough research into the policies and character qualities of the two aspiring presidents. As a student at Baylor University – a Baptist University in Texas – this became particularly evident.

The decision to vote Republican, especially in support of Donald Trump, seemed less of a political decision and more of a religious obligation. Statements such as “a Christian cannot vote Democrat” or “Trump is a Christian, so he has my vote” proliferated among my peers.

Baylor University

Having grown up in Massachusetts, a comparatively progressive environment, this sense of political certitude was new. Many seemed to hold the belief that to be an evangelical Christian necessitated Republican support. I wrestled with this belief and began to question if this correlation has always been present in American politics.

This, however, wasn’t the first time I wrestled with my political understanding and heritage.

Growing up, conversations at the dinner table often revolved around politics. I quickly became acquainted with the “good party”, the Republicans, and the “bad party”, the Democrats. Through the years my dad became increasingly involved in politics, even hosting fundraisers at our house to support Republican candidates and making numerous personal donations.

I trusted in his enthusiasm, and the beliefs my dad held became my own. In 2020, George Floyd was killed by a police officer in Minneapolis, leading many Americans, my dad included, to question the state of racism in our country.

While reading Heather McGee’s The Sum of Us , my dad learned about redlining – a discriminatory practice that historically denied financial assistance to non-white communities. This discovery was unsettling for him.

My dad’s most compelling discovery dealt with economic theory. As a businessman he initially supported the Republican party’s economic policies, particularly “trickle-down economics,” which was enacted by Ronald Reagan. My dad soon learned that this theory has not worked. After seeing the stark economic disparities this policy exacerbated – the top 10% now control 67% of the nation’s wealth while the bottom 50% only own 2.4% – my dad shifted his allegiance from Republican to Independent.

Both conservatives and evangelicals, and especially conservative evangelicals, should be seeking a political engagement marked not by fighting and destruction, but peace and edification.

In The Politics of Prudence, philosopher Russell Kirk defines a conservative “as one who finds the permanent things more pleasing than Chaos and Old Night.” – someone who abides by tradition rather than progress. My dad’s shift brought me into the Chaos and Old Night of critical reflection, and I was prompted to embark on my own path of political exploration. I was especially interested in the intersection of religion and politics, and how this influenced conservative evangelicals and the republican party. I found the history of this intersection to be a prescient hermeneutic for what I witnessed at Baylor during the 2020 election.

Originally established as an anti-slavery group, the Republican Party was solidified with Abraham Lincoln’s 1860 presidential victory and the subsequent abolition of slavery. Distinguished history professor Dr. Phillip Jenkins also noted in an interview that the Republican Party was traditionally more “sympathetic to women’s causes and feminist causes through the 1950s.”

The social upheaval of the 1960s and 1970s, however, driven by movements for civil rights, women’s rights, and reproductive freedoms, fundamentally altered the political landscape. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Roe v. Wade in 1973 were landmarks in the fight for racial and gender equality. Many conservatives, however, saw these advancements as a threat to the traditional order. Conservative Americans, particularly evangelical Christians, grew frustrated with the direction of America and sought an outlet to express their distaste and effect change.

The Jesus Movement

Amidst these social progressions, the Jesus Movement in the late 1960s and early 1970s brought vibrancy back to evangelical church communities. The movement drew disillusioned youth who, unsettled by societal changes, turned to the counter-cultural teachings of Jesus on love and peace. The disorganization of this movement, coinciding with the social upheavals of the 60s and 70s, set the stage for the evangelical leader and political activist Jerry Falwell.

As an individual favoring conservative policy, Falwell consistently opposed the social progress of the 1960s and 70s. In 1979, he formed the Moral Majority, a political organization that sought to unite evangelical Christians around conservative values. By 1980, the Moral Majority helped propel Ronald Reagan to a decisive victory, ushering in an era of conservative dominance in American politics marked by the united support of a large evangelical Christian population.

Statements such as “a Christian cannot vote Democrat” or “Trump is a Christian, so he has my vote” proliferated among my peers.



With this history in mind, I began to see parallels between the political engagement of conservative evangelicals led by Falwell and the current political engagement of conservative evangelicals for Trump—notably a common thread of fear and rhetoric centered on opposition.

Four decades after Falwell’s Moral Majority, the United States is encountering shifts in social dynamics reminiscent of those leading up to the Reagan administration. Issues such as abortion and LGBTQ+ rights have become volatile and polemic in American political rhetoric. Conversations around immigration, especially enforcement of the U.S. southern border, are similarly engaged. The same frustration with the direction of society and politics that united Christians under the republican banner in 1980, seems to have worked similarly in the 2020 election.

Jerry Falwell (left) and Ronald Reagan (right)

In Republican election campaigns, this frustration is expressed as fear of the “other,” rather than the traditionally conservative exhortation to preserve and care for the known. Rather than preserving and edifying, current Republican rhetoric gravitates toward fighting and fear-mongering.

This is particularly evident within issues such as migration to the United States, where charged rhetoric is utilized to stoke fear and division. During his most recent campaign, President Trump issued statements such as “the migrants [are] attacking villages and cities” and labeling them as a “threat from within” that have plagued the way Americans view this critical issue. Language is presented to invoke fear in the voter base, not inspire. This rhetoric is destructive, not cultivating.

While this rhetoric and disposition of the current Republican party is problematic, it does not mean that every evangelical Christian must declare allegiance whole heartedly to the Democratic party, deeming them the new “Christian” party. This is especially clear if we reflect on the two presidential candidates presented in 2024.

The first was a Democratic candidate who, while holding some good policies, celebrated and supported policies and actions generally opposed by the Christian ethos, such as early pregnancy termination. The second was a Republican candidate who, while often appealing to the Bible and the support of “Christian” groups, spoke and acted in ways that clearly diverged from the examples modeled for us in scripture.

This dilemma, for which there is no good solution, reveals a telling truth for both conservative and liberal evangelicals —there is no “Christian” party today. For my conservative evangelical peers at Baylor, there is no room to blindly vote for a candidate just because they claim to be a “Christian.” Similarly, one cannot deem someone less of a Christian because they voted differently than us.

Our vote has some impact, but as we approach political engagement today, we must strive to perpetuate small acts of love in our community each day.

In scripture, there is no Republican or Democrat distinction. To be faithful in politics, evangelicals have a duty to impartially compare the messaging of all candidates with the truth of scripture. There is a need to earnestly seek answers without settling on them through charged rhetoric or popular drift. Once this is done, a voting decision can be made with trust that the LORD is in control of any earthly authority.

Conservative evangelicals today must approach politics with more deliberation than ever before. Both conservatives and evangelicals, and especially conservative evangelicals, should be seeking a political engagement marked not by fighting and destruction, but peace and edification. We must, as Christian John Mark Comer puts it, “look hard to make little moves against destructiveness.”

On both sides of the aisle there is brokenness and flaw. Our vote has some impact, but as we approach political engagement today, we must strive to perpetuate small acts of love in our community each day. Through this, conservative evangelicals can reject complete alignment with a party increasingly centered on fear and destruction. Instead, they may return to alignment with the Way of Jesus—a way marked by humility, peace, and relentless love.

item.title: Is Trump’s Foreign Policy More Conservative than Traditional Conservatives?
item.description:
Donald Trump’s return to the White House promises to challenge previous approaches to foreign affairs seen in the past century. Trump’s foreign policy revives elements of 18th- and 19th-century strategies, emphasizing territorial control and regional dominance. In his inaugural address, President Trump captured his second term’s vision of the nation in a promise that the U.S. “will once again consider itself a growing nation” that “expands our territory” and “carries our flag into new and beautiful horizons,” while reminiscing on former President William McKinley’s (1843-1901) territorial expansion and tariffs. These ideals have been significant in the early Administration’s foreign policy, seen explicitly in Trump’s suggestion of U.S. control over Greenland, the Panama Canal, and Canada.

Trump’s foreign policy recalls elements of the Founding Father’s 18th century Monroe Doctrine, by focusing on a secure Western Hemisphere, free from foreign interference, as the key to success and power on the world stage.

The Founding Father-era presidents, while avoiding European conflicts, emphasized the peaceful resolution of issues and preferred ties of commerce to the threat of force. The Monroe Doctrine pressed European powers to calculate the risk of contravening the will of the U.S. in its own neighborhood, the Western Hemisphere, while avoiding an entanglement in European wars through security alliances.

Bettmann Archive/Getty Images

While Trump questions the benefits of U.S. alliances in Europe and Asia, especially Ukraine recently, he has become incredibly stout in prioritizing the Western Hemisphere. A Trump America-First foreign policy involves mitigating the flow of illicit drugs and illegal immigration from south of the border.

Additionally, Trump is focusing on forcing the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) out of Latin America, specifically Panama, due to their supplying of precursor chemicals and financial laundering assistance to transnational crime groups in the Western Hemisphere, designed to harm American interests. Trump leverages an important weapon in today’s world: economic power. Threatening tariffs and withholding of previously committed aid, Trump forces states to grapple with choosing between access to U.S. markets and risk economic harm if they go against Trump’s will.

Trump’s foreign policy revives elements of 18th- and 19th-century strategies, emphasizing territorial control and regional dominance

With heavy tariffs specifically enacted on the PRC, Canada, and Mexico, Trump forces these states to help the U.S. in mitigating the effects of illegal immigration and fentanyl trafficking. In Panama, Trump has forced a commitment to remove all remnants of the PRC’s BRI and sale of the Canal’s ports to U.S. companies. Trump is bringing back the vision of the Founders to force an adversarial foreign power out of the Western Hemisphere and using the U.S.’s greatest strength, its economic power, to secure its backyard, while shifting away from perceived one-sided security alliances.

Trump’s foreign policy revives Founding-era ideas, however, a direct return to these strategies overlooks the evolution of America’s global role.While 18th- and 19th-century foreign policies had merit, traditional conservative foreign policy has adapted to America’s evolved global role.

Trump announcing tariffs on “Liberation Day”

The Founders and McKinley crafted policies for a rising power focused on national unity, economic strength, and strategic expansion. The Founders did not neglect commitments in Europe in a move towards isolationism but regularly engaged with European powers for trade and diplomatic measures. They navigated international engagement with a view of the future, carefully avoiding entanglement in European wars while simultaneously using European interstate rivalries to strengthen America. They strategically consolidated this growing power in North America through westward expansion. Alexander Hamilton established beneficial trade relations and national financial credit with Great Britain, Thomas Jefferson conducted the Louisiana Purchase, and James Madison obtained Florida and halted European colonization in the Western Hemisphere.

In the 19th century, America began to take a stronger and more assertive role as a rising power in the international sphere. Under McKinley, they pushed their influence in the Asia-Pacific region where McKinley obtained vast islands in the Pacific, most notably Hawaii, negotiated the Open Door Policy in China, and won the Spanish-American War, expanding American territory into the Philippines, Puerto Rico and forcing Spain out of Cuba.

McKinley was also famous for his use of tariffs to promote self-sufficiency and strengthen domestic industry in a rapidly industrializing economy prone to rely on foreign manufacturers, primarily Europe, to defend against economic recessions. Trump too has championed tariffs as a way to revitalize U.S. manufacturing and domestic industry, address national security concerns with critical supply chains, counter unfair trading practices, reverse the American debt, and expand domestic manufacturing jobs available. In the strategy of reshoring American industry, Trump’s tariffs appear similar to McKinley’s. However, Trump’s tariffs deviate from McKinley’s in his tactical use of tariffs to ensure foreign alignment to U.S. interests beyond issues of trade.

Trump’s foreign policy revives Founding-era ideas, however, a direct return to these strategies overlooks the evolution of America’s global role.

An “America First” policy does not mean an “America Alone” policy. Neither Trump nor historical conservative presidents are isolationist; instead, they engage globally to advance American interests. The key debate is not whether to serve U.S. interests, but how to do so effectively in today’s geopolitical landscape. While the American diplomatic and foreign policy strategies of the 18th and 19th centuries led to American success at its time, these strategies were designed for America as a rising power not suited for the America of today.

The diplomatic strategies of the 18th and 19th centuries helped America rise, but they were designed for a weaker nation, not a global superpower. Early American leaders recognized that the U.S. lacked the military and economic power to lead the international order. This could mean that Trump views the U.S. as a declining power, taken advantage of by the international system, allies and adversaries alike, in unfair trade deals and multilateral institutions.

In contrast, conservative foreign policy post-World War II, most notably under Reagan, embraced a strategy of peace through strength, close military alliances, free trade, promotion of global democracy, and American primacy. It established and grew the U.S.-led international order after the most brutal set of wars in humanity’s history. This strategy created the most successful international order the world has ever known, providing long-lasting peace between great-powers, bolstering prosperity and democratic supremacy. These benefits, now taken for granted, are pillars of conservative foreign policy.

President Ronald Reagan and Soviet General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev signing the arms control agreement banning the use of intermediate-range nuclear missles, the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Reduction Treaty.

Traditional conservative foreign policy principles should continue guiding America as the leader of the world, advancing moral leadership alongside strong defense and resisting a world ruled by power and coercion. This does not mean abandoning the nation’s founding ideals but applying them pragmatically to today’s challenges. History offers wise lessons on strategies proved effective and how they can be adapted to today’s realities.

The Trump Administration has an opportunity to challenge many of the obsolete assumptions in contemporary foreign policy by understanding that order flows from power and can hardly be preserved without it. Powerful authoritarian regimes around the world threaten this international order because it restrains their inmost desire to exert their strength through military expansion and regional dominance. Russia, Iran, North Korea, and China all seek to recreate the world in their image, one of repression and predation, through war and the threat of war.

Traditional conservative foreign policy principles should continue guiding America as the leader of the world, advancing moral leadership alongside strong defense and resisting a world ruled by power and coercion.

Trump must readopt aspects of the 20th century conservative foreign policy to retain America’s success on the international stage. While the pursuit of peace as an end is necessary, the pursuit of a just and lasting peace is sufficient for not only obtaining but maintaining a peaceful world.

American strategists after the Second World War took several lessons from the past decades in their formation of the American-led international order, securing of the greatest peace between great-powers the world has ever known.

First, while Woodrow Wilson had an admirable and appealing vision for the world in the League of Nations, he lost the lasting peace by forsaking public and Congressional support. The Great Depression of the 1920s and 30s displayed the benefits of free trade between nations both for economic and political recovery and cooperation, avoiding divisive blocs of autarkical states.

World War II taught Americans one final and simple lesson: appeasement fails to satisfy dictators. Only strength could deter these dictators’ expansionist dreams of empire. For Trump to ensure this just and lasting peace against the new tensions facing the international order, he must retain the support of the public and Congress, prioritize free trade with our allies, and build U.S. military strength. Without the traditional conservative’s high valuation of such peace, Trump’s move seems reckless and destructive by both allies and adversaries alike.

Trump must readopt aspects of the 20th century conservative foreign policy to retain America’s success on the international stage.

In his second term, Trump has the opportunity to bring together the best of American foreign policy from the 18th to the 20th century. Amidst the flux of changing American policies under Trump, conservatives should reflect on what a traditional conservative foreign policy should look like today.

We should recognize the 20th century concern for supporting the strength of democracies abroad through USAID, security alliances, and free trade agreements, while also acknowledging the 18th and 19th century importance of exerting influence to hold both allies and adversaries accountable, protect domestic economic strength, and force adversarial powers from the Western Hemisphere, our own backyard.

While many foreign policies require recalibration under Trump, the consistent thrust of American foreign policy must remain—we must balance Eurasian power and prevent any single actor from dominating the continent through a strategic threat of force. By so doing, we recognize that the power that controls Eurasia controls the world.

item.title: Donald Trump is the Fulfillment of a Founder’s Vision
item.description:
When I was thirteen, I attended my first political rally in my home state of Pennsylvania. I went with my father, a middle-school American history teacher. He had raised my brothers and me on stories of great heroes both historical and fictional. As a boy, I was disposed to works like The Lord of the Rings, Chronicles of Narnia, Star Wars, The Odyssey, The Iliad, King Arthur, Beowulf, The Bible, and numerous stories of our American Founders and national heroes. I admired great men—especially those who had a divinely ordained mission. I wanted to be just like the heroes I read in books and watched on the screen.

In 2016, I learned an important lesson: politics is an active application of history. Indeed, all eyes were on this election. Two staunchly different candidates battled for command of the world’s highest helm. One of them I knew could actually win it. He defied expectation.

Donald Trump

Here I now stood as a boy in 2016 on time-trodden grounds watching history unfold before my eyes. At this Trump rally, I understood for the first time that great men still exist, and I could associate myself with one of them. I recognize Trump’s persona is not wholly admirable. He is, however, undeniably a man on a mission. Flawed, yes, but invigorated by a burning sense of purpose. I took him to be like one of these great men I grew up reading about.

I do often wonder how our great Founders would view our 45th and 47th President. There is no way to know for sure, but years of personal association with one particular Founding Father has led me to believe that Trump may actually fulfill a presidential ideal. In early 2022, I joined a national organization called the Alexander Hamilton Society. Two years ago, I was tapped to lead the Baylor chapter. Having immersed myself in Hamiltonian perspectives for over three years, I now propose that Donald Trump is the fulfillment of Alexander Hamilton’s executive vision. This is my view alone and does not reflect my organization. This is simply my observation several years in the making. Donald Trump’s national policies and powerful personality are squarely in line with the Hamiltonian ideal.

To understand Trump’s economic perspective, one only needs to reference Hamilton’s written thoughts on the subject. Hamilton’s plan to bolster the American nation was rooted in the belief that geo-economic strategy works, and that government investment in the economy and protection over trade was to be the foundation of growth. With federal support, the American private sector would, in turn, stabilize the American military, social, and political domains. Hamilton thus recognized the importance of economic statecraft when aiming at global power.

I recognize Trump’s persona is not wholly admirable. He is, however, undeniably a man on a mission. Flawed, yes, but invigorated by a burning sense of purpose.

In an era when Adam Smith’s free trade theory began to make waves, Hamilton remained a proponent of tariffs and protectionism. Free trade has become the prevailing philosophy in our global 21st Century. Trump’s recent implementations of tariffs and his consistent support for protectionist policies have come as a shock to contemporary economists. However, these ideas are not so far-fetched. Economic security is national security. In these matters, even Adam Smith believed the government should be involved to protect the nation-state.

For liberal democracies, free trade can be a net positive. When dealing with totalitarian regimes like China, which openly flouts the rules, free trade can hurt a country. Other nations have implemented relatively high tariffs on the United States whereas American trade barriers have remained low. Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs are a product of revived protectionism. Reciprocity in trade can allow the United States to counter poor agreements with adversarial and allied nations alike.

Alexander Hamilton

President Trump embodies Hamilton’s national economic philosophy. Trump is—as Hamilton was—unabashedly “America First.” He has already leveraged American economic power to elevate our global political power and national security. Tariffs not only offer industry protection and external revenue, but Trump has begun to use them as a negotiating tool. His threat of tariffs on Canada and Mexico have resulted in agreements to increase international cooperation on border security and the fight against drug trafficking. His joint public-private investments in artificial intelligence, energy, space travel, and manufacturing have bolstered our national security. Trump’s economic agenda may seem frightening to status-quo economists, but it’s nothing new. Hamilton’s ideas have worked before. With a modern application, they can work again. They just need an energetic executive to enact the vision.

To Americans, power is a provocative word. It conjures images of men who have corrupted positions of authority for their own gain—men who used their power to bring evil into the world. But power is not evil. Power can be used for good. Trump is leveraging the presidential powers vested in him by the U.S. Constitution. His rapid course of action has come to frighten critics who say he is concentrating executive power. While these claims are disputed, there is a truth that is impossible to deny:

Donald Trump is powerful.

When Trump walks into a room, the air thickens. When he speaks, people listen. What he asks is done with haste. Trump is a powerful individual. He leverages his natural gifts to fulfill Hamilton’s ideal of the most powerful office in the world. Federalist no. 70 envisions an energetic executive at the helm of the Oval Office. This does not mean a power-hungry or power concentrating president, but a president that is quick and energized to accomplish his goals.

Hamilton’s ideas have worked before. With a modern application, they can work again. They just need an energetic executive to enact the vision.

Since a certain Broadway play was produced, it’s frequently forgotten that Hamilton was also a controversial figure during his day. Hamilton displayed a shameless audacity in pursuit of his goals. He was a non-stop machine-like high-energy individual. I believe Hamilton would admire these same qualities in President Trump today. I will add that President Trump is not the only American president who has fulfilled Hamilton’s ideal. Savvy, spirited, and swashbuckling, Teddy Roosevelt embodied policy positions and a powerful personality that would have adhered to Hamilton’s liking. Franklin D. Roosevelt also possessed a powerful Hamiltonian persona and energy to accomplish his grand New Deal vision. Trump’s energy and savvy matches that of fellow presidents like the Roosevelts. In simple terms, these men just get things done.

How history ultimately views Donald Trump is not up to us. Regardless of current perception, Trump has made his mark in the history books. He forged a new political era. Three consecutive election cycles have been centered on him. Years of slander, courtroom trials, impeachments, and a would-be assassin’s bullet ought to be enough to slow a man down, but Trump kept on going.

Alexander Hamilton was unquestionably a great man of his day. He surrounded himself with other great men of similar caliber. Thomas Jefferson once remarked that the Constitutional Convention had been composed of an “assembly of demi-gods.” These were the men that would chart the course of the nation, and such people still exist today. After three contentious election cycles, Donald Trump has earned his mark in history as a great man. His policy aligns with Hamilton’s vision. His power and persona fulfill Hamilton’s executive ideal. In turning back the pages of history, one will see that Alexander Hamilton’s vision lived through President Trump, may just be the key to Make America Great Again.

cover image from salon.com

item.title: Calvin Coolidge and the Paradox of Conservative Journalism
item.description:
For a free press, reporting facts for their objective significance rather than their perceived benefit to society is a principle long prioritized by conservatives.

In 1925, for example, President Calvin Coolidge commended the American Society of Newspaper Editors for printing recently revealed income statistics in their news columns while their editorial columns advised that publicity for those statistics would be harmful for society. Coolidge praised the newspaper editors for maintaining this necessary tension in their craft. “As practical newsmen they printed the facts. As editorial idealists they protested that there ought to be no such facts available.”

Calvin Coolidge’s Address at the Celebration of the 150th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence

This paradox illustrates a key principle of conservative news journalism: disinterest—printing significant facts as objectively as possible with little care for the social consequences.

I use the term “disinterest” similarly to how Baylor Professor Elizabeth Corey used it in a 2018 essay in National Affairs, “Defending Disinterest.” Corey writes that “the practical-political university is intensely concerned with future outcomes; the disinterested university is focused on the process of learning in and for itself, right now.” Disinterested universities pursue the immediate function of schools as learning environments.

Similarly, disinterested journalists pursue the immediate function of journalism as delivering accurate information on the state of our country rather than using their institutions as platforms for their personal agenda.

When we think of our institutions as performative, rather than formative , they become harder to trust.

Elizabeth Corey

Objectivity—the primary application of disinterested journalism—is widely valued in news reporting. But I believe that objectivity is a specifically conservative value, one supported by the most fundamental conservative principles. Broadly speaking, conservatives believe in a transcendent reality, which allows them to value truth for its own sake. Conservatives advocate slow and prudent reform, which leads them to preserve the norms that give journalism credibility as an institution. And most importantly, conservatives see themselves as fulfilling a social role, which motivates them to act as servants to an institution rather than reformers using the institution as their stage.

In the Coolidge example, the “practical newsmen” were fulfilling their social role of providing information to the people. The duty of a newsman is to give all the significant facts, even those he does not believe should be public. A disinterested newsman serves the truth, not the direct good of society. This is why newsmen ought to be in tension with policy makers, and the editorial columns that advise them. They each serve goals that are noble, necessary, but sometimes contradictory.

Our culture seems to find this tension much easier to accept in the realm of law. A defense attorney who capably defends a guilty client does direct harm to the public good by empowering a criminal, but indirectly contributes to the public good by supporting a justice system in which everyone is given a defense. A virtuous defense attorney and a virtuous prosecuting attorney ought to be in tension, because they serve noble, yet contradictory goals.

For journalism to maintain its credibility, we must dedicate ourselves to building it up as an institution, rather than using it as a stage for our activism.

“Disinterest,” in journalism, universities, and our broader culture, is going out of style. In his book A Time to Build, Dr. Yuval Levin explains why Americans are losing trust in our institutions, and why that trust is important to preserve. He writes:

When we don’t think of our institutions as formative but as performative—when the presidency and Congress are just stages for political performance art, when a university becomes a venue for vain virtue signalling, when journalism is indistinguishable from activism—they become harder to trust. They aren’t really asking for our confidence, just for our attention.

Yuval Levin

For journalism to maintain its credibility, we must dedicate ourselves to building it up as an institution, rather than using it as a stage for our activism.

A conservative is not the world-changing, activist hero in the story he tells of himself. He is an economic contributor, a vital check in a balanced government, a voice in a stable justice system—advancing society as, in the words of Edmund Burke, a partner with “those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.”

Opinion journalism plays an important role in synthesizing information into arguments and advice, just as it did in Coolidge’s day, but we must resist the temptation to place news journalism in the service of opinion pieces. Conservatives should lead the way in embracing the uncomfortable paradox of disinterest.

item.title: Is Trump’s USAID Shutdown Conservative?
item.description:
“CLOSE IT DOWN,” President Donald Trump declared on his social media platform, Truth Social. Hours later, the metal letters spelling “US Agency for International Development” (USAID) lay in a heap on the floor.

Letters spelling “US Agency for International Development” lay in heap after being stripped from building; Photo from Business Insider

Established in 1961, USAID is the principal federal agency responsible for aiding countries recovering from disasters, combating poverty, and promoting democratic reform. The dismantling of the USAID headquarters is a striking symbol of the broader effort by President Trump to disband the agency.

The saga began on January 20, when President Trump issued an executive order halting foreign aid programs pending a 90-day review. By February 6, over a thousand USAID employees were placed on leave, and the administration announced plans to reduce the agency’s global workforce from more than 10,000 to just 100. By February 26, another 2,000 employees were fired, and thousands more put on leave. Court documents revealed that the administration intends to cut 90% of the agency’s operations.

Despite a temporary waiver from Senator Marco Rubio allowing lifesaving aid to continue, USAID employees reported that aid is still halted due to obstacles such as the shutdown of the agency’s payment system.

On March 5, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s request to freeze nearly $2 billion in foreign aid payments for completed USAID and State Department projects.

While debates about USAID’s effectiveness and the proposed reforms are valid, the Trump administration’s attack on the agency seems driven by an ethos of destruction rather than improvement, a mindset incapable of seeing the good within the structures it seeks to dismantle.

Mindy Belz, a distinguished foreign correspondent and firsthand witness to USAID’s impact, shared her insights on the Trump administration’s actions.

Mindy Belz

Belz recalled her early experiences with foreign aid, reporting on the flaws within an NGO’s structure. Despite these problems, she emphasized that real, tangible good was still being done. “It wasn’t an all-or-nothing problem,” she said.

“By dismantling USAID, we are taking away one of our most effective tools for projecting American interests abroad and taking away the face of America which has been a humanitarian face in the midst of some of the worst calamities,” Belz noted. “What does the Trump administration hope to achieve with this?”

While the Trump administration’s goals in shutting down USAID remain unclear, the actions reflect key characteristics of its ethos. These characteristics are incongruous with traditional conservatism, a mantle the administration tries to wear.

Belz’ insight contrasts sharply with the Trump administration’s current campaign against USAID. Trump’s calls to “CLOSE IT DOWN” and Elon Musk’s claim that USAID “is not an apple with a worm in it…but actually just a ball of worms” reflect the “all or nothing” approach Belz rejects. The destruction of the agency, she argued, will harm U.S. diplomatic relations and reputation by diminishing trust with allies and nations that rely on American support.

The first characteristic is the administration’s inability to see the good before them. Contrary to Belz’ insight that flaws may exist alongside real benefits, the Trump administration seems focused only on exposing problems, ignoring the positive contributions of USAID

Historically, however, both republican and democratic administrations have viewed the activities of USAID—building up civic society, repairing roads, building hospitals, reconstructing sewer systems—as integral to America’s global presence and identity. To be a force for good in the world was once a bipartisan aim. The current administration, however, refuses to acknowledge any value in these efforts. For them, USAID is nothing more than a tangle of corruption to be eradicated.

The administration’s failure to see the good before them contradicts the conservative ethos of gratitude. Michael Oakeshott (1901-1990), a notable conservative philosopher, once wrote that a true conservative is one who can “delight in what is present rather than what was or what may be,” who has “an appropriate gratefulness for what is available.” For he sees the present as a gift to be cared for.

In contrast, Trump’s administration embodies a spirit of condemnation, not gratitude. Belz affirmed this, observing that by shutting down USAID, the administration is “drawing a circle around what America has, not recognizing it as a gift we received, a gift to be shared with the world.”

Michael Oakeshott

The conservative value of caring for the present is glaringly absent in Trump’s handling of USAID. Belz highlighted the administration’s disregard for NGOs and faith-based organizations abroad, which have been left in crisis without promised U.S. funding. She pointed out that the instinct to help and share resources is no longer part of the administration’s approach. If this mindset extends to all areas of diplomacy, Belz warned, “we cease to be the country we have been.”

What follows this inability to see and be grateful for the present good is a willingness to enact radical change for a utopian “bliss,” the second characteristic of Trump’s ethos.

The conservative according to Oakeshott, however, believes change “entails certain loss and possible gain,” and who, if change is indeed warranted, prefers “small and limited innovations to large and indefinite.” This is not the attitude of the Trump administration. They seemingly pay little regard to the certain loss they have prompted by the large and sweeping shutdown of USAID. They are too focused on “making America great again,” the “possible good” of utopian bliss, to care for the America of the present.

Belz acknowledged the need for reform within USAID operations, while still maintaining and caring for the existence of the agency and U.S. diplomatic presence. Belz affirmed that the power of the presidency lends itself to a variety of strategic ways to clean up business and reduce excess without completely gutting the agency and uprooting U.S. diplomacy. While the issues may be complex, they are not hopeless.

Oakeshott writes that the conservative prefers change which “resembles growth,” as opposed to change that is “merely imposed upon a situation.” What USAID needs is not the imposed destruction of the Trump administration, but rather a hopeful renewal built upon thoughtful collaboration and careful strategy. The Trump administration’s attack on USAID is not simply a product of USAID shortcomings, but a product of the administration’s lack of creativity and hope.

This hopeless destructiveness is the third characteristic of the Trump administration’s ethos. While Trump’s mantra is “make America great again,” rather than seek to renew or improve American institutions, Trump’s leadership is defined by a relentless drive to tear them down. His approach is one of destruction, not creation.

This is antithetical to the conservative ethos of hope. Hope does not tear down but builds up. True conservatives are not in the business of dismantling what has been built but of renewing and preserving it for the future. Hope comes from recognizing the gifts of the present, not from fantasizing about an idealized future.

Amid so much destruction and hopelessness, Belz offered a way forward: “Train your eyes to see what you haven’t been seeing.” Instead of focusing on the bad, look for the good in our trials. Draw resilience from the great examples in our country of those who overcame great trials with faith and hope. As an example, Belz shared the moving strength of the African American churches who started their work by singing.

This seemed to me a very conservative approach: see the good and give thanks, return to the past and learn, hope in goodness and renew our present time. As the USAID shutdown continues apace, may we find the strength to resist despair and seek the work of renewal. May we follow the example of our forbearers and start this work with singing.

Cover Photo: Celal Gunes/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

item.title: Trump Isn’t The Answer to the Gender Wars
item.description:
Donald Trump is a masculine icon. Conservative men venerate him for his frank speech and his business-savvy politics. In the 2024 presidential race, podcast appearances and “alpha male” language seemingly cemented Trump’s influence over young men.

It appears that Trump made men more conservative. But the facts show otherwise.

Photo from the New York Times : https://static01.nyt.com/images/2024/11/05/multimedia/pol-trump-wins-hfo-new0101-qzgw/pol-trump-wins-hfo-new0101-qzgw-mediumSquareAt3X.jpg

According to Gallup polling, the percentage of young conservative men has held relatively stable. Meanwhile, the percentage of young liberal women has jumped in the last decade.

This gender gap suggests that Trump has not persuaded more men to be conservative. Rather, he emboldened existing radical men and alienated previously moderate and conservative women.

How did Trump widen this political chasm between the sexes? And how can true conservativism win back radicals of both sexes?

The political divide between the sexes began well before Trump’s first presidency. Until 2013, Gallup polling shows that the political gender gap was relatively narrow. After 2013, a considerable number of conservative and moderate women shifted to the left, more than doubling the previous separation.

While Trump himself did not cause the political gender gap, he is emblematic of its underlying cause: a perversion of true conservative masculinity. Trump’s presidency spread this perversion publicly, further widening the political divide between the sexes.

Trump has not persuaded more men to be conservative. Rather, he emboldened existing radical men and alienated previously moderate and conservative women.

Contrary to conservatism’s emphasis on personal moral duty and accountability, Trump’s words and deeds reflect disregard for personal morality.

For example, Trump’s marital history is rife with infidelity and lack of commitment. Ivana Zelnickova, his first wife, divorced Trump after discovering his affair with Marla Maples, the woman who would become his second wife. Amid his divorce to Maples, Trump began dating Melania Knauss, his third and current wife. Trump is the only U.S. president with this kind of marital history.

In 2023, a jury awarded E. Jean Carroll millions of dollars in relation to Trump sexually assaulting her and defaming her. In 2024, a jury convicted Trump in connection with hush money payments made to a porn star who claimed to have sex with him. Both cases concern sexual encounters Trump allegedly had while he was married.

E. Jean Carroll. Photo taken from NPR; https://media.npr.org/assets/img/2023/04/26/ap23116485022449-20d60f61beda7b50d2bdeb7acd158221b85db2f0.jpg?s=1100&c=50&f=jpeg

Trump infamously boasted that his celebrity status allowed him to kiss women and grab their genitals. “When you’re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything,” Trump said in the 2016 “Access Hollywood” recording. When the recording leaked, Trump gave a half-hearted apology and defended his comments as “locker room banter.”

Despite Trump’s known habits of promiscuity and lewdness, he and his allies are all too willing to dismiss legal attempts at accountability as political “lawfare.”

Many women reject conservatism because of this Trumpian behavior masquerading as conservative. They believe that conservatism fails to hold men accountable for their actions. Viral movements such as #metoo and #churchtoo seemed to expose the inadequacy of traditional institutions. Thus, many women seek liberal alternatives to counter male capriciousness and elevate female autonomy.

Conservatives should be the first to recognize Trump’s sexual practices as unconservative.

But if Trumpian masculinity isn’t conservative masculinity, then what is? Can true conservativism be a real solution to the political gender gap?

True conservative masculinity must be distinguished from the frauds. Barry Goldwater defines conservatism in The Conscience of a Conservative as “look[ing] upon politics as the art of achieving the maximum amount of freedom for individuals that is consistent with the maintenance of social order.”

Conservatives emphasize individuals’ responsibility for their own improvement and the dangers of concentrated political power. Conservatives also generally recognize humans as spiritual and ensouled beings, a quality which imbues each person, no matter their gender, with inviolable worth and dignity.

Following these principles, conservative masculinity respects others’ freedoms and responsibilities. True conservative men recognize that the concentration of power requires self-restraint and accountability, especially if that power lies in their own hands. Ultimately, conservative masculinity submits personal autonomy to moral duty.

To win back liberal converts, conservative men and women must actively combat abuses of power, especially if they occur within structures conservatives seek to promote. Conservatives should be the first to call out misogynistic patriarchy as tyranny. Conservatives should be the first to demand consequences for sexual abusers who infiltrate institutions, such as the church. Conservatives should be the first to recognize Trump’s sexual practices as unconservative.

If modern conservatives were as enthusiastic about punishing sexual violence as they were about punishing illegal immigration, the political gender gap could look drastically different.

Men have become so hardened by their fight against liberalism that they risk losing their sensitivity to true conservative values.

Conservatives must demand consistently moral leaders. Trump’s crackdown on transgender athletes and gender ideology correctly upholds the distinction between the sexes. However, protecting women-only spaces reads as hypocritical for someone found liable for sexually assaulting someone in a women’s dressing room.

Additionally, conservatives must win back men who have gone too far in the name of “conservatism.” Such men have become so hardened by their fight against liberalism that they risk losing their sensitivity to true conservative values.

For example, when 67 people died in a collision between a military helicopter and a commercial airliner this January, Trump blamed the incident on DEI policies and the gender of the pilot. Online outrage was quick to focus on the female helicopter pilot, regardless of her merit. Trump’s reversal of DEI policies is only a victory for meritocracy if it does not embolden discrimination and hatred.

Reining in “red pill” culture and the “manosphere” means catechizing young men in conservative values. Respect for all persons, accountable leadership, and moral responsibility are central to conservative masculinity.

In the end, winning back both liberal converts and radicalized men requires compassion. Ideological splintering hints at the immense suffering experienced by men and women alike. In such a hurting world, let us bridge the political gender gap by seeing beyond ideological caricatures and caring for humanity’s deepest needs.

Cover Photo from Christianity Today

item.title: Can Great Texts Be Friends?
item.description:
I really enjoy reading books with friends and wrestling with the fundamental questions of “the great conversation” together. I love picturing past contemporaneous authors doing the same, the Inklings and Maecenas’ circle gathering over something a little stronger than Dr. Pepper. Seriously, imagine being friends with C. S. Lewis or Virgil! In fact, I would like to think that, in a way, we are, and that brings me to the question I want to reflect on with you. How can we read books not only with friends, but as friends? In other words, can these authors, despite our separation by time, become our friends through our study of their great texts? Some striking similarities do stand out between friendship and studying great texts, and this essay explores the value of those great texts through this metaphor of friendship.

Before progressing, let me clarify that a real difference exists between the friendships we experience with those alive with us today and those commemorated in books. While I draw out similarities that help us enter into our readings more deeply, I encourage my readers to enter simultaneously more deeply into relationships with their neighbors. God has given each experience its own riches; I wish for neither’s deprivation. Great texts offer wonderfully relevant wisdom, consolation, humor, and inspiration, but you cannot offer the same to them in the reciprocity of the truest friendship. Neither can you physically nourish one another. I once mused, “You cannot hug a poem like you cannot hug a phantom”—and a cup of water is not life-giving to a page. You gasp in horror, but you know we have all been there. In short, the quasi-immortality authors achieve through great texts does not preserve a whole person (sorry, Horace and Ovid). Consequently, our friendship with great texts is metaphorical, which does not make it worthless, but rather worthy in a different way. But enough caveats—let us ponder the beneficial similarities between great texts and friendship that spark the metaphor in the first place. Both extend to us faithful companionship, longed-for relatability, maturing conversation, and increasing degrees of influence.

How can we read books not only with friends, but as friends?

Our friends are the people we go through life with. While our authors must endure the downside of being dead, they possess the marvelous advantage of traveling around in their books wherever we go, mimicking friends’ close companionship. Cicero commends the constancy of studying great texts in his Pro Archia:

Other pursuits belong not to all times, all ages, all conditions; but this gives stimulus to our youth and diversion to our old age; this adds a charm to success, and offers a haven of consolation to failure. In the home it delights, in the world it hampers not. Through the night-watches, on all our journeying, and in our hours of country ease, it is our unfailing companion.

Is this not praise enough for such studies? In a world of change, we yearn for intimate and long-term connection. We want people to be there for us while we are young and “new” at life, and when we grow old and are still trying to figure out how to live well. We crave their shared joy through our happiness, as well as their comfort through our sadness. We want them with us in and outside our homes. And here is Cicero describing that kind of desired companionship—but through literature! If his comparison of great texts to friendship is not already obvious, a passage from his De Amicitia (“On Friendship”) makes it even clearer. Gaius Laelius recalls his friendship with the late Scipio Africanus Minor:

In it I found agreement on public questions; in it, counsel in private business, and in it, too, a leisure of unalloyed delight. . . there was one home for us both; we had the same fare and shared it in common, and we were together not only in our military campaigns, but also in our foreign tours and on our vacations in the country.

Specific words in this depiction of togetherness enhance the connection between the passages. Cicero uses oblectationis to convey the “delight” of friendship, which contains the same root as both his wording for the great texts’ “diversion” of “old age” (oblectant), as well as their “delights” at “home” (delectant). The pairing of the friends’ “foreign tours” and “vacations in the country” (peregrinationes rusticationesque) likewise takes on the corresponding verb forms in great texts’ companionship through “our journeying” and “country ease” (peregrinantur, rusticantur). I need not even mention that the next sentence in De Amicitia remarks that Laelius and Scipio shared their studiis together.

Given Cicero writes his De Amicitia in 44 B.C., one cannot help but wonder if, as he speaks of the studies he defended in Pro Archia in 62 B.C., he further references his speech with these verbal parallels. He first paints a picture of books as friends. Now, he recycles his wording to emphasize the companionship of friends. This echo highlights for us the “friendishness” of books, insofar as they can accompany us faithfully through life.

But how do we make friends with them in the first place? As with our present-day friends, we first relate to authors when we discover similarities to ourselves in them. C. S. Lewis famously wrote, “The typical expression of opening Friendship would be something like, ‘What? You too? I thought I was the only one.’” We all know the thrill of finding a person shares a niche interest or relates to an experience that before felt unique, even isolating. The same bond occurs when we find past authors that are like us, addressing a question in humanity’s “great conversation” dear to our hearts.

Just as in friendship, we best begin—and continue—by being elated, or at least intrigued, to know someone shares an experience with us.

For instance, maybe you lost loved ones and suffer from chronic illness. May I introduce you to the life of Flannery O’Connor, who lost her father to lupus when she was 15 and then struggled with the same illness until she died at age 39? She once penned in a letter, “In a sense sickness is a place, more instructive than a long trip to Europe, and it’s always a place where there’s no company, where no one can follow.” She reflected on her suffering’s loneliness, but, ironically, hearing how others feel this way can offer a sort of companionship in our suffering.

Or maybe you are navigating the intricacies of love and friendship (or “freindship” for the doctus lector), secrecy and deceit, assumption and correction, patience and wisdom in your local community. Upon opening a Jane Austen novel, you may be surprised to find uncannily parallel situations. Austen seems to understand you as you understand her characters.

Connections like these draw us in to listen to what else an author has to say. Just as in friendship, we best begin—and continue—by being elated, or at least intrigued, to know someone shares an experience with us. Even with authors we anticipate disagreeing with in parts, finding common ground can be very helpful to stay engaged with getting to know the author. This relatability also comforts and encourages us down the line, as those who have been through the same things offer consolation, insight, and advice. After all, this makes their constant companionship, even in sorrow, pleasing.

And then, just as friendship grows through conversation, we keep reading and interacting with our texts through metaphorical dialogue. Authors write of an idea or situation, we respond with our own in margins or papers, and we keep reading to see if they answer our questions or raise even more in the pages to come. Although great texts cannot read the annotations inscribed upon them and truly listen to the thoughts we offer, they still have a knack for replying to them somehow in their work anyway. Sometimes it is when we listen to what they are actually saying more carefully, which is a key (but often neglected) step in friendship, as well. This process produces an ongoing exchange of thought, which turns out to be Aristotle’s definition of friends’ living together: “For in the case of human beings what seems to count as living together is this sharing of conversation and thought, not sharing the same pasture, as in the case of grazing animals.” Even though it is a great gift to eat with our living friends, it is our dialogue with both these friends and our books that draw us into an even deeper connection with them.

And wonderfully, just as friends sharpen one another toward virtue, we find ourselves maturing through this conversation, for wrestling with an author’s ideas can yield wisdom we would not have reached on our own. Solomon commented on the value of such togetherness in Ecclesiastes: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow.” We can read this in a figurative sense as well as a literal one. Friends are there to pick each other up when they fall physically, but also when they fall into error. Sometimes we have the eyes to recognize an author has slipped into one erroneous ditch characteristic of his age, and the next chapter the author drags us out of the other treacherous trench that we, stuck in our own time, were previously blind to (an idea C. S. Lewis describes in his preface to Athanasius’ On the Incarnation as well). For example, the pages of my reading list this past semester grew ornate with comments such as “Is this a bit gnostic?” as well as “Oh dear, this is convicting about humility… Dear Lord, vanquish my pride.” Both Aristotle and Cicero discuss the important pursuit of virtue in friendship; our conversation with great texts thus refines how we see we ought to live.

Wrestling with an author’s ideas can yield wisdom we would not have reached on our own.

Lastly, just as quality time with friends increases their effect, our time with great texts increases their metaphorical friendship’s influence. Seneca also compares reading to friendship:

You should be extending your stay among writers whose genius is unquestionable, deriving constant nourishment from them if you wish to gain anything from your reading that will find a lasting place in your mind. To be everywhere is to be nowhere. People who spend their whole life traveling abroad end up having plenty of places where they can find hospitality but no real friendships.
