Just as hastening between many acquaintances hampers more substantial relationships, reading many different authors gives us a little knowledge spread over much but not a richer knowledge about specific areas.

While I might disagree with Seneca here slightly and suggest the value of literature surveys for context, I do gain much more from authors when I spend significant time focusing on them. Instead of knowing a few soundbites, I am familiar with their different stories and their tensions, the ways they try to handle the world, and aspects of their personalities I can sense from their writing. They feel like old friends, and I call them that. You have met them through my references in this piece. Intensive classes on these authors seared their words and ideas into my mind, and these often guide me through analyzing my grief and joy and deciding how to act amid them. Reading generally provides us with guidance when we stumble on a relevant passage, but reading on this more intimate level gives their guidance a “lasting place in your mind.” These experiences, Seneca tells us, are like “real friendships,” and we end with an application of that bit of gold.

A great thing about books is that we can carry them with us pretty much anywhere. But the even greater thing is, we can spend so much time with an author that our very brains become the books that accompany and teach us through day and night, youth and old age, success and failure, private and public decisions, home-making and sojourning, work and rest—even prison, if you follow Boethius’ footsteps. That is, I suppose, a sort of “sticking closer than a brother.” I hope that in this new year we enjoy that kind of friendship with great texts, taking advantage of their close companionship throughout our lives, always connecting over our common ground, and developing through conversation with our special interlocuters. Maybe even do it with your living friends, too.

item.title: Hey, Christians, Who Picked up the Pitchforks?
item.description:
In a world of growing political division, Christians should be leading the charge on connection.

This election cycle, nearly every house in my neighborhood put out the same signs. I went to an election party where nearly everyone voted for the same candidate. I didn’t know there could be “liberal Christians” until I got to Baylor and met them, and I still think a lot of the “conservative Christians” don’t think they’re real. That smaller, liberal demographic—the “nearly” in my neighborhood—tends to be pushed away by the majority into their own, fenced-off group. The “less” is reduced of its complexity—thereby its humanity—by the “more,” relegated to caricatures and joke fodder. If this was the secular world, I wouldn’t be surprised by this. Division and lacuna are stock-in-trade in modern politics. However, Christians aren’t supposed to go along with the outside world. Their teacher was notorious in His time for crossing social boundaries, dining with both tax collectors and zealots. He led the way for radical unity. So, where’s the disconnect?

Jesus eats with sinners and publicans by Alexandre Bide

With some exceptions, I’ve been inside a bubble of the same socio-political sphere my entire life. I grew up in a more-or-less conservative, Christian household that sent me to a more-or-less conservative, Christian private school which set me up for a more-or-less conservative, Christian university. As I’ve trudged through the relative homogeny, it’s seemed easiest for the people I’ve grown up around to follow their Christian commandments within the sameness of their chosen communities, rather than outside them; shared values mean less friction, as it turns out. The golden rule to “love God, love others” is a lot easier to follow when your God and your others are a lot like you.

And I think that was the whole point of the commandment. The people of Jerusalem didn’t need help loving their in-group, and we don’t need help now. In John 13:15, Jesus makes it clear that his humility towards all people is an example for us. And if a Christian can’t reach across the party line and wash the feet of their neighbor, then what example are we setting?

Separation restricts people’s ability to relate to one another. If you’re closed off from other people, then you’re keeping yourself from loving as Christ calls us to.

I don’t know if I can propose a singular “Christian” party in American politics, despite efforts from either side. I have friends that are united by hardly more than their belief in the resurrection, and knowing these types of Christians matured my own views on faith and politics in a way that makes stark categorization seem impossible to me. Also, I should say: although the majority demographic that makes up my world is conservative, the same rules for in-groups and out-groups apply to majority liberal demographics, as well. We’re all complicit in division. So, if it’s not the establishment of a “Christian” party, what needs to change?

When leading Baylor’s chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society through political dialogues, President Luke D’Ambrosio has a guiding principle in his club: the foundation for productive political discussions is a fundamental respect for the other person. This is easy to say, but practice is a different story (think of the person who makes your eyes roll). And what happens if you’re in a neighborhood like mine, where you’re rarely exposed to people of a different view? Separation restricts people’s ability to relate to one another. If you’re closed off from other people, then you’re keeping yourself from loving as Christ calls us to.

God gave humanity free will, and we’ve done some admittedly odd things with it (I still question my thought process behind a particular high school haircut); however, it fuels the diversity in our world. Differences, in that sense, are holy, and loving our neighbor as ourselves means trying to know them like we know ourselves: fully, richly, and graciously. There’s a glorious weight to the idea that our neighbor is made in God’s image. When we overlook our theologies in favor of stereotypes, a significant aspect of the Christian calling is lost.

Seeking to love those different than us doesn’t simply mean tolerance; it means loving with our actions, by forming connections across our differences.

One of my favorite books of 2023 was Jeff Sharlet’s The Undertow, a collection of longform narrative journalism that occupied various pockets of America’s fractioning political sphere. An area of continual return was Evangelical Christianity: Sharlet gave his readers a hard look at a reality of far-right Christianity, to be sure; but the reason his book struck me was his earnest attempt at understanding these demographics. He tried to listen, really listen, to people radically different than himself. And in a world where Jesus tells us to cross differences and love our neighbor, Sharlet, a nonbeliever himself, should be noticed for going in the right direction.

Political differences are not the same as haircuts, however. Issues carry enough power between democrats and republicans to tear relationships apart. And it’s these issues’ fidelity to separation that sour people on the idea of connection. So, when does this “loving your neighbor” business cross the line? When should we dig our trenches?

I cannot imagine being told, amidst Roman persecution, to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s. I cannot imagine, as Nero burned and crucified Christians, being told to pray for those who persecute you. And yet, in the midst of serious threats and imminent danger, Christians were told to do just that. Remember Sharlet? He threw himself into dangerous places for the sake of understanding. The rest of us don’t get a paycheck for listening; going to those lengths means unspeakable compromise, whoever you voted for. It’s radical. It’s asinine upon first glance. It’s something I could never, ever tell someone to do. And yet, Jesus commands it. When I read what He asks of us, it’s never, “thou shalt vote republican or democrat.” He never claimed that November 5th was our salvific event. It’s pretty heavily implied, though, that the Kingdom of Heaven is bigger than Washington; also, Luke 17:21— “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” He’s adamant that we seek it.

Jesus exemplified a life of expansive connection, one that certainly makes room for the glory and mystery of our neighbor, whether we agree with them or not.

As we look to the Kingdom, we must remember that our neighbor belongs there, too. Seeking to love those different than us doesn’t simply mean tolerance; it means loving with our actions, by forming connections across our differences. We’re not digging trenches but tearing down fences. If you’re not around those different than you, seek them out. I mentioned at the beginning that I couldn’t define a “Christian” political party because of myriad Christians I’ve had the beneficial, albeit confusing at times, experience of meeting. I learned as I loved, and Lord knows I’m all the better for it.

Learn from that guy who makes your eyes roll, so that you might love them better (also, try to stop rolling your eyes at them). Wash their feet, as He did for us. Christians should be setting the example for modern political interaction, not falling into division. Jesus exemplified a life of expansive connection, one that certainly makes room for the glory and mystery of our neighbor, whether we agree with them or not. And who knows? If Christians become known for radical connection, we might be bringing the Kingdom of Heaven a little closer to Earth.

item.title: We Are The 99: Rethinking Our Place in the Biblical and Political Narratives
item.description:
Like many people who grew up in evangelical contexts, the local church was my second home. My Sunday mornings were reserved for service and Tuesday nights for youth groups. I went to church camp every summer and played Mary in the Christmas pageant every holiday. Reflecting on these experiences, I now see how formative the biblical stories we learn as young children are. These stories shaped me into the woman I am today. However, I have also seen problems with how these stories are often told and the consequences on our political and social engagement.

Think about the biblical stories you were taught as a child. How were you taught these stories? More specifically, how did you factor into the stories?

It seems that we are too often brought up to see ourselves on the “right side” of these stories—as the heroes or victims, rather than the perpetrators of injustice or violence. We are always the “in-group” rather than the “out-group” and the “good guys” instead of the “bad ones.” We are David, not Goliath. We are the prodigal son returning home, celebrated by his father rather than the jealous brother. We are the 1 sheep Jesus searches for rather than the 99 who must join him in the long and faithful pursuit of the lost. We are taught to view the biblical narrative through the lenses of “hero” and “villain” and to always identify ourselves with the victor. By always thinking we are on the “right” side of the stories, we fail to see the in-between space where we must do the hard work of reflection and discernment of our own lives. This framing affects not only how we see ourselves in the biblical narrative but is also formative of our political and social theologies.

Sometimes, we are not the one sheep that Jesus is chasing. Sometimes, we are the 99 who must welcome the lost.

Let’s consider how this rigid dichotomous framework affects our political thinking. There is a growing group of Christians who see themselves as political heroes; the “right” side fighting against the “wrong” side in support of “Christian” policies and candidates. It is no secret that most Americans believe Christianity is synonymous with Conservatism and assume that all evangelicals vote Republican in primary elections. Indeed, the recent election numbers seem to harden this assumption.

Defining a Christian candidate, however, and what makes a policy Christian, is actually really difficult. In ascribing one side to the “Christian” label, we exchange the difficult work of discerning Christian praxis for a dogmatic adherence to a political group and its figureheads. But how did we get here? Has it always been this way? Has there ever been a time when Christianity wasn’t culturally synonymous with the Republican or conservative party?

To understand the connection between Christianity and Conservatism, we should look back and start with the rise of the Moral Majority and Jerry Farwell.

Reverend Jerry Farwell was a fundamentalist preacher, religious broadcaster, and author. He is also known for being a force in the political arena and was particularly popular with Evangelicals. Farwell was the leader of a movement known as the Moral Majority which sought to rally together Christians on cultural and political issues such as abortion.

As Farwell grew in popularity, specifically through his televised program, “Old-Time Gospel Hour,” his following multiplied. The Moral Majority raised millions of dollars and was supported by countless volunteers. The organization was credited with playing a role in the election of former president Ronald Regan. The rise of the Moral Majority was the first time Americans saw a noteworthy connection between Evangelicals and the Republican Party.

We are too often brought up to see ourselves on the “right side” of these stories—as the heroes or victims, rather than the perpetrators of injustice or violence.

Before Farwell and his campaign, however, Evangelicals were rather mixed in politics. While, Billy Graham, the pioneer of the neo-evangelical movement, was sympathetic to Republican administrators he was also a registered Democrat and had a close friendship with Martin Luther King Junior. He paid King’s jail bond after his 1962 arrest in Albany, Georgia, and remarked after King’s death that the country had lost “a social leader and prophet.”

Jerry Farwell (right) with Ronald Reagan (left)

This all changed with Farwell and the Moral Majority, for if it wasn’t for Farwell and his campaign many Christians would have likely still voted for Jimmy Carter over Ronald Reagan in the 1980 election. Indeed, Carter seemed the more moral choice. While Reagan was an actor from California and would become the first divorced president, Carter was a committed Southern Baptist and Sunday school leader. Farwell’s evangelical support for Reagan now seems an ominous foreshadowing of the recent evangelical support for Donald Trump.

The Moral Majority and the legacy of Jerry Farwell help explain much of how we got to our current political climate and help us understand the “right side” and “wrong side” dichotomy we see in much of our Christian thinking about politics (where one has to vote Republican to be considered a “good” Christian) has not always been the norm.

This also means that, in the not-so-distant past, Christians did not see themselves as political heroes fighting for a political party. They saw their true allegiance to Christ and not a “Christian” party. Many evangelicals today, however, tend to think allegiance with Christ is synonymous with allegiance to a certain political party. They make political decisions based on what is best for the victory of their party, rather than first considering the poor, the hungry, and the vulnerable—people whom Christ seemed most concerned for.

In ascribing one side to the “Christian” label, we exchange the difficult work of discerning Christian praxis for a dogmatic adherence to a political group and its figureheads.

This can be seen in the growing “hero archetype” within Christian culture. By associating the victory of their party with the victory of Christianity, a growing sect of Christians have grown deeply concerned with engaging in culture wars. They spend hours a day on social media or watching the news. They become expert conspiracy theorists and find themselves constantly on edge and angry. Rather than feeding the poor and clothing the naked, they are “crushing” their opponents on Twitter. Rather than seeking peace, they are sowing further discord. This seems far from the example of Christ in the New Testament.

We must shift away from this dichotomous political model in which one is inherently right and the other wrong and instead align ourselves with a political theology that reflects Mark 12:31: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”

The Good Samaritan, Jean François

When engaging with Biblical stories and politics, we should not begin from a state of self-righteousness but rather a state of humble love. We need to stop seeing ourselves as David overcoming Goliath and see ourselves as the hands and feet of Christ: the suffering servant who loved the unlovable. We must be less concerned with winning battles and coming out on top, and more concerned with the active advancement of peace and justice. As Christians, we are not called to vote a certain way but to lay down our lives for others, to turn the other cheek, and to give away all our resources to those in need. We need to check our hearts the moment we find ourselves more concerned with winning culture wars than loving our neighbor, more concerned with being the hero than the servant.

Sometimes, we are not the one sheep that Jesus is chasing. Sometimes, we are the 99 who must welcome the lost. Sometimes we are not the prodigal returned, but the older brother who must learn to love. We are not always the center of the narrative but always get to partner with Jesus in relentlessly pursuing the lost, advocating for justice, and putting others’ needs before our own. When we learn how to identify ourselves with not only the heroes in the biblical narrative but also with the lost, the wanders, the sinners, the tax collectors, the Pharisees, and the background characters – we find ourselves shifting away from a faith that is inward focused to one that is outward focused. We move from a Christianity that is one-sided to one that encompasses every side – one that is boundless in love.

item.title: Facing the Dark and Finding the Sun: A Semester with Nietzsche and Murdoch
item.description:
“What angers you?” “Who do you admire and why?” These questions were posed to me by my moral philosophy professor at the beginning of this semester. He clarified. “I’m not asking about what merely irritates or annoys you but what you find deeply unjust. I’m not asking about what you simply like but what you find morally excellent in others.”

These questions remained with us throughout the semester as we engaged with thinkers from Plato and Aristotle to Martin Luther King Junior and Elizabeth Anscombe. At the end of the semester, we were asked to reflect on two thinkers who influenced or challenged our responses to these questions the most. How did they deepen our understanding of injustice and moral excellence? For me, these two thinkers were Friedrich Nietzsche and Iris Murdoch.

“I’m not asking about what merely irritates or annoys you but what you find deeply unjust. I’m not asking about what you simply like but what you find morally excellent in others.”

Beginning with Nietzsche, I recalled sitting in class on the first day reading The Madman and Thus Spake Zarathustra and being struck by how much I resonated with these stories! It was the crowd’s response to the Madman and Zarathustra that captured what I found so unjust and angering at the beginning of the semester: the rejection and hindrance of full life and full existence.

Friedrich Nietzsche (credits: Wikipedia)

The Madman opens with the man “who lit a lantern in the bright morning hours, ran to the marketplace and cried incessantly: “I am looking for God! I am looking for God.”” A crowd of those who did not believe in God see him and laugh They mock him, asking: “Have you lost him?” “Did he lose his way like a child?” “Is he hiding?” “Is he afraid of us?”

The madman responds to the crowd, saying “we have killed [God]—you and I.” He asks them:

“What did we do when we unchained the earth from the sun? Whither is it moving now? Whither are we moving now? Away from all suns? Are we not perpetually falling? Backward, sideward, forward, in all directions? Is there any up or down left? Are we not straying as through an infinite nothing? Do we not feel the breath of empty space?

The crowd is astonished by these questions. For they have not wondered how their rejection of God and all moral absolutes effects their reality and role in it. They are blind to their own killing of God and the empty nothingness into which they now fall. It is this smug blindness to reality and one’s role in it that ultimately leads to a complete degeneration of life and an open acceptance of a small existence.

This outcome is captured in the crowd’s response to the last men in Thus Spake Zarathustra. Similar to the crowd in the Madman, the last men are those who, when faced with the great questions – “What is love? What is creation? What is longing? What is a star?” – merely blink. Unlike their foil, the Superman, who creates his own value and meaning in the world, who indeed is “the meaning of the earth,” these last men “make everything small.” Indeed, they are small. Rather than overcome the life of man like the Superman, they succumb to the life of fleas. For “they have left the regions where living was hard,” and huddle together for warmth. They are a herd without a shepherd. They are all the same. When Zarathustra finishes describing these men, the crowd interrupts him and cries “Give us this last man, O Zarathustra! … Make us into these last men!”

Reading both the Madman and Thus Spake Zarathustra, I felt like Nietzsche captured exactly the hindrance and rejection of full life which I found so angering and unjust at the beginning of the semester. Nietzsche also captured another dimension of this injustice for me: cowardice and laziness. Both crowds fear the great questions of life. They are too lazy to face the empty nothingness and create their own suns. Nietzsche showed me that a full life requires us to “remain in the region where living is hard.” We must have the courage and vitality to step out and face the darkness of our own lives, the places of question and doubt.

While I resonated with Nietzsche’s condemnation of the crowds, I was challenged by his alternative. For Nietzsche, the alternative to becoming last men is to become a Superman, to transcend the human state and create our own meaning and value in the empty void. This was a huge challenge to my beliefs that 1) humans are fallible and limited, and thus 2) don’t create value but receive, find, and participate in value, and thus 3) don’t start from an empty void. While Nietzsche and I agreed on the injustice of a diminished life, I couldn’t swallow his starting point in nothingness and his confidence in a human self to create value. While I knew I didn’t like Nietzsche’s superman, I was left wondering how I would respond. I wanted a vision of moral excellence that could courageously stare into the darkness of the unknown and not count it as emptiness, but rather a mystery to be wondered at. I wanted a vision that saw the expansion of the human person, not in an assertion of the individual self, but rather in deep communion and love.

Nietzsche showed me that full life requires us to “remain in the region where living is hard.” We must have the courage and the vitality to step out and face the darkness of our own lives, the places of question and doubt.

The philosopher who gave me an alternative to Nietzsche’s Superman is Iris Murdoch. In her essay, The Sovereignty of the Good Over Other Concepts, Murdoch presents a way of being in the world that is deeply attentive to mystery, full of wonder, and grounded in selfless relation with reality. For she begins with the assumption that humans are blinded and isolated from reality by the “veil of self.” Unlike Nietzsche’s superman, the self for Murdoch is a hindrance to full life. Murdoch is aware, however, that we must begin with our selves, with an act she calls “unselfing.” It is by removing the veil of self through attention to art, nature, and study that one ultimately ascends to a contemplation of the “Good.” Leaning heavily on Plato’s Cave Analogy, she writes that “the mind which has ascended to the vision of the Good can subsequently see the concepts through which is has ascended (art, work, nature, people, ideas, institutions, situations, etc., etc.) in their true nature and proper relationship.”

Iris Murdoch (Credits: New York Times)

Murdoch, despite denying any unifying metaphysic of life, acknowledges a universal desire for this “Good.” She takes a jab at the Nietzschean superman writing that “no ordinary person, unless corrupted by philosophy, believes that he creates value by choice. He thinks that some things really are better than others and that he is capable of getting it wrong.” It is precisely this acknowledgement of our ability to get it wrong that made me so skeptical of Nietzsche’s Superman. Murdoch helped me see that the Superman gets it wrong by mistaking the darkness for emptiness, by not realizing that perhaps there is a greater mystery in the dark, a Good beyond what we can see. Murdoch captures this when she writes that the “Good is mysterious because of human frailty, because of the immense distance which is involved.”

And yet we keep trying to reach the Good, Murdoch acknowledges. We keep trying because we are drawn to the Good by the power of love. For the “Good is the magnetic center towards which love naturally moves,” Murdoch writes. It is this love, refined in the search for the Good, which “joins us to Good and joins us to the world through the Good.” Murdoch writes further that “[love’s] existence is the unmistakable sign that we are spiritual creatures, attracted by excellence and made for the good. It is a reflection of the warmth and light of the sun.” Unlike the madman who declares that we “have unchained the earth from all suns” and are perpetually falling into a cold infinite nothing, Murdoch suggests that the sun, its rays and its warmth, may still be felt in the power of love and relationship with the world.

In Murdoch’s vision I found the picture of moral excellence that I craved. For she acknowledges the vast unknowns in the world, the deep darkness which Nietzsche calls emptiness. Murdoch showed me, however, that we may face this deep darkness with courage and not count it as emptiness, but rather as a mystery to be communed with in wonder. I would even argue that it requires more courage to stare into the darkness and trust there is light beyond our eyes, mysteries yet to be met.

Unlike the madman who declares that we “have unchained the earth from all suns” and are perpetually falling into a cold infinite nothing, Murdoch suggests that the sun, its rays and its warmth, may still be felt in the power of love and relationship with the world.

Murdoch also showed me that it is by losing ourselves in wonder before the world, art, each other, etc. that we receive ourselves back. While she doesn’t precisely say this, I found that the Christian ideas of love and communion met her argument well on this point. What Nietzsche would see as an unegositic negation of life, was actually an expansion and returning of life through communion. For it is by meeting another in the selfless communion of wonder that we are drawn further by the power of love toward that excellence and good we were made for. In Murdoch I saw Christ’s claim that “whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” in a new light. Whoever loses himself in Love will indeed find his real life—a life surrounded by mystery and wonder, a life made for communion and love.

I’m grateful for my semester with Nietzsche and Murdoch. They have joined the family of those who shape my moral vision and philosophy. Like any family member, I can see their flaws and yet I feel greatly indebted to them. For in each of their philosophies I received a gift of moral wisdom and virtue. Nietzsche gave me courage–courage to remain in the region where living is hard, courage to face darkness and doubt. Murdoch gave me hope–hope in a wonderful world sustained by Love, hope in a Sun beyond what our eyes can see.

Cover Photo Credits: Photo by Dan Cook on Unsplash

item.title: How To Know A Person by David Brooks: A Review
item.description:
David Brooks’ How to Know a Person leaves a transformative impact on me. He explains the importance of being deeply seen and seeing others deeply. Many people today lack the ability to communicate and build strong relationships with each other, leading to other worldly problems.

I read David Brooks’ How to Know a Person for a reading project this past summer and was intrigued to find how much this book impacted me. After reading this book, I was inspired to strengthen my interpersonal skills and strive to become an “illuminator.”

In his book, Brooks explains the importance of education to grow interpersonal skills. Most schools teach how to read and solve math problems, but not how to enhance our interpersonal skills. Skills like communication, responsibility, active listening, and empathy amongst others, are not taught in the education system, leading to societal problems. Brooks writes that “our social skills are currently inadequate to the pluralistic societies we are living in.” If the issue is left unresolved, Brooks explains that we will see more employees who are untrustworthy, irresponsible, and unable to get along with their coworkers and supervisors. Brooks not only recognizes issues we have in the education system but provides solutions.

I was inspired to strengthen my interpersonal skills and strive to become an “illuminator.”

Brooks describes the concept of “illuminators” and “diminishers” as categories of people we meet in the world. He describes an encounter with a peer whose conversation skills resembled an illuminator’s. “To speak to him was to be seduced by an inverse charisma, a sense of being listened to with such intensity that you had to be your most honest, sharpest, and best self.”

Brooks describes an illuminator as possessing the qualities of tenderness, receptivity, active curiosity, affection, generosity, and a holistic attitude. However, I believe he missed a crucial characteristic. Trustworthiness. This may seem like a basic characteristic, but I believe it is fundamental to illuminators. If you truly want to be seen and deeply see others, you must be a trustworthy person. In other words, for someone to open up to you, they must trust you.

Brooks’ personal examples, woven prominently throughout the book, support his arguments and boost his credibility. For example, he tells the story of how he used to be a diminisher, describing his childhood years, and how that impacted him emotionally.

He even goes to the extent of saying that he is still not an expert, which I found to be an appropriate representation of the message of How to Know a Person. To me, some “self-bettering books” sound condescending, which make it harder for me to be open to what the author has to say. However, Brooks uses an understanding tone to relate to the reader on a personal level, which I found impactful.

Brooks also describes the effect that people’s experiences have on their lives. What someone struggles through and how they move forward says a lot about a person. To understand people, you must see how they were before their losses in life and how they turned their life around in response.

The examples Brooks provides are relevant to the point he is making. The character of a person has to do with their outlook on life and not just what they have experienced; but how they overcame the negativity in their lives.

“our social skills are currently inadequate to the pluralistic societies we are living in.” David Brooks

Brooks also makes the powerful point that many people do not truly listen to one another. “Once you are in response mode, your ability to listen deteriorates.”. In conversations, we merely think about what we are going to say in response, instead of what the person is truly saying. We have developed the selfish mindset of only caring about what we are going to say next. This defeats the purpose of listening to one another by preventing us from understanding each other on a deeper level. I completely agree with this claim Brooks makes and found that the way he supports his claim to be powerful.

Brooks not only explains how we can build deeper relationships that are truly meaningful but describes what exactly we are doing wrong. What is the root cause of these issues and why do people think like this today? Brooks answers these key questions by stating that the media has an impact, but our life experiences play a more prominent role.

Overall, How to Know a Person is a great book for people seeking professional and personal development, and people who are interested in psychology and self-bettering books that provide an analytical approach to tough concepts.

I found David Brooks’ book to be eye opening in terms of professional and personal development. He goes in depth on the way these skills are used in the workplace, to how these skills strengthen relationships. How to Know a Person dives into an abundance of poignant questions leaving the reader reflecting on how they approach relationships and small talk in their day-to-day lives. After reading this book, I am inspired to become an “illuminator” in a world where they are needed most.

item.title: Hospitality: Revisiting the Roots
item.description:
Hospitality is not a new or foreign idea. For many of us, the word hospitality likely conjures up images of southern grandmothers setting picture perfect place settings in sterile white homes, or perhaps your mom telling you to clean your room before guests come over. While these might be common cultural associations with hospitality, neither of these images, or ones like it, seem to communicate the ancient core of hospitality found within the Christian tradition.

Rather than a cultural nicety or polite obligation, hospitality in the Christian life is the very celebration of our soul’s embodiment and the extension of Christ’s welcome and love to our neighbor. For the Christian, hospitality is the recognition of the brokenness and needs of the people around him coupled with the desire and motivation to meet these needs without grumbling. It is openly and unreservedly inviting others into one’s life simply because of their value before the living God.

The command for hospitality can be found throughout both the Old and New Testaments. Beginning in Leviticus, God commands the Israelites that “The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt. I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 19:34). The Israelites are instructed to welcome the foreigner with hospitality because they were once foreigners who had been brought near by their God. Hospitality receives its basis from the character of God as One who welcomes the outsider and brings His people near.

In the New Testament, Jesus’ teachings are filled with the exhortation to show hospitality, particularly to the most vulnerable and outcast in society. For Christ says that when hospitality is offered to the least of these, it is being shown also to Himself. Likewise, when it is withheld, it is withheld from Himself (Matthew 25:35-40). Clearly, hospitality is important to God, and its absence is grievous. For when we extend hospitality to those outside, we join in the work of a God who became flesh, died, and rose again in order to save and welcome the lost.

Rembrandt: Return of the Prodigal Son

Hospitality receives its basis from the character of God as One who welcomes the outsider and brings His people near.

I came to see the significance of Christian hospitality while hiking the Camino de Santiago in Northern Spain. For all the beauty, adventure, and history of the trip, one daily occurrence sticks out to me as I recall my time on the trail. Every afternoon, after arriving at the hostel for the night, nearly all of the other pilgrims on the trail would walk to the nearest tavern and sit at a long table together, laughing and recounting the joys and mishaps of the day and learning each other’s stories. And every afternoon, my hiking partner and fellow English speaker and I would sit at a nearby table and watch as friendships began and flourished among these Spanish speakers.

We longed to be a part of the community and camaraderie of the table, but because of our language barrier, we were never invited. Never being on the outside of a language barrier, I felt this longing to belong in a new way. I felt strongly the perennial pains of being an outsider and not invited to the table, pains which seem to especially plague our current generation. For we are an isolated people, desperate for assurance that we are welcomed and accepted. We long for a seat at the table. We fear deeply that our brokenness excludes us from the table.

The practice of hospitality meets this deep longing with grace and compassion.

What a mysterious beauty that the living God would create His people with the need to eat, with the ability to make tables, with the creativity to cook delicious meals, and with the longing to sit around the table with fellow pilgrims to rest along the journey of this life.

Photo from author’s hike of Camino de Santiago

Often, in our attempts to show the incomprehensible love of God, we end up doing nothing at all, for how could we possibly display the depth and perfection of the love of God? But when we seek to show hospitality, providing for the physical needs of the physical people around us, we honor the embodiment of God’s image in the people around us. We rejoice in the glorious mystery of the Incarnation, God dwelling with us. We choose to be people who proclaim Christ’s descent to earth as the greatest mystery and greatest gift we could ever know.

We are an isolated people, desperate for assurance that we are welcomed and accepted. We long for a seat at the table. We fear deeply that our brokenness excludes us from the table.

This is indeed the mystery of the incarnation: that the living eternal God would condescend to the form of a man and eat with sinners and tax collectors. The gospel cannot remain abstract and theoretical in our minds when our Savior knew the painful experience of hunger and the beautiful satisfaction of a meal enjoyed with His closest friends. Rather, this gospel is found in invitations of hospitality to the least of these, from sinners who know they have been freed from shame and invited to the wedding feast of the Lamb.

The Christian relies on the true origin of hospitality in order to be able to invite freely and graciously. Our welcome to the greatest table, of which we “are not worthy so much as to gather up the crumbs from underneath” (Book of Common Prayer), makes the welcome we extend to the hurting world a cosmic participation in the genuine and shocking hospitality of Christ. Our invitations to others are not desperate attempts to gain social superiority or hidden requests to be invited back in return. Rather, they are rooted in the scandal of our own undeserving welcome, rooted in the redeeming and welcoming blood of the Lamb.

At Christ’s table there is a place for all, even the sinners and tax collectors, even the people you don’t like, even you.

The practice of hospitality is not a sentimental or naïve cliché, as so many perceive it today, but a courageous recognition of the vast brokenness around us. It is the stepping into and healing of this brokenness through the meeting of tangible needs. It is the antidote to the unfortunate tendency for Christians to feel burdened for the souls of our neighbors and forget that they are first men who must eat, pay rent, raise children, and grieve lost family members. Hospitality is not a shallow once-and-a-while act, but a foundational and life-long practice. True Biblical hospitality honors the people around us as worthy of our time, resources, and inconvenience regardless as their station or status in society. For biblical hospitality sees all humans as valuable gifts, as images of God–the imago dei.

For the Christian, the Eucharist is the greatest manifestation of hospitality in our current time and respective places. For it is both a physical meal eaten alongside fellow pilgrims, and a divine communion with a holy God. We come to the eucharistic table over and over again so that our weak and apathetic hearts might be filled by the presence of our Savior—“that we might dwell in Him and He in us” (Book of Common Prayer). Before kneeling beside our neighbor at the altar table, we welcome them with the passing of the peace. In this we see that the hospitality of God to us in the Eucharist is inseparable from the hospitality due our neighbor. For at Christ’s table there is a place for all, even the sinners and tax collectors, even the people you don’t like, even you. In the Eucharist we learn to be people of radical hospitality and welcome.

Jesus with the Eucharist at the Last Supper by Juan de Juanes, mid-late 16th century

Thus, let us embrace the potential discomfort of extending invitations freely and joyously to those far different from us. And as our bodies are offered up as living sacrifices to the Holy God, let our tables be offered as the answer to humanity’s longing cry in the voice of the Israelites: “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78:19). Let our hospitality display the miraculous and resounding “yes” for which we are so desperate. Until the Wedding Feast of the Lamb, let us feast at tables in the wilderness.
