item.title: Experiments in Virtue: Byron Johnson on Religion in Prisons
item.description:
Liberal democracies like America claim neutrality on deep questions of human nature, meaning, and morality. But prison policy stands out as an exception: here, governments openly theorize and experiment on how to turn bad people into good people — people who will not return to prison.

Several California prisons provide inmates plots of land to plant gardens. Dozens of state and federal prisons give convicted felons shelter dogs to train. Utah women’s prisons dress their inmates in a flattering shade of plum and allow them to wear makeup. Each of these initiatives is built on deeper theories about reforming broken people: assigning responsibility, encouraging compassion, or enabling a dignified appearance. Religious people have their own theory, one that has existed for millennia: faith is the most effective means for moral reform.

Some prisons are applying this principle with positive results that should make both government and religious people take notice.

Mr. Walters is an assistant pastor at the prison’s largest church, called Leadership Village.

(https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2013/10/06/us/bible-college-helps-some-at-louisiana-prison-find-peace.html)

Dr. Byron Johnson, a senior fellow at the Religious Freedom Institute and the founder of Baylor University’s Institute for Studies of Religion, has authored four books and more than three dozen articles on religious programs in prisons. He has found that religion helps inmates find meaning, transform their identities, and serve others.

Prisons are one of the very few places where our government explicitly aims to improve the personal moral character of its citizens.



For example, in 1995, an unusual program was launched at America’s largest maximum security prison: a prison seminary. The seminary students at the notorious Louisiana State Penitentiary (known as “Angola”) learned how to minister to their fellow prisoners, lead worship services, and care for the dying. Johnson spent several years studying the program and interviewing the inmates. He found that religious education gave the inmates a sense of belonging and purpose. He writes that “Angola’s seminary graduates describe the message of love and service outlined in the Christian gospel as their blueprint for personal change—and the inmate minister program as an opportunity for them to demonstrate that change in practice.”

Dr. Johnson’s research has produced similar results across time and place. In 2018, Dr. Johnson’s study in a South African prison found that religious inmates were more likely to report meaning in their lives and less likely to report negative emotions. His 2023 study of a Colombian prison found that religious behaviors were positively associated with forgiveness, self-control, and gratitude, and inversely associated with anger, depression, and anxiety.

Religious education gave the inmates a sense of belonging and purpose.

This research confirms what religious people have always known: faith has the power to transform even the most fallen people in our society. Turning away from a life of crime requires more than vocational training. In Dr. Johnson’s words, it requires “identity transformation.”

Reflecting on countless conversations with people behind bars, Dr. Johnson described some of the barriers to identity transformation he has seen in prisons: “Many of these people are in prison because they experienced the most horrible types of things their whole lives.… you can imagine there’s a lot of anger and bitterness that they’re in a place like prison.” Addressing that depth of bitterness requires a depth of healing that secular programs struggle to provide. “They need to forgive others, and they need to forgive themselves. And forgiving others and forgiving yourself is something that’s hard to do outside of faith.”

Dr. Johnson’s research is a powerful reminder to our society that crime is not a disease that can be treated with a concoction of therapy and drugs. Nor is it the inevitable result of poverty or suffering. Crime is a moral problem, and that’s just what religious communities are most equipped to address.

Dr. Johnson points out that, while these programs ought to be applauded, they are severely lacking in diversity. “A vast majority of prison volunteers are evangelical. My question is, where is everybody else? I think it’s a great thing that people are responding. However, I think that it’s not necessarily a good thing that prisoners are overwhelmingly exposed to just a particular religious tradition.”

“God is merciful,” intoned Mr. Walters to fellow inmates, most facing life sentences. “God gives us so many benefits.”

Credits: New York TImes (https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/2013/10/06/us/bible-college-helps-some-at-louisiana-prison-find-peace.html)

Religious freedom requires religious options. And religious options require religious diversity. “In a religious freedom environment, what more can you do? Well, if you’re Catholic, you should be telling your Catholic friends ‘why aren’t we in there?’ People need to respond to a need. Where are the mainline denominations? They aren’t there either.”

Religious freedom in prisons doesn’t just require governments to step back, it requires religious organizations and leaders to step forward. Organizations like the Religious Freedom Institute and the Becket Fund fight for the right of prisoners to attend church services in prisons, but churches aren’t stepping up to provide enough services.

Forgiving others and forgiving yourself is something that’s hard to do outside of faith. Dr. Byron Johnson

This is a massive missed opportunity for religious people who want to bring their faith into the public square. Prisons are one of the very few places where our government explicitly aims to improve the personal moral character of its citizens.

So why are prisons the exception? Even the most libertarian prison experts admit that neglecting to engage with questions of moral development in prisons can have deadly consequences. Next year, over 600,000 people will be released from American prisons. They will live in our neighborhoods, work with us, teach our children, and become part of our communities. If prisons do nothing to improve the character of the criminals who enter their doors, those same people will exit those doors with just as much likelihood of hurting their fellow citizens, if not more.

Our prisons have become labs for experimenting with human nature. Right now, most of those experiments are failing. According to US Department of Justice data, 82% percent of inmates who are released will be arrested again within 10 years. Dr. Johnson believes that religion is the key to beating those numbers, and he has the evidence to prove it. Now, it’s time for religious people to do their part.

Cover Photo Credits: New York Times

item.title: The Meaning Behind the Words: Methods of Interpreting the Constitution
item.description:
While the text of the Constitution has remained unchanging, methods of interpreting it have varied greatly over the history of the United States. The two methods of interpretation dominating the courts and academic thought today are originalism and living constitutionalism. Living constitutionalists seek to allow for a certain amount of judicial discretion to incorporate values of current society, creating a responsive, ‘living’ constitution. On the other hand, originalists seek to constrain judicial discretion in constitutional interpretation by emphasizing textual and historical evidence. We will briefly examine the arguments and leading figures of both methods, and you will be left to decide which better fulfills the framer’s intention.

The Case for Originalism

Often referred to as the father of originalism, Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia argues ardently for an originalist method of interpretation in his essay Originalism: The Lesser Evil. As the title of his essay concedes, Justice Scalia did not find originalism to be a perfect method; however, he believed it to be much more practical than non-originalist methods and, therefore, the better choice. Originalism can be broadly defined by the use of historical and textual evidence to guide and justify the decision of a case, making constitutional interpretation an analytical process that purposefully leaves little room for personal judgement. By practical necessity, Justice Scalia believed the constitution was intended to be a general framework. Creating a constitution which details all subdivisions of power and subsequent means of execution is an insurmountable task. Thus, interpretation of its text must be done with an understanding of its broad nature.

Conversely, if constitutional interpretation was intended to evolve with circumstances, broadly interpreting its text would be unnecessary. In opposition to originalism stands living constitutionalism, which Scalia defines as “a body of law that (unlike normal statutes) grows and changes from age to age, in order to meet the needs of a changing society. And it is the judges who determine those needs and ‘find’ that changing law.” A living constitution allows for the rights it protects to change by means other than formal amendment. Unlike originalism, living constitutionalism does not require judges to be historians but instead leaves room for judges to incorporate what they discern to be fundamental societal values.

Many non-originalists seek to treat the Constitution like a common-law document, which is formed by custom and judicial precedent instead of statutes, which are passed by legislatures. On a theoretical level, Scalia disagrees with non-originalist arguments because such claims are inconsistent with the practice of judicial review of constitutionality. Despite the supremacy of the Constitution, Scalia believes it is still a law with “a fixed meaning ascertainable through the usual devices familiar to those learned in the law.” Because the Constitution functions as a law and not an innovatively mutable document, it can be assumed that the role of expressing society’s values falls within the legislative branch. Elections work to ensure the values of current society are reflected in our government through the legislation representatives pass. Thus, many originalists argue their interpretation method is more consistent with democracy as it respects that legislatures determine the content of laws while judges determine their constitutionality. Scalia fears that non-originalist interpretations enable judges to engage in lawmaking because it gives judges the liberty to recognize, narrow, or overrule precedents as they please in the name of ‘societal values.’ Many originalists argue that Constitutions cannot be characterized as living because their purpose is to prevent change by embedding certain rights in text so that they cannot be revoked easily by future generations. Similarly, bills of rights are created because citizens are wary that ‘evolving standards of decency’ will always be positive progress; determining whether to protect rights based on mutable standards ascertained through ‘society’ allows rights to be expanded and removed more easily – for the better or worse – and potentially threatens the permanence of important rights. Thus, Scalia thinks it is quite clear that it is the role of the legislature – not the courts – to respond to changes in society’s values. Allowing judges to incorporate what they determine to be the views of society poses a problem of consistency and potentially endangers the protection of important rights. Instead, Scalia advocates that we should interpret text according to its original meaning when it was drafted and adopted, creating a more consistent interpretive method that protects right according to the text’s fixed meaning.

Another practical concern regarding living constitutionalism is the lack of consensus on what values should be used as the bedrock of the interpretive methods. Critics of originalism agree to oppose it but offer no viable alternatives. Whose fundamental values are to be used to guide judicial decisions? Should judges use newspapers, national polls, well-respected political philosophers, personal conversations, or other means to discern the will of the majority? It is undoubtable that originalists disagree on how to discern the original meaning of a text such as how free speech – protected by the First Amendment – applies today. However, he believes that the challenges faced by proponents of originalism in modern application are trivial in comparison to the uncertainty of discerning a guiding philosophy in living constitutionalism.

Whose fundamental values are to be used to guide judicial decisions?

Scalia is by no means asserting that originalism is a perfect system of interpretation. A major criticism of originalism that Scalia acknowledges is the difficulty in applying it. Performed correctly, originalist interpretation requires study of immense amounts of material. Even then, historical records may be unreliable. Proper examination of historical documents also commands a great understanding of the political and intellectual climate of the time. Additionally, Scalia’s argument for originalism is largely practical and focuses on the faults of what Scalia characterizes to be the only alternative – non-originalism – though real-world interpretation methods are more nuanced and varied than strictly originalist or living constitutionalist. But what is the fundamental problem of abandoning original meaning? Scalia would respond practically: there is no better alternative, and Americans are bound by the fundamental and intentionally unchanging values and rights embedded in the Constitution. Scalia argues that if we assume living constitutionalists are correct in that the Constitution was intended to evolve over time, there is still no compelling reason why judges should be charged with determining the direction of this evolution by discerning the will of the people. Vesting judges with the responsibility of executing the will of the people and the changes they desire arguably violates constitutional separation of powers by allowing judges to legislate. Scalia proclaimed regarding the Constitution “it’s dead, dead, dead” and, though he can no longer remind us of it, he would argue its meaning remains the same today.

The Case for Living Constitutionalism

Because of the greater disunity in the living constitutionalist movement, we will examine the views of two academics with starkly different ideas. Professor David Strauss of the University of Chicago Law School advocates for a changing constitution based in a common law legal system. Strauss’s justification is that attributes of constitutional law that would be considered correct today would not be acceptable one hundred years ago and vice versa. Our understanding of constitutional law has significantly changed in ways other than formal amendment. An example of this is the evolution of civil rights law. Scalia asserts in his article Do We Have a Living Constitution? “If having a ‘living’ Constitution means having a Constitution that changes over time in ways other than by formal amendment, then in a fundamental way there is only one plausible answer to that question,” which is an emphatic ‘yes.’

Living constitutionalism does not require judges to be historians but instead leaves room for judges to incorporate what they discern to be fundamental societal values.

For Strauss, the largest practical problem with originalism is its inability to account for changes Brown v. Board of Education (1954) to end segregation and Reynolds v. Sims (1964) enforce equal representation – cases which are universally accepted in constitutional law today – are irreconcilable with the original views of the framers who wrote and adopted the provisions. Thus, he finds that the originalist method of interpretation is not valid as it fails to explain these major changes in the understanding of many constitutional provisions. Though their view cannot explain such changes, judges should accept originalist doctrines because they are so well established. According to Strauss, following originalist methods leaves us unsure of what changes in understanding are justified and denies the reality that major changes in our understanding of constitutional provisions reveal how our legal system should work. Strauss’s alternative is applying common law methods to constitutional interpretation.

Common law has been influential to the American legal system since its inception and earlier dominated the English legal system. Strauss understands the American constitution as “a common law constitution in the sense that the principal mechanism of change is the evolution of the law through the development of precedent.” A major concern of originalists is that living constitutionalism allows for ‘judicial activism’ or allowing judges to decide based on their personal view of societal implications instead of abiding strictly by legal texts. Strauss believes his common law method of interpretation restrains judges through precedent and tradition while leaving room for innovation. In most cases, clearly established precedents dictate the judge’s decision. In the rare circumstance that the outcome is not directly determined by precedents, common law allows for judicial discretion. Strauss finds this incorporation of “fairness and good policy” when precedents are not clear as essential to judges’ decisions. Strauss argues that sometimes the moral dispositions of judges surely play a role in their decisions; thus, allowing the court to ground their decision in precedent and acknowledge how their morality shaped the outcome is more honest than attempting to justify the decision on purely historical and textual evidence, according to Strauss.

Therefore, Strauss believes the Constitution is ‘living’ in that its interpretation changes gradually The legal text provides an essential skeleton but – to Strauss – it would be remiss without acknowledging the influence of tradition, precedent, and common law practices.

Strauss believes his common law method of interpretation restrains judges through precedent and tradition while leaving room for innovation.

Yale law professor Jack Balkin agrees with Strauss on the living nature of the constitution, but their perspectives diverge on the weight they give to different factors shaping constitutional interpretation, namely institutions. To Balkin, “a constitutional regime combines a range of beliefs about constitutional meaning together with a set of accepted, customs, practices, and institutions.” While the common law method may compose a part of constitutional construction, the constitution is mutable because of the role all branches play in driving change over time. The “engines of change” to Balkin are governmental institutions and civil society; only acknowledging the common-law aspects yields an incomplete understanding. Thus, Balkin believes a constitutional regime is twofold; it is composed of not only fundamental principles of constitutional rights, responsibilities, and the proper role of government but also the institutions and traditions surrounding these basic principles. Therefore, while Strauss emphasizes precedents, practices, and traditions, Balkin points out that much of the constitutional regime is institutionally created through administrative regulation and statutes.

Balkin thinks Strauss fails to acknowledge that constitutional construction is a product of all the branches of government over time. To Balkin, living constitutionalism does not outline the methods judges should use to decide cases in a manner compatible with democracy. Instead, it describes the process through which constitutional change occurs in the three branches of government as well as civil society and shows how such processes promote legitimate democracy in our legal system. Perceptions of what practices promote or hinder democracy are relative to the fundamental values of the current constitutional regime; thus, competing conceptions of what promotes democracy in America exist between different groups.

Additionally, constitutional construction is a process of building on and rejecting elements of previous regimes. While Strauss portrays the Courts as reacting to changes in public thought, Balkin considers the judicial branch an active participant in constructing the current constitutional regime. According to Balkin, viewing the courts in an active light better explains sharp changes in doctrine while common law constitutionalism only accounts for gradual shifts.

Strauss and Balkin also differ in the way they respond to the criticism that non-originalist doctrines allow for too much judicial discretion. Strauss believes the value that common-law method places on precedent limits judicial discretion. On the contrary, Balkin pegs institutional factors as the primary restraint on judicial activism such as structural restrictions on judicial decision making, requirements for judicial candidates, and the professional and constitutional climate in which judges attempt to convince others of the legitimacy of their decision.

Balkin finds that most constitutional development occurs beyond the text and history that originalists emphasize or the common law method that Strauss relies on. In Balkin’s view, doctrinal development is motivated by “an entire political and legal culture” from public opinion platforms to NGOs to competing institutions of civil society. This ‘culture’ motivates change in the way we understand the constitution over time in both the public and legal sphere. According to Balkin, these institutions both restrict and foster constitutional change.

In summary, originalists like Justice Scalia advocate for an interpretive method founded in historical and textual evidence that constrains judicial discretion and provides consistency in its protection to the fixed, original meanings of rights. Conversely, living constitutionalists tend to agree on the mutable nature of the constitution and its ability to respond to changes in societal values in ways other than by formal amendment. However, living constitutionalists diverge greatly in their interpretive methods, as Strauss grounds his method in common law and Balkin in institutions. Though means of interpretation may differ, one thing is agreed upon by constitutional scholars: the question of how to interpret the Constitution is irrefutably important.

item.title: “Getting What We Deserve”: A Lecture by Jeff Polet
item.description:
On September 23rd, Dr. Jeff Polet was hosted by Baylor University in the Honors College reading room as the guest speaker for the Laura Jackson Endowed Lectureship in World Issues. Polet is the Director of the Ford Leadership Forum at the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Foundation and a former professor of political science at Hope College.

Jeff Polet

The lecture, “Getting What We Deserve,” was a timely reflection on the widely perceived crisis of leadership in America and the broader West. Although the crisis seems to be endemic to our current political landscape and social fabric, Polet explained that “our leadership class is reflecting a much deeper trend in political life.”

“When we think about ‘getting what we deserve,’” he said, “we might well ask: Who’s this we? What are we getting? And why do we deserve it?”

Polet began his remarks by mildly challenging the all-too-common assumption that democratic governments are a fountain stream of blessings, devoid of any major imperfections. “Among the advantages of monarchy,” he said, “not having to live through quadrennial elections and strenuous campaigns ranks high in the list.” This may be especially relevant during this election cycle, when a fateful many undecided voters seem weary and disappointed with the binary choices.

Good leaders will be persons of high character and sound judgement. Jeff Polet

In this sense, “monarchy also gets subjects off the hook,” as they cannot be blamed — at least not directly — for the cruelty or incompetency of their sovereign. Of course, Polet conceded, monarchy could easily bring about reckless and incontinent rulers, “but it’s not as though democracy has such a great record these days.” Moreover, the rhetoric of this being “the most important election of our lifetime” has become a tiring repetition every four years, fomenting skepticism over the authenticity of each election’s actual importance.

Yet, Polet clarified, too narrow a focus on politics may blur the depth of our problems. He cited Tocqueville to explain the relationship between the health of all civic associations, from one’s trust in one’s neighbors to collective trust in institutions, and how the crisis is not merely political, but also inherently social. The breakdown of associations has arguably led to a major disconnect between the “few” and the “many,” as Aristotle would have described it. In our contemporary parlance, the divide is described as that between “ordinary people” and the “elites,” but the concept is essentially the same.

“Today,” Polet said, “it is a costly fact in the United States that the most outstanding men are rarely called to public office.” The once-esteemed class “of American statesmen has become significantly smaller” than what past generations had to offer. Why is this? Polet seemed to argue that it has something to do with the aforementioned societal disconnect.

The crisis is not merely political, but also inherently social.

Addressing the particularities of the crisis in the American context, he cited some of Madison’s insights from The Federalist. He explained how “the essence of politics involves the resolution of conflict,” given that conflict is embedded in “the human condition.” Many elements of the Madisonian republicanism we find in the pages of The Federalist are directed at such ends. Polet pointed out that “Our Constitution, for example, is a compromise document,” arguably designed “for a contentious people.” Furthermore, “one of the reasons why it has worked for as long as it has is [that] it tries to channel this contentiousness into energetic action; and that end is largely accomplished through executive power.” This is why “we tend to equate the health of the country with the quality of our most visible leaders, and in this day and age that means the presidency.”

James Madison; photo from the Library of Congress

This was reminiscent of Joseph de Maistre’s insight that “properly speaking, all governments are monarchies which differ only in whether the monarch is for life or for a term of years, hereditary or elective, individual or corporate.” In his famous case for a mixed regime, St. Thomas Aquinas also maintains that good governments require a monarchical element, which we now refer to as “executive power.” Thus, if a given society were experiencing a crisis of leadership, it would eventually be reflected at the executive level.

Polet also emphasized how, in contrast with Aristotle and the Angelic Doctor, “Hamilton and Madison provide a sober,” even pessimistic “view of human nature.” But, they both “acknowledge that we need good leaders.” Polet’s presentation of the Founding, therefore, seemed to follow the interpretation that conceives the American experiment as an effort to reconcile Enlightenment principles with a characteristically ancient pursuit of the common good. He maintained that “republican systems seem to assume the following: good leaders will be persons of high character and sound judgement, and as such we trust them with the enormous powers invested in them.”

Republicanism for Polet, then, depends on there being good leaders, and that they be willing to partake in public life. As for what makes a good leader, Polet cited Madison and Hamilton to contend that it must be one who shares a certain bond with the people he is tasked to represent. Madison’s words could not be more relevant today: “But if those ties which bind a representative to his constituents are ever weekend, then the very possibility of republican government becomes unthinkable.”

“Our current crisis of leadership results directly from the loosening of those bonds,” said Polet, “not only in our political institutions but in all institutions. We increasingly feel distant from those in positions of authority.” Indeed, these are the seeds of the populism we have seen emerge over the last two decades, stemming from the perception that our ruling class is “too often operating from a set of interests contrary to the good as we understand it, or to the wellbeing of the institutions they run.”

Polet acknowledged recent populist trends as being legitimate, insofar as they are the justified reaction to the loosening of bonds between leaders and ordinary people. Yet, in terms of the broader crisis, he identified three sources from which it arises:

The loosening of bonds between leaders and their respective constituents, exacerbated by contempt. Earning back the trust of ordinary people will be impossible without sharing in their fate and their misfortunes.

The rise of a centralized administrative state, whereby average citizens experience themselves as being at the mercy of anonymous powers — these powers being at the hands of elites who then use them to reward friends and punish enemies.

The desire for material comfort, and the role of money and securing it.

The latter two are just as consequential as the first, Polet argued. And, to some degree, they are all interrelated. The expansion of the administrative state is largely responsible for the loosening of bonds, and the desire for material comfort among the masses fuels the existence of such a state. Quoting Tocqueville, Polet expounded on how materialism leads to “a soft despotism that could turn democratic peoples into timid and industrious sheep, with government as their shepherd.” Lacking a common pursuit of the good, a common telos, the quest to attain material wealth has come in its place, reaping the venomous crops of greed, isolation, and constant competition among those who would otherwise relate to one another as neighbors and kin.

Alexis de Tocqueville; photo from Wikipedia

Our current crisis of leadership results directly from the loosening of those bonds, not only in our political institutions but in all institutions. Jeff Polet

As a remedy for the crisis caused by these interrelated problems, Polet concluded by proposing restraint — not merely for the governing, but also for the governed. Restraint, he contended, is opposed to both the “imperial impulse” of the administrative state and the acquisitional impulse of the masses. Lack of restraint, on the other hand, is the reason “our Constitution no longer operates from the principle of limited government,” and is now a “fluid adaptation to changing mores.” Our ills could thus be summarized as “unrestrained appetite, either personally or politically.”

But how shall we reintroduce restraint into our social and political life? Polet alluded to some alternatives, including a process of “decentralization” in the political sphere, while fostering “lives of mutual dependence” in the social sphere. Amidst the sobriety of the diagnosis, there was an air of hope in the concluding remarks. If we begin to work toward these aims, Polet implied, we may yet be able to save our nation from the calamities that have befallen other, once-great civilizations. Whatever happens, one thing is clear: we have deserved it. In the words of de Maistre, “every country has the government it deserves.”

item.title: A Call for Unity: Braver Angels
item.description:
How good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity. Psalm 133:1

A weekend ago, I sat around the dinner table as my grandmother blew out her birthday candles. Family and friends shared laughter and tears while recalling memories of my grandmother’s unbelievable care for each of us over the years. My uncle, who had always been the more rebellious one, tearfully testified of my grandma’s belief in him and the security she had provided him with all these years. The room was full of joy, fellowship, and peace. My grandma showed no partiality in her love. She saw the person, valuable and worth believing in, even when she did not agree with them.

Why does this kind of acceptance feel almost foreign? Why does it feel like a pastime? As the election approaches, our country is not promoting fellowship, but instead disregarding and discarding anyone whose views do not align with ours. The question we must ask ourselves is: Where is this kind of thinking leading our country? More than ever, we are in desperate need of unity.

David Blankenhorn; photo from Deseret News

David Blankenhorn is a cofounder of Braver Angels, a citizens’ organization that seeks to unify and depolarize America. He was having similar thoughts around the time of the 2016 presidential election: Donald Trump v. Hillary Clinton. “This was a very, very difficult time and a very difficult election. Highly polarized. Much, much anguish and fear. People were really rattled.”

He recalls the highly polarized reactions of citizens in different regions. “Some regions were feeling good, thinking the election would be good for the country. While in Manhattan, people were devasted, walking around like someone had shot them in the side.”

It was during this election that Blankenhorn realized that the problem wasn’t that people didn’t agree on certain issues, it was that people weren’t willing to engage with the people they didn’t agree with.

“Disagreement and conflict are normal and healthy in a free society. You don’t want to eliminate them, but where it becomes toxic is when it’s not just disagreeing, it’s hating. It’s not that I disagree with your opinion, it’s that I don’t like you. I don’t find you to be a trustworthy or a good person. That’s when it becomes toxic, and you get the kind of social breakdown that we’re experiencing.”

The problem wasn’t that people didn’t agree on certain issues, it was that people weren’t willing to engage with the people they didn’t agree with.

In December of 2016 with the hope of bridging the divide, Blankenhorn and his fellow cofounders held a meeting at a local church in South Lebanon, Ohio consisting of ten Trump voters and ten Clinton voters. They simply asked them to talk to each other. “It might seem tame, but it certainly wasn’t going on anywhere in the country.”

What set this kind of meeting apart, Blankenhorn explains, is that “you’re not just marshalling facts to try to defeat your opponent; you’re actually interacting with one another. It’s a collective search for truth.”

A Braver Angels debate; photo taken from Braver Angels

The experience was transformative, and the response was enormous. People couldn’t get enough. Braver Angels has grown from one chapter to now having 102 chapters around the country that host debates, workshops, and discussions. They have trained around 4000 people to host meetings similar to the first. They regularly hold national conventions with over 750 delegates from their chapters around the country. Braver Angels has even started taking their method directly into the halls of political power, working with state legislatures and even members of Congress. Braver Angels’ message of unity continues to spread across America with features in major news outlets, including ABC, Fox News, CNN, The New York Times, and many others.

Another way to be a good person is to essentially be a peacemaker. We can find ways to communicate and cooperate. That’s not a sign of being weak. Actually, it probably requires more strength and more moral fiber to do that. David Blankenhorn

As from the very beginning, the movement seeks to “bring Americans together to bridge the partisan divide and strengthen our democratic republic.” They stand for stating views “freely and fully, without fear,” while also treating those who disagree with “honesty, dignity, and respect.”

When asked about our moral responsibility toward fostering unity, Blankenhorn noted many young people’s desire to “be a fighter for your cause, to stand up and fight for what you believe in.” He said this is what many young people believe makes them a good person.

Blankenhorn responded, “I respect it, however, another way to be a good person is to essentially be a peacemaker. We can find ways to communicate and cooperate. That’s not a sign of being weak. Actually, it probably requires more strength and more moral fiber to do that.”

Braver Angels exists in the tension of finding peace with others while also not watering down our views. Braver Angels recognizes the danger of fighting so hard for a cause that the people the cause is meant to help are sacrificed along the way. When we give way to division and hatred, we are not damning our opposing party, we are ultimately damning our nation and, in turn, ourselves.

So with the election at hand, let us be people that learn from the work of Braver Angels and collectively search for truth, not just seek victory over our neighbor. Let us be people, like my grandma, who respect and believe in one another. May we foster the fellowship and peace that only comes from valuing people just as they are.

item.title: Fall 2024 Issue: Preserving Humanity Amid Election Year
item.description: The fall issue of The Standard is a shared reflection and exploration of what it means to be human in the midst of an often dehumanizing and turbulent political landscape, namely the election season. In preparation for the November election, we wanted to ask ourselves questions not about the merits or demerits of left and right, but about the responsibility we owe to our neighbor, to our common life, and our own humanity. What does it mean to be fully alive? How do we truly know a person? What does polarization and a politics of war do to our personhood and humanity? Our goal in this fall issue is to offer ourselves and our readers an edifying path through the destructive polarization of the present political landscapes and discourses. By engaging with the wisdom and stories of those who are looking beyond the battles between left and right, we hope to habituate ourselves and our readers to the virtues of charity, magnanimity, and hope. For we believe that these durable and lasting virtues will make for a healthier and more meaningful civic life.

item.title: Claire Cochran Studio: Paintings
item.description:
Claire Cochran is a student at Baylor University studying Art and Classics. Below is a couple of her recent pieces series accompanied by her thoughtful reflections. More of her work may be found and acquired on her instagram @clairecochranstudio. She is also open for commissions.

Madonna and Child

2024

3 5/8 in. x 5 1/8 in.

Flashe acrylic paint on Arches paper

A few months ago, my mother and I both had a good, long cry.

Not for any particular reason other than the general pressures and anxieties that are our lot in a broken world. But we cried. We cried on each other’s’ shoulders and sniffled as our tears wet our shirts. And as we sat there with the late afternoon sunshine lapping at our backs, our tears gradually settled into a soft sigh of acceptance and deep sense of belonging.

The moment was profoundly transcendent in its own quiet way. Mother and daughter alike bearing the burdens of life, stooped together beneath a shared weight of disappointment and discouragement—but not alone. As I sat there, I remembered painfully that our lives are steeped in tears and suffering. That is inevitable. Yet even as the streams of heartache wash through and over us, we are swept ever nearer into the loving embrace of a God who meets us with compassion and kindness, a God who came to sit with us in our tears until he one day wipes them away completely.

I was drawn this scene because to me it was a beautiful representation of the way Christ makes his care and nearness known to us in our daily lives. Rather than meeting our grief or misunderstanding with anger or frustration, he responds with the gentleness of his own presence, which he often makes felt through the loving touch of our fellowmen. The moment presented that rare divine intersection between hope and sadness, the momentary and the eternal, when we are suspended motionless (as T.S. Eliot would say) “at the still point of the turning world” and acutely perceive our nature as spiritual and relational beings.

Loose vertical brushstrokes, a subdued color palette, and nods to Christian imagery evoke this soft, spiritual quality and convey a sense of mingled sadness and calm restfulness. The long, dramatic sweep of the daughter’s arm around her mother recalls both the gravity of traditional pieta scenes and the hopefulness of a Madonna and Child. At the same time, more mundane details like the dog pressed against the mother’s leg lend a sense of comfort, security, and homeliness that ground the scene in the everyday.

I deliberately worked on a small scale to communicate the intimacy and humility of the moment. The understated size invites the viewer to lean in close, much as one would in a conversation, while at the same time establishing a sense of intimacy between the figures that the viewer cannot completely broach. In the same interest of creating a piece that felt as quiet, informal, and unassuming as the scene itself, I chose to work on paper rather than canvas. The opaque quality of the paint grounds the scene in a specific moment of time and lends the scene a sense of permanence. At the same time, the fading afternoon light and translucent wash on the lower half of the work suggests the onward movement of our lives and quietly celebrates the rarity of these precious “still points” we experience in communion with one another.

Being

Acrylic on wood panel

5″ x7″

2024

General Artist Statement

My work explores personal longing for physical and spiritual homecoming through the lens of my own family relationships. My approach fuses sentimentality with figurative abstraction to reimagine humble moments of connection between family members as still points existing along two axes—the horizontal (temporal) and the vertical (transcendent).

Vertical and horizontal streaks of color take on a metaphorical quality as they appear to dissolve from partially obscured figures like warp and weft threads coalescing into a unified image. The effect is an ambiguous sense of motion and of stillness. It is in this intersection that human and divine communion seem to meet.

Select areas of beautiful rendering float in and out of tension with rough incompleteness and emphasize the face and hands as centers of human connection. By holding loss and loveliness together, this tension makes sense of the ever-moving present and the aching anticipation it awakens for a permanent home and unbounded relational fulfillment.

item.title: Election Discord and National Security: A Presidential Transition Expert’s Visit to Baylor
item.description:
When America’s foreign enemies attempt to spread election disinformation online, their aim is usually not to support one candidate or the other, but simply to “sow discord” between Americans, warned election expert Dr. Paul Lettow.

Dr. Lettow, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute researching foreign policy, visited Baylor on Thursday, Sept. 26, for a speaking event hosted by Baylor’s chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society (AHS). More than 150 students gathered in McClinton Auditorium to hear Dr. Lettow speak on his experience facilitating presidential transitions, and what our upcoming transition could mean for US foreign policy. Dr. Lettow has served both on the White House National Security Council and in the State Department, and helped facilitate two presidential transitions.

Paul Lettow speaking to students at Alexander Hamilton Event

Overcoming division for the sake of national security became a theme throughout Dr. Lettow’s talk. When asked about foreign interference in US elections, Dr. Lettow responded that “You can be darn sure that China and Russia and Iran and North Korea and any number of other actors are indeed very active, particularly online.” He noted that this social media interference was rarely targeted at specific candidates or policy positions, but “simply sowing discord.”

In the 2020 election, for example, Russia and China “were promoting on the one hand, Black Lives Matter and causes like that, and simultaneously promoting some of the kind of far-right causes. And the sole intention is to sow discord and mistrust among us so that we’re at each other’s throats.”

Social media interference was rarely targeted at specific candidates or policy positions, but “simply sowing discord.

It is notable that when our enemies are doing their best to weaken America, they choose to target our civil discourse itself rather than any particular policy position. Dr. Lettow emphasized what our enemies’ choices can teach us about ourselves. “Undoubtedly the greatest strength that we have as a country in our competitions with China and Russia is the fact that we self-correct through elections every two years, every four years… and that, I think in the end, will be our greatest strength, just like we proved through the Cold War. But it’s messy.”

In the midst of a polarizing election year, it can appear that everyone working in politics is fighting for a side. Dr. Lettow described his job differently. Through his position on President George W. Bush’s National Security Council, Dr. Lettow played a key role in the transition from President Bush to President Barack Obama.

In 2008, as the campaign between then-candidates Barack Obama and John McCain was heating up, Dr. Lettow said that President Bush and his National Security Advisor (Steve Hadley), “were emphatic… that whoever won, we were going to do everything we could from the White House side and throughout the government, to turn over the government to the president-elect with as much information-sharing and as much cooperation as we could possibly muster.” The nonpartisan “Center for Presidential Transition” called the Bush to Obama transition the “gold standard” of presidential transitions.

We self-correct through elections every two years, every four years… and that, I think in the end, will be our greatest strength, just like we proved through the Cold War. But it’s messy. Dr. Paul Lettow

Paul Lettow and members of the Alexander Hamilton Society

In the latter half of his talk, Dr. Lettow outlined the actual foreign policy records of each presidential candidate, their major successes and failures, and their stated plans for their administrations. Jazmine Fajardo, a junior political science major at Baylor, said she found this particularly helpful as an undecided voter.

“He gave me a lens of looking into the future depending on who I vote for, . ” Fajardo said. “What I told him after the event was that this conversation was more informative than the actual presidential debate… We just hear Trump’s iconic quote ‘I have concepts of a plan’ but he [Lettow] was actually able to say, based on what Trump has done before and what he’s been proclaiming… what is actually going to be happening if he were to go into office.”

Luke D’Ambrosio, the president of the AHS chapter at Baylor, shared his perspective on handling sensitive topics emerging at events like this one.

D’Ambrosio said that he is not concerned about student questions getting too controversial. “I think in the past I used to be worried about that, but honestly, controversial questions are what’s needed because those kinds of questions are what’s on people’s minds… It’s good to give a speaker a tough question. They’re qualified, they’re experienced… that’s what they’re there for.”

D’Ambrosio reported that this will not be their last event on the election. AHS plans to host a student forum in late October to discuss the election, and possibly a separate professor panel. On Thursday, Oct. 17, they will host a speaking event on Christian nationalism.

In 2019, Baylor’s AHS was founded as one chapter of a national organization based in Washington, DC. Baylor’s AHS “brings Washington to Waco” through foreign policy speaking events, movie nights, and book clubs. AHS also “brings Waco to Washington” by providing students with funding and job opportunities in DC. In 2023, Baylor AHS received the award for “Baylor Organization of the Year,” as well as the national award for “AHS Chapter of the Year.”

Reflecting on the success of AHS at Baylor, D’Ambrosio said “we’ve shown throughout our years on campus that we’re able to talk about controversial topics in a cordial manner.” He said that it would be good for Baylor to host more events that field controversial topics and encourage people to talk across the aisle this election season. “I’m very confident in the abilities of Baylor students to have a constructive dialogue.”

item.title: Renewing the Role of Religion in Global Affairs
item.description:
In 1977, President Jimmy Carter, while attending a New Year’s Eve party hosted by the Iranian Shah, famously described Iran as “an island of stability in a turbulent corner of the world.” Just a few months later, religious extremists orchestrated a revolution that culminated in the seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran, triggering a 444-day hostage crisis. This dramatic shift in Iran’s political climate raised questions about how a nation, once deemed exemplary in conduct, could spiral into chaos. The Carter administration’s failure to anticipate the religious forces driving Iran’s upheaval highlights a deeper issue: the United States’ lack of religious literacy in diplomacy.

Crowds rush the gates at the U.S. Embassy in Tehran on November 4, 1979 (CNN.com)

The Iranian Hostage Crisis was not just a political failure but an outcome of Washington’s broader negligence in understanding the religious dynamics shaping global affairs. In its post-crisis review, the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) admitted that U.S. diplomats had little to no interaction with religious leaders in Iran before the revolution. This oversight proved fatal. In dismissing the growing influence of Iran’s Islamic clerics, the U.S. undermined its diplomatic strategy and found itself blindsided by the revolution. As the crisis unraveled, it became clear that diplomatic engagement requires more than just relationships with government elites; it demands an understanding of the religious forces at play in society.

The Iranian Hostage Crisis revealed a broader issue in U.S. foreign policy: a systemic underestimation of religion’s role in international affairs. Former diplomat Eric Patterson, in his book Politics in a Religious World, argues that U.S. diplomacy operates with a “deliberate blindering” to religious factors, resulting in poor policy decisions. This secular bias, deeply ingrained in the U.S. State Department, has led American diplomats to ignore religious dynamics that drive political and social change across the globe.

Religious freedom, Patterson argues, is not just a moral good but a fundamental human right, essential to the functioning of democratic societies. Countries that protect religious freedom tend to uphold other democratic liberties, such as freedom of speech and assembly. Moreover, religious freedom can serve as a defense against authoritarianism. As former diplomat Thomas Farr notes, “tyranny often begins when the government claims the authority to define what is true.” When governments restrict religious expression, they in turn undermine the very freedoms that keep authoritarianism at bay.

Diplomatic engagement requires more than just relationships with government elites; it demands an understanding of the religious forces at play in society.

While U.S. diplomacy has long promoted democracy and human rights abroad, it has often ignored the religious context in which these rights are exercised. This oversight has left American diplomats ill-prepared to engage with religious leaders and movements that shape the political landscape in many parts of the world.

The roots of the U.S. government’s religious illiteracy can be traced to the secularization of its foreign policy. The U.S. Constitution’s Establishment Clause, intended to prevent government-imposed religion, has been interpreted in modern times as a mandate to keep religion out of public life altogether. This approach, while safeguarding against religious imposition, has led to a secular bias that dismisses the importance of religion in public and international affairs.

The faulty interpretation of the separation of church and state can be traced to the French Revolution, where the principle of laïcité seeks to keep religion out of the public sphere entirely. In contrast, the U.S. model was designed to protect religious expression, not to eliminate its influence from public life. However, over the past half-century, U.S. policy has increasingly marginalized religious voices in both domestic and foreign affairs. This trend has left American diplomats unequipped to optimally engage with deeply religious societies, where faith plays a central role in politics and governance.

Secularization has also influenced the academic field of international relations. In the 1960s, political scientists developed “modernization theory,” which posited that economic development alone could advance U.S. foreign policy objectives in religious cultures. This theory largely ignored the role of religion in shaping political outcomes, leading to diplomatic strategies that were ill-suited for religiously devout societies. As Patterson points out, this secularist bias continues to influence U.S. diplomacy, often to its detriment.

To address these shortcomings, experts like Patterson and former Secretary of State Madeline Albright argue that U.S. diplomats must be trained in religious literacy. Religious literacy, as defined by scholar Stephen Prothero, is “the ability to understand and use the basic building blocks of religious traditions.” It allows diplomats to engage effectively with religious leaders and traditions, recognizing their influence on governance and society.

Madeline Albright (right) and Mawlana Hazar Imam the Aga Khan (left) at a State Department dinner,

Religious literacy is not just a tool for preventing crises; it is a means of building relationships and fostering trust in an increasingly religious world.

In practice, this means going beyond the “old diplomacy,” which focuses solely on engaging with government elites, to what Patterson calls “new diplomacy,” which recognizes the influence of non-governmental actors, including religious leaders. In many countries, religious groups wield significant power and shape public opinion. For example, in Muslim-majority countries, religious leaders often have more credibility and influence than secular political elites. Ignoring these actors can lead to missteps, as the U.S. learned in Iran.

Albright has been a vocal advocate for incorporating religious understanding into diplomatic training. She asserts that “no American ambassador should be assigned to a country where religious feelings are strong unless he or she has a deep understanding of the faiths practiced there.” Currently, the U.S. State Department mandates language training for diplomats, but there is little emphasis on religious education. A comprehensive religious literacy program could mirror the language training model, with diplomats undergoing courses tailored to the religious landscape of their assigned countries.

Religious literacy is not just a tool for preventing crises; it is a means of building relationships and fostering trust in an increasingly religious world. Understanding the religious motivations behind political decisions can help U.S. diplomats navigate complex social landscapes, avoid misunderstandings, and promote policies that align with the values of the societies they engage with.

In a world where religion plays an ever-greater role in shaping politics, governance, and social movements, the U.S. must prioritize religious literacy as a key component of its diplomatic strategy. By doing so, it can better protect its interests abroad, prevent future crises, and promote a more stable and democratic international order.

item.title: Reading to Transcend
item.description:
“All that is done under heaven… is an unhappy business that God has given the children of man to be busy with,” reads one ancient Hebrew verse. Indeed, it seems the allotted fate of mankind to be burdened by the mundane, of all that is done under heaven. Man is no longer master over his daily task, but often becomes the task itself. People are not fulfilled by the mundane, so they seek escape from their lives through other means. Some are captivated by pleasure, others seek the games of mankind, while another digs himself further into work.

That same Hebrew source, however, tells us that God “has put eternity into man’s heart.” Man was not made to be simply a political observer, an athlete, or a teacher bound by time and circumstance. For there is a part of man which cannot be filled by such mortal things. Rather, he was made for something transcendent. Yet, how does one transcend the human condition? One way is to read books as sacred texts, as places of possible interaction with divine truth and wisdom.

Man was not made for reading but reading for man. Yet few read, and fewer read anything worthwhile. Most men, as Henry Thoreau writes, “have learned to read to serve a paltry convenience.” While the few who do read books are often content if “for the rest of their lives [they] vegetate and dissipate their faculties in what is called easy reading.”

How does one transcend the human condition? One way is to read books as sacred texts, as places of possible interaction with divine truth and wisdom.



Transcendence through reading requires engaging with ideas and truths that have stood against time. For Thoreau tells us that “in dealing with truth, we are immortal, and need fear no change or accident.” For “the oldest Egyptian or Hindoo philosopher raised a corner of the veil from the statue of the divinity; and still the trembling robe remains raised, and I gaze upon as fresh a glory as he did.” Whether they carry the title ancient, great, or classic books does not matter. It matters only that the books attempt to uncover and understand universal truths.

Though a laborious task, it is one that provides far more than it cost. However, one must humble himself in order to receive something he does not understand. The ends of reading cannot be pursued in advance. It is the activity itself which is good. To gaze upon that fresh statue of divinity requires reading books that are confusing, hard, and often unattractive. A vulnerable approach to reading invites revelation.

While not every single idea encountered is entirely true, it is the readers’ responsibility and gift to wrestle with the ideas presented. For in this wrestling, despite the frustration, one is led closer to wisdom. A spark is lit within us, a chance to peak behind the veil, with every great book we read.

This spark is not merely for a select few. While a notion persist that reading is only for the educated, Thoreau contends that “[e]ven the college-bred and so-called liberally educated men have really little or no acquaintance with” the English classics, far less anything beyond. One group does not hold claim to reading good books. It seems all groups alike tend to neglect nor desire to sacrifice time and attention for reading.

It is a failure to suppose that reading is only for the few and stops beyond the walls of a school or university. The goal is not to be a scholar removed from the world in solitude. Nor is it about the number of books one consumes. A few pages a day, even a couple lines here and there can suffice. For example, Socrates’ short declaration that it is not divinely “sanctioned that a better man be harmed by a worse” does more than enough to edify the mind for some time.

Every man can be a student who hears the richest thoughts ever spoken. Every man can transcend the unhappy business of everyday and glimpse at eternity.

The pursuit of something higher is not an activity confined by walls or a set day of the week. It is lifelong and daily. “It is,” Thoreau says, “time that we had uncommon schools, that we did not leave off our education when we begin to be men and women.” Each individual must take it upon himself to create a university within his mind. The burden does not rest on the university to do for us what each individual must do for himself.

Transcendence through reading offers a natural cultivation of the individual, a responsibility that rests far higher than the modern obsessions pervading the culture. “A man, any man, will go considerably out of his way to pick up a silver dollar; but here are golden words, which the wisest men of antiquity have uttered, and whose worth the wise of every succeeding age have assured us of.” The modern man does not treasure these golden words. He’d rather gather and collect and be left unsatisfied. Too many people believe, unconsciously or not, that there is nothing to transcend from.

Perhaps if the sages of the past were consulted, the human condition would appear clearer. “There are probably words addressed to our condition exactly, which, if we could really hear and understand, would be more salutary than the morning or the spring to our lives, and possibly put a new aspect on the face of things for us.” The ideas that have been considered for centuries are not old and dead but alive and breathing. Reading offers one the ability to transcend his time and speak with the greatest philosophers, kings, and statesmen that have ever lived. Every man can be a student who hears the richest thoughts ever spoken. Every man can transcend the unhappy business of everyday and glimpse at eternity.

The ends of reading cannot be pursued in advance. It is the activity itself which is good.

Moreover, mankind does not have to rely on itself for the seemingly unanswerable challenges of today. “These same questions that disturb and puzzle and confound us have in their turn occurred to all the wise men; not one has been omitted; and each has answered them, according to his ability, by his words and his life.” Man has at his fingertips many lives which he can live and many worlds he can transverse. Though man’s daily toil wastes him away, for a moment, time does not overcome him.

By reading with attention and wonder we may commune with timeless wisdom. For we may do what we were made to do, become who we were made to be.

item.title: The “After Party:” A New Christian Political Movement
item.description:
There’s a sickness in modern politics. Readers don’t need to be told about it—they feel the tensions at family dinners, the ridicule on social media, the sadness of people moving across the country to live with more “like minds.” Churches, neighborhoods, even entire towns are longing for hegemonic similarity.

There is a great separation going on. Something has changed in recent years, and people are forgetting about the “before.” But the tumult of our current political environment takes on new meaning under the teachings of Christianity: this world, though broken, is temporary; that the greater treasure is ahead. Christians are called to love their neighbor, to live in truth and in service to their neighbors, looking forward to a kingdom that is “not of this world.”

Therein lies the rub—different people who call themselves Christians consistently disagree about the way they ought to implement Christ’s commandments in their voting habits and advocations in this world.

There is a great separation going on. Something has changed in recent years, and people are forgetting about the “before.”

The After Party Book; Photo taken from Amazon

Considering this division, Curtis Chang, David French, and Russell Moore, friends across political lines but united under faith, developed the “After Party Project,” a course designed to teach Christians how to move together in love and hope for a better future. Their goal was not to negate anyone’s political convictions, but to elevate the Christian hope for transformation above politics—to shift the emphasis from what someone believes, to how we interact with humility and hope. This message was developed into a book by Curtis Chang and Nancy French called The After Party: Towards Better Christian Politics.

Chang and French remind their readers that the political atmosphere of Jesus’s time was similar to our own. The people of Israel were either in support or refusal of cooperation with their oppressors, and the two camps were contentious, with clear lines drawn between us and them.

And yet, Jesus walked over the dividing line. He had dinner with tax collectors and Pharisees, indiscriminately crossing over the dividing line to engage deeply with members of both camps. The authors point out that if we are to walk as Jesus walked, then it’s necessary to commit to deep engagement with people across the spectrum is necessary.

Nancy French; Photo taken from Amazon

We don’t know what is to come; neither do the politicians who claim otherwise. Accepting this admission of ignorance creates an intellectual humility, which translates to a relational humility. Not knowing everything, the authors suggest, should flow into the mindset that it’s not all about us. Tomorrow isn’t promised; we’re only given today, and we’re called to fulfill God’s will of servanthood in whatever time he gives us.

From left to right: Russell Moore, David French, Curtis Chang; Photo taken from City Church Network

This isn’t easy. There are many different attitudes towards political engagement formed from past experiences and personality differences. Chang and French acknowledge this: every Christian has a personal approach to politics—categorized by the authors on axes of hope and humility—which identifies a profile on the Hope/Humility graph. Below is an abridged description of their four political “types.”

And yet, Jesus walked over the dividing line. He had dinner with tax collectors and Pharisees, indiscriminately crossing over the dividing line to engage deeply with members of both camps.

The Combatant: This profile is high in hope and low in humility. They’re zealous in what they believe, but struggle to see nuance in issues and opposing views. And since they care the most about their issues, they exert significant influence.

The Exhausted: This profile is low in hope and high in humility. Opposite the combatant, they’re humble to the point of inaction. They’re dominated by fear and conflict-aversion, and prefer to withdraw themselves from a political environment they see as hopeless.

The Cynic: This profile is low in hope and low in humility. They’re certain of their pessimistic worldview, and due to the supposed sophistication and confidence of their position, they exert unusual influence. They are corrosive to themselves and others through their mix of pride and despair.

The Disciple: This Profile is high in hope and high in humility. They have submitted themselves and their politics fully to Jesus, and in that, they find freedom to approach situations with humility and nuance. They’re willing to learn from others and accept they don’t always have the answers.

After discussing these profiles, Chang and French make one thing clear: exhibiting faith in your politics means leaving the mindset of us vs. them. We are called by Jesus to resist conforming to the binary, but rather to approach each other with the Kingdom of Heaven in mind, leading lives filled with hope and humility, and moving forward together with a recognition that not this world, but the next, will be made well by the intervention of Christ at the end of time.

item.title: Connection Amidst Polarization: A Conversation with Elizabeth Oldfield
item.description:
Polarization sounds a deafening pitch in our common life today. With the 2024 election looming, the pitch only grows louder. For humans who deeply desire connection, this cacophony of division and wrath is a sign not only of civic but soul danger. Elizabeth Oldfield, host of The Sacred Podcast and author of the new book, Fully Alive: Tending to the Soul in Turbulent Times, is one of those humans. In an interview with Elizabeth, we discussed her own work and vocation across divides, the social and theological marks of polarization, and the hope and healing found in connection.

Photo taken from Yale Center for Faith and Culture

The first question I asked Elizabeth was one of her own, a question she asks at the outset of every podcast and interview—“what is sacred to you?” Her answer, relationships and interconnectedness, illumines the heart of her vocation. “It sounds like a sort of abstract thing,” Elizabeth said, “and yet it is my sense that we get into so many problems when we are disconnected as human beings.”

It was precisely to foster connection in the face of polarization that Elizabeth began her podcast, The Sacred, in 2017. Elizabeth recalled the vapid disconnection and the tense social and political climate around that time. She remembered the questions that confronted her: “How did my very mixed group of friends politically and theologically get to the point where I can’t put them around the same table?” “What is this desire to dehumanize that I see in others and feel also in myself?” “Where is it coming from and how do I respond?”

The Sacred was Elizabeth’s response. In each episode Elizabeth sits down with a public intellectual or figure and talks with them about their deepest values and influences as well as the stories that have shaped them. Guests span the political and ideological spectrum, and if you listen long enough, you are bound to encounter a guest you disagree with.

The goal of these conversations, however, is not eristic victory, but empathy and understanding. “I want the listener to see that while you may disagree with someone about abortion, climate change, whatever issue it is, they are still a human being with a complicated life worthy of our curiosity and care.”

How did my very mixed group of friends politically and theologically get to the point where I can’t put them around the same table? Elizabeth Oldfield

The Sacred Podcast, Theos. Photo taken from Spotify.

The ability to see someone as an interesting, complex human worthy of attention and care cuts against the predominant public and media impulse to label and dismiss, categorize and attack. Today, in the shadow of the coming election, our prejudices seem to be hardening and our categories tightening. The ability to hold tension in a heart-expanding way, what educator and author Parker Palmer deems our hope, is dissolving as people close themselves and others in neat little boxes.

And yet, “people are so interesting,” Elizabeth emphasized. She spoke of the neurological reward we feel when we are surprised by another person, when we find ourselves outside of the preconceived map we drew around them. For it seems that we were not made for labeling and classifying, but care and connection—that our humanity and others’ is not meant to be closed in a category but opened up and attended to.

In a chapter of her recently released book, Fully Alive: Tending to the Soul in Turbulent Times, Elizabeth presents polarization not merely as a social problem, but a soul problem—a problem of sin, the sin of wrath. In her book, Elizabeth writes that “wrath allows the tension of balancing in complexity to dissolve in a joyous freefall of certainty, akin to a sugar high, addictive.” She points to the monk, Evagrius, who characterizes wrath as an irritant to the soul. For it is wrath that works in us to categorize, label, and divide—to close us up and off from another.

Wrath, Elizabeth told me, is more than anger. “It is anger mixed with disgust. It is any anger that undermines relationship.” It is that impulse to say, “Screw you. You don’t deserve me or my attention. There is nothing good in you.” If we believe that we were made for connection, this wrath appears gravely dangerous. For it is disconnection from both our neighbor and our own selves. Moreover, if we adhere to the imago dei, this wrath is ultimately division from the communal and relational Source. This wrath is sin.

“Wrath allows the tension of balancing in complexity to dissolve in a joyous free fall of certainty, akin to a sugar high, addictive.” Elizabeth Oldfield, Fully Alive

This may seem dramatic to some. And yet, sin, Elizabeth told me, while often and historically twisted and misused, really does make sense of a lot of things. “We all want wisdom,” Elizabeth said, “and I believe that religion still has something to teach us.” In the Christian tradition and New Testament writings, Elizabeth encountered the wisdom and example of radical non- tribalism and hospitality, a direct and practical counter to the wrath and disconnection of polarization.

Photo taken from Baker Publishing Group

Elizabeth recalled the example of Christ. “Jesus is constantly going between different racial and social groups—Ethiopians and Samaritans, the poor and victimized—and doing so with care and compassion, seeing them as fully human.” This was a radical position then, and still so today. Today, our tendency is to engage only with our own political tribes. Increasingly, we begin to view those unlike us as mere political categories and derogatory labels—not humans like ourselves. We divide and polarize. We call ourselves righteous and leave.

And yet, “Christ stayed,” Elizabeth emphasized. “He did not stand his ground and attack, but he stood his ground and listened.” When asked how we resist the wrathful impulse to polarize, Elizabeth pointed to this practical example of Christ. “Stay,” she said, “ask another question.” This doesn’t mean you have to agree, but rather, in the words of theologian Willie Jennings, “keep holding hands.” Elizabeth shared her personal practice of inviting someone she disagrees with to dinner. She explains this with a verse from 1 Peter, which more or less reads, “The end of all things is near, so show hospitality.” In other words, be open, resist wrath, stand your ground and offer the other cheek.

I ended my conversation with Elizabeth the same way she ends her chapter on wrath and polarization—with blessing. In her book, Elizabeth describes blessing as “holding someone in the light,” as “creating room for connection and love to grow.” In blessing, Elizabeth shared, we speak life over someone. We name them, seek protection over them, turn our focus of care on them.

The end of all things is near, so show hospitality.

For blessing is the opposite of polarization. It affirms and cares for another’s complex humanity. Blessing is both a physical and spiritual reaching out for another, a uniting in love. Blessing is not for the select religious few, Elizabeth told me, but is available for us all. It is an act of love, “the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real,” writes philosopher Iris Murdoch. It is a mother blessing her child before school. It is a parent giving his or her child the care they never received themselves. For love covers a multitude of sin.

As we continue navigating this election season, it is my hope that we not only see polarization for what it is, wrath and sin, but also recognize the opportunity for real connection, reconciliation, and love. May we bless those we disagree with, who disagree with us. May we recognize the reality of another’s beautifully and painfully complex humanity. And if we call ourselves Christians, may we be those who carry the hope of communion, the fragrance of Love.

item.title: David Brooks: Knowing People in Uncertain Times
item.description:
The inability to “see” others lies at the root of America’s increasingly hostile sociopolitical climate, claims New York Times journalist and bestselling author David Brooks.

Brooks opened President Linda Livingstone’s Baylor Conversation Series on civil discourse with a lecture given to almost 2000 Baylor students, faculty, and local Wacoans. Given just hours before the Presidential debate, the bright-eyed audience appeared eager for an effective antidote to the polemic tumultuousness of the next hours and months.

Linda Livingstone sits with David Brooks during Q&A segment of event. Picture taken from https://news.web.baylor.edu/news/story/2024/salt-and-light-baylor-focuses-year-long-series-events-civil-discourse

Brooks began by diagnosing the state of the nation as a greater reflection of the current state of the individual soul. He shared several recent statistics pointing to the increase in cases of severe depression, feelings of isolation, and those who consider themselves to have zero close friendships, ultimately asserting that “America is a sadder country, and a sadder country means a meaner country.”

For Brooks, this is where politics comes in. As a result of social isolation and feelings of invisibility, more and more people are misplacing their desire for deep and meaningful connection in the political sphere. For many, politics has become a sort of “self-solving” of this inner sadness—mere medicine for a loneliness that requires a tangible cure.

“America is a sadder country, and a sadder country means a meaner country.” – David Brooks

Brooks explains that politics has given an increasingly isolated public the illusion of tight knit community. People feel a sense of belonging or identity when they subscribe to the worldview and opinions of a certain political group, and yet no one truly knows them as a unique and individual person. They are only a number counted, not a person seen.

Because of this, the world of politics has become a grand scale war of identity. To disagree with someone’s politics is to deny and reject the entire person. The person is generalized down to a political label with a set of opinions, rather than seen as a whole person, complex and interesting. The human person, says Brooks, has become a “land of permanent warfare.” Where there should be connection and seeing, there is division and attack.

If a lack of real human connection is the core of our charged political atmosphere, what is the effective response? Brooks offers a solution so ancient and innate to the human experience it might appear lackluster in the modern age: conversation and friendship.

Brooks argues that in our age of digital distraction and false connection, the average person simply does not know how to get to know someone in a deep and meaningful way, especially when that person is unlike them. This void of social skills both produces and exacerbates the issue—obstructing human fellowship and its corollary, civil discourse. This is where Brooks’ most recent book comes in. Fittingly titled, “How to know a person,” the book offers itself as a humble guide to help every individual learn “the art of seeing others deeply and being deeply seen.”

Brooks urged the audience at Baylor and those reading his book to recognize that everyone has room to grow in the art of knowing and seeing people deeply. He outlined his book’s main points of advice for growing in this art.

There are two types of people, Brooks told us — illuminators and diminishers.

Illuminators are those who shed light on another person, encouraging them to open up about their life and experiences.
