An illuminator recognizes that each person’s story is more nuanced and detailed than they could possibly imagine and is thus quick to give their attention and always 100% of it—they do not listen in hopes to respond, but because they are simply interested and care.

A diminisher, on the other hand, is quick to lessen another by putting them in a box. With little true attention, they merely listen for answers they want to hear and judge someone based on their own preconceived generalizations. Brooks urged all of us to habituate ourselves to the careful and caring attention of an illuminator and watch as it changes not just ourselves, but American culture at large.

Even so, the idea that a climate as hostile as American politics could be healed by deep connection and humble conversation across divides, still seems idealistic to some. And yet, Brook’s call for true connection strikes a deep and innate chord. If you could boil down the daily argumentative, polarized, and hate-speech rampant interactions (within politics and outside), one major metaphysical and ethical question is at stake—do human beings have intrinsic value that does not depend on what I think of them? Or is every person’s value dependent on their values, beliefs, or actions?

“These failures of seeing are not failures of vision or failures of intellect—they’re failures of the heart.” – David Brooks

Brooks would answer the first. If every human person has intrinsic value dependent on something outside of one’s own perception of them, then the desire to understand one another quickly enters the fray. Conversations quickly turn from hostile tennis matches to unified discussions, disparaging comments to respectful interaction, asserting one’s own will without care for the devastation inflicted to listening carefully with a desire to understand. Brooks argues that disagreements between people will and should remain—but the ultimate goal (for all people to flourish) is remembered.

As Brooks noted while closing his speech; “these failures of seeing are not failures of vision or failures of intellect—they’re failures of the heart.” As the United States prepares for yet another combative election season, one cannot help but wonder what might happen if we all admitted where our own hearts fail—fail to see, to respect, to know. Perhaps America, as with any truly free state, may return once more to the art and privilege of civil discourse. A practice that, as President Livingstone noted, “is both timeless and timely.”

item.title: Retrospective Memory: A Series by Claire Cochran
item.description:
Claire Cochran is a student at Baylor University studying Art and Classics. Below is her recent series on retrospective memory and her reflections and statements on each piece. More of her work may be found and acquired on her instagram @clairecochrancreative. She is also open for commissions.

Blocks

2024

20 in. x 12 in.

Oil and charcoal on stretched fabric

Through the light of retrospective memory, this piece explores my relationship with my grandfather from a ‘contemplative distance’ and reflects on the coalescence of singular, seemingly insignificant moments into the unified bonds of human connection. I am interested in the idea that repeated moments like these, though forgotten themselves, are collectively remembered and compounded into a distinct impression of the particular place or person to which they are connected. Considering how the past life of the canvas material imbues the image with additional meaning, I worked the painting onto the surface of fabric salvaged from my grandparents’ house, where I spent much of my childhood. As such, the place is literally ingrained into the image itself, in much the same way that these familiar places compose the backdrop of our lives and become an integral part of them.

Though I do not actually remember this scene, moments like this were profoundly formational both in my relationship with my grandfather and in my personal development. The image unfolds as a subconscious memory that crystalizes as it settles on his familiar figure, which appears in greater focus than the still-developing figure of the infant. Abstracted horizontal and vertical strokes represent the tension between the aspects of our lives passed along the “horizontal axis” of the space-time continuum and the aspects positioned along the transcendent “vertical axis” of memory and relationship. In this way, I hope to communicate that we can appreciate the people, places, and things in our lives both for what they once were and for what they are now.

9 a.m

2024

13.75 in. x 11 in.

Oil and charcoal on naturally-dyed cotton

This piece likewise considers how repeated experiences of a particular place gradually compound into the fabric of our human experiences. I continue to be interested in how my family’s generational cabin has remained an immutable refuge and place of family communion from my early childhood all the way into my adult life.

In further exploration of place and how the story ingrained into the canvas itself informs the story depicted in the overlaid image, my grandmother’s figure appears over cotton dyed with fallen oak leaves from around the cabin where this scene occurs. In fact, we collected these leaves together over the Thanksgiving holiday, and she assisted me in dyeing the fabric. Contemplating repetition and the passage of time, the piece engages with the ambiguity of memory as our lives pass in and out of a space.

Mama Bird

2024

22 in. x 15 in.

Oil and charcoal on stretched fabric

This piece again explores incorporation of patterned textile into the world of the painted image. More concerned with the fabric’s pattern than its past life, I sought here to communicate the subtle, nurturing shades of my mother’s personality. I also played with the convergence of the musical and visual arts, translating Beethoven’s Grande Sonata No. 8 (which I strongly associate with my childhood) into color and form. In this way I sought to depict a scene both singular and repeated—both within and without temporal confines—like a snapshot frozen in time and seeping out from the moment.

item.title: Still Lingering: On Poetry
item.description:
“Be still and know that I am God,” exhorts Psalm 46:10. Mere knowledge of the Divine is insufficient for communion with Him. God asks for stillness to accompany such knowledge. In the context of this psalm, however, such a request appears unreasonable. Before the call to be still, the psalmist recounts desolations (v. 8), wars (v. 9), and the very mountains toppling into the sea (v. 2). How are we to be still?

We ask this question of our own lives in the face of the––less poetic yet seemingly no less drastic––chaos that surrounds us, the constant noise that drowns out the peace we might otherwise know. We flee from fleeting season to fleeting season, ever looking ahead for a reprieve, a rest. But even our vacations are meticulously packed and planned, and we come home more exhausted than when we left. Again, how are we to be still?

The psalm, by its content, offers a difficult but not dissatisfactory answer to the question. Its form, however, also serves to provide the answer, for insofar as it is a poem, it works to produce the very thing it asks of its reader. All poetry, no matter its form or content, requires of and simultaneously produces in its reader one thing: stillness.

At the still point of the turning world. Neither flesh nor fleshless;

Neither from nor towards; at the still point, there the dance is

Neither arrest nor movement. And do not call it fixity,

Where past and future are gathered. Neither movement from nor towards,

Neither ascent nor decline. Except for the point, the still point.

Thus writes T.S. Eliot in lines 62-66 of “Burnt Norton.” What is this so-called “still point”? Eliot is generous in providing us with exactly what it is not, but he offers very little information as to what it is––other than its name and that “there the dance is.” These are the only two images: a point and a dance.

T.S. Eliot

How are we to be still?

Perhaps by dance he insinuates a ballroom dance, where couples rotate and circle the floor, all turning together, yet each couple a particular spinning sphere in a larger space. One partner’s eyes are on the other’s and, while all the world is frantic with motion, they are still to one another. Yes, they move, but in relation to one another they have not changed. They hold and are held, and though the rest of the world be in motion, they share a kind of stillness together. Perhaps Eliot meant dance in this way.

Perhaps, however, the image is not the only thing he wished to communicate to his reader. I can summarize and describe a dance to you, but I cannot––short of writing a poem of my own––communicate all that Eliot would if his reader were attentive to what he is writing. Through all the beauty and confusion of his language he makes his readers stop and ask of the poem, “What does this mean?” The poem’s words offer no variation, no explanation beyond what is already there. The reader, frustrated by such unresponsiveness, has only three remedies at hand: to slam the book shut and never open it again (an understandable response to reading T.S. Eliot); to turn to the internet (alas); or to linger.

While I will not fault anyone for the first option, I would offer some counter-intuitive encouragement: some poetry is simply hard. Perhaps difficult, complex, esoteric poetry is not what you wish to read (and oftentimes I do not wish to read it, either). Pick up a copy of Emily Dickinson and enjoy some poetry that does not drive you to tear out your hair. However, I do endorse Eliot as being worth a certain measure of premature baldness.

For the second option, the urge to turn to the internet for explanation, I would beg of you to reconsider. A confusing poem is not some kind of math problem with a single solution. Perhaps some scholar or avid fan has written some elegant prose online about the imagery of dancing in a certain T.S. Eliot poem and can explain in vivid detail the underlying themes and motifs in “Burnt Norton.” All that information may be true and good, but if Eliot wished merely to communicate such information, he could have done so. But he chose not to. In order to read a poem, one must trust its poet. If Eliot did not write exact information in a clear and systematic manner but instead chose to present it through negation and a couple of images, then we must trust that he did so with an intent. If we are willing to trust him as an author, then we may be content to be still even in the face of complex and confusing language.

Here we come to the third option when encountering a difficult bit of poetry: lingering. Our initial question, “What does this mean?” arrests our reading of the poem. We reread what we just read, thinking, drawing connections, noticing things we did not first observe. Perhaps a certain level of confusion remains, and yet at the same time there begins to arise a sense of wonder and familiarity. The page becomes worn, annotated, highlighted, warm. All of a sudden, the spell is broken, and we realize that we had lost ourselves in a small stanza, a line, a phrase. Thus, in contemplating a bit of poetry such as “the still point,” we ourselves are stilled.

Perhaps a certain level of confusion remains, and yet at the same time there begins to arise a sense of wonder and familiarity.

If Eliot had been clear in his meaning (or if we had resorted to easy answers on the internet or elsewhere), we would have gained the knowledge but lost the knowingness, the experience of having been brought to stillness. Taking the time to reflect on the image of dancing in “Burnt Norton” provides the reader with a lens through which he or she might consider the rest of the poem. In surrendering ourselves to a poem––in lingering––we open ourselves up what a poem offers: the experiential knowingness is more important than the factual knowledge.

Lingering, engaging in the classical notion of leisure, is a practice we would do well to rediscover. In continuing the theme of time, Eliot ends the same section of “Burnt Norton” by writing line 89, “Only through time time is conquered.” We speak of ‘having no time’ and of ‘making time,’ as if time were a commodity (‘time is money’) and not a moment in which we lived. We look to the past overfondly and to the future overanxiously. But what about right now? Instead of trying to conquer time as if we were outside of it, what if we boldly entered into it? This would require a firm conviction that the moment is an end unto itself and not merely a means to the future (though we have been taught the latter). A moment is all we have; as finite creatures, we can only experience time right now through this moment. If we cannot be still in this moment, when will we ever learn how?

Poetry will not spur you on to the next great thing. It is not a page turner––most poems are only a page (if even that long). If you read it hastily, it will likely seem vague and uncompelling. While novels might reward the insatiable reader who can tear through two hundred pages in a day, poetry only asks slowness. However, if you yearn for a breath of peace, for a renewed sense of wonder at this world of ours, for a deeper ability to be still in the presence of God, then poetry may guide you in the right direction. In lines 44-46, Eliot writes that “Time past and time future / What might have been and what has been / Point to one end, which is always present.” Heeding his words, let’s learn to linger in the present.

item.title: Magnolia: A Catalyst for Renewal in Waco
item.description:
The Waco many know today is unrecognizable from 50 years ago. A massive catalyst for this change is thanks to Chip and Joanna’s Magnolia Silos.

In recent history, Waco has grappled with economic stagnation and urban decay. But now the city has undergone a remarkable transformation thanks in part to the vision and efforts of Magnolia, founded by Chip and Joanna Gaines. Magnolia has helped renew the town’s reputation and economy through the company’s various business ventures. One person who understands how Magnolia has impacted Waco is Jonathan Gulley, former head of operations. I recently spoke with Gulley about the company’s role in Waco’s revitalization.

The reputation of Waco reflected poorly on the city prior to Magnolia, Gulley remembers. It conjured images of extreme poverty, homelessness, the Branch Davidian Compound, and scandals involving Baylor athletics. But, as Gulley observes, Magnolia has played a massive role in lifting this “dark cloud” and renewing Waco’s identity.

Chip & Joanna Gaines

One of Magnolia’s significant contributions has been job creation and talent attraction. In the past, Waco struggled to provide white-collar jobs and attract experienced creatives, innovators, and managers. But Magnolia has brought and continues to bring people from across the nation to Waco.

Gulley said that “Magnolia provided a place where true creatives could come together and succeed in their businesses.” The company’s executive decision to pull talent from far and wide has allowed Magnolia to fill essential roles within the company and stimulate economic growth within the city as well.

This influx of skilled professionals has increased employment opportunities within Waco contributing to the broader revitalization of Waco’s job market. Not only bringing in outsiders, but also offering opportunities for talented locals. “Magnolia hires people who want to make a difference,” Gulley told me. Chip and Joanna have always had a deep-rooted commitment to their community in Waco.

As part of their efforts to contribute to the city’s betterment, Chip and Joanna actively sought partnerships with other businesses in Waco, recognizing that collaboration and cooperation were critical to a meaningful impact on the city’s growth and development. These partnerships were not merely transactional but were built on shared values and a common vision for improving the quality of life for all residents of Waco.

Chip and Joanna have always had a deep-rooted commitment to their community in Waco.

Magnolia has also turned Waco into a desired tourist destination. The flood of visitors from across the world has provided Waco with far more opportunities and resources for renewal. Waco was ranked second on Trip Advisor’s list of top vacation destinations for Americans in 2018, with one and a half million people visiting the Silos each year. Bringing such massive numbers of people to the small city has increased the city’s revenue tremendously, allowing the economy to boom like never before.

This influx of visitors to Waco also sparked a revolution in Waco’s dining and hospitality scene. Before the Silos, there was very little open outdoor dining for families and friends to come together and have a nice meal in the sunshine. Magnolia Table and the many food trucks at the Silos brought an iconic dining experience to Waco. “Magnolia really catalyzed a move of beautiful outdoor spaces where families can gather together and eat.” This dining experience spilled over into other local restaurants, further boosting the city’s economy, and creating more spaces for gathering with community.

Magnolia Table Outdoor seating area

Magnolia’s partnerships with local organizations like Mission Waco and the Salvation Army have also strengthened the local community. “Magnolia was and is a very generous company,” Gully testifies. The company understood that true generosity was not about seeking recognition or praise but about selflessly serving others and making a tangible difference in people’s lives.

Magnolia’s collaborative efforts facilitate community outreach programs and support budding entrepreneurs. Their endorsement and support of local artisans and small businesses fosters unity and development within the community, further displaying the company’s commitment to revitalization and renewal.

Moreover, Magnolia Foundation’s mentorship program aids and supports Waco small businesses. The program’s events, such as the Christmas Silobration and the Silos half marathon, provide small businesses with vendor spots and opportunities for further growth and outreach. By bringing people together, these events cultivate and strengthen the sense of community in Waco.

“Chip and Joanna’s passion is Waco. They had a love for the city and the people here. Everything they did and are working to do is to make this city better.” Jonathan Gulley

Beyond just providing opportunities, Magnolia also works personally with local Waco entrepreneurs and businesses. Jonathan Gulley and other experienced entrepreneurs at Magnolia would meet with struggling startup business owners in Waco and give them free tips and advice on how to succeed in their business endeavors. They did this for no other reason than that they wanted these individuals and businesses, as well as the community around them, to thrive.

Magnolia has also contributed to a revitalizes Waco through its efforts to fight drug abuse, sex trafficking, and child homelessness. Recently, Magnolia fought alongside the City of Waco and others to tear down the last strip club in the city. Magnolia has also helped the city convert places that were once drug and sex trafficking hubs into beautiful parts, better serving the community of Waco.

Waco has undergone tremendous renewal thanks to the visionaries behind the Magnolia Foundation. Jonathan Gulley says it best: “Chip and Joanna’s passion is Waco. They had a love for the city and the people here. Everything they did and are working to do is to make this city better.”

Waco’s revival is a testimony to the transformative power of community, collaboration, and vision. Magnolia’s journey from a small operation to a massive catalyst for change illustrates the potential for positive impact when businesses and communities work together toward a shared vision of growth, restoration, and renewal.

item.title: Winter 2024 Issue: Renewal
item.description:
When a year ends and a new one meets us, there descends upon our culture a spirit of evaluation and change. There is a sense of looking back—we evaluate our life, pinpointing what isn’t working and what must change. In this mindset, we look back to cut out. While in some cases this cutting out is necessary for growth and health, it is not the primary way in which we grow. There is a looking back, a returning to, that doesn’t force us to cut down, but rather invites us to soak in and feed on that which brings us life. It is a season of renewal that prepares us for new life and growth.

In this issue our writers were invited to think about this aspect of renewal in their lives — where and how it might be found, its value and importance for their individual and common life. Many of our writers focused on daily habits of renewal. Keira Konson invites us to cultivate a rhythm of sabbath in our lives. Lottie King welcomes us into the habituation of winter, a season long practice of wintering where we may find healing and rest. A delightful defense of leisure and feasting is offered us by Julianna Kazemi through her lovely analysis of Babette’s feast. Nicolas Horne encourages us to welcome stillness through the practice of lingering on poetry.

Following this theme of renewal in the spiritual and religious domains of life, Jonathan Perkins helps us understand the renewal woven into the practice of liturgy as both the work of the people and the worship of God. A Christian renewal of the Feminine and Masculine ideals is presented by Mike Ortiz, drawing from his interview with Dr. Mike and Alexandra Foley. Mike Ortiz also offers us a renewed understanding of Catholic Guilt that points us towards spiritual renewal and redemption. For my part, I interviewed the Rector-Elect of Christ Church Waco to discuss questions of spiritual renewal–what it is and how we might cultivate it within this Lenten season and beyond.

Our writers also found examples of renewal on Baylor’s campus. Emily Livesay and Luke Babler illustrate the renewing quality of storytelling and listening through their interview with Dr. Stephen Sloan of the Institute for Oral History. Danielle Miller presents us with a renewed understanding of civil discourse that points one toward renewed openness, charity, and truth seeking. Ashley Turner reviews Baylor professor Alex Fogleman’s new book, “Knowledge, Faith, and Early Christian Initiation,” which renews the age old question of how one may know God.

Not only at Baylor, but in the wider culture and community did our writers turn to find wellsprings of renewal. Madeline Alfonso shares the renewing impact Chip and Joanna Gaines’ Magnolia has had on Waco. Mark Raines renews a 1952 film “Ikiru” and points us toward its themes of renewal both in old age and community. Mike Chapple provides us thoughts on civic renewal from his interview with Justin Giboney of the AND campaign.

As this winter looks increasingly to spring, I invite you to read these pieces and consider the ways in which renewal is possible in your life. It is my belief that this is the purpose of winter (and Lent for those who practice.) It is the time to return to the soil and feed on the nutrients that will usher in our spring. It is the time to foster renewal, not just by pruning, but by returning to and soaking in the sources of life that have been lost or overlooked in the course of a year. In this issue, we hope to do just that, and we invite you to join us. Thus, may we foster renewal together as we give thanks for the soil that grounds us and look for the spring to come.

item.title: Embracing Catholic Guilt
item.description:
The idea of “Catholic guilt” usually carries with it some negative connotations, namely the excess of religiously-induced remorse and the toxicity of such feelings. It is not uncommon, for instance, to read op-eds or blog posts about “leaving Catholic guilt behind” or “how to recover from Catholic guilt.” In this article, however, I want to propose an alternate view, and dare to argue on behalf of Catholic guilt. I will first draw from my personal experience as a recent Catholic convert and former evangelical protestant, and then make some broader points about why I think guilt is a necessary ingredient for those who take their religious faith seriously, especially for Catholics and for Christians generally.

In the Catholic tradition, I have found a healthy embrace of guilt which, instead of pushing me away from redemption, points me straight to it.



Growing up, I was seldom confronted with religious guilt. Of course, our moral conscience can often be our most zealous accuser, but it is also the case that some environments and belief systems can be more or less conducive to adequately “listening” to our conscience. For example, a child who is immersed in moral relativism will likely be less aware of a personal wrongdoing than his religiously-raised counterpart. But even among the religious, some traditions are more conducive to this awareness than others. While awareness is not synonymous with virtuous action, it is nevertheless a crucial step toward acting virtuously. I say this only to highlight the importance of external influence on one’s moral formation and development.

In my middle school days at a Wesleyan academy, I was often reminded of God’s mercy and forgiveness, usually phrased in such a way that emphasized the point in the past tense: i.e., “you have been forgiven.” I thought little of it at the time, but as I reflect on the meaning of that statement, I am reminded of why I began to drift toward Catholicism. If we are attentive to our conscience, guilt is inescapable. If we ignore it as a merely fleeting sentiment or, worse, as a sign of weakness for “saved” Christians, then we do so at our own peril.

I remember the night that I decided to embrace my own guilt: I was sitting alone, reading St. Augustine’s Confessions. It was quite the liberating experience, too metaphysical to accurately describe with words. What I can say is that I was no longer made uncomfortable by those feelings which too many of my fellow Christians had advised me to ignore. Rather, I began to grow more uncomfortable with the “come as you are” messaging that is ever so prevalent in modern churches today. In the Catholic tradition, I have found a healthy embrace of guilt which, instead of pushing me away from redemption, points me straight to it.

Catholic guilt, in spite of the heavy scrutiny it receives, is a virtue, for it stands as a mean between the extremes of moral apathy and scrupulosity.

I do concede that guilt is not an intrinsic good. It is not inherently good to feel guilty, as it is a sign of personal wrongdoing. But it can in fact be a good means to higher ends; it is, in my view, the only means through which we can access certain goods, namely repentance, the inclination to confess our sins, and a desire to attain spiritual perfection and holiness. Guilt implores the Christian, first and foremost, to pray for forgiveness and mercy. Indeed, one of the oldest Christian prayers is the Miserere Mei, Deus, i.e., “God, have mercy on me,” which is still prayed by Catholics (as well as by many Anglicans, Lutherans, and other “high church” protestants). For only those with a sense of guilt can truly desire mercy.

Thus, what I have found is that guilt, and Catholic guilt in particular, takes us out of our spiritual comfort zones and demands that we seek the sacraments of reconciliation, both confession and penance, in hopes that we may lead holy lives and partake in the divine nature. Of course, it is possible for this sense of guilt to become overly scrupulous, leading to unhealthy obsessions which may hinder us from moving further. But this would obviously be an excess. As Aristotle taught in his Ethics, a virtue is the mean between two extremes. Catholic guilt, in spite of the heavy scrutiny it receives, is a virtue, for it stands as a mean between the extremes of moral apathy and scrupulosity. Thus, this Lenten season, I invite every Christian to embrace Catholic guilt, that we may fast and perform penance, increasing in holiness and devotion. For it is in this embrace that spiritual renewal awaits us this Lenten season.

item.title: Truth, Not Victory: Civil Disagreement at Baylor
item.description:
Does going to college make you better or worse at having a disagreement?

One of the primary goals of a liberal education is to learn from people you disagree with through civil discussion. However, the numbers show that America’s current education system is doing the opposite.

In September, a PEW Research Center poll found that about 6 in 10 American adults say that political conversations with people they disagree with are stressful, while only 36% say they are “interesting and informative.” The same poll found that those with a postgraduate degree are actually 8% less likely to find political disagreements “interesting and informative” compared to those who never attended college.

Is it possible to reverse this troubling trend? How can we turn our universities into places that promote informative disagreement rather than eroding it?

There are many at Baylor who believe they have an answer: find people who disagree with each other, give them a controversial topic, and guide them in civil discussion.

About 6 in 10 American adults say that political conversations with people they disagree with are stressful, while only 36% say they are “interesting and informative.”

Baylor Conversation Series on Improving Civil Discourse

On January 22nd, President Linda Livingstone moderated the first in a series of “civil discourse” panel discussions on politics and faith. On April 12-13th, Baylor will host the 2024 National Bioethics Bowl, in which teams will debate difficult ethical dilemmas in the medical field. And throughout the spring semester, the Bo Bo Spiritual Life Center will be hosting a “Bridging the Gap” course, part of a national initiative attempting to train students across the political spectrum to seek common ground on contentious issues.

Behind each of these projects are people who have hope that Baylor students can grow from their disagreements.

Annalise Shero, co-president of the Baylor student organization “Table Talk,” is one of those hopeful people. Table Talk hosts weekly student conversations on controversial topics, such as the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, affirmative action, and feminism in the Barbie movie. Annalise clarified that Table Talk discussions are not competitions. Rather, “this is a conversation where we are all trying to learn from each other.” Despite this spirit of charity, Annalise never encourages participants to water-down their true opinions. “We want people to come in with strong opinions and vocal opinions, because if we didn’t talk about the things we think, then there would be no point to having the club.”

The dynamic that Table Talk has cultivated is so antithetical to America’s polarized culture that it seems almost contradictory. Moderators ask people to express their unmitigated opinions on the most divisive issues, while still preserving an atmosphere where, in Annalise’s words, “everyone would listen when someone talked rather than mentally preparing what they were going to say in response.”

While Table Talk simply aims to provide a space for open discussion, Drs. David and Elizabeth Corey, two Baylor political science professors, are taking a more structured approach. This semester, they are teaching a class together titled “The Hardest Issues of Our Age” as part of a national initiative to promote civil discourse on college campuses. The class asks students to discuss controversial political topics such as immigration and gender identity in a framework of freedom, charity, humility, and curiosity. According to Dr. David Corey, “the course is designed to help students understand that most people’s views are based on fundamental goods to which they are committed; and learning how to discover those goods is the first step toward political understanding.”

In their own way, each of these projects is teaching Baylor students to disagree in civil, informative ways. However, it is important to acknowledge that building a community which rewards disagreement, even civil disagreement, comes with dangers as well.

The goal of having a conversation with someone you disagree with should always be to come closer to the truth or at the very least to understand why people hold the views they do.

Over the past seven years, I have been immersed in just such a community: competitive policy debate. I have observed competitive debate culture from a variety of roles: debater, judge, coach, tournament organizer, and even reality TV show contestant. Because a debater must prepare to argue both sides of an issue, competitive debate rewards not only listening to arguments that oppose your own, but actually learning to make opposing arguments yourself. The critical thinking, creativity, and rigorous research that this atmosphere encourages are all crucial for developing informed opinions on political issues. However, if used in the wrong spirit, those same skills can work against the truth rather than for it.

I once heard the story of a champion college debater who would often get Jehovah’s Witnesses knocking on his door. Whenever this happened, he would pick a random religion in his head, and through subtle persuasion and careful questioning, attempt to convert the Jehovah’s Witness to that religion. He is reputed to have sometimes succeeded.

This kind of relativist attitude is common among competitive debaters. Many of those debaters would enthusiastically place themselves among the 36% who find political disagreement “interesting and informative,” but they are clearly still missing something. It is not enough to make our disagreements civil, or even for them to be “interesting and informative.” The goal of having a conversation with someone you disagree with should always be to come closer to the truth or at the very least to understand why people hold the views they do.

Illustrations of these types of disagreements abound in Plato’s dialogues and other cornerstones of liberal education.

Alcibiades being taught by Socrates; (1776) by Marcello Bacciarelli (1731-1818)

In the “Republic,” Socrates’ friend Glaucon makes a robust case for living an unjust life, even though he does not believe the argument himself. Socrates thanks his friend for the strong opposition, and the difficulty of the argument prompts Socrates to spend the rest of the dialogue forming a detailed theory of justice.

Whenever Thomas Aquinas sets out to engage with a question in the “Summa Theologica,” his first step is to list “objections” to his view: several well-formed, persuasively written counter-arguments. He then refutes the objections individually and presents his argument at the end.

In a similar vein, John Stuart Mill argues in “On Liberty” that no dissent should be forcibly silenced, no matter how wrong we may believe it to be. Beyond the possibility that the dissent may in fact be true, he adds that even wrong opinions can lead to a “clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.”

What each of these thinkers has in common is that they ask more of themselves than mere civility. They ask more of themselves than disagreeing in an “interesting, informative” way. They ask of themselves something that requires much more vulnerability and courage: to expose their most dearly held beliefs, the foundations of their identity and worldview, to the most compelling opposing arguments.

In the midst of a polarizing election season, that degree of bravery may seem like a lot to ask. But the growth of opportunities at Baylor for civil disagreement is a promising first step toward a campus culture of renewed openness, charity, and truth-seeking.

item.title: Mardi Gras: A Meaningful Mix of Tradition and Local Pride
item.description:
Growing up in Louisiana, I believed Mardi Gras to be the most anticipated holiday of the year. It was not until I went to Baylor that I realized its celebration is constrained largely by the Louisiana border, only managing to seep out around the gulf coast. Since this epiphany, I have vowed to bring the joy and festivity of Mardi Gras to wherever life takes me, and in the spirit of renewal, I believe now is the time for a renewed appreciation of this wonderful holiday.

How Mardi Gras Came to Be

For many, Mardi Gras evokes the festive shades of green, yellow, and purple that color the streets as children catch beads thrown from stunningly decorated floats, and men and women dance to zydeco tunes (originating from French creole artists). Despite its modern depiction, Mardi Gras festivities have evolved with time.

Instead of disregarding Mardi Gras as just a silly parade with masks, we should renew our thinking and celebration of this lovely holiday.

https://assets.editorial.aetnd.com/uploads/2009/11/mardi-gras-GettyImages-515507822.jpg

Mardi Gras was deemed a statewide holiday in 1875, but its origins trace back to the Middle Ages and the French celebration of Carnival in several European countries. “Carnival,” originates in the French phrase “carne vale,” meaning “farewell to flesh,” a reference to the Christian fasting practices of Lent, the Church’s 40 day period of solemn remembrance and preparation for the celebration of Easter. “Mardi Gras” means ‘Fat Tuesday,’ which refers to the tradition of consuming all the forbidden foods and having a final feast before fasting begins the following day on Ash Wednesday. Carnival’s sponsorship by the French House of the Bourbons and later Napoleon helped augment its popularity.

The ever-present French influence in Louisiana, from street signs to common last names, can be attributed to the large number of ‘Cajuns,’ or descendants of French Canadians who settled in the bayous of south Louisiana after being driven from the French province Acadia in the 18th century. French Canadian explorer Jean Baptiste Le Moyne Sieur de Bienville arrived south of New Orleans in 1699, naming the area “Pointe du Mardi Gras” to commemorate their landing on the evening before the holiday. Nearby Fort Louis de la Mobile celebrated the first recorded Mardi Gras in the French-Canadian settlements four years later. A “Boeuf Gras Society” was established in 1710 and began the organization of parades. Bienville later founded New Orleans in 1718, and Louisiana governor Marquis de Vaudreuil was known for hosting elaborate Mardi Gras balls, which still occur today.

Mardi Gras’ festivities not only persisted but grew as the holiday was openly celebrated from the 1730s on. By 1830, processions of masked participants in carriages guided by torches marked the Mardi Gras celebration. The first Mardi Gras ‘krewe’ – an organization that provides and often rides on a parade float – was formed by six Mobile residents. Naming themselves ‘Mistick Crewe of Comus,’ they entered the Mardi Gras parade in 1856, helping to further grow the holiday by suppling ornate floats and hosting masked balls which maintained the anonymity of the Krewe members. They were later joined by the Twelfth Night Revelers krewe, which introduced the custom of ‘throws’ – now beads – that are specially made to fit the symbols of each krewe.

Acknowledging the origins of Mardi Gras allow us to appreciate the people that contributed to its traditions and add some of our own. By joining the festivities, we renew the joy of past generations who came together in good times and bad to celebrate.

Current Traditions: Reminiscent of Past Origins, Present Excitement, and Future Persistence

Modern-day Mardi Gras, the culmination of which occurs in New Orleans, has expanded into innumerable parades and krewes, the largest of which occur in the five days leading up to Fat Tuesday. Despite its great growth in popularity and participants, Mardi Gras still retains much influence from its religious and cultural origins. Depictions of a fatted ox – ‘Boeuf Gras’ – representative of the last meat consumed before Lent, is still a hallmark symbol of Mardi Gras today. A large, white smoking bull is a well-known symbol of the Rex parade.

The staple dish of any Mardi Gras goers diet is King Cake, a combination of coffee cake and cinnamon roll fashioned into a circle. King Cake is adorned with the colors of Mardi Gras and harbors a surprise inside – a plastic baby! King Cakes appear in markets around the beginning of Epiphany, the season and feast day in which Jesus Christ’s manifestation to the Magi, the three wise men, is celebrated. The lucky finder of a King Cake’s plastic baby (representative of the King Jesus, after which the cake is named) is obligated to provide the next King Cake, a clever way to keep the festivities going!

One of the great beauties of festivals with deep cultural roots is the participation and contributions later generations and communities bring.

As expected, Mardi Gras parades occur all over Louisiana and parts of neighboring states, but this celebration has even made its way to the nation’s capital. The Washington Mardi Gras Ball is held annually, usually organized by representatives from Louisiana. It occurs over four nights, showcasing Cajun culture as well as Louisiana-pride to attendees from across the nation. This year’s Washington Mardi Gras featured former New Orleans Saints quarterback Drew Brees as its king. Seeing how far the traditions of Mardi Gras have spread is evidence of how it has touched participant’s lives in impactful ways.

Mr. Tony Richardson: From Outsider to Leader in the Mardi Gras Community

One of the great beauties of festivals with deep cultural roots is the participation and contributions later generations and communities bring. While Mardi Gras has a specific cultural origin, its festivities have become custom to Louisiana residents with diverse cultural backgrounds, inviting newcomers to partake in centuries-old customs and sustaining the practices that have given joy to generations.

In the true spirit of renewal, Mardi Gras invites all of us to share in the rich heritage of Louisiana while bringing it into our own communities and practices today.

Mr. Richardson was one of these newcomers. As a Michigan native, Mr. Tony Richardson never anticipated what a large role Mardi Gras would have in his life. After moving to Bossier City, Louisiana, he attended the Krewe of Gemini Parade with his family and remembers the delight he felt seeing his daughters catch beads and stuffed animals from vibrantly dressed float riders.

PARADE FLOATS ROLLING DOWN SAINT CHARLES AVENUE https://mardigrasinsidertours.com/history

A few years later, a close friend invited him to join the Krewe of Gemini and ride in the parade. Grateful for the good memories Mardi Gras provided his family, Mr. Richardson happily participated, taking part in every event from the theme announcement and coronation to the Twelfth Night Celebration and Grand Ball. Despite the exhilaration of the countless events leading up to it, the day of the parade was a “game changer” according to Mr. Richardson. He recounted mirthfully, “After riding in the parade and having one of the best times in my life, my wife and I were hooked. The experience was simply overwhelming. Seeing how much excitement and joy the parade brought to the community was beyond incredible.” Motivated by his float riding experience, Mr. Richardson applied for a more proactive role within the Krewe and became Float Lieutenant. He served in this role for ten years, managing a 50 foot float and its krewe.

While reminiscing on his leadership, Mr. Richardson reflected on the often-overlooked impact of Mardi Gras on not only the community that gathers to watch the parade but the krewe members who help make it possible. He remarked, “Who would have ever thought float riders would come from such a diverse background: lawyers, doctors, politicians, administrators, engineers, business owners, builders, nurses, accountants, and bankers – all together working hand in hand on the float or on various Krewe events. The children of friends we made on the float often referred to as Uncle Tony and Aunt Carla, which is so incredibly humbling.”

While the motto of Mardi Gras – laissez les bons temps rouler, ‘let the good times roll’ – is surely true during the parade, the good times stretched beyond celebration day as Mr. Richardson and his wife witnessed first-hand how being part of a Krewe brought people with a multitude of professions and pasts together to share in Mardi Gras traditions. Mr. Tony Richardson and his wife are being honored for their impact on the Mardi Gras community by being chosen as the Captain Elect for the Krewe’s 36th year. His story of coming into Mardi Gras after being raised outside of the tradition is one of many testimonies to welcoming community Mardi Gras fosters.6

Instead of disregarding Mardi Gras as just a silly parade with masks, we should renew our thinking and celebration of this lovely holiday. For the celebration of Mardi Gras not only sustains the rich culture of many Louisianians’ ancestors, but also invites new individuals to join and become part of a diverse community that brings families together and creates a sense of local pride. In the true spirit of renewal, Mardi Gras invites all of us to share in the rich heritage of Louisiana while bringing it into our own communities and practices today.

item.title: On American Civic Renewal: An Interview with Justin Giboney
item.description:
Last month, Baylor facilitated a panel discussion on civility, moderated by our very own President Linda Livingstone. The panel included some well-recognized names: Curtis Chang of Redeeming Babel, author Kaitlyn Schiess, and Justin Giboney of the AND Campaign.

After the panel, I interviewed Mr. Giboney on the topic of “American Civic Renewal.” Giboney was well equipped to speak to this topic: an ordained minister, Vanderbilt JD, two-time delegate to the Democratic National Convention, and Georgia community organizer, Giboney knows a lot about Christian political engagement. He also shares with many Christians today a sense of disillusionment and aversion towards politics.

Justin Giboney speaking at Baylor’s Conversation Series on Politics and Faith

“So, let’s start right there,” I said. “What comes to mind when you think, ‘American civic renewal,’ Mr. Giboney?”

“Well,” he said, “does this mean we’re ‘going back’ in a sense? To me, this is problematic for a number of reasons.”

We discussed moments when our society just didn’t get it right in the past. This is perhaps why so many Americans baulk at the concept of renewal. It seems like an invitation to repeat past mistakes.

“Well, maybe let’s use another word. Maybe instead of ‘renewal’ you’re suggesting ‘recognition’ or even a ‘realignment’ of sorts?”

“Sure,” I said, “and a recommitment to American ideals, to the principles and integrity of the Constitution.”

Giboney, however, argued that this necessarily begins with a survey of our shortcomings, or what he describes as “what we got right and wrong” in the past.

We discussed moments when our society just didn’t get it right in the past. This is perhaps why so many Americans baulk at the concept of renewal. It seems like an invitation to repeat past mistakes.



“Certainly – so where did we get it right?”

“Well, I’d look at the ‘progressive’ era,” said Giboney. “And by this, I’m not referring to the early 20th century ‘Progressive Era movement,’ but those years in which the United States made significant progress in the area of civil rights.”

Giboney then referenced, for example, the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of what we now call the “protected class”: race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. But how did the America of yesteryear, stuck in the practice of institutionalized discrimination, achieve such progress?

Agreeing with me that ideology plays a fundamental role in either progress or renewal, we moved to the question of theory and practice.

“Theorizing” is what the Academy is doing today; scholars exchanging ideas in a lingua franca accessible only to those keeping up with the conversation. But whatever their activity, we agreed, it’s all for naught without practice. “So how do we marry theory and practice?” I asked. “How do we take Baylor’s panel discussion, for instance, and make it go?”

Giboney started by focusing on organizations: creating “guiding principles and a framework of disciplines” had proven to be his most successful tool. This reminded me of Baylor’s Commission on Historic Campus Representations, a 2020 campus committee that made formal recommendations to Baylor’s administration on our racial legacy and strategic future. During those conversations, many were of the belief that Baylor already had a sufficient set of guiding principles and disciplines that would animate their response to the revelation of our painful history: the Christian faith.

Yet we all know the Christian “type” who wants to marshal the whole of Christian faith not behind the truths of Christ’s sovereignty, but behind a particular candidate or cause.

According to Giboney, “Christians have to be rooted in a love for neighbor,” not just in proclamations about their faith. Yet “today, we’re plagued by a ‘politics of Christian self-interest.’” We seem to harbor hidden and unfaithful motives behind the guise of Christian conviction. Or, we use our Christianity as a Trojan Horse, an attractive outer shell in which we barely disguise our warring intentions.

But for Christians, says Giboney, “we can’t put ‘winning’ before ‘witnessing’—and it’s not just [conservative] evangelicals: those on the Left have to stop following what is essentially secular progressivism.”

Christians of all traditions—Catholic, Protestant, or Orthodox; conservative, liberal, or simply jaded – cannot abandon the responsibility we have to be in the world, but not of the world. For Giboney, the Christian is the most equipped person to translate the guiding principles and frameworks of redemptive faith into organizations, and on a larger scale, into society writ large.

we can’t put ‘winning’ before ‘witnessing’ Justin Giboney

Simply put, Christians play a pivotal role in renewal.

“You cannot be a devout Christian without impacting politics,” says Giboney. “Our faith has to inform everything about our lives.”

It was all making sense. “American Civic Renewal” really means re-aligning ourselves with principle; and it requires recognizing the past (its successes and failures) in order to rise to the challenge of engagement. Who but the Christian is best equipped to inculcate the virtues of love, compassion, truth, and conviction in the conversations and movements where they matter most.

Wrapping up our conversation, I finally asked Giboney what his best advice was for Gen Z in light of that challenge.

“This is Gen Z’s opportunity to throw away the culture war,” said Giboney. “You have to challenge both sides of the culture.” Giboney credits his ability to do this to his academic training as well as his life in his church and community. “The Academy shouldn’t tell us what to believe,” he says, “but it helps us understand how to arrive at our own understanding, namely of what a civic community is. Moreover, community is not about ‘affirming you’ but about the exchange of ideas.”

Giboney’s parting encouragement was to read the words of Frederick Douglass. “Douglass did not attempt to destroy the Union; he understood that its institutions were those that would afford his rights.” Therefore, Giboney advises us to do something quite different from what so many of our peers are doing. His advice is this: “Help your institutions. Don’t tear them down.”

item.title: Can We Know God?: A Review of “Knowledge, Faith, & Early Christian Initiation” by Alex Fogleman
item.description:
We live in an era marked by religious divergence. According to a recent study conducted by the Pew Research Center, the U.S. alone is home to over six significant religions and eight Christian denominations. Facing an increasingly secularized culture, many religious groups have turned to new forms of worship and marketing to appeal to the next generation. From the use of social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram to modern concert-style worship sets—Christians today are doing everything they can to attract young people to the church. Yet amidst this movement, a rising tide of young individuals is defying convention by rediscovering the historical roots of Christianity. New interest in traditional Christian practices like liturgy and Catechesis (spiritual instruction received before baptism) has followed, priming the intellectual landscape for scholars specializing in how early Christians developed these practices—scholars like Alex Fogleman.

Fogleman is an Assistant Research Professor for the Institute for Studies of Religion at Baylor University. Holding a Ph.D. in Patristics and Theology from Baylor, Fogleman has extensively researched spiritual instruction in the Patristic age. His new book, Knowledge, Faith, and Early Christian Initiation, examines the role and development of catechetical instruction throughout the early church, offering unique insight into the ancient question—how can humanity know God?

The book explores Catechesis as a potential answer to this question, focusing on writers from the close of the second century to the mid-fifth century, particularly in Italy and North Africa. “[The] hope,” Fogleman writes, is for readers to understand that “what it means to know God is inseparable from the ways in which such knowledge is experienced,” i.e., “medium and message are tightly linked.” Diving into the writings of several key figures, including Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Augustine, Fogleman approaches the study from a theological and historical perspective—distinguishing his work by highlighting the specific role that educational institutions and practices played in communicating knowledge of God. Fogleman accomplishes just that, beautifully delineating the gradual change of Catechesis as not merely a change in beliefs surrounding if and how individuals should be trained before baptism, but rather that it reveals far more nuanced questions of how Christians are to gain knowledge of God and what role divine grace plays in the understanding of faith. Should the individual go through years of instruction before being baptized? or “hurry to the font”? For Fogleman, these questions are not strictly about baptism at all. Instead, he argues that the church fathers are asking how to teach others best to know God—is it through intellectual lessons and practices? or does God bestow understanding through baptism? The answer, for Fogleman, is both and more.

Fogleman adds his voice to the chorus of church fathers in discerning the relationship between mythos and logos—asserting the vital role of Catechesis in this age-old conversation.

The study’s primary limitation (though one readily acknowledged by Fogleman) is its narrow selection of catechetical writings. What Fogleman lacks in breadth, however, is more than compensated by the depth and complexity of his analysis of the writers and writings he interacts with. This allows him to explore the historical, philosophical, and theological convictions of each figure, expertly weaving together the book’s comprehensive view of both the practical components of Catechesis and the underlying posture towards questions surrounding knowledge, Christian learning, the role of mystery in faith, and even the Incarnation. Fogleman both tracks pre-baptismal instruction and explores its impact on the mind and soul. In doing so, he suggests that Chatachesis is not merely training for baptism—but for beatitude, the state of complete blessedness. In short, through his analysis of early Christian Chatachesis, Fogleman adds his voice to the chorus of church fathers in discerning the relationship between mythos and logos—asserting the vital role of Catechesis in this age-old conversation. As such, Knowledge, Faith, and Early Christian Initiation has established itself as a resource for scholars and laypeople alike, proving a valuable resource for anyone seeking to engage with Catechesis and, in doing so, “encounter the fullness of God in a way that initiates the ascent to eternal beatitude.”

item.title: Listening Well: An Interview with The Institute for Oral History’s Dr. Stephen Sloan
item.description:
Both of us met Dr. Sloan before our interview; Luke, two years ago at the Palladium downtown, and Emily, four months ago at a crowded UPS store on 8th Street.

Emily stood shoulder to shoulder in line, a box of homemade cookies in her arms. Suddenly, the tall gray-haired man behind her broke the silence and asked, “Who are the cookies for?” As she told him about her boy five states away, Dr. Sloan intently listened, only interrupting with thoughtful questions.

Luke, fresh on campus and surrounded by unfamiliar faces, had an evening saved by conversation with Dr. Sloan, started only by a single family connection. The encounters left both of us feeling known. As it turns out, Dr. Sloan, the Director of the Institute for Oral History, is no novice at listening to people’s stories.

Years and months after these encounters the two of us sit opposite Dr. Sloan in his office located in the Carole Science Library. Accolades, family photos, and books line the shelves (as well as parts of the floor). Dr. Sloan confidently and comfortably leans back in his chair, leg crossed over his knee. His words are imbued with a commanding electricity, and more—a deep sincerity.

“I direct the Institute for Oral History, which has been around since 1970. We’re the largest oral history collection in the state. We conduct and collect and partner with oral history projects on all sorts of different topics: community based, academic based, undergraduate, graduate. We run our own projects, but we also collect other people’s work.”

Dr. Stephen Sloane

“Hey, I’d like to show you this.” Dr. Sloan leads us out of his office and towards the opposite wing, coming into a room lined with shelves. He moves towards a corner and starts drawing his finger along the wall, looking for something. I realize we’re looking at walls of cassettes, years of hard-copied interviews. He draws one out–dated 1989–and opens it, revealing the spool. “Leon Jaworski. This is the man that prosecuted Nixon.”

There are hundreds more of these interviews, dating back to the Institute’s founding in 1970. The Institute’s purpose, demonstrated by these tapes, is to collect and conduct interviews with various people across historical periods. Their efforts, as well as partnerships with other Oral History projects across the country, have developed a web of primary resources spread across time and space. And in the time since their founding, the Institute has grown to become the largest in the state.

Dr. Sloan talked with us about one of the institute’s current projects: recording interviews with the first generation of African American students at Baylor. “The idea being, you got the statues, which are wonderful, but they don’t live, talk and breathe, and they don’t communicate the experience of being black at Baylor in the late sixties and seventies. And so, these stories do that. It’s within those stories that that experience lies.”

The Institute records these stories by first reaching out to the individual for an interview, conducting it, and then transcribing with artificial intelligence before undergraduate students revise and format the transcript. This transcript is then reviewed by the interviewee, and upon their approval, goes online in the Institute’s digital collections.

“You got the statues, which are wonderful, but they don’t live, talk and breathe, and they don’t communicate the experience of being black at Baylor in the late sixties and seventies. And so, these stories do that.” Dr. Sloane

The Institute views this collection as having three primary functions: Project, Public, and Private. The Project purpose is what you think of first where the interviews are used in academic research.. Dr. Sloan also emphasizes oral history as an outward-facing medium; the project serves not only academia, but the community and beyond. That’s where the Public purpose comes in. The Institute’s digital collection is a community resource “that’s going to be available 50 to 100 years from now.” Dr. Sloan spoke most passionately about the Private purpose. “The private value is:what does it mean to this individual? What does it mean to this family?”

Dr. Sloan shared anecdotes of family members coming back to the Institute to hear the voice of a deceased loved one. He emphasized the value of preserving an individual’s story. “Everything else is going to be stripped away. But we have our stories and our experiences. I want whatever we do to operate on all three of those levels.”

Dr. Sloane conducting interview https://library.web.baylor.edu/oralhistory

Dr. Sloan recalls a series of interviews conducted with a woman for a project about housewives in Waco. “I think it changed her relationship a little bit with her own story that someone thought, ‘hey, they’re recording this and they’re typing it up and they’re writing it down, and they’re spending money to make sure it’s archived.’ […] Not that she thought it was unimportant, but it elevated maybe even how she thought about her own experience.”

“Everything else is going to be stripped away. But we have our stories and our experiences”

The conversation turned to the use of AI to conduct interviews, the argument being for increased efficiency. Dr. Sloan believes differently.

“Let’s leave a little humanity in it. The humanity part is extremely important. And so, it’s not just about the story. Without a listener it’s not the same. […] You need the human element there. Interacting and listening deeply.”

The Institute is making waves through individuals and families with their ability to simply listen. We want to tell our stories. We want to be known. The Institute for Oral History is creating space for people to tell their stories, even when they may not feel worthy to tell them. The Institute is bringing new life to the stories that we have overlooked, and by returning us to these stories, they return us to our humanity. Through each of the Institute’s interviews, there is an opportunity: by listening, we are bringing renewal to our communities and to ourselves.

item.title: Hills and Valleys: The Meaning and Purpose of Liturgy
item.description:
Growing up, I went to a very large southern Baptist church. Because of this, my Sunday mornings were loud, exciting, and inspiring. I grew up thinking that all Christians’ spiritual practices were like this: passion gilded with spotlights, wisdom embroidered with rhetoric. It wasn’t until I left for Baylor that I really began to understand what religious life was like for Christians of other denominations.

After leaving home, I visited several different kinds of churches, trying to find the place that would grow me in my walk with Christ best. For a while I kept to the same tradition, attending a church very much like the one I attended growing up. It wasn’t until a friend of mine invited me to a much more traditional, structured service at a different church that I began to really understand what a centuries-long liturgical tradition looked like, and why it was worth engaging with.

What is liturgy? No doubt any discussion of the topic requires a good definition. Growing up I had understood liturgy to mean written words to be recited, in a similar manner to the pledge of allegiance, as a part of some religious activity. Certainly, this is how the word is often used, and for good reason. As Fr. Jonathan Kanary, a priest at Christ Church Waco, points out, liturgy, traced etymologically, means “the work of the people.” This is an important thing to note, because it is the first hint that liturgy is not merely words: it is a sort of “work.”

The nature of this work is something to be carefully considered. From a spiritual perspective, what is “the work of the people?” Certainly, there is not merely one answer. However, it might be said that the general spiritual work of the people is chiefly worship. Worship is a complex activity, a demonstration of the worth someone puts on something or someone else. Liturgy is the way that we accomplish this work, worshiping our creator well.

Liturgy is not merely words: it is a sort of “work.”

Book of Common Prayer

How does liturgy do this? In my mind, there are two ways of thinking about liturgy that answer this question. The first I will call “Practical Liturgy.” this understanding of liturgy conceives of its role in worship as essentially spiritually practices. Practical liturgy is a combination of both words and actions, things like praying out loud a thoughtfully written prayer, or bowing your head when Jesus’ name is spoken. Both should equally be considered liturgy.

These practices are designed to grow us in a specific way: they help us to be consistent in how we reorient our hearts towards God. Fr. Jonathan aptly described this using phrases like “turning toward God” and “being drawn to God.” He characterized much, if not all of the Christian life this way: as a fundamental turning of the heart; that is, changing the primary object of our love from ourselves to God instead. This change is something we are not naturally inclined to do. Instead, like an illness, our sinful tendencies draw our affections away from God and onto ourselves. This is why this “turning” of the heart is such an important part of Christian life: it directly fights these sinful tendencies.

It is because the Christian life is composed of such a consistent activity that spiritual health is composed of such a consistent practice. The consistent nature of practical liturgy is a fitting prescription for the illness: a habit to meet a habitual need.

However, many do not think of the consistent nature of liturgy in this way. In fact, many people believe that the repetitive nature of practical liturgy (repeating the same words and the same actions, day after day) is actually a detriment to our spiritual health, not a benefit.

This objection is based on the idea that habitual activities tend to become mindless muscle memory. For many habits, this is fine, but for practices like prayer, this can be a big problem. After all, a prayer isn’t really a prayer if you aren’t really thinking and meaning the words you’re saying. No doubt, repetitive words can be mindless if we let them be. Think about the last time you said the pledge of allegiance. Did you really think about all the words that are a part of that pledge? Did you mean all the words you said with full conviction?

While this is a real concern, there are two reasons why it shouldn’t keep Christians from practicing practical liturgy. First of all, mindless prayer is certainly possible, albeit in a different way, in both extemporaneous and pre-written prayers. This is because thinking about which words to say can actually distract you from the meaning of the words you say.

This is a dangerous trap especially in extemporaneous prayer, because often those prayers are spoken in front of other people, who are listening to you pray. I admit that it is often a strong temptation for me: to try to make my prayers “sound good.” In trying to pray eloquently, I find that I am not really praying at all. I am speaking to the people around me, not to God. And as surprising as it is, building a habit of this approach to prayer can cause you to make your prayers “sound good” even when no other people are present.

If liturgy is the work of the people, and the work of the people is to worship God, then liturgy is how we worship, it’s the countless ways that we glorify God with our thoughts, our words, our actions, and our lives.

With pre-written prayers, this is still a challenge, but a different one. Usually, you might get concerned with praying the correct words, while you are still learning the prayer. However, once you have learned it, you are no longer concerned with saying the wrong words, because you know them by heart.

This memorization need not be disingenuous, you can mean words just as much even if you didn’t come up with them. Fr. Jonathan reminded me that all language is this way in fact, because we all learn to speak by repetition. Because of that, it would be ridiculous to say that merely repeating someone else’s words makes them no longer genuine.

Fr. Jonathan also called to mind a poignant image from his knowledge of C.S. Lewis on the topic: comparing the practice of pre-written prayer to a well-known dance. The more you have done it, the better you can be. When you stop having to think about the steps, that’s when you can really have your mind in the dance. The principle is just as true with prayer as it is with dance, because after you’ve learned the steps (the words) you can really devote your mind to the meaning, focusing on a particular word or phrase, or even just an idea. This is why the repetitive nature of practical liturgy is not necessarily a flaw, it can be a great strength.

I mentioned at the beginning of this article that there are two kinds of liturgy. Here at the end, I’d like to introduce you to the second, broader conception of liturgy: “glorifying liturgy.” I’ve chosen to call it this because this conception of the meaning of liturgy takes the word much more seriously. If liturgy is the work of the people, and the work of the people is to worship God, then liturgy is how we worship, it’s the countless ways that we glorify God with our thoughts, our words, our actions, and our lives.

In this way liturgy is not merely a set of practices that helps us to set our minds on God when we need it, it is also a fundamental way of life. Glorifying liturgy is transformative: living every moment as an act of worship makes us into the people we were always meant to be; the people who were made, as the Westminster Shorter Catechism states, “to glorify God and enjoy him forever.”

item.title: Ikiru: A Story of Renewed Life & Community
item.description:
Over the summer of 2023, I made a point to watch some of the movies I had seen in the preceding semester with my dad. At the time, I felt that besides simply providing him with a little bit of what I had been watching recently, I could somehow express how my time at college was slowly shifting my taste. Something like that. I didn’t get through a ton with him, unfortunately, largely because my summer schedule is built on late nights and early mornings, whereas my parents make an effort to be in bed by 9:30, basically every day of the week. Among the few films my father and I were able to cram into our limited viewing time, was the classic ‘52 Kurosawa flick, Ikiru, or in English “To Live.” (Just as a disclaimer… I am obviously going to be “spoiling” this movie. It has a runtime of 2h 23m which… is like watching ~7 episodes of Friends. It is DOABLE. And it is free to watch on the Baylor Library Website!) Being somewhat of a fan of existential thought, I really enjoy this movie. It is one of a handful of my favorite films that explore finding purpose and meaning in life, specifically, in old age (Among others are Taste of Cherry, The Sacrifice, Wild Strawberries. Check ‘em out!).

The narrative approach in Ikiru is something that only a short list of directors would dare to attempt. Akira Kurosawa presents our sweet old protagonist, Kanji Watanabe, as an elderly gentleman working a somewhat oppressive and unfulfilling position within his local government. What is unique is that Kurosawa kills him off with almost an hour to go.

It is one of a handful of my favorite films that explore finding purpose and meaning in life, specifically, in old age.

In his introduction, the narrator word-for-word says that Mr. Watanabe has “yet to live” despite being in his 80’s. Shortly following this initial presentation of Mr. Watanabe, a woman approaches him and expresses that there is an area of her neighborhood which has fallen into utter disrepair, with stagnant water and filth accumulating on the streets. What follows is one of the more iconic scenes from the movie. The camera flits through a bureaucratic nightmare, from office to office, each new person delegating what one might assume is a simple task from public works, to the parks department, to the mayor’s office where it is finally deemed nothing can be done… sure.

After leaving work, Mr. Watanabe goes to a doctor’s appointment which turns out to be anything but a rudimentary checkup. The doctor informs him (somewhat roundabout – ly) that he has terminal cancer. He gives him less than a year. This is his catalyst. His first response is to seek out his estranged son and revitalize their relationship…to little avail. He then begins to pursue a life of partying and dancing (the geriatric can get down too!) with a much younger lady who he meets on a night out and who takes pity on him. Quickly, Watanabe finds all that unfulfilling for an old soul like himself. He instead chooses what, I think anyone would consider, a more noble path. He decides to push through the intricacies of the bureaucracy and help the community of the lady who had come to him, asking for change, simultaneously trouncing a plot to put in a brothel at the same location, a move which would damn the then residential area to a state of immorality and crime.

It took an old man, with what boils down to a death sentence, and the conviction that he must do something with the waning hour of his life, to actually bring about some significant difference.

The real charm of this movie lies in the last 50 or so minutes, at which point our protagonist has already passed away. This chunk of the film is less concerned with showing what our characters are up to, and more focused on reassessing and revivifying the main character’s…well character, in the eyes of the public and we, the viewers. The narrative resumes with a crowd shuffling in for his wake. (Beyond being one of the more heartfelt sections of the movie, this part provides some insight into traditional Japanese funeral practices, which is a cool cultural aside.) One of the people who attends his wake, a police officer, recalls seeing Mr. Watanabe swinging in the park that Watanabe had made his life mission to build, softly singing to himself on a cold winter night. This sparks a conversation amongst the crowd about what Kanji Watanabe did with the last months of his life, his motivation, and where the flame that pushed him to fast track a project through all their offices came from. Many of the gathered officials claim that if they were given the diagnosis that Watanabe received, they would have done the same. One brave man, however, stands up in opposition, pointing out that what the Watanabe did was significant, precisely because people like the officials have made a career out of inhibiting progress and change. It took an old man, with what boils down to a death sentence, and the conviction that he must do something with the waning hour of his life, to actually bring about some significant difference.

The very last shots from this movie are extremely poignant. Akira reveals the moment that was described at the dead man’s wake: Watanabe swinging in the park that he toiled over, singing a song from his youth as snow begins to fall. It is in these last couple frames that we see the culmination of a life well lived, in this beautiful moment of childlike bliss, as an old man who has turned the trajectory of his life on its head, sits on sleek new playground equipment. He has turned something stagnant and decaying into a place where children, a symbol of continued life, can grow and flourish and play.

I don’t really know how much my dad liked the movie. He was doing dishes and car shopping online for a significant portion of it and not completely locked in to the subtitles, so it is possible he missed some of the gem one liners that Kurosawa blesses the viewer with and perhaps whole chunks of the plot. Regardless, it was still a pleasant and impactful experience.

It is in these last couple frames that we see the culmination of a life well lived

As the movie started to wrap up, I began to make ties between the plot and my own life. Unlike the man and his son in the movie, I have a great relationship with my parents, but in college, I am no longer growing with them by my side. This can in a sense simulate the isolation that the characters felt in the movie. A more direct comparison I drew between an element in the film and my own life experience, was with those old rickety striped swings out on Baylor’s Founder’s Mall. My parents both went to school at Baylor and when I was little, they told me about sitting on those swings together when they were first falling for each other. Each time we drove over to Waco for a football game or to visit my cousins, we would wander around amongst the flowers as a family and sit and talk on one of those swings. On move-in day freshman year, right before we said those emotional last goodbyes, we went out together and crammed ourselves onto one of those swings. These days, I’ll sometimes go out in the wee hours of the morning with a book and a flashlight and read on one of those swings. In these quiet moments, I give thanks for my loving (middle-aged) parents who had hoped that I might find this school to be a place for growth and maturation, a place where I might learn “to live” – IKIRU.

I don’t think you need to have a connection with a swing to get something valuable out of this classic movie. Ikiru is a story about a life and legacy renewed because of an honest and focused investment in a community in need. It also presents an interesting thought exercise: if you only had six months to live, how would you leave your mark on the world? I am certain we would all have a different answer to that, but I would hope that, as we enter a new year and face new obstacles, this story of an elderly man’s hope and resilience might serve as inspiration for each of us.

item.title: Spiritual Renewal: A Conversation with Father Nick
item.description:
With the start of a new year, and now with the start of Lent in the church’s liturgical year, many people are thinking about renewal: what can we change in our overly cluttered lives? How can we get back to basics, return to the childlike simplicity of earlier days? What even is renewal?

Last week I had the opportunity to put questions like these to Father Nicholas Chandler Athanaelos, the rector-elect at Christ Church Anglican here in Waco. Father Nicolas, or “Fr. Nick,” as he is called, is moving to Waco from Athens Georgia, where he has served as rector of St. Stephens Anglican Church since 2011. Before that, he served as rector of Saint Bartholomew’s, New Bern, North Carolina and Saint Andrew & St. Margaret of Scotland in Alexandria, Virginia.

How can we get back to basics, return to the childlike simplicity of earlier days? What even is renewal?

When I asked Fr. Nick how to approach renewal during Lent, he said, “you begin in darkness and end in light. You start in the dead of winter, and end in the blossoming life of spring.” The humble acts of confession and penance begun on Ash Wednesday, are the beginning of renewal.
