They bring light to the sin hidden in darkness and empower believers to begin again in the light of Christ. Patience and reliance on the Holy Spirit throughout the 40-day season are the ingredients of spiritual renewal.

This patience and humble reliance on the Holy Spirit were exemplified in the long process of renewal Father Nick recounted within his own parish, St. Stephens. When he first arrived at St. Stephens, Father Nick recalled that finances, attendance, and overall morale of the church were hurting. Taking on the mission to recharge and bring the church back to where it had once been, Father Nick began by knocking on doors and inviting back all who had left the parish. He told me that what followed was a lengthy period of intense prayer focused on where they had been, where they were going, and where they should have been going all along.

At each gathering, the congregation prayed “Come Holy Spirit, renew the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love.” Though the process was long and difficult, St. Stephens saw tremendous growth and restoration and is now thriving once again.

Father Nick emphasizes the patience and humility that this process required. “Give it time,” he advised, “Let the Holy Spirit work.” His reliance on the Holy Spirit and the daily act of showing up even when results seem obscure were vital to the renewal of St Stephens. They are similarly vital for all us today, especially in this Lenten season.

Father Nick reminded me, however, that spiritual renewal is not relegated to the season of Lent but is fixed and graciously extended in the sacraments of the Church—specifically the sacraments of confession and eucharist taken weekly and communally.

The sacraments, features of the church liturgy sometimes viewed as “traditional” or even “antiquated,” sparked a question I’ve been wrestling with: “How does one reconcile renewal with tradition? How do we find something new in that which is old?”

“Renewal calls us to return to that which we have known to have been from the beginning.” Father Nick

Father Nick told me that despite appearances to the contrary, people are actually looking for “something traditional—something that has been there, that has worked, that is solid and unchanging,” and that this is “the faith delivered once for all to all the saints.” He told me that renewal, and especially spiritual renewal, begins with tradition, that those who leave traditional and sacramental forms of worship for more non-denominational styles often come back—not because the word proclaimed elsewhere isn’t fresh, solid, and true but because they miss the sacraments. Renewal requires both: the word and the sacraments.

“People are looking for renewal everywhere,” Father Nick told me, “but it’s right here.” It is right in front of us. Instead of going out to find something “new,” the act of renewal starts with the people and gifts given to us already. “It is what you make it. It is open to everyone,” Father Nick said. Renewal begins with looking at what is in front of us and acknowledging where we have gone astray. “Renewal calls us to return to that which we have known to have been from the beginning.”

Father Nick shared another beautiful story of renewal that exemplified this “returning to that which we have known from the beginning.” It was the merger he oversaw between St. Andrews & St. Margaret of Scotland Anglican church in Alexandria Virginia—a powerful reconciliation between liturgical and evangelical church bodies.

When Father Nick came to St. Andrews & St. Margarets, about the only thing shared in the parish was the building. “There was a chalk line drawn down the church. They had to vestries, two choirs, two alters.” The church even had a cross that switched sides, one side plain and the other depicting the crucifixion, depending on the service!

All this had to go, Father Nick told me. “The church had left its roots. They were arguing about nothing to do with the Christian commitment and the great commandment.” Through a series of retreats and Lenten practices of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, the two sides of the church were able to renew and unite their church body. By returning to core Christian commitments, St. Andrews & St. Margarets was able to overcome their disputes and become truly one.

This story of reconciliation and unification brings to light the essential quality of spiritual renewal: it is above all a returning to “that which we have known to have been from the beginning.”

Renewal is to bring into being again, to take what we already have and make it better. I believe the Church is the starting point. Father Nick

The deep parallels between this understanding of renewal and that of confession and the Eucharist struck me. Spiritual renewal truly is right in front of us. It is kneeling in front of the altar and confessing the sins set before us. It is coming to the table set before us and sharing in bread and wine, being cleansed by the body and blood of Christ, returning to that which we have known from the beginning. It is the sacraments.

Christ Church Waco

I finished our interview with a question: how, practically speaking, can cultivate renewal in our lives and what obstacles should we watch out for? Father Nick told me we must first recognize our need for renewal and have the willingness to make it happen. This requires daily examination, a quiet moment of prayer and meditation on what we have done and left undone, on why we may be frustrated or stressed. Daily prayer affords a time for looking back to moments of health and joy, examining what we have lost or where we have gone astray.

It was precisely in such daily prayers that Father Nick felt God calling him to something different—which turned out to be Waco, Texas.

“Renewal is to bring into being again, to take what we already have and make it better. I believe the Church is the starting point,” Father Nick said. As we continue in Lent this winter, let us all find renewal by returning—“returning to that which we have known to have been from the beginning”—the faith delivered once and for all, the gifts put before us, and the hope of eternal life.

Special thanks to Father Nick for giving his time and wisdom for this interview.

item.title: Leisure: One Hour of the Millennium
item.description:
It is a peculiar fact that among all living things, human beings alone spend their free time throwing parties. Indeed, the party is so central to our social life that we have highly regulated it by etiquette. If I asked you to describe the formal features of a party, you could come up with a list, perhaps even a definitive one. This feature of human existence—our propensity for celebrating—has led some to call us homo ludens, the playing man.

Josef Pieper, the author of Leisure: The Basis of Culture, assumes a playful, celebratory ontology of man in his defense of leisure. Pieper argues that leisure is a basic power of the human person and that to enjoy leisure is part of what it means to live a fully human life. He defines leisure as “a mental and spiritual attitude”—we might say, in Aristotelian terms, a virtue or habit of soul—that enables us “to overstep the boundaries of the workaday world and reach out to superhuman, life-giving existential forces that refresh and renew us.” As a spiritual habit, leisure is not reducible to any one external act: playing a video game, going for a stroll, or reading a book. Rather, leisure is fundamentally an internal disposition. A disposition to what? To celebrate.

Among all living things, human beings alone spend their free time throwing parties.

Celebration is the core of leisure. By celebration, Pieper means something specific: “man’s affirmation of the universe and his experiencing the world in an aspect other than its everyday way.” Pieper goes on to connect this deep affirmation of the universe to the practice of divine worship, in which we affirm the world by praising its Creator. Indeed, the essential basis for the sabbath festival is God’s leisure at the end of the first creation account. Seeing that the world is good, God rests from work to enjoy it. God himself embodies a disposition to celebrate creation.

Like any other habit of soul, we can realize leisure more or less well. Pieper laments that most people are at risk of failing to be leisurely—and so failing to be fully human—because our culture is marked by a work ethic that invades and degrades attempts to enjoy leisure. We are obsessed with work. Our careers define us. Our jobs creep into the precious hours and spaces of our home lives. In this context, leisure appears silly or only incidentally useful as a quick refresher before returning to work.

Pieper identifies three contrasts between the life-giving attitude of leisure and the dehumanizing ideology of total work:

Leisure means being inwardly calm and receptive—as opposed to the busyness and anxiety of work.

Leisure is an effortless affirmation of the world—as opposed to effortful toil upon the world.

Leisure exists for its own sake—as opposed to work, which is (or should be) oriented toward leisure.

Pieper’s exhortation to leisure is challenging and countercultural, for leisure resists the widespread notion that work determines the basic value of a person. Furthermore, a commitment to true leisure reveals the superficiality of most contemporary “recreation,” which often functions as a vapid brain-anesthetic for the overworked.

What if we took Pieper’s challenge? What would it look like to truly celebrate the world’s goodness?

Celebration is the core of leisure.

Isak Dinesen’s short story “Babette’s Feast”, better known through its Grand Prix-winning film adaptation, gives us a remarkably vivid depiction of leisure. The story unfolds among a small Pietistic congregation living in rural Jutland. With the passing of the founding pastor, religious life now revolves around his two elderly daughters, Phillipa and Martine. The congregation can hardly be said to be thriving: internal disputes and offenses against charity are, troublingly, the norm.

Against this backdrop of quarrelsome religious life comes the central action of the tale. One day, a woman named Babette, a refugee from Paris, arrives at the village. During her stay, Babette wins a lottery and decides (Spoiler alert!) to use the money to prepare a French feast honoring the pastor’s centennial. And it is a feast: seven delightful courses—including turtle soup, blinis topped with caviar, quail en croute—each served with its own outrageous o-be-joyful.

As preparations for the feast begin, the story juxtaposes two perspectives on the goods of creation. On the one hand, the community embodies a puritanical suspicion and fear of nature’s pleasures. On the other, Babette shows an exuberant and artistic embrace of nature. Consider Babette and Martine’s conversation about the wine for the third course:

[W]hen Martine saw a barrow load of bottles wheeled into the kitchen, she stood still. She touched the bottles and lifted up one. ‘What is there in this bottle, Babette?’ she asked in a low voice. ‘Not wine?’ ‘Wine, Madame!’ Babette answered. ‘No, Madame. It is a Clos Vougeot 1846!’ After a moment she added: ‘From Philippe, in Rue Montorgueil!’ Martine had never suspected that wines could have names to them, and was put to silence.

Both Martine and Babette judge that the bottles contain “not wine,” but for two vastly different reasons. Martine, who is so little an imbiber that she does not know the tradition of wine appellation, must describe the liquid in purely negative terms: “What is there in this bottle?…Not wine?” Ironically, Babette agrees—the label “wine” doesn’t cut it! Her familiarity with the goods of creation emerges in this scene as she names not only the vintage but also the vintner, thereby affirming both creation and its human caretakers.

The conflict is replayed in the matter of the Turtle (an ingredient for the first course), which looms like some chthonic beast over the congregation as they await the feast. Martine first catches sight of the Turtle hauled in by a helping boy:

Martine is wrong. Babette is not a hedonist. She is, rather, a leisurely celebrator who affirms the Creator through creation.

[H]e lifted a big, undefinable object from the barrow. In the light of the lamp it looked like some greenish‐black stone, but when set down on the kitchen floor it suddenly shot out a snake‐like head and moved it slightly from side to side. Martine had seen pictures of tortoises, and had even as a child owned a pet tortoise, but this thing was monstrous in size and terrible to behold. She backed out of the kitchen without a word.

Again, notice Martine’s ignorance about the Turtle and her subsequent inability to consider it good: she sees it as undefinable, a stone with a reptile’s head, incommensurate with her memories of other turtles. The Turtle raises suspicions about the enjoyment of creation. Its snakish head recalls the tempter in Eden and his garden goods. From Martine’s perspective, the Turtle represents a disordered hedonism, the choice of nature over and against supernature.

But Martine is wrong. Babette is not a hedonist. She is, rather, a leisurely celebrator who affirms the Creator through creation. And so, when the feast finally takes place, its exquisite sumptuousness does something wholly unexpected for the community. It offers them a glimpse of heaven. The guests perceive that the dining rooms “had been filled with a heavenly light, as if a number of small halos had blended into one glorious radiance… Long after midnight the windows of the house shone like gold, and golden song flowed out into the winter air.” In this heavenly space, an internal spiritual renewal among the brethren quite naturally occurs. Participants own up to past mistakes, retake lost opportunities, and in the process, resentments melt away. They laugh, kiss, and play, having been restored to childhood vitality.

Through her feast, Babette accomplishes a tremendous act of leisure: she allows the world—here, food and drink—to be experienced outside of its everyday fashion. This is no mere dinner. This is more of a sacrament, and Babette is something like a priestess. Instead of succumbing to hedonism, as Martine had feared, the feast elevates nature to its proper dignity as a divine amuse-bouche: “[T]he vain illusions of this earth had dissolved before their eyes like smoke, and they had seen the universe as it really is. They had been given one hour of the millennium.”

Babette’s Feast

This is no mere dinner. This is more of a sacrament.

Pieper’s reflections and Babette’s example should provoke us to rethink our leisure practices. Do we really affirm creation? Are we merely suspicious, avoiding the goods of creation or using them only to replenish ourselves for work? Are we merely hedonistic, seeking the highs of this life without understanding their relation to the next?

Friends, I offer you this spiritual challenge: Throw a party. A real one. I don’t mean to advocate spending all your money on preparing a seven-course meal. (Where can you even find caviar in Waco?) Instead, immerse yourself and others in the sublime. Get to know the goods of creation—both people and things—and take the time, in a spirit of peace and receptivity, to celebrate them as fundamentally valuable. With the right attitude, even a simple walk in the forest or contemplation of art can achieve this.

In sacramental terms, I challenge you to be a priest or priestess, especially for those who do not see the enchantedness of the world. Give to them, and to yourself, one hour of the millennium.

item.title: A Christian Renewal of Feminine and Masculine Ideals for Today’s Society
item.description:
A prominent feature of modernity, as manifested after the sexual revolution of the 1960s and 70s, is the decline of distinctively masculine and feminine ideals. By “ideals” I do not mean to evoke the more common term of “gender roles,” or at least I think that “ideals” should not be reduced to a mere prescription of roles.

Instead, what I mean is this: a healthy understanding of the differences between men and women, and how those differences, when accompanied by virtue, are strengths rather than weaknesses; i.e., a complementary vision of the sexes under which both “roles” are equally valuable and indispensable, both for the sustenance of society and individual flourishing.

Increasingly, men and women lack a positive understanding of their identities as such, and—perhaps more importantly—of how best to relate with one another. In spite of these trends, Alexandra and Dr. Mike Foley, hosts of the Drinking With the Saints podcast, still have hope for the future of masculine and feminine ideals (as I have defined the term).

As with all problems, it is best to start by addressing the root causes.

Increasingly, men and women lack a positive understanding of their identities as such, and—perhaps more importantly—of how best to relate with one another.

Dr. Michael and Alexandra Foley https://cicdc.org/speakers/michael-p-foley/

“It’s a really hard time to be a woman,” asserts Mrs. Foley, adding that “it’s also a really hard time to be a man.” But it has become exceptionally hard to “embrace the specialness of being a woman.” Agreeing, Dr. Foley finds the cause of this in “a lack of respect for human nature,” the belief “that there is a nature to maleness and femaleness.” Modernity seems to reject this.

The problem, says Mrs. Foley, is that without the distinction between the sexes, “you can’t highlight the beauty of each role.” And you can’t ask what it means “to be perfected” in either maleness or femaleness, or how best to “integrate” our strengths. After all, she adds, “to recognize distinctions is to recognize great things.”

As for how a renewal of feminine and masculine ideals would look like in modern society, Dr. Foley explains that the answer does not lie in a return to chivalry. It is not that the chivalric code is in tension with modern sensibilities, but that “it was already in tension” with Christianity because of its insistence on the particularity of certain virtues, casting them as gender-specific.

For instance, in “the code of chivalry, courage for a male was supremely important,” while “chastity for a female was supremely important.” Hence, says Dr. Foley, “that’s actually not an ethical code,” but it is rather “an honor code.” He adds: “According to Christian moral theology, all the virtues are equally important.” Thus, “a man is equally called to be” as “chaste as a woman,” and “a woman is equally called to be” as “courageous as a man.”

“The honor code,” Dr. Foley elucidates, “which is in our DNA from the very beginning, does indeed have a double-standard. We want men to be courageous and women to be chaste. Chivalry was a Christian truce between these two competing worldviews, and I say ‘truce’ because it did its best, but it wasn’t a fully integrated solution. I would like to see a code of chivalry brought back, but it can’t be brought back in a … brutish way, or in the same key that it was.”

“a man is equally called to be” as “chaste as a woman,” and “a woman is equally called to be” as “courageous as a man.” Dr. Michael Foley

Dr. Foley’s point on the universality of Christian virtue is perhaps best illustrated by St. Joan of Arc. Mrs. Foley agrees and says that St. Joan is “such a wonderful example for us nowadays because she was perfectly feminine,” graceful and modest, “and yet God gave her this role” which involved both chastity and courage.

Indeed, Christianity has much to offer in terms of societal renewal, especially on the question of male and female identities.

In contrast with pre-Christian thought and culture, it rejects double-standards; and likewise, contrary to post-Christian thought and culture, it rejects the notion of there being no distinctions between the sexes, and is worrisome of the reduction of men and women to mere individuals with no necessity of relating to one another—i.e., the view that is probably best incapsulated by the famous, or rather infamous, feminist slogan: “a woman needs a man like a fish needs a bicycle.”

Moreover, Catholic theology and doctrine in particular may be helpful guides in the pursuit of feminine and masculine ideals. “One of the great things about Catholic theology,” says Dr. Foley, “is that it understands the principles—the first principles, the important things—but it also understands the role that prudence plays in all of this; in adjudicating a myriad of circumstances.”

In the words of Mrs. Foley, the Church’s approach to questions of roles is one of “prudence informed by charity.” She explains that “in charity you see the other as the child of God, always thinking of that person in light of God—the light that shines upon your understanding of each other—and then you prudentially make decisions.”

Therefore, in terms of general principles, the Foleys “land on three different truths”:

“That God created male and female, and it is good. The maleness and femaleness of the homosapiens is good.” “That does imply that there’s certain roles that male and female should assume.” “Those roles are” flexible or “up for grabs, given political circumstances and individual circumstances.”

The third principle may seem surprising to those who would have expected a prescription of specific “to-do’s.” But “there are no two marriages that are alike,” says Dr. Foley. “I, personally, am very skeptical about drawing up a laundry list for roles that the husband should play and the wife should play.” He adds: “I affirm the binary of male and female,” but acknowledging distinctions is not the same as “drawing up a nice, tidy list about what that means.”

In charity you see the other as the child of God, always thinking of that person in light of God—the light that shines upon your understanding of each other—and then you prudentially make decisions.” Alexandra Foley

Of course, there are non-negotiables, as Mrs. Foley points out. “Birthing children,” she says, is obviously a uniquely female role, while “the male is the protector.” Dr. Foley agrees: “In a generic way, I would say that the male is in a sense the protector of the sacred,” while “the woman is an incarnation of the sacred.” But these roles can take a variety of forms, depending on “different circumstances, and this is where the virtue of prudence” is crucial.

This, once again, is another way in which Catholic tradition can help illustrate the healthy binary of male and female. “The sacred is consecrated,” says Dr. Foley, “set apart, and you see this in the liturgy: the males are in the sanctuary, protecting the sacred,” while “the woman is in many respects a profound symbol of the sacred, and we get this from the Blessed Virgin Mary. She is the new Ark of the Covenant, she is this keeper of the sacred, but she needs to be protected by St. Joseph.”

Icon of our Lady of Perpetual Help https://www.monasteryicons.com/product/Story-of-the-Most-Famous-Icon-of-the-Virgin-Mary/did-you-know

The Holy Family exemplifies this because Mary “literally embodies the sacred by having the Word of God in her womb, and St. Joseph needs to protect that at all costs.” Thus, Dr. Foley says: “I treat that as a basic starting point—the woman is sacred and the man is there to protect her, so he is at the service of his wife.”

Mrs. Foley embraces this paradigm and says that “it works both theologically” and “naturally.” The Holy Family, therefore, can serve as our highest ideal, and we can strive to prudentially emulate the spirit of what each member’s role embodies.

The sacred is consecrated, set apart, and you see this in the liturgy: the males are in the sanctuary, protecting the sacred, while the woman is in many respects a profound symbol of the sacred, and we get this from the Blessed Virgin Mary. Dr. Micheal Foley

“When a woman is pregnant,” Mrs. Foley observes, “she’s vulnerable and she needs protection, and that’s an important role of the man.” But child-bearing and protection do not necessarily constrain an individual couple to gender-specific duties in and out of the household. The man, for example, may be the protector and the one who cooks most meals.

It may still be difficult for some women to consider these ideals without the suspicion that, at their core, they are merely masquerading the same restrictiveness of ages past. But perhaps this cynicism is due to a scarcity of feminine “icons,” i.e., women who perfectly embody virtue and are not “oppressed” by it, but rather empowered.

Once again, we may think of the Blessed Virgin Mary. As a Catholic woman, Mrs. Foley speaks of being ever inspired by “Mary as someone who is so important and so valuable.” She describes her as someone who “is valued for her relational quality,” as seen in “the way she relates to Jesus, St. Joseph, and then St. John.”

But the Blessed Virgin’s most important role, explains Mrs. Foley, is that of being at “the center of the Trinity: she is the daughter of God” the Father, “she is the spouse of the Holy Spirit, and she is the Mother of Christ. How can the role of the woman not be important?” It is in this way that “Mary’s role in my life has been so helpful.” Her intrinsically relational nature gives women “a sense of value.”

Likewise, for men, the Faith provides countless examples of virtuous masculinity, the first of which is, of course, “the everlasting man,” Christ Himself. But renewal need not be limited to those who subscribe to Christian orthodoxy. It begins by acknowledging differences, avoiding double-standards, and—in the words of Dr. Foley—prudentially embracing a healthy and wonderful “complementarity of the sexes.”

item.title: Sabbath: A Renewal of Celebration and Slowness
item.description:
Pastor and widely read author John Mark Comer recently noted Corrie ten Boom’s insight about busyness: “If the Devil can’t make you sin, he’ll make you busy. There’s truth in that. Both sin and busyness have the exact same effect- they cut off your connection to God, to other people, and even to your own soul” (John Mark Comer).

These words are haunting in our current culture of efficiency, busyness, and overloaded schedules. If the devil has made us so busy that we are losing sight of true goodness and beauty, then how do we combat this and seek to cultivate an unhurried soul?

Throughout the history of the Christian tradition, there have been countless spiritual disciplines practiced with the intention of promoting slowness and stillness in the body in order that the soul might be likewise slowed and stilled. In addition, there have been spiritual disciplines practiced in order to celebrate and rejoice in the hope of Christ and the joy of life with Him.

At the intersection of these two intentions of slowness and celebration, we find the discipline of Sabbath. One of the original Ten Commandments but largely neglected in the practice of American Christianity today, I believe the Sabbath is vital to growing and maintaining a healthy view of work, reminding ourselves of the future rest that Christ has secured for us, and becoming people marked by patient love and peace. In order to uncover the beauty of the Sabbath, we will explore why we practice the Sabbath, how we practice the Sabbath, and the fruit of consistently practicing the Sabbath.

First, we must establish the motivation behind practicing the Sabbath. In the world of self-help and motivational speakers, it’s easy to approach this discipline as simply another tool to become more efficient with our time and create the illusion of more margin in our lives. And while I believe that setting aside one day of rest a week will affect our productivity and motivation, these can not be the primary reasons for practicing a spiritual discipline. In the words of John Mark Comer, “hurry is the death of prayer and only impedes and spoils our work.”

At the intersection of these two intentions of slowness and celebration, we find the discipline of Sabbath.

Sabbath is an invitation to slowness for the specific purpose of deepening our communion with our Creator. Choosing to commit to a rhythm of Sabbath is not a command to simply work harder, be more efficient, and get ahead in hopes that by Sunday, all our work will be completed. Rather it is an acknowledgement that in this life, and especially throughout college, the work will not end.

Photo taken by Lottie King

Many of us can affirm the truth that if periods of rest are not planned for, they simply will not happen. We practice the Sabbath to train our souls to rest in the midst of stress, not just when it is over; in doing this, we declare that our work is not the place from which our identity is derived. We loosen our tight grip on the things in our lives that promise to give us value and look to our Savior instead. We trust that in Him, we are offered freedom from death and the fullness of life.

Next, we will discover how to practice the Sabbath. For if we are going to take part in this practice, we must confront the misconception of the Sabbath as a white-knuckled form of legalism and accept it as a gift instead. For some of us, the idea of the Sabbath brings up ideas of boredom, joylessness, and rule-following. Maybe we picture the Pharisees enforcing thier strict Sabbath regulations, pointing fingers at Jesus Himself for wrongly healing a man on the Sabbath. But as people of the New Covenant, living under grace and not under the law, this discipline of Sabbath is an invitation to freedom, not an added chain of bondage. Practically, we start with subtraction.

as people of the New Covenant, living under grace and not under the law, this discipline of Sabbath is an invitation to freedom, not an added chain of bondage. Practically, we start with subtraction.

By removing schoolwork, frustrating tasks, and anything solely aimed at achievement, we make space for beautiful, life-giving, and enriching activities. The beauty of a Sabbath free from legalism is the freedom to create a day of rest that succeeds in connecting us to our Creator and grounding us in Biblical truth. Because of this freedom, the Sabbath may look different for each individual. Of course, some practices ought to be prioritized- corporate worship, intentional prayer, and time in His Word. But beyond that, we can trust the words of Jesus: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

We have been given the freedom to enjoy God in a vast number of ways. For some the Sabbath might be spent in nature rejoicing in God’s intentionality and creativity; others might spend it reading their favorite author and marveling at the ways that humans are made in God’s image; still others might paint or cook or garden. When the two core intentions of slowness and celebration are held central, we find ourselves looking forward to this day all week, longing for the time we will spend in worship and in rest. If the Sabbath is a dim picture of what Heaven will be like, we must rid ourselves of pictures of deprivation, bleakness, and boredom, replacing them with images of enjoyment, freedom, feasting, and delight.

Lastly, we turn to the fruit of consistently practicing the Sabbath. In choosing to rest in the midst of business rather than naively hoping the business ends of its own accord, we affirm this resounding truth: rest does not receive its value from the simple fact that our work has been completed, but rather from the knowledge that our Creator calls it good.

Sabbath is a gift freely offered to us, not a burden that we must unhappily endure.

While resting reminds us of our finiteness, need for daily sustenance from our Creator, and weakness, it ultimately derives its value from following an example set by an infinite, limitless, and all-sustaining God. Sabbath is a gift freely offered to us, not a burden that we must unhappily endure. And while it may be unnatural, frustrating, and difficult at first, we will never regret acting in obedience in the imitation of our God.

When we recognize our own brokenness, we can pursue wholeness in Christ as we seek to follow the example of God resting after Creation. We are fueled by the promise that one day our fallen home will be restored and made new, and our identity has already been made secure as children of the living God. With this assurance, we can rest. If the burden of work feels unending and far too heavy, I encourage you to begin the practice of Sabbath and set aside one day devoted to celebration and slowness. We will never regret the time we spend pursuing joy and rest in our Savior.

item.title: Wintering: An Invitation to Heal, Rest, and Renew
item.description:
I was recently in a conversation with a family member about the asperity of winter. With the longer nights, colder weather, and lack of sun, it’s no wonder wintertime is associated with perpetual gloom. However, I recently came across a term and practice that could serve as a helpful paradigm shift: wintering.

In Katherine May’s book, Wintering: The Power of Rest and Retreat in Difficult Times, she writes that “Plants and animals don’t fight the winter; they don’t pretend it’s not happening and attempt to carry on the same lives they lived in the summer.” To understand wintering simply look at the intrinsic rhythms of nature during the colder months. Birds migrate south, whales withdraw to tropical climates, and bears hibernate just to name a few. When winter comes they engage with the season in a way that is most conducive to their well being. This begs the question: why don’t we do the same?

One of my favorite aspects about wintering is how it invites you into an alternative approach to coping with the colder season: a fresh perspective on times of trial. May writes that wintering “is the active acceptance of sadness. It is the courage to stare down the worst parts of our experience and to commit to healing them the best we can. Wintering is a moment of intuition, our true needs felt as keen as a knife.”

May shares her own story of how the act of wintering helped her family through a personal period of hardship. In discussing a hard time of life for her son, May shares that they persevered through the hardship together by diving into activities that brought them great joy and comfort. Her main goal was to teach him how to create space in which he was safe to feel whatever was needed. This cultivation of space, of feeling and acknowledging our difficult times, is key to wintering.

Transformation is the business of winter. Katherine May

One of the most imperative points to May’s take on wintering is the skill of feeling sadness. It is leaning into our God-given instinct and recognizing that “perhaps through other terrors we are taught to ignore sadness, to stuff it down into our satchels and pretend it isn’t there” May argues that it is within the struggle of the season in which we find recuperation for the rest of the year, an opportunity to come out on the other side with a “new coat.”

This “new coat” that wintering gives us is an emblem of the renewal and restoration of wintering. May writes that, “transformation is the business of winter.” Not every winter is marked by grief and loss, however, every winter can be an opportunity for slowing down, taking mental stock, and returning to or rediscovering what we have lost in the course of a year. In this way, wintering renews us and prepares us for the blossom of spring.

I’m no stranger to the reality of how quickly life moves. A multitude of responsibilities and commitments demand much of our time, often calling the shots of how our precious time is spent. Our commitments, calendars, and deadlines are certainly important, yet too much involvement and exhaustion during a time when our body is naturally craving rest, decompression and a slower pace will eventually take a toll on us.

In a way, I imagine the beginning of each year as a new plot of land. The winter provides time to prepare for how I will utilize the land. Does something need to be built? Torn down? Grown? If I don’t do the arduous and somewhat boring act of planning ahead and checking my supplies, the land will go to waste.

Wintering is both a thought provoking philosophy and an action you can complete. The beauty of it all is that similar to most things, you can’t place it in a box. It can look like seeking rest and reset through a multitude of avenues.

The wisdom of wintering simply leaves you with this truth: it is a gifted time to heal, decelerate our pace, and return to things we love–the things that make us… us.

For me, wintering looks like being snuggled in the corner of my couch sipping a cup of tea with a book. Other times, I find more rest in a deep clean and organization of my home. The act of taking ownership of my own space and decluttering the unneeded excess in my life can even serve as a reminder of what I should allow to be stored in my mental headspace.

While everyone’s way of wintering may differ, there is in each a sense of grounding and reorienting, of opening our eyes a little more to the loveliness in life we may have overlooked over the year. The wisdom of wintering simply leaves you with this truth: it is a gifted time to heal, decelerate our pace, and return to the things we love–the things that make us… us.

Dreading winter has become the norm for many people, but I don’t believe it has to stay that way. Maybe the idea of slowing down and regrouping makes you squirm in your seat– but this practice is anything but passively waiting for the winter to move on before we get to the good part of the year. It’s about grasping the restoration in front of us, open mindedly exploring our emotions, and moving in tandem with the difficulties and delight of it all.

In this time of winter, may the shorter days remind us that life is fleeting, and may this reality invite us to give thanks and delight in that which makes life rich. May the longer nights beckon us to an extended time of restfulness and contemplation, an opportunity to meet our deepest fears and dreams head on, to further evolve into the people we are made to be.

In this winter, let us answer the call of wintering and embrace the renewal set before us.

item.title: Finding Blessings in Imperfect Days
item.description:
On a chilly Tuesday night in late February this year a crowd gathered at the National Press Club to hear Kate Bowler discuss questions of suffering, blessing, and how we can live faithfully amongst the two. Months later, I still reflect on Bowler’s hopeful and honest insights into suffering, grief, and blessing.

The Trinity Forum, a DC based organization engaging life’s greatest questions in the context of faith, hosted this conversation entitled “Finding Blessings in Imperfect Days.” This event featured Kate Bowler, a New York Times bestselling author, professor of the History of Christianity in North America at Duke Divinity School, and self-described incurable optimist.

Bowler is the author of many books, including “Blessed: A History of The American Prosperity Gospel,” “Everything Happens for a Reason: And Other Lies I’ve Loved,” “No Cure for Being Human (And Other Truths I Need to Hear).” Bowler’s discussion this night was on the topics explored in her new book, “The Lives We Actually Have: 100 Blessings for Imperfect Days.”

A simple scan of Bowler’s books reveals the witty yet heartfelt approach she brings to life’s toughest realities. Many of her titles prod at the glitzy yet ineffective responses we give to suffering. Martin Luther King calls these “easy answers and half-baked solutions.” These can be the prosperity gospel’s loud and glaring promises of health, wealth, and popularity. They can also be the seemingly innocuous phrases we hear during tribulation, such as but not limited to: “Everything happens for a reason” and “It’s all God’s plan.”

Standing before a crowded room, Bowler joyfully joked about these “easy answers and half-baked solutions”, kindly mocking the “#blessed” and “live your best life” mantras. She acknowledged however, with sobering honesty and deep sadness, their hollow attempts at alleviating human suffering.

Bowler remarked “We all have become our own televangelist of good, better, and best” and “We live under the weight of the person we thought we would be.” She likened us to runners going through life as though it were an obstacle course, grasping for empty statements at every setback and trying our hardest to believe them. Yet we find little comfort in our efforts, and as Kate makes clear, little truth and little love.

Bowler shared her own story of suffering: diagnosed with stage IV colon cancer at the age of 34. A young mother and wife, Bowler grappled with how this could possibly be God’s plan. She told of her own attempts to muscle out a reason for her suffering, a lesson to tell, a bright side to find.

“We all have become our own televangelist of good, better, and best” and “We live under the weight of the person we thought we would be.” Kate Bowler

Instead of a self-concocted reason for her suffering or a bright side to her pain, Bowler told about a God who walks with us to the edge of our suffering. Rather than comfort in answers and reasons, Bowler found comfort in presence and love—the presence and love of God even in her own anger and pain—the presence and love of the church expressed in simple acts of care, like offering rides to the doctor and putting warm socks on her feet while she slept.

Bowler spoke about the “blessings of these imperfect days.” They weren’t blessings she forced or pitiful “on the bright side” statements—like her hair not falling out during chemotherapy (as some tried to convince her). “Truly”, she told us, “Blessing and gratitude must mean something greater than that.” Bowler spoke of blessing as similar to joy: a surprise transcendent gift.

A stillness fell on the room as Bowler spoke about blessing. She spoke of how blessing comes through recognition of our own limitation and dependency, and our acceptance, our surrender, to receive a gift we did nothing to illicit or deserve. Blessing might reveal itself in the loving presence of a friend, the joyful laugh of a child, the beautiful blue of a sky, the feeling of God with you, around you, and before you. We have done nothing to earn or create these moments, Bowler said, yet here they are, surprising us with joy despite our grief and happiness despite our pain.

Blessings awaken us to a “God who walks with us to the edge of our suffering” and comforts us not with explanations and reasons but simply himself.



These “blessings in imperfect days” call us to wake again tomorrow and live. As Bowler demonstrated, they invite us to fall into the arms of loving community and accept the grace we all too often exchange for perfectionism, obstacle courses, and false fronts.

They remind us that life is not an obstacle course for us to conquer, but perhaps a winding journey with beautiful pastures and craggy shores. Most importantly these blessings awaken us to a “God who walks with us to the edge of our suffering” and comforts us not with explanations and reasons but simply himself.

On the other side of our suffering, we may look back and see a lesson learned, a loveliness forged out of the shards of sin and pain. Yet amid brokenness when we can’t see a lesson or fathom a reason for such grief, we receive a God who walks with us to the edge, who meets us in our suffering. Instead of twisting the knife of reason into the wounds of our suffering, we can, like Bowler, be able to say “God is here. We are loved. It is enough.” Perhaps that is better than any reason.

Listening to Kate Bowler, it was clear that she knew suffering, yet also the love it called for. She listened thoughtfully and compassionately to the crowd’s own questions about suffering, their own experiences with brokenness and pain. She responded with love—shared tears and honest encouragement. She closed out the night with a prayer from her newest book. We all sat together and listened to her simple yet beautiful words of faithfulness, humility, and love. In that moment we were not only united in our shared experience of suffering but also a shared hope. It was a beautiful moment, a blessing on an imperfect day.

item.title: Nationalism and Solidarity
item.description:
Can nationalism be a force for good? This question may seem jarring in a time when nationalism is only discussed in the negative. But perhaps nationalism can be a good if it incorporates an affirmation of a nation’s particular merits and an informed solidarity for other nations. Groups such as the National Socialist Party represent an ugly type of nationalism, a collective egoism, in which the state becomes obsessed with affirming its own specific traits while negating traits it sees as “other.” Collective egoism results in conflict. In the words of Leo Tolstoy, “the egoism of the individual is terrible. But the egoists of private life are not armed. . . . Quite otherwise with states.” An egoistic state cannot stand that which is not itself. It works to find and destroy the other.

Here, one thinks of Mr. Fenchel in John Steinbeck’s East of Eden, which is set in California during WWI. Fenchel is a kind old German tailor who encounters “every cruelty” for his cultural ties. The narrator writes of his encounter with the German:

“He broke into a smile and said, ‘Gut efning, Chone.’ ‘Gut efning, Mary.'”

“We stood stiffly side by side and we said in unison, ‘Hoch der Kaiser!’”

“I can see his face now, his startled innocent blue eyes. He tried to say something and then began to cry. Didn’t even try to pretend he wasn’t.”

For the crime of sharing a language and culture with the enemy, Mr. Fenchel is bullied by his whole town, eventually fleeing after his house is lit on fire by American patriots.

Collective egoism cannot stand difference. When the public “exalts as the virtue of patriotism” the theft of other people’s property, nationalism has become egotistically obsessed with the other, set on conquering their differences and therefore defined by destruction. This nationalism is rightly condemned.

A better, though still imperfect kind of nationalism is “collective camaraderie.” This type of nationalism is not motivated by hatred of the other. On the contrary, it is motivated by a love of the real merits of a nation. And it has the positive result of unifying citizens and feeding their affections. That is because the merits it celebrates, while virtuous per se are also (as Alasdair MacIntyre points out) “the merits and achievments of this particular nation.”

But the problem with collective camaraderie becomes evident when we hear the way it is defended. Mao Tse-tung once said, “We are at once internationalists and patriots, and our slogan is, ‘Fight to defend the motherland against the aggressors.’” Love of country (collective camaraderie) is here in the form of patriotism and a willingness to be internationalist: no necessary hatred of the other is sensed. But there is also a note of defensiveness, an assumption that “aggressors” will be a problem. Ronald Reagan expresses a similar sentiment, saying, “If we lose freedom here, there’s no place to escape to. This is the last stand on earth.” The quote is a cry to defend freedom, yes, but in its focus on America it implicitly casts other nations aside as others or even enemies. We can use collective camaradarie to rally a nation through loyalty to a particular country’s merits, but while it is better than collective egoism, it is still problematic from the vantage point of cooperative international relations.

The best form of nationalism is one that is compatible with international solidarity. For all its potential, collective camaraderie cannot meaningfully interact with differences unless it learns to love that which is not a part of it. Love of one’s nation for its merits and love of others for their merits is then the completion of this nationalism. This love is expressed through solidarity.

The great film Casablanca exemplifies this perfectly. When Nazi soldiers oppresively sing their national anthem to a Moroccan nightclub full of French refugees, Victor Laszlo, a leader of the Czechoslovak Resistance, orders the band to play La Marseillaise. He bellows out the opening lines and is soon joined by dozens of voices, drowning out the Nazi officers. Though not a Frenchman himself, Laszlo is able to use French nationalism to express solidarity for a people occupied and oppressed. His love has motivated him to not only learn of France’s character but also to stand beside her as she is attacked. He loves his nation but that love extends to others, meeting them in ways informed by their own national character.

The best form of nationalism is one that is compatible with international solidarity. John Austin DeLozier

Somehow collective camaraderie must make itself compatible with a parallel collective camaraderie of other nations. In the words of the Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara it must stand “in solidarity with all the oppressed peoples of the world,” even to the point of struggling “ for the independence of other countries.” The love of one’s own is good, but if we cannot meaningfully meet other nations in their own nationalisms, then we risk isolating ourselves completely and engaging internationally only in a posture of aggressive “defense.” We must then tread a middle ground, loving our own nation as well as others for their merits. We do so in powerful displays of solidarity founded upon a patriotism for one’s own nation and others. Solidarity is then the ultimate perfection of nationalism.

So what is nationalism’s place in our world? How can we both love our nation for its unique merits and love others for theirs? How can we engage in difference with love and without conflict? The answer to these questions is not obvious. Here, then, are the questions that need urgent attention as we think about the phenomenon of nationalism and the proper attitude toward it.

item.title: A Vital Nexus: Why Conservatives Should Care About Religious Freedom
item.description:
Why do conservatives place such high value on religious freedom? While religious freedom does not serve conservatives only—indeed it serves everyone, even the non-religious—it seems often especially valuable to conservatives. Here’s why.

I. Preserving Tradition and Values

Conservatives often emphasize the importance of preserving tradition and values in society, as well as recognizing the value of what is tried and true. Religious freedom is integral to this preservation, as it safeguards the right of individuals and religious institutions to uphold and pass down their traditional beliefs and values. Conservative thought has a deep respect for established institutions, norms, and moral codes; and religious freedom ensures the continuity of these cultural and ethical foundations.

Furthermore, many conservatives are deeply rooted in religious traditions, with 85% of conservatives reporting to be Christian according to the Pew Research Center study, in addition to other faiths that comprise 3%. The ability to practice one’s faith freely is integral to identity. According to Pew findings, 70% of Conservative Christians report that “Religion is very important in my life.” The preservation of this faith and its traditions fosters cultural continuity, ensuring that time-honored customs, rituals, and morals remain a vital part of society.

II. Limited Government and Individual Liberty

One of the core tenets of conservatism is the belief in limited government intervention in individuals’ lives. Conservatives advocate personal liberty, emphasizing that government should protect the rights of its citizens rather than infringe upon them. Religious freedom aligns with this principle, as it prohibits the government from encroaching on the individual’s right to practice their faith and many of the strong moral beliefs that so many live their lives by.

Conservatives see religious freedom as a necessary bulwark against government overreach allowing individuals to make their own choices regarding faith and spirituality.This aligns with the conservative ethos of self-reliance and personal autonomy.

III. Moral and Ethical Foundations

For many conservatives, religion provides a moral and ethical compass. They draw from religious teachings and beliefs to guide their actions and decision-making. This is reflected in their voting patterns. Conservatives and religious communities are often in agreement about hot button issues like abortion, same-sex marriage, and other forms of sexuality or gender expression. It is vital in a pluralist society that these opinions are not silenced but rather respected, even if not agreed with.

IV. Protection Against Discrimination

Conservatives also appreciate the role of religious freedom in protecting individuals and groups from religious discrimination. Religious freedom ensures that people can express their faith without fear of discrimination or persecution, safeguarding the principle of equality under the law. This protection is consistent with conservative values of justice and fairness. In addition, religious freedom protections ensure that the government does not favor one religion over another or discriminate against those who hold different religious convictions.

While many conservatives desire protection against discrimination, the concept of religious freedom is often interpreted by LGBTQ activists as a force of discrimination and injustice against them. Because of this, religious freedom is especially under attack today. This type of conflict is common in liberal democratic life where people build their lives around certain (sometimes rival) goods. In this case, religion seems to clash with justice. For both LGBTQ activists and religious communities – these goods are highly emotionally charged and can become grounds of bitter conflict when there are feelings of infringement. However, people on both sides of this issue can find common ground. Both LGBTQ activists and religious communities understand the desire to protect their core beliefs. This is the objective of religious freedom- not to push religion on everybody, but to be free to include our faith in the spaces and the practices that we choose to freely participate in. As the Christian faith instructs us to be hopeful, I am confident that this conflict will eventually find resolution. Whether by a legislature or a court, the conflict between religious freedom and minority justice will be worked out. It is vital, however, that whatever such a resolution looks like, it allows wide scope for religious freedom.

V. Voluntary Social Services

Religious institutions play a substantial role in providing voluntary social services and charitable work that comes from the community. Many conservatives believe that such organizations are often more effective, compassionate, and efficient than government programs in addressing the needs of the less fortunate. Religious freedom ensures that these institutions can continue to provide their essential services without government interference.

The ability of religious organizations to operate freely and provide assistance to those in need is a testament to the positive impact of religious freedom on communities. Conservatives see this as an example of the power of civil society and voluntary efforts to address societal issues, aligning with their preference for limited government involvement.

VI. Defense of Traditional Marriage and Family Values

Some conservatives strongly associate religious freedom with their beliefs regarding traditional marriage and family values, even as traditional beliefs are becoming less common. They argue that religious freedom safeguards the ability of individuals and religious institutions to uphold their views on marriage and family life, often rooted in religious doctrine.

In summary, religious freedom holds a principal place in the conservative ethos, aligning with a range of conservative beliefs and values. It preserves tradition, limits government intervention, upholds individual liberty, protects moral and ethical foundations, defends against discrimination, preserves cultural identity, enables voluntary social services, and safeguards traditional family values. By promoting religious freedom, conservatives ensure that individuals can live in accordance with their faith, and that religious institutions can continue their vital role in communities. The protection of religious freedom is not only a matter of principle for conservatives but also a fundamental aspect of preserving a society that makes room for their values and beliefs.

item.title: Conservatism and the First Kind of Order
item.description:
It is broadly understood that conservatives value order. This is usually meant in terms of social and political order; conservatives value norms which hold society together, as well as laws which enforce a series of standards upon citizens. There is, however, a second kind of order, which is really prior to the first, and which many conservatives also value. Although there may be several ways of describing this prior kind, I will use the words of Russell Kirk and call it “transcendent moral order.”

Oftentimes the conservative’s sense of right and wrong is informed by something greater and more mystical than societal norms and positive law (whatever those may be at a given time and place). He does not value one, but “two aspects or types of order: the inner order of the soul, and the outer order of the commonwealth.” He understands that the inner order “is made for man, and man is made for it,” and that “human nature is a constant, and moral truths are permanent.”

Russell Kirk

This does not mean that all conservatives embrace some specific religion, or that they always subscribe to orthodoxy. Kirk himself wrote of many thinkers in his Conservative Mind who were not orthodox Christians (e.g., John Adams and George Santayana). Kirk’s argument is simply this: that conservatives, even those who do not subscribe to a religious creed, embrace a specific ontological conception of human nature: namely that human existence cannot be reduced to materialism, and that there is a transcendent order—insofar as it is constant, unchanging, and thereby independent from cultural and societal contexts—to which the soul should always conform.

There are, of course, disagreements among conservatives as to the exact contents of this order. Kirk knew this well, which is why he rejected the notion that conservatism is an ideology. Ideologies, like religions, have creeds which induce individuals to agree on specific matters of belief and doctrine. But conservatism does not have a creed, in this sense, and is therefore not an ideology.

This is precisely why a Whig such as Edmund Burke and a Tory like Samuel Johnson—or, in the American context, a Federalist such as John Adams and a Jacksonian Democrat like John C. Calhoun—can both be described as conservatives of some sort despite their differences. Adams and Calhoun, for instance, did not agree on the morality of slavery, but they each held their respective views on transcendent moral grounds. For Calhoun, slavery was not an accident of circumstance or, in the words of Robert E. Lee, a “necessary evil.” However strange he seems to us today, Calhoun viewed slavery as a divinely sanctioned institution that reflected a natural order prescribing certain roles to certain peoples. Likewise, for Adams, the immorality of slavery was not based on the move toward industrialization and the emergence of more convenient means of labor, but on the conviction that it was an “abhorrent” practice, contrary to the natural order of humanity.

At a time such as the one inhabited by these men, conservatism could be a united banner for the slaveholder or the abolitionist. Rather, what it offered were anti-utilitarian answers that, regardless of the conclusions drawn from them, were inspired by an understanding of the human soul and the moral order to which it is bound.

Nevertheless, even amid variety and disagreement, there are some grounds of consensus among most conservatives on the habits which lead the soul to moral virtue. As Sir Roger Scruton maintains, “conservatism as a political philosophy traces its roots as far as the Greeks.” Indeed, most conservatives hold the ancients in high regard, and find their ontological insights of particular value. Aristotle’s moral and intellectual virtues, for instance, are among the most significant foundations of Western ethics, and thereby of conservatism in the West. All four of his virtues, as well as the so-called theological virtues developed later in the Western tradition (e.g., faith, hope, and charity), are generally held by conservatives to be the pillars of the moral constitution and the ends to which the soul is naturally ordered.

To this general truth that conservatives value a transcendent source of order, it is sometimes objected that some conservatives are skeptical of, or altogether opposed to the notion of a “transcendent moral order,” but still value social and political order. But this objection is misplaced, as we can see from reflecting on Kirk’s “two aspects or types of order.”

There is meaning in conservatism, and an essential part of this meaning is an ontological understanding of the human soul, namely that it is teleologically structured and that moral virtue is its end. Nor is conservatism merely the preservation of the status quo. Mike Ortiz

Implied in Kirk’s explication of this concept is the inherent interrelation between “the inner order of the soul, and the outer order of the commonwealth.” The thread of conservative thought, in all its variety, illustrates a way of relating these two forms of order, and expressing the latter’s dependence on the former. Thus, it is only because of a perceived moral order that human beings found it necessary to establish a political order. The political is modeled after the moral in a constant pursuit of imitation and perfection. Hence, though there may in fact be such a thing as a conservative who denies the existence of transcendent order, his conclusions on matters of the commonwealth will still be informed by some view of moral constants. If not, then he may not be a conservative after all, but a utilitarian.

There is meaning in conservatism, and an essential part of this meaning is an ontological understanding of the human soul, namely that it is teleologically structured and that moral virtue is its end. Nor is conservatism merely the preservation of the status quo. In times of moral confusion and fog, the conservative may find himself opposed to all establishments, even if he is skeptical of revolution and the destruction of institutions, which he always is. His means are reform, not revolution; but reform presupposes the need for improvement and perfectibility, which he would not value if he were merely concerned with maintaining the status quo.

The fundamental mark of a true conservative is her commitment to an order prior to the order of laws. Thus, Kirk writes that the “great line of demarcation in modern politics [is] . . . not a division between liberals on one side and totalitarians on the other. No, on one side of that line are all those men and women who fancy that the temporal order is the only order, and that material needs are their only needs, and that they may do as they like with the human patrimony. On the other side of that line are all those people who recognize an enduring moral order in the universe, a constant human nature, and high duties toward the order spiritual and the order temporal.

item.title: Hills & Valleys: Wonder in Learning
item.description:
Two months have passed since I moved to Oxford to begin my studies, and this place is nothing short of enchanting. The streets, spires, bicycles, and books give Oxford its own unique style, one that is not easily emulated. A treasure trove of knowledge, Oxford has been around for nearly a thousand years. And it shows. To walk down a street where every building is older than the United States is surreal.

Living in such an amazing environment, infused with the spirit of learning, evokes a sense of wonder within me. As I engage in my own studies here, I am often left wondering about the things I’ve learned. Truths of Theology and Philosophy, the logic embedded in the universe, these topics leave me with so much to contemplate. This brings to mind a question: what is wonder, and what is the relationship it has with learning? In this latest installment of the “Hills and Valleys” column of The Standard, I hope to gain some ground on this question.

It seems that many educational institutions view the purpose of wonder in purely practical terms. Many schools, teachers, and administrators regard wonder as a helpful disposition that will motivate their students to learn. But this instrumental view of wonder is fundamentally incomplete.

First of all, wonder isn’t merely the bare desire for knowledge or truth. That kind of desire is more akin to curiosity, which is similar to, but not the same as, wonder. Curiosity is an avid desire to gather information and to understand. But wonder does not always seek to understand.

wonder isn’t merely the bare desire for knowledge or truth. Jonathan Perkins

Think of it something like this: say you and a friend are looking out over the Grand Canyon. His response is to visit every visitor’s center, read every pamphlet, and memorize the entire Wikipedia page. He simply must know everything there is to know about how the canyon was formed, and what it can tell us about the history of the earth.

You may be very interested in all those facts, but unlike your friend, you do not seek to grasp the truth, you let it grasp you. Your soul is inextricably gripped by how amazing the mere sight of the canyon is. Learning more about the canyon only increases this feeling, it leaves you in awe, leaving you speechless in the face of something so much greater than you. You want to learn more, but you would be happy just basking in the wonder of the way the world is, in the way that God’s creation proclaims his name. Wonder like this can only be understood as an end in itself, an activity that is so meaningful all on its own that nobody should need any other reason to do it.

In this example, your friend would be best described as taken by curiosity. However, your attitude would not be one of curiosity, but of wonder. There are a few important takeaways from this: first, wonder isn’t really about acquiring knowledge as much as it is about appreciating it. Of course, wondering at knowledge may lead you to desire more of it, but it is not the same as curiosity, which is merely a desire to learn.

wonder isn’t really about acquiring knowledge as much as it is about appreciating it. Jonathan Perkins

Second, wonder doesn’t have to understand everything to be in awe of it. Moreover, there’s something about wonder that is heightened when you don’t (at least completely) understand what you’re wondering at, when you feel as though the thing you are beholding is beyond you.

As I define it, wonder is a response of the self (perhaps it could even be said, the soul), to something meaningful beyond the human power to fully grasp. This is most naturally seen in connection with beauty. After all, beauty is a perfect thing to point to as a trigger for wonder, since by its nature it induces the sort of awe that wonder ought to be, a simple speechlessness in the face of something so great and worthy.

Another important way that wonder takes place in our lives is in love. When we love another person, wonder is there. Something about the nature of real love involves a deep recognition that our beloved is something beyond us, a person too complex and too beautiful to encompass with our knowledge.

Think for a moment about someone you love and care deeply about: a significant other, a family member, a friend. Now take some time to consider how truly incredible and complex they are, just because they’re a person. There’s something behind the eyes of every person that is totally beyond us; and in some unique way, its that part of someone that our love calls out to and stands in awe of. Love is built on the notion that the people we love are so unfathomably meaningful, they are worthy of our minds and our hearts.

When we love another person, wonder is there…our beloved is something beyond us. Jonathan Perkins

This raises an interesting question: why is wonder such a natural and proper part of love? A sort of awe at “otherness” doesn’t seem natural to apply to a lover. In fact, a lover should be the opposite, held close, known as much as possible. Yet, wonder is natural to love.

How can this be? Can the one held so close to one’s heart simultaneously be inexpressibly distant? This must precisely be the case. However, the distance is in this case no detriment. Instead, it serves as a sort of essence of love, a sort of reaching out into infinity in a way that is both complete and incomplete, whole and yet only a part of something greater.

Perhaps, just perhaps, wonder’s place in love, as well as in the world, is a reference to a higher object of our wonder, an eternal and wonderful God. A being so beyond us, yet so near to us, that we can recognize His beauty in all things, for He indeed is beauty. He is one who is worthy of unending appreciation for His own sake, who as an object of our wonder is eternally satisfying to the wonderer.

This is why we feel comfortable in the midst of wonder, because the infinite and ineffable is also the God who is there, who is with us and in us at every moment. Wonder teaches us to approach the unfathomable God the way He is meant to be approached: with an attitude of adoration, not a desire for possession or comprehension. This is the meaning of true wonder. In the world we find God’s signature everywhere, and through the beauty He leaves behind we catch glimpses of His infinity.

This is what learning is all about, what it has always been about. Tasting and seeing that the Lord is good, that He is wonderful in the fullest sense. The more we experience, the more that we learn, the more that we can stand in awe before God and what He has made, at who He is, the Great I Am.

This is why the approach of many schools, teachers and administrators is fundamentally flawed. Wonder and learning are related and mutually motivate each other, but this is not because wonder is for learning. It is precisely the reverse, that learning is for wonder. Truth is useful, but it is worth seeking for its own sake because it takes its essence from the truth and being of the God who is.

This is what learning is all about, what it has always been about. Tasting and seeing that the Lord is good, that He is wonderful in the fullest sense. Jonathan Perkins

No matter your role in life, whether or not learning is still a large part of your life, no matter if you’re in Oxford or in a small town that doesn’t even have a library, don’t forget the importance of learning. Because learning gives us a gateway to one of the most profound activities: we can see God through His universe, and glorify Him each day, appreciating Him through appreciating what He has made.

Proverbs 25:2 reminds us that “it is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.” God made us to learn, to see Him in all He has made, and there are few things more satisfying and fulfilling than wonder: taking a posture of humility, and gazing into the infinite.

Large portions of this article were drawn from my essay: “Wonder, Curiosity, and Studiousness,” written for Dr. Elizabeth Corey’s “What is Liberal Education?” Philosophy class.

item.title: Halloween, Vindicated?
item.description:
Well, it’s October. You wouldn’t know it by how hot it still gets in our great state, or how green the trees are. But fall is here, nonetheless. And Halloween follows with it! If you’ve stepped foot in an HEB or Home Depot any time after the fourth of July, you’ve felt the slow creep of Halloween in all its fake cobwebs and colourful skulls. Personally, I love Halloween . . . I really do! While I don’t like horror movies (they’re scary) or candy corn (it’s chalky and vile), I love that Halloween is a creepy celebration of the year’s winding down, coming to a close, the world settling in for the winter.

There are two popular opinions about Halloween, and both are misguided: the first is more common and approving of the holiday. This camp holds that Halloween is great because it’s freakish and occult, and there really aren’t any other holidays like that, except April Fool’s Day (maybe, if you’re committed enough to the bit). To those holding this opinion, Halloween is a unique time to embrace the dark side of life. The second opinion is more commonly held by many Christians these days who disapprove of the holiday. They insist upon not celebrating Halloween due to its supposed connections to the demonic–they see people dressing up like demons and decorating their houses with bones or pentagrams and assume that the holiday itself is unholy. The amount of Baylor students that refuse to celebrate Halloween shocked me my first year here.

I argue these two views presume incorrectly the nature of Halloween. To vindicate our beloved Halloween, we must first ask the question: what was Halloween originally about in the first place?

Etymologically, Halloween is a sort of contraction of All Hallows’ Eve. The Scots got rid of the v in eve, added an n, and combined hallow and eve, making it Hallowe’en. Hallow is an archaic English word for holy, and although it has fallen out of use, it’s where we get the adjective hallowed.

Historically, Halloween is the first day of a three-day-long series of a vigil and two feast days called Allhallowtide, which comprises Halloween on the 31st of October, All Saints’ Day on the first of November, and All Souls’ Day on the second. Allhallowtide has fallen out of fashion among many Christians, having waned both in comparison to Christmas and Easter, and facing a negative swing in popular opinion surrounding the holiday. But Allhallowtide is a period of time with a feast and a vigil, just like Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, or the days from Good Friday to Easter. The day after Halloween is Hallowmas, or the feast day of all the saints. In fact, if Christmas Eve followed the same etymological pattern as Halloween, we’d be calling it Christeen (or, something along those lines). On the second day of November is All Souls’ Day, the final day of the feast, in which Christians remember the ordinary departed–not the saints and martyrs who, with grand gestures, dedicated their lives to the Church—but regular people.

As we keep the Christ in Christmas, so too can we keep the hallowed in Halloween.

This all sounds wonderful to me, so how did Halloween get the bad rap? Just as Christmas has been influenced by the old Roman holiday of the rebirth of Sol Invictus, their Sun god, and carries with it themes of birth, light, and renewal, so too has Halloween been influenced by ancient pagan holidays that occur at the same time of the year which celebrate death and conjure the idea of a veil between this life and the next growing thin. Some scholars say Halloween has connections to the Celtic holiday of Samhain, a seasonal festival about the end of the season of the harvest and beginning of a dark winter. On the vigil before the Day of the Dead, practitioners were indeed vigilant, adopting disguises so that the souls of the dead would pass them by unharmed before celebrating the lives of the saints the next day. This snowballed over time from celebration of the dead into ideas of occultism and Satanism in today’s world, and we ended up with some of the views on Halloween we know today–not a solemn vigil before a major liturgical feast day, but a pointed rejection of religion. This is, of course, not to say that trick-or-treating, hanging cobwebs, gorging on candy, and dressing up like your favorite axe-murderer is bad. It is, instead, that arguments pointed towards the infernal gravity of these traditions–be they for or against–hold no power over a person versed in the holiday’s rich history.

Halloween is a night of spiritual asceticism and contemplation, a night in which we are to heed well the end of life, before spending the next two days celebrating all the dead–ordinary as well as extraordinary.

This whole history lecture is all to say that there is no reason a Christian ought to reject Halloween based on how it is perceived by the many. As we keep the Christ in Christmas, so too can we keep the hallowed in Halloween. Liturgically, it is the vigil day that precedes the celebration of the lives of the saints and recognition of their martyrdom. The inclination to be averse to death and the occult should not discourage us from exploring ideas that are uncomfortable and celebrating the history of our religion. The aversion to death is understandable. It is that final, gaping maw which Christ himself died to conquer. Christians celebrate life’s triumph over death, so it’s no surprise that a day recognizing death might makes us uncomfortable. And yet. Allhallowtide, shrouded as it is in historical mystery and out of style as it may be, has a lesson for us: death is ever near, and we, too, shall die. Evil exists, and we ought to be vigilant of it. Halloween is a night of spiritual asceticism and contemplation, a night in which we are to heed well the end of life, before spending the next two days celebrating all the dead–ordinary as well as extraordinary. On Halloween, we remember the terror of death, that greatest and most final of unknowns. But the very next day, we celebrate that on account of Christ, death did not, and cannot, have the last word, and we relish in the promise of eternal life thereafter. And I promise that buying a plastic skeleton, posing it in the corner of your house, and naming it Hank is not letting the devil have the final word, no matter what anybody says. Trust me.

item.title: Conservatism or Orthodoxy?
item.description:
Is conservatism basically a form of what G.K. Chesterton (1874-1936) once called “orthodoxy”? Or is it something different?

According to Jerry Muller, a secular Jew and conservative thinker, the answer to this question has important ramifications. In his anthology on conservatism, he argues that if the two are the same then conservatism is wholly irrelevant to politics in our pluralistic and largely secular age. Muller values conservatism in the realm of society and politics, but he believes that orthodoxy is only relevant in the realm of religion. Even if conservatism and orthodoxy reach the same or similar conclusions, they have distinct and independent ways of reasoning. To Muller, this is not an arbitrary distinction but a fundamental one.

As an agnostic conservative, Muller would seek to put some distance between conservatism and orthodoxy. However, he seems allergic to the association between the two. In fact, if orthodoxy is the same as conservatism, Muller is prepared to abandon conservatism entirely. He argues that what makes conservatism and orthodoxy different is that conservatism opposes liberalism and progressivism on the grounds of enlightened principles using reason, rather than pointing to some transcendent truth like orthodoxy does.
